National and international health agencies and multiple epidemiological studies have found vaccines to be overwhelmingly safe, with only very rare serious adverse events; passive reporting systems contain unverified reports that do not establish causation. Excess mortality during the pandemic has been overwhelmingly attributed to SARS-CoV-2 infection and its indirect effects, not mass fatalities from vaccination.

claim: "There was a raid on the Biden residence yesterday by the military!"
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official confirmation that the U.S. military conducted a raid on President Biden's residence. Such an event would be extraordinary, widely reported, and is constrained by domestic law and the Secret Service's protections for the president and presidential residences.

claim: "Mitt Romney has been asked to lead Health and Human Services in Biden administration."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden asked Senator Mitt Romney to lead the Department of Health and Human Services. Biden nominated Xavier Becerra as HHS Secretary and he was the administration's publicly announced pick and later confirmed. Claims that Romney was asked appear to be rumors or misstatements, not documented outreach or an official offer.

claim: Says Jon Ossoff is "a socialist."
rationale: Jon Ossoff is a Democratic U.S. senator who is generally described as a mainstream/progressive Democrat, not a socialist; he has not identified as a socialist nor been publicly affiliated with socialist organizations. Labeling him a 'socialist' is a partisan characterization rather than an accurate description of his stated ideology and record.

claim: "March 2019 and on-going food benefits WILL NOT be available until further notice. Clients are encouraged to use their food benefits as soon as possible in case SNAP benefits are unavailable in March."
rationale: The claim that March 2019 and ongoing SNAP/food benefits were universally unavailable until further notice is incorrect. SNAP issuance is managed by state agencies under USDA and there was no nationwide suspension of benefits in March 2019; isolated local outages or administrative notices can occur, but a blanket cessation did not happen.

claim: Says Republican Gov. Phil Scott "just voted to impeach President Trump."
rationale: Governors do not participate in federal impeachment votes; only members of the U.S. House of Representatives vote to impeach a president. Phil Scott is the Republican governor of Vermont and, in that role, would not have 'just voted to impeach' President Trump.

claim: "There's not a single, solitary example that" signing the bill to end Glass-Steagall "had anything to do with the financial crash."
rationale: The claim is false because numerous analysts, regulators, and academic studies have identified links between the 1999 repeal of key Glass-Steagall restrictions (Gramm–Leach–Bliley Act) and the 2007–2009 financial crisis, arguing that allowing commercial banks, investment banking, and insurance activities to combine increased systemic risk and encouraged risk-taking. While scholars disagree about the magnitude of the effect and many other factors (housing bubble, securitization, weak oversight) were also crucial, it is incorrect to say there is 'not a single' example connecting the repeal to crisis-related failures and losses at large financial firms.

claim: Says Marco Rubio endorsed Obamacare for his own family.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Marco Rubio publicly endorsed the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) for his own family. Rubio has been a consistent critic of the law, and reputable reporting does not show he recommended ACA marketplace coverage for his family or explicitly enrolled them under that characterization.

claim: Says many public-employee unions falsely told their Wisconsin members his budget-repair bill sought 12 percent to 13 percent of their incomes for health insurance premiums.
rationale: During the 2011 Wisconsin debate several unions did circulate claims that employees would be required to pay about 12–13% of their pay for health insurance, but independent fact-checkers judged that figure to be misleading or exaggerated. The budget-repair law set employee premium contribution rules and caps that produced much lower percentage-of-pay costs for typical workers and varied by plan and salary, so the broad 12–13% claim was not an accurate representation of the law's effect for most members.

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: Reporting and government reviews have found that many individuals placed on terrorism-related watchlists (including the no-fly list) have nonetheless passed background checks and purchased firearms; multiple investigations have identified figures in the low thousands. The underlying point—being barred from flying does not automatically prevent a gun purchase—reflects a documented gap between watchlist use for aviation screening and the federal background-check system.

claim: "Nearly 70 percent of all federal spending will go towards Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid" in fiscal year 2014.
rationale: The claim is incorrect. In fiscal year 2014 Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid together accounted for roughly half of federal outlays (around 45–50%), not nearly 70%. Each program was a large share (Social Security ~24%, Medicare ~14–16%, Medicaid ~8–10%), but their sum was well short of 70%.

claim: Says a photo shows a "lithium mine for hybrid cars."
rationale: A standalone photo cannot be reliably identified as a lithium mine for hybrid-car batteries without provenance, metadata, or independent reporting. Lithium is produced both from brine evaporation ponds and hard-rock (spodumene) mines with different visual signatures, and images are frequently miscaptioned or misattributed.

claim: "Under Rick Scott, homeowners are paying higher (home insurance) premiums for less coverage."
rationale: While homeowners' premiums in Florida rose during and after Rick Scott's tenure, increases are attributable to multiple factors (hurricane losses, insurer insolvencies, rising reinsurance costs and market shifts) rather than a single clear causal effect of his policies. Scott did sign insurance reforms aimed at reducing litigation and stabilizing the market, but there is no consensus evidence that his actions directly produced uniformly "higher premiums for less coverage."

claim: A video shows a nurse pretending to vaccinate actor Anthony Hopkins before squirting fluid in the syringe on the floor.
rationale: Independent fact-checking and news reporting do not support the claim that the clip shows Anthony Hopkins being faked-vaccinated; the video is misattributed or edited and there is no credible evidence Hopkins was the person in that footage. Additionally, routine clinical practice does not involve pretending to inject a patient and then ejecting vaccine onto the floor.

claim: "Biden resigned, Pelosi was detained."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden resigned or that Speaker Nancy Pelosi was detained; both continued to carry out public duties and major news organizations and official sources did not report any such events. This statement matches patterns of misinformation circulated online rather than verified fact.

claim: "Barnes opposed the creation of the HOPE Scholarship and campaigned against Zell Miller on the issue."
rationale: The HOPE Scholarship was created by Governor Zell Miller in 1993 and is widely recorded as a Miller initiative; there is no clear historical evidence that Roy Barnes (the Georgia politician likely referenced) formally opposed its creation or ran a campaign centered on opposing Miller over HOPE. Barnes later ran for governor and had policy disagreements with Miller at times, but opposing the creation of HOPE and campaigning against Miller specifically on that issue is not supported by common historical accounts.

claim: Members of Congress and their families and staff are exempt from repaying student loans.
rationale: There is no blanket statutory exemption that frees members of Congress, their families, or congressional staff from repaying federal student loans. Individual members or staff may qualify for existing forgiveness or repayment programs (e.g., Public Service Loan Forgiveness or income-driven repayment forgiveness) if they meet the program criteria, but that is not the same as a general exemption for Congress or their relatives.

claim: Says with "Gov. Chris Christie and bipartisan reformers" New Jersey had "the most job growth in 11 years."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated as presented: it gives no timeframe or metric (absolute jobs vs. percentage) and attributes broad job growth to Gov. Chris Christie and "bipartisan reformers" without evidence. State employment data across Christie's tenure show variable year-to-year gains, and there is no clear, broadly recognized finding that New Jersey achieved "the most job growth in 11 years" in a way that definitively supports that attribution.

claim: "We have the lowest beer tax in the nation."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which jurisdiction 'we' refers to or the time frame. Beer excise taxes vary widely across states and localities (and change over time), and several jurisdictions have very low or zero beer taxes, so a blanket assertion of having the lowest rate is unlikely without current comparative data.

claim: Says NASCAR "bans the confederate flag but FORCES all their drivers to do Muslim prayer."
rationale: NASCAR did enact a ban on display of the Confederate flag at its events in June 2020, but there is no credible evidence that NASCAR forces drivers to perform Muslim prayer. Requiring drivers to engage in a specific religious practice would be unprecedented, unlawful under U.S. constitutional protections, and would have been widely reported; no such policy exists.

claim: Ted Cruz "helps run two national organizations that have been leading the push to give amnesty to illegal immigrants."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Senator Ted Cruz helps run two national organizations that have been leading a push to give amnesty to illegal immigrants. Cruz's public record and political activity have consistently opposed broad amnesty measures and supported stricter immigration enforcement. The claim appears to conflate or misattribute actions to him that are inconsistent with his known positions. Without specific organizations named, the assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Steve Southerland "voted to keep the shutdown going."
rationale: There is no clear single roll-call in which Rep. Steve Southerland explicitly 'voted to keep the shutdown going.' While Southerland voted with many House Republicans in 2013 on measures tied to defunding the Affordable Care Act that contributed to the October 2013 shutdown, the statement as phrased is misleading because it implies a distinct vote to prolong the shutdown rather than support for legislation that failed to pass the Senate and thus resulted in a shutdown.

claim: "Hillary ignored multiple requests for security, didn’t respond for 13 hours, & let 4 Americans die in Benghazi. Trump rushed in reinforcements, threatened to destroy Iran, & made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad."
rationale: The statement mixes true elements with misleading or unsupported assertions. Four Americans did die in the 2012 Benghazi attack, and reviews found systemic security failures and missed opportunities, but multiple official investigations did not find evidence that Hillary Clinton personally ignored explicit requests or intentionally delayed response for 13 hours. Donald Trump did use aggressive rhetoric toward Iran and authorized strikes (including the Soleimani strike), but the claim that he "rushed in reinforcements" and thereby "made sure no lives were lost in Baghdad" is misleading—violence and casualties related to U.S. operations and embassy unrest occurred and responsibility/causality are disputed.

claim: "Some people are going to die from the vaccine directly. But a large number of people are going to start getting horribly sick and get all kinds of autoimmune diseases."
rationale: Broadly claiming that vaccines will directly kill people and that a large number will develop widespread autoimmune diseases is not supported by evidence. Vaccines undergo extensive safety testing and ongoing surveillance; serious adverse events (e.g., anaphylaxis, rare myocarditis, or very rarely Guillain-Barré after specific vaccines) are documented but are uncommon, and population-level studies do not show vaccines causing large increases in diverse autoimmune diseases. The claim exaggerates and misrepresents the frequency and scope of known risks.

claim: "A new ruling by the EPA would force dairy farmers to comply with the Spill Prevention, Control and Countermeasure Program when dealing with spilt milk -- the same regulations oil and natural gas producers must follow."
rationale: This is incorrect. The EPA's SPCC program regulates discharges of 'oil' to waters (generally petroleum and certain animal/vegetable oils) and is aimed at oil storage and spills; ordinary milk is not the target of SPCC and there has been no EPA ruling forcing dairy farmers to apply SPCC to routine spilled milk. Dairy operations can, however, be subject to other state or federal water-quality or waste-management rules, and farms that store oil/fuel still must follow SPCC where applicable.

claim: Potential Foxconn changes are due to "the wave of economic uncertainty" from Evers administration
rationale: Attributing Foxconn’s project changes primarily to a ‘wave of economic uncertainty’ caused by the Evers administration is not supported by available evidence. Major documented drivers of Foxconn’s scaling back were company business decisions, global LCD panel market collapse, shifts in technology demand, and the original deal’s terms negotiated under the previous administration; there is no clear causal linkage showing Evers’ policies caused the changes.

claim: "You had (4,925) out-of-state voters… in Georgia."
rationale: The claim as stated is ambiguous and unsupported: it gives a precise number but no election/date or source. Public Georgia election reports and official canvass documents do not corroborate a widely reported, standalone figure of exactly 4,925 “out-of-state voters” without additional context, and such counts vary by definition (registration address vs. where a ballot was cast).

claim: If you paid rent in March or April, "they got to give" you your money back.
rationale: The statement makes a universal claim that anyone who paid rent in March or April is entitled to a refund. There is no general federal or global rule mandating landlords must return rent paid in those months; during COVID some jurisdictions had eviction moratoria or rent-relief programs that offered assistance or deferred obligations, but they did not broadly require refunds of already-paid rent.

claim: "Moderna chief medical officer admits: mRNA alters DNA."
rationale: There is no credible record of a Moderna chief medical officer admitting that mRNA vaccines alter human DNA. Moderna and independent experts state that mRNA acts in the cytoplasm, lacks the enzymes needed to integrate into genomic DNA, and is transient. While some laboratory studies have shown that viral or cellular reverse transcriptases can reverse-transcribe mRNA under artificial conditions in cell culture, that is not evidence of in vivo genome alteration or an admission by Moderna leadership.

claim: Says recent studies indicate that nationally, only 8 percent of white voting-age citizens but 25 percent of African-American voting-age citizens lack government-issued photo IDs.
rationale: Those exact nationwide percentages (8% of white voting‑age citizens and 25% of African‑American voting‑age citizens lacking government photo ID) are not supported by a single credible national study. Different reputable analyses (Brennan Center, Pew, Census-based estimates, and GAO/state studies) produce varying figures and often report lower national rates overall or higher rates for specific subgroups or states rather than the precise national split claimed. The 25% figure is sometimes cited for particular subpopulations or in certain states, not as a uniform national rate.

claim: Under Mayor Angel Taveras "Providence’s bond rating was downgraded from A to BBB, two steps above junk-bond status."
rationale: The claim is misleading: credit ratings differ by agency and notch (e.g., A, A-, BBB+, BBB, BBB-), and public records do not uniformly show Providence being downgraded from a generic 'A' to a generic 'BBB' specifically under Mayor Taveras. Also, BBB is generally considered the lowest investment-grade category, and whether it is 'two steps above junk' depends on the agency and which plus/minus notches are counted, so the blanket statement is inaccurate without specifying agency and date.

claim: GOP candidate for California governor Travis Allen "on the floor vote … refused to join Republicans opposing driver licenses for illegal aliens."
rationale: Travis Allen, while serving in the California Assembly, opposed legislation (notably AB 60 in 2013) to allow driver’s licenses for undocumented immigrants and voted consistent with Republican opposition; he did not 'refuse to join Republicans opposing' such proposals. Public roll-call records and Allen’s own statements show he opposed granting driver’s licenses to undocumented immigrants.

claim: The Republicans' alternative health care plan "will still let insurers raise premiums four times faster than wages."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific, universal numeric outcome (premiums rising "four times faster than wages") as a direct effect of a Republican alternative health plan. No GOP replacement bill contains a provision that mandates or guarantees premiums will rise at that specific multiple of wage growth; independent analyses of repeal/replace scenarios show varied results and impacts by state and population rather than a single 4x rule.

claim: Republican state Sens. Paul Newton and Warren Daniel "refused to even give testimony" in North Carolina’s latest redistricting case.
rationale: I could not find reliable evidence that both Republican state Sens. Paul Newton and Warren Daniel categorically "refused to even give testimony" in North Carolina's most recent redistricting litigation. Coverage of NC redistricting cases shows some Republican legislators invoked legislative privilege or declined certain subpoenas, but the blanket claim that these two specifically refused all testimony is unsupported or ambiguous without a specific proceeding identified.

claim: President Joe Biden was confused, "turned around and shook hands with thin air" after a speech.
rationale: Video footage and contemporaneous news coverage documented President Biden finishing a speech, turning and extending his hand where no one was to reciprocate, appearing to shake 'air.' Characterizing him as 'confused' is interpretive, but the physical gesture of reaching for a handshake with no partner is supported by footage.

claim: Says Donald Trump said, "Alec Baldwin, a total loser, has taken his impression of me to a new low by testing out this theory" by shooting someone.
rationale: There is no credible record in news reports, Trump’s public statements, or his social media posts of Donald Trump saying that exact line about Alec Baldwin ‘testing out this theory’ by shooting someone. The phrasing attributes an endorsement of violence and appears to be fabricated; major outlets would have reported such a provocative comment and did not. Given available public archives of Trump's remarks after the Rust shooting, this quote cannot be substantiated.

claim: "Dr. Oz releases COPD gummies that help quit smoking, detox lungs and stop COPD."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Dr. Oz has released a proven 'COPD gummy' that cures or stops COPD. COPD is a chronic, generally irreversible lung disease and cannot be 'detoxed' or cured by gummy supplements; evidence-based quitting aids are nicotine replacement, medications, and counseling. Claims that a gummy both stops COPD and detoxes lungs are medically implausible and unsupported.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: This is a specific, private claim about correspondence and payments that cannot be independently verified from the information given. Without copies of the letters, transaction records, or corroboration from the named individuals, the statement is unsubstantiated. Because I cannot confirm the asserted counts, I treat it as false per the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain.

claim: "The United States was paying for anywhere from 70 to 90 percent of (NATO), depending on the way you calculate."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The U.S. does not pay 70–90% of NATO’s budgets: it contributes roughly 20–25% of NATO’s small common-funded budgets but accounts for roughly 60–75% (not 90%) of the total defense spending by all NATO members combined in recent years. Conflating ‘share of NATO members’ total defense spending’ with ‘paying for NATO’ (common budgets and collective activities) produces the exaggerated 70–90% claim.

claim: Says opposing the Paycheck Fairness Act is part of the Koch brothers’ agenda.
rationale: Koch-funded organizations and allied conservative groups (notably Americans for Prosperity and other Koch-network entities) have publicly opposed the Paycheck Fairness Act and lobbied against similar pay-equity legislation. Opposition to such regulatory and labor-related bills is consistent with the Kochs' broader free-market, anti-regulation policy agenda.

claim: "Mayor Barrett saved Milwaukee $25 million, thanks to Gov. Walker’s reforms."
rationale: There is no clear, independently verified budget or audit showing Mayor Tom Barrett "saved" Milwaukee $25 million solely as a result of Gov. Scott Walker’s reforms; media and fact-checkers have found such dollar figures to be disputed or the result of mixed accounting, timing and bargaining changes. Reported savings after Walker’s Act 10 and other measures were often smaller, incremental, or arose from multiple actions (employee concessions, benefit shifts, accounting moves) rather than a single $25 million, mayor-led savings directly attributable to the governor.

claim: "Virginia papers called (Scott) Rigell’s campaign ‘Mostly False.’"
rationale: The statement is misleading: Virginia news organizations and PolitiFact have sometimes rated specific claims made by Scott Rigell or his campaign as "Mostly False," but they did not broadly label his entire campaign as "Mostly False." Fact-check ratings apply to individual statements or ads, not whole campaigns.

claim: "COVID ends next Wednesday."
rationale: There is no scientific basis or authoritative announcement that COVID-19 will 'end' on a specific upcoming day; pandemic status is determined by evolving epidemiological data and formal declarations from public health bodies. Predicting an exact end date like 'next Wednesday' without official confirmation or supporting data is unfounded.

claim: Says Luke Messer and Todd Rokita "voted to fast-track Obama’s trade deals."
rationale: Both Luke Messer and Todd Rokita voted in favor of the 2015 Trade Promotion Authority (commonly called 'fast-track') bill in the House, which granted the Obama administration expedited procedures to seek approval for trade agreements. That vote enabled agreements such as the Trans-Pacific Partnership to be negotiated with limited floor amendments and expedited up-or-down votes.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: I cannot verify this specific assertion and there is no independent, contemporaneous public reporting or official confirmation that a 13-year-old in Halifax went into critical care with cardiac arrest 'right after' receiving a vaccine. Temporal proximity to vaccination does not establish causation, and extraordinary medical events affecting a child would typically be confirmed by hospitals or public health authorities before being reported as fact. Without verifiable evidence (hospital statement, public health bulletin, or reputable news coverage) the claim should be treated as unverified and therefore false for fact-check purposes.

claim: In Hillary Clinton's tax returns, "you saw a lot of income coming from donors to the Clinton Foundation and people who benefitted from her State Department term as well."
rationale: Hillary Clinton's publicly released tax returns show substantial income from speaking fees, book advances, investments, and salary, and while some payers who hired the Clintons or paid speech fees also gave to the Clinton Foundation or had dealings with the State Department, independent fact-checks found only limited overlap. There is no clear evidence that a large share of her reported income came from Foundation donors or people who directly benefited from her State Department role, so the claim overstates the situation.

claim: Says video shows "Ukrainian forces shoot down Russian plane carrying hundreds (of) troops on Kyiv airport."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Ukrainian forces shot down a Russian plane carrying ‘hundreds’ of troops at Kyiv airport. Major news outlets and official sources did not document such a dramatic airlift and shoot-down, and the claim likely misattributes or sensationalizes unrelated footage.

claim: Says Barack Obama "endorsed a total ban on the manufacture, sale and possession of all handguns."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama ever endorsed a total ban on the manufacture, sale, and possession of all handguns. His public record and campaign positions called for measures like reinstating the assault weapons ban, expanded background checks, and limits on high-capacity magazines, not a blanket prohibition on all handguns. Multiple contemporary fact-checks and his public statements do not support the quoted claim.

claim: Says U.S. Senate rival Tommy Thompson said he wants to "do away with Medicare."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Tommy Thompson publicly saying the literal phrase he wants to "do away with Medicare." While opponents have criticized his support for market-based Medicare reforms and privatization-like proposals as effectively ending traditional Medicare, that is a characterization of his policy positions rather than a direct quote. Therefore the claim that Thompson said he wants to "do away with Medicare" is not supported as stated.

claim: Says Matt Rosendale "consistently supported land use rules that would help developers like him and hurt farmers in Montana."
rationale: There is no public record of Matt Rosendale himself saying the quoted line. While opponents and news accounts have accused him of supporting development-friendly land-use policies that could disadvantage farmers, that is not the same as Rosendale explicitly stating he "consistently supported land use rules that would help developers like him and hurt farmers in Montana." The claim presents a direct quote that cannot be substantiated.

claim: No one "with a concealed carry permit ever committed a mass shooting."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement and is inconsistent with reporting and criminal records. While definitions of 'mass shooting' vary, journalists and researchers have documented instances where individuals who held concealed-carry permits have later carried out multi-victim shootings or similar mass-attack incidents.

claim: Says Scott Walker supports "a health care plan that would gut protections for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Scott Walker explicitly endorsed a specific health‑care proposal that would outright eliminate (gut) statutory protections for people with pre‑existing conditions. Walker has supported repeal of the ACA and measures such as state waivers, high‑risk pools, and expanded sale of alternative plans that critics say could weaken protections in practice, but those positions are not the same as publicly backing a plan that explicitly removes the legal prohibition on denying or charging more for pre‑existing conditions.

claim: The Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine contains an "undisclosed ingredient. … How is informed consent possible?"
rationale: Regulatory filings, EUA and product fact sheets for the Pfizer‑BioNTech (Comirnaty) COVID‑19 vaccine publicly list the active ingredient (mRNA) and all excipients (named lipids, salts, and sucrose). There is no credible evidence of an additional undisclosed ingredient; proprietary lipid codes are disclosed in regulatory documents, so informed consent can be based on available ingredient lists.

claim: "The number of killings of citizens by police is at a two-decade high."
rationale: The claim lacks a specified country or time frame and is not supported by available U.S. evidence: independent tallies show annual police killings have generally ranged roughly 800–1,100 per year over the past two decades with year-to-year variation. While some years (e.g., 2020) were elevated compared with immediately prior years, there is not clear evidence of a sustained two-decade high overall.

claim: "One man (New Castle, Del., County Executive, Chris Coons) thought property taxes should be hiked almost 50 percent."
rationale: There is no well‑documented record that Chris Coons, while serving as New Castle County Executive, publicly advocated raising property taxes by nearly 50 percent. A tax increase of that magnitude would have been widely reported and is inconsistent with the available accounts of his county budget positions, which described more modest adjustments. Given the lack of corroborating evidence and the implausibility of such an extreme, singular proposal, the claim is unlikely to be accurate.

claim: "If you stop testing (for COVID-19) it all goes away and people just have colds like before."
rationale: Stopping testing does not make the virus disappear — it only reduces detection and reporting. SARS-CoV-2 continues to infect, cause illness, hospitalizations, and deaths even when testing is scaled back, so cases would not simply become ordinary colds just because surveillance is reduced.

claim: Over the last 10 years, incomes for the top 1 percent "have grown." Meanwhile, the bottom half of the country, "they've seen their wages stagnate."
rationale: Multiple U.S. data sources show that incomes for the top 1% have risen noticeably over recent decade-long periods, while income and wage growth for the bottom 50% has been minimal or essentially flat in real terms. Analyses using IRS, CBO, and BLS data consistently find gains concentrated at the top and weak real-wage growth for lower-income workers over comparable ten-year spans.

claim: "United Nations Resolution is the single largest economic sanctions package ever on North Korea. Over one billion dollars in cost to N.K."
rationale: The statement is misleading. UN Security Council sanctions on North Korea have accumulated over many resolutions; while 2017 measures that barred major exports (coal, iron, seafood, etc.) were estimated by some analysts to reduce DPRK export revenue by around $1 billion, no single UN resolution is universally identified as the "single largest" package and published cost estimates vary and typically refer to combined effects or annual revenue losses rather than a definitive one-time cost.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's "been very clear where she stands on trade."
rationale: The statement that Hillary Clinton has "been very clear where she stands on trade" is misleading: her trade positions have evolved and at times been inconsistent. She supported certain trade agreements or elements earlier in her career and as a presidential candidate shifted to oppose the TPP and emphasize protections for workers, producing mixed messaging rather than a single clear stance.

claim: "Biden won’t allow Delta-variant COVID patients to get proven and effective monoclonal treatments even though there are 50,000-100,000 Americans infected by Delta EVERY DAY."
rationale: The claim is false: the federal government did not categorically ban monoclonal antibody treatments for Delta-variant patients. Several monoclonal antibody therapies were authorized by the FDA and distributed during the Delta surge, though supply, allocation, eligibility criteria, and product-specific effectiveness against particular variants affected access and use. The stated 50,000–100,000 daily infections may be a rough estimate for parts of the Delta wave depending on the date, but it does not support the assertion of an intentional nationwide prohibition.

claim: "Wisconsin Republicans have not passed a single bill in 6 months."
rationale: The assertion is implausible and contradicted by public legislative records: Wisconsin's Republican-controlled Legislature has routinely passed multiple bills and budgets within six-month spans in recent years. The claim lacks a specified timeframe and appears inconsistent with documented session activity and news coverage of enacted legislation.

claim: "92 million Americans aren't working."
rationale: The claim gives no date or definition of 'aren't working' and is therefore misleading. U.S. labor statistics distinguish 'unemployed' from 'not in the labor force' (which includes retirees, students, caregivers, and disabled people), and while the count of people not working has at times been near the low 90 millions, the exact number fluctuates monthly and requires context to be meaningful.

claim: "In Harrisburg, I passed more bills than all the Democrats combined, in terms of legislation affecting the city."
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported as stated: it names no person or timeframe and offers no evidence that a single official enacted more city-affecting bills in Harrisburg than all Democrats combined. Legislative records for state and local bodies are public and generally show bills are authored and passed by many members across parties; it is extremely unlikely one individual would outpace an entire party caucus. Without specific identity, dates, and a clear definition of "affecting the city," the claim cannot be verified and is almost certainly false.

claim: Says swabbing a tick with a soap-soaked cotton ball is a "safe, easy way" to remove them from skin.
rationale: Public-health agencies and medical guidance do not recommend swabbing ticks with soap as a safe removal method; such agents can irritate or make the tick detach unpredictably and may increase the chance of the tick regurgitating pathogen-laden fluids into the bite. The recommended method is to use fine-tipped tweezers to grasp the tick close to the skin and pull upward steadily, then clean the area and monitor for symptoms.

claim: Marco Rubio's "income skyrocketed while his power increased."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Marco Rubio’s income "skyrocketed" in direct correlation with increased political power. U.S. Senators receive a fixed salary and Rubio’s publicly filed financial disclosures show some increases from book advances, speaking, and investments over time, but not the dramatic, sudden surge implied by the term "skyrocketed."

claim: Video shows Biden saying "salute the Marines" after hearing the words in an earpiece before his inauguration.
rationale: The viral clip shows Biden repeating the phrase after someone nearby speaks it aloud; there is no reliable evidence the prompt came from an earpiece. Multiple contemporaneous video analyses and fact-checks found Biden heard the words in the environment and there was no visible or documented in‑ear prompt feeding him that line.

claim: "We paid down the debt for four years -- paid down $600 billion on the national debt."
rationale: The statement is misleading and cannot be verified as given because it omits the timeframe and which debt measure is meant. U.S. federal debt has generally trended upward; only a few years in the late 1990s saw small declines in debt held by the public, and those reductions over four years do not clearly match a $600 billion paydown of gross federal debt. Without specifying whether this refers to gross debt, debt held by the public, or a particular four‑year span, the claim as stated is false or at best misleading.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because while multiple studies and official records find voter fraud rates are extremely low, they do not show that fraud is completely non-existent in Texas. Texas has had documented incidents, investigations, and prosecutions of various types of election fraud, so the absolute assertion of "non-existent" is contradicted by evidence.

claim: Says Alaska Sen. Mark Begich "is on record supporting a carbon tax, even pushing Harry Reid to make it a priority."
rationale: There is no clear public record that Sen. Mark Begich explicitly endorsed a standalone carbon tax or publicly pressed Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to make a carbon tax a priority. Begich did express support for addressing climate change and backed market-based or emissions-control approaches in some statements, but sources do not show him publicly lobbying Reid to prioritize a carbon tax specifically. The claim overstates and mischaracterizes his documented positions.

claim: "Justin Amash is rated Michigan’s No. 1 conservative" by National Right to Life.
rationale: The National Right to Life is an anti‑abortion organization that issues pro‑life voting scores, not an overall “Michigan’s No. 1 conservative” ranking. There is no evidence that NRLC labeled Justin Amash as Michigan’s top conservative; that phrasing appears to conflate different types of scorecards or a different organization’s ranking.

claim: "Welders make more money than philosophers."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and not universally true: wages depend on country, experience, and whether a person is a tradesperson or an academic. Median wages for welders in many countries are competitive with or above earnings of contingent/entry-level philosophy instructors, but tenured philosophy professors often earn more than many welders. Because pay distributions overlap and depend on role and location, the blanket statement is false.

claim: Says that according to a report, "the tech sector now drives more than one-quarter of Austin’s economy."
rationale: There is no single authoritative, widely-cited report that unambiguously states the tech sector now drives more than 25% of Austin’s entire economy. While technology is a major employer and contributor to growth in Austin and some measures (employment share, payroll, or sectoral influence) are often reported in the mid-20% range, the claim overstates without specifying the report, metric, or timeframe.

claim: Says Bill White is refusing to debate.
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as presented — it does not identify which Bill White, which debate, or when the alleged refusal occurred. Without a specific event or reliable source documenting a refusal to debate, the assertion cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false. If a particular incident is cited, it could be fact-checked separately.

claim: "A lot of the move to free the slaves ... did not come from the federal government. It came from a growing movement among the people, particularly people of faith."
rationale: The abolition of slavery in the U.S. was driven in large part by grassroots movements, including religious groups and reform societies, even though federal actions (the Emancipation Proclamation and the 13th Amendment) ultimately ended legal slavery. Quakers, evangelical reformers from the Second Great Awakening, abolitionist societies, Black activists, and women’s organizers played central roles in building public pressure and organizing campaigns against slavery.

claim: "It is more difficult to obtain a Costco membership than it is to get a NYC Municipal ID"
rationale: This claim is false because obtaining a Costco membership generally only requires paying an annual fee and providing basic proof of identity, while the NYC Municipal ID (IDNYC) requires submission of multiple documents to prove identity and New York City residency, an in-person enrollment with photo, and often an appointment. For most people the administrative and documentation requirements for IDNYC make it as or more involved than signing up for a retail membership.

claim: "Obama-Nelson economic record: Job creation ... at slowest post-recession rate since Great Depression."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supportable as stated. While early years of the post-2007–09 recovery saw unusually slow job growth compared with many postwar recoveries, authoritative analyses and BLS/CBO data do not support a simple, documented finding that Obama-era job creation was the slowest 'since the Great Depression'—the comparison depends on the exact time window, metric (private vs. total jobs), and baseline used. Common, accurate characterizations note this recovery was slower than typical postwar recoveries, but the dramatic 'since the Great Depression' phrasing exaggerates and conflates distinct measures.

claim: Tapping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve would immediately lower gasoline prices
rationale: Releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve increases crude supply, which can lower crude oil futures, but it does not immediately translate to lower retail gasoline prices. Gasoline prices depend on refining capacity, regional inventories, distribution logistics, taxes, and market expectations, so any pump‑price effect is typically delayed, partial, and depends on the size and timing of the release. Historical SPR releases have generally produced modest or temporary impacts on pump prices rather than an immediate drop.

claim: "[The] unemployment rate in the Philadelphia metro area is now at its lowest level ever recorded."
rationale: The statement gives no date or source and thus claims a historical record without verification. Official unemployment time series (BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics) are required to establish an "ever recorded" low for the Philadelphia metro; historically the metro had very low rates in 2018–2019 and wide swings during the pandemic, so asserting a new all-time low without citation is unsupported.

claim: "I certainly supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden. ... I was there both times for them."
rationale: The claim is a first-person statement about an individual's past political support and presence at events, but no speaker identity or independent evidence is provided to corroborate it. Voting choices are private and attendance at specific events requires documentation; without supporting records or attribution the claim cannot be verified and should be treated as unproven.

claim: Rubio's "got more experience than Obama had."
rationale: The statement as phrased is ambiguous and subjective. Objectively, Marco Rubio’s elected-office résumé (Florida House 2000–2008; U.S. Senate beginning 2011) and Barack Obama’s résumé (Illinois Senate 1997–2004; U.S. Senate 2005–2008) are broadly comparable and which one counts as "more experience" depends on which offices and timeframes are compared. Because the claim is presented categorically without context and hinges on a subjective judgment, it cannot be verified as true.

claim: Says scientists are "in dispute" over whether being gay is a choice.
rationale: Major medical and scientific organizations and the bulk of peer-reviewed research do not endorse the view that sexual orientation is a voluntary choice; they describe it as arising from complex biological, developmental, and environmental factors. Although researchers debate the precise causes and their relative contributions, there is not a mainstream scientific dispute that being gay is simply a personal choice.

claim: The federal government requires "COVID passports to visit the movies."
rationale: There is no U.S. federal requirement that people show a "COVID passport" to attend movie theaters. Proof-of-vaccination or test requirements were set by some state or local governments and by private theaters at various times, while federal mandates applied to specific groups (federal employees/contractors, and certain travel rules) but did not impose a nationwide rule for visiting movies.

claim: The Obama administration "was successful in rushing a massive spending bill through Congress in just two days — after which it sat on the president's desk for three days, while he was away on vacation."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific, atypical timeline (passed in two days and then left unsigned on the president’s desk for three days while he vacationed). Major Obama-era “massive” spending bills (for example the 2009 stimulus and annual omnibus appropriations) involved longer legislative processes and different signing timelines; I find no corroborating evidence that any such large bill was rushed through in two days then intentionally left unsigned for three days while Obama was on vacation. The statement appears to conflate or exaggerate events and lacks factual support as presented.

claim: "We’re also using a sterilization process ― some great equipment that will sterilize masks up to 20 times per mask. So that’s like ordering 20 times more masks."
rationale: While some decontamination systems authorized early in the COVID-19 response (notably one program) were reported to allow up to about 20 decontamination cycles for certain N95 models, that is not equivalent to literally 'ordering 20 times more masks.' Reuse after decontamination depends on mask model, strap and filter integrity, and specific validated processes and conditions; not all respirators tolerate that many cycles and regulatory authorizations were limited and conditional.

claim: When the United States "first created the federal income tax, frankly, nobody below a million dollars a year paid anything."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. The federal income tax implemented after the 1913 16th Amendment (Revenue Act of 1913) taxed incomes above relatively low exemptions (roughly $3,000 for individuals) at 1% with graduated surtaxes on higher incomes, so people earning well below $1,000,000 paid tax. Earlier Civil War–era income taxes also taxed far lower incomes.

claim: "We only have 2 percent of the oil reserves in the world, and we consume 25 percent of the world's oil on a daily basis."
rationale: The first part is approximately correct — the United States holds only about 2–3% of the world’s proven oil reserves. The second part is overstated: U.S. oil consumption is roughly 20–21% of global daily consumption in recent years, not 25% (25% was closer to early-2000s figures).

claim: The Democratic Party "is the oldest continuous political party in the world."
rationale: The U.S. Democratic Party traces its organizational roots to the Jeffersonian Democratic-Republicans of the 1790s and was organized in its modern form around Andrew Jackson in 1828, continuing to operate nationally since then. No other currently existing national political party is generally documented as older and continuously active. Some historians note debate over what counts as uninterrupted continuity when party names and coalitions change.

claim: "Our state economic development agency under Walker, WEDC, actually isn’t even using the funds that are appropriated to it."
rationale: Available public oversight and audit records from the Walker era show WEDC awarded grants, loans, and tax credits and did spend appropriated and program funds; criticisms focused on mismanagement, improper awards, and reserve levels rather than a complete failure to use appropriations. While WEDC sometimes carried balances or delayed expenditures, characterizing it as 'isn't even using the funds' overstates the situation.

claim: Under President Barack Obama, "We’ve got the lowest labor force participation in over three decades, since 1978."
rationale: BLS labor force participation data show the civilian labor force participation rate fell into the low-62% range during Obama's terms, levels not seen since the late 1970s. Contemporary reporting and BLS series noted monthly lows in 2015 that were the lowest since around 1977–1978, so saying it was the lowest in over three decades (since 1978) is consistent with official data.

claim: The national debt is "larger than our entire annual economy."
rationale: For the United States, the commonly quoted total (gross) federal debt has been larger than annual GDP in recent years, so the national debt exceeds one year’s economic output. That said, alternative measures such as 'debt held by the public' can be closer to or below GDP depending on the date, so the accuracy depends on which debt measure is intended.

claim: "Drug overdose deaths decreased in 2018 for the first time in 30 years."
rationale: U.S. provisional CDC data showed a decline in drug overdose deaths in 2018 compared with 2017, which many public-health reports described as the first year-over-year drop in roughly three decades. The wording in news coverage referenced the long-term upward trend since the late 1980s/early 1990s, making 2018 the first reduction in about 30 years.

claim: Ketanji Brown Jackson "says she gave pedophiles lighter sentences (because) it’s different when they use computers vs mail to get volumes of child porn. This makes ‘total sense’ according to Jackson."
rationale: This claim misstates and sensationalizes Judge Ketanji Brown Jackson's record and remarks. In her judicial opinions and during confirmation hearings she described applying statutory sentencing rules and requiring proof before imposing specific enhancements (for example, for use of a computer or for distribution), not a policy of deliberately giving “lighter sentences” to people convicted of child pornography offenses. News coverage and hearings show critics framed routine legal distinctions about proof and guideline application as improper leniency, but her explanations concerned legal standards rather than an endorsement that "this makes total sense" as a permissive policy.

claim: "28.2 million Americans are still waiting under Obamacare and remain uninsured!"
rationale: The statement is misleading. While the U.S. Census Bureau reported about 28.2 million people uninsured in 2016, that number refers to the total uninsured population that year, not people who are "waiting under Obamacare" or have enrolled and are awaiting coverage. Many uninsured people are ineligible for marketplace plans, unaware of options, or choose not to enroll, so it is incorrect to equate the entire 28.2 million with being "still waiting under Obamacare."

claim: "Queen Elizabeth d-e-a-d at age 95."
rationale: Queen Elizabeth II died on September 8, 2022; she was born April 21, 1926, which made her 96 at the time of death, not 95. Official announcements and widely reported obituaries give her age as 96.

claim: Says "of the 2,000 Portland households in the year-long (composting) pilot, 87 percent of participants reported being satisfied with the overall system."
rationale: I cannot verify that a Portland year-long composting pilot involved exactly 2,000 households with 87% overall satisfaction; publicly available city program summaries and news coverage do not corroborate those specific figures and the claim may conflate different pilots or survey results. Absent a cited official report showing those exact numbers, the statement is unverified and treated as false.

claim: "Medicare does just as good, if not better, at keeping people healthy" as Medicare Advantage.
rationale: The statement is a broad claim that Original Medicare (fee-for-service) performs as well or better than Medicare Advantage across keeping people healthy; evidence is mixed and does not support a clear, general conclusion. Many analyses find Medicare Advantage plans report higher performance on preventive care measures and sometimes lower mortality or readmission rates, but these differences are affected by selection (healthier people disproportionately enroll in MA), more intensive diagnostic coding, and measurement differences. Because results vary by outcome, population, and adjustment methods, it is incorrect to assert as a general fact that Traditional Medicare does just as good or better overall.

claim: Twenty-seven percent of Californians, almost 11 million, "were born in a foreign land."
rationale: California's population is about 39–40 million; 27% of that range is roughly 10.6–10.8 million, which is reasonably described as "almost 11 million." American Community Survey/Census estimates for recent years report the state foreign-born share around 27%, corresponding to about 10.5–11 million people.

claim: Says President Barack Obama wants to raise "the lowest (income) tax rate from 10 to 15 percent."
rationale: There is no credible record that President Barack Obama proposed raising the lowest individual income tax bracket from 10% to 15%. Obama's tax proposals during his presidency generally targeted higher-income taxpayers (e.g., the 'Buffett Rule' and higher rates or fewer preferences for top earners) while preserving or expanding tax relief for low- and middle-income households. Claims that he sought to raise the bottom rate to 15% are inconsistent with his published budgets and public statements.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution "doesn’t say anything about (redistricting) being fair. … it’s set up to be partisan."
rationale: The Constitution does not contain explicit language requiring that redistricting be 'fair' or nonpartisan. It generally leaves regulation of times, places, and manner of elections to the states (with Congress able to regulate), and historically state legislatures have been responsible for drawing district lines. Later constitutional doctrine and federal laws (e.g., equal-population rules from the 14th Amendment, the Voting Rights Act, and court limits on racial gerrymandering) impose constraints, but the text itself does not mandate partisan fairness.

claim: Says Fox News gave Republican senators twice the air time as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State.
rationale: The statement is a specific numeric claim but provides no date, program, or source, and there is no well‑known, independently verified timing analysis showing Fox News gave Republican senators exactly twice the airtime as Democrats during a hearing about the Islamic State. Media monitoring reports on partisan airtime exist but results depend heavily on which segments and time windows are measured; absent a cited study or transcript timing, the 2:1 figure is unverified and likely incorrect.

claim: Say Ohio Reps. Marcia Fudge, Marcy Kaptur and Dennis Kucinich are "socialists who are openly serving in the U.S. Congress."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. None of the three are known to self-identify as "socialists" or to be members of socialist organizations, and two of them (Marcia Fudge and Dennis Kucinich) are not currently serving in the U.S. Congress. Marcy Kaptur is a long-serving Democratic congresswoman but is not an openly self-described socialist.

claim: Benzene has "never been proven to be harmful."
rationale: This claim is false: benzene is a well-established human toxicant and carcinogen. Multiple epidemiological studies and occupational health investigations have linked benzene exposure to bone marrow suppression and increased risk of leukemia (notably acute myeloid leukemia), and major health agencies have classified it as carcinogenic.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh "refused to uphold key patient protections in the past."
rationale: The claim is too broad and lacks specifics; without naming which “key patient protections” or which actions are alleged, it cannot be verified as a factual blanket refusal. While critics and advocacy groups have pointed to Kavanaugh’s D.C. Circuit opinions that limited aspects of the Affordable Care Act and challenged employer contraceptive mandates, those points do not support an unqualified assertion that he categorically "refused to uphold" patient protections in every relevant instance.

claim: "Schumer and Pelosi sneak funding into COVID bill."
rationale: The claim is vague and alleges that Schumer and Pelosi secretly inserted funding into an unspecified 'COVID bill' without citing a particular bill or provision. While congressional leaders have negotiated amendments and sometimes added unrelated provisions to legislation, those changes are part of the legislative record and not inherently 'sneaky'; asserting clandestine action requires specific documented evidence. Absent a concrete example, the blanket accusation is unsupported.

claim: "The minimum number of infrastructure (needs) in Atlanta is $900 million."
rationale: The statement gives a precise minimum figure without any sourcing or context (time period, scope, or methodology) and cannot be verified. Estimates of Atlanta's infrastructure needs vary by agency and planning horizon and are typically reported as multi-year capital needs or specific program totals, not a single unsupported $900 million 'minimum.'

claim: "If a statue of a person in the park on a horse has both front legs in the air, the person died in battle. If the horse has one front leg in the air, the person died as a result of wounds received in battle. If the horse has all four legs on the ground, the person died of natural causes."
rationale: This is a widespread urban legend about 'hoof code' for equestrian statues, but it is not a reliable rule. Art historians and numerous documented examples show many statues whose horse poses do not match the rider's cause of death, so the pose is determined by artistic choice, balance and design rather than a fixed code. For example, the well-known Andrew Jackson statue shows a rearing horse though Jackson did not die in battle.

claim: "In 2009, Jim Doyle and the Democrats rushed through a budget repair bill with billions in tax increases and held no public hearings."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. The well-known "budget repair bill" controversy occurred in 2011 under Republican Governor Scott Walker (Act 10), not in 2009 under Democrat Jim Doyle. Doyle did not rush a single 2009 "budget repair bill" with "billions in tax increases," and routine legislative budgets involve committee processes and hearings rather than the description given.

claim: "It costs nearly five times as much in California to build and maintain a mile of road as it does in the rest of the nation."
rationale: Available evidence and expert analyses show California’s road construction and maintenance costs are higher than the national average but not uniformly ‘nearly five times’ higher. Typical cost differentials cited by transportation analysts and federal/state data are much smaller (often under two- to three-fold for specific projects or urban areas), and a fivefold gap is unsupported as a general statewide average.

claim: "For every $1 spent on mitigation, $4 in post-storm cleanup and rebuilding is saved."
rationale: The statement presents a universal, fixed ratio but empirical studies report varying benefit–cost ratios for mitigation. U.S. government and research reports often cite different averages (for example some FEMA-related analyses have cited about $4 saved per $1 for specific flood mitigation programs, while broader studies such as the Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves report have found about $6 saved per $1 on average); results depend on hazard type, mitigation measure, region and time horizon. As a blanket claim it is therefore misleading.

claim: "Obama said he would unilaterally renegotiate the North American Free Trade Agreement."
rationale: Barack Obama did not say he would "unilaterally renegotiate" NAFTA. Public statements from his administration described modernizing or updating trade agreements, but renegotiation of a trilateral treaty requires agreement with Canada and Mexico and cannot be done unilaterally by a U.S. president.

claim: A space shuttle the National Museum of the United States Air Force near Dayton would be "within a day's drive of 60 percent of the U.S. population."
rationale: The claim is implausible because 'a day's drive' is ambiguous but normally implies roughly 6–8 hours (~400–500 miles); using that range, large population centers on the U.S. West Coast and parts of the Mountain states are well beyond a single day's drive from Dayton. Publicly available population-distribution analyses and common-distance isochrones do not support 60% of the U.S. population living within that driving distance of Dayton.

claim: "Only in the Third World do you see this habitual use of prosecutions of former leaders."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: prosecutions of former leaders occur in many developed democracies as well as in developing countries. Examples include legal cases against former leaders in France (Jacques Chirac), Italy (Silvio Berlusconi), the United States (indictments of a former president), and Israel (indictments of a former prime minister).

claim: California’s marijuana legalization initiative, Prop. 64 "allows marijuana smoking ads in prime time, on programs with millions of children and teenage viewers."
rationale: Prop. 64 does not explicitly permit cannabis ads that target or primarily reach minors. The measure contains restrictions banning advertising designed to appeal to children and limits placements where a substantial portion of the audience is under 21 and near schools or youth centers, so the claim that it broadly "allows" smoking ads in prime time on programs with millions of children is misleading.

claim: Says he met a teacher in Dallas "who was only in his third year of teaching and already making more than $90,000 a year in salary."
rationale: This is an anecdotal, unverified claim and is unlikely given typical pay schedules: third-year public school teachers in the Dallas area generally earn well below $90,000. While it is possible a rare individual could reach that total with substantial stipends, outside income, or employment in a private/charter setting, no corroborating evidence is provided for the specific meeting described.

claim: "We spent $3-million of your money to study the DNA of bears."
rationale: The statement is unverified and lacks critical context (who 'we' refers to, which agency, timeframe, or program). While government and academic grants sometimes fund wildlife genetics research, there is no clear evidence of a specific $3 million expenditure by a government entity solely 'to study the DNA of bears' as a general claim.

claim: Says "Bruce Starr voted to throw 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Bruce Starr literally cast a single vote described accurately as "throwing 6,000 Oregonians off unemployment." While Starr has voted for bills that changed unemployment rules or funding and critics sometimes estimated those changes would affect thousands, the claim as stated is an unsupported simplification and conflates projected impacts with a direct, quantified action.

claim: "Last year, (Bill McCollum) spent more than $2.2 million dollars to produce and air campaign-style TV ads where you were featured in almost every frame."
rationale: The claim is unverified and implausible as stated because it gives no specific year or identity for “you,” and campaign finance records are required to substantiate a precise $2.2 million ad buy. Independent expenditures by PACs or media vendors can account for large sums, but without documentary evidence (campaign filings or ad-buy records) the assertion that Bill McCollum personally spent that exact amount and that a named individual appeared in ‘almost every frame’ cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says the unemployment rate for African-American youths is 59 percent.
rationale: A 59% unemployment rate for African-American youths is not consistent with national labor statistics; BLS data show Black teen (e.g., 16–19) unemployment has at times been very high but typically in the ~20–40% range during severe downturns, not 59%. A 59% figure likely arises from a misinterpretation, a very narrow local subgroup, or mixing in measures like 'not in the labor force' rather than the official unemployment rate.

claim: Says the U.S. government caused the coronavirus pandemic because it sent mRNA coronavirus vaccine candidates to university researchers weeks before the COVID-19 outbreak.
rationale: There is no credible evidence the U.S. government 'caused' the COVID-19 pandemic by sending mRNA vaccine candidates to researchers. SARS-CoV-2 emerged in late 2019 and genomic sequencing was published in January 2020; mRNA vaccine platforms and coronavirus vaccine research existed beforehand, but sharing research materials is normal and does not imply creation or release of the virus. Epidemiological and genomic analyses favor a natural zoonotic origin and do not support the claimed causal link.

claim: Says "the New York Times wrote about" Barack Obama wiretapping Donald Trump during the election.
rationale: The New York Times did not report that Barack Obama ordered wiretapping of Donald Trump during the 2016 campaign. NYT and other outlets covered FISA-authorized surveillance of some Trump associates and reported that there was no evidence that Obama personally ordered a wiretap, and official investigators did not substantiate Trump's claim.

claim: Florida retirees and families "lost tens of thousands of dollars" in deposits on failed Trump condo projects, but he "pocketed their money and walked away."
rationale: Reporting shows that some buyers of Trump-branded condo projects — including in Florida — did lose substantial deposits when those third‑party developments failed, but there is no reliable evidence that Donald Trump personally 'pocketed' those deposits and 'walked away.' In many cases the Trump Organization licensed its name and the developer or escrow agents held buyers' funds, and liability depends on project-specific contracts and outcomes rather than a general pattern of Trump taking deposits.

claim: Democrats say Chafee wants to tax equipment that enables amputee veterans to drive
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated record that Democrats broadly asserted Chafee wanted to tax equipment that enables amputee veterans to drive. While opponents have attacked Chafee on tax issues, the specific claim about taxing adaptive driving equipment is unsupported by widely reported evidence and may be a misleading framing of a tax proposal or budget position.

claim: "We have that program where immigrants come here and they have to bring a million dollars in order to get a green card if they’re going to create jobs."
rationale: There is an EB‑5 immigrant investor program that can lead to a green card for investors who create jobs, but the claim that immigrants "have to bring a million dollars" is an oversimplification and not universally true. Historically the standard EB‑5 threshold was $1,000,000 (with a $500,000 lower threshold for targeted employment areas), and statutory/administrative investment minima have changed over time; approval is conditional on job creation and other requirements, not automatic upon depositing a sum.

claim: "Today’s minimum wage worker making $7.25 an hour has less buying power than a minimum wage worker in the 1960s."
rationale: Adjusted for inflation, the federal minimum wage reached its peak real value in the late 1960s and that nominal $1.60 then is equivalent to roughly $11–13 per hour in recent dollars. Therefore a worker paid $7.25 today has substantially less purchasing power than a minimum-wage worker in the late 1960s.

claim: TriMet is "spending 4.2 million in fed funds to save $168K per year."
rationale: The claim is a precise arithmetic assertion about TriMet spending $4.2 million in federal funds to achieve $168,000 per year in savings, but there is no authoritative context or documentary evidence provided to confirm those exact figures. Without identifying the specific project, time period, or source, this reads like a misleading summary that compares a one-time capital outlay to recurring operating savings without showing full cost-benefit details or funding rules.

claim: Says Tony Evers wants to give in-state tuition and drivers licenses to "illegal aliens."
rationale: Governor Tony Evers has publicly supported policies to allow undocumented immigrants to obtain driver’s licenses and to make in-state tuition available to eligible undocumented students (often described as DACA or DREAMer-type students). Those positions have been part of his campaign platforms and policy proposals, though legislative action has been required for implementation.

claim: "There are actually only 30 countries that practice birthright citizenship."
rationale: Most comparative legal surveys and reporting find that roughly 30–33 countries worldwide grant unconditional birthright (jus soli) citizenship, with the majority located in the Americas. Many other countries either restrict birthright citizenship by parental status or residency or do not grant it, so saying 'only 30 countries' is a reasonable approximation.

claim: The Benghazi probe is "the longest-running congressional investigation ever."
rationale: The House Select Committee on Benghazi operated roughly from mid-2014 to the end of 2016 (about 2–2.5 years). Numerous other congressional investigations in U.S. history have been longer or ongoing for many years — for example the House Un-American Activities Committee existed for decades and major probes like Iran–Contra involved multi-year congressional inquiry — so calling the Benghazi probe the longest-ever is inaccurate.

claim: "Trudeau's foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics which makes mechanic lipids for Pfizer."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any Trudeau-linked foundation owns 40% of Acuitas Therapeutics. Acuitas is a private Canadian company developing lipid nanoparticle technology and while it has collaborated with vaccine developers, ownership by the Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation or a 40% stake has not been reported.

claim: "The very first Republican convention after the Civil War was held in Virginia in a Black church."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated: the first post–Civil War Republican National Convention after the war was held in Chicago in 1868, and Republicans held numerous state and local conventions in 1865–67 across the North and South. While Black churches were often used as meeting sites during Reconstruction and Virginia held important Republican and constitutional conventions, there is no clear evidence that the very first Republican convention after the war occurred in Virginia in a Black church.

claim: "Leah Vukmir OPPOSES Buy American legislation."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that Leah Vukmir has publicly opposed 'Buy American' legislation. Her public record and campaign materials do not contain documented statements or votes expressly opposing Buy American provisions, and major news coverage does not attribute such a stance to her. Without a specific bill or time frame, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "Daniel Webster said he's out. Now he says he's in."
rationale: The claim is vague and provides no time, office, or source; there is no clear, verifiable public record that Daniel Webster universally declared he was 'out' and then later 'in' for a specific race. Without contextual details or corroborating reporting, the statement cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: "Big pharmaceuticals pay off — they literally pay off — generics to keep the prices and the competition off the market."
rationale: There is documented evidence that brand‑name drugmakers have paid generic manufacturers to delay market entry — a practice called 'pay‑for‑delay' or reverse‑payment settlements. These arrangements have been the subject of FTC investigations, antitrust lawsuits, and the Supreme Court's 2013 FTC v. Actavis decision, and regulators have concluded they can keep prices higher by postponing generic competition.

claim: "I'm not taking any corporate PAC money."
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable without knowing who said it and the relevant time period; many politicians publicly pledge not to take corporate PAC money but may still receive funds via affiliated PACs, joint fundraising committees, or party/leadership PACs. Because the statement lacks a specific actor and campaign-finance records would be required to confirm no corporate PAC contributions, I rate it as false under uncertainty.

claim: "Wisconsin took a break, and when they returned, Biden coincidentally came back ahead by 100k."
rationale: The claim is too vague and presents a suspiciously specific outcome without date, source, or evidence; I cannot verify that Wisconsin officials paused counting and that Biden 'coincidentally' regained a 100,000-vote lead at that specific moment. Vote totals often shift when counting pauses and later includes different ballot types (e.g., mail-in or provisional ballots) that favor one candidate, so a change in the lead is plausible but the asserted coincidence and exact figure are unproven. Without concrete timing and official tallies, the statement is not supported.

claim: Democratic lawmakers who voted in favor of short-term spending bills "just voted to deport Dreamers."
rationale: Voting for a short-term spending bill (a continuing resolution) that does not include language changing immigration policy is not the same as voting to deport Dreamers. Most CRs simply extend existing funding levels and programs; they do not themselves rescind DACA or order deportations. Saying lawmakers "just voted to deport Dreamers" is a misleading characterization unless the specific bill explicitly authorized or funded deportation actions or repealed DACA protections.

claim: "More than half of women under 30 who give birth do so outside of marriage..."
rationale: The claim as stated lacks a country and year and therefore cannot be taken as universally true. Nonmarital birth rates vary widely by country and time; in many places (including the United States overall) births to unmarried women are under 50% of all births, though certain younger age groups can have majority nonmarital births. Without clear context the blanket statement is not reliably true.

claim: Oregon concealed gun applications include "home phone numbers, home address, Social Security numbers, what kinds of guns you have in the house … whether you were dishonorably discharged from the military, what controlled substances you are taking and  were you ever accused of -- accused, mind you -- of stalking."
rationale: The Oregon concealed handgun license application does request contact information (address, phone) and an applicant's Social Security number for processing and fingerprinting, and asks about disqualifying conditions such as dishonorable military discharge, unlawful or dependent use of controlled substances, and certain stalking-related convictions or restraining orders. However, it does not require you to enumerate 'what kinds of guns you have in the house,' nor does it ask only whether you were merely 'accused' of stalking; questions focus on convictions, restraining orders, or other disqualifying legal findings. Therefore the quoted formulation mixes true elements with incorrect or exaggerated items.

claim: "Germany owes ... vast sums of money to NATO & the United States must be paid more for the powerful, and very expensive, defense it provides to Germany!"
rationale: Germany does not legally owe “vast sums” to NATO; NATO is funded by agreed national contributions and common budgets rather than an accounts receivable system, and there is no large outstanding invoice that makes Germany indebted to NATO. The United States provides forces under NATO and bilateral stationing arrangements and has long argued allies should increase their defense spending, but that political position is not the same as a binding obligation that Germany must pay the U.S. additional sums for providing defense.

claim: Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated — Multnomah County’s finances have not shown an indisputable, year‑over‑year reduction for 11 consecutive years. County budgets fluctuate, some years included increases or one‑time federal/state relief (e.g., pandemic funds), and public budget records do not support a simple 11‑year straight decline.

claim: Israel has seen a "90 percent reduction in terrorist attacks" that it attributes to building a 500-mile fence.
rationale: Israeli officials and security reports have publicly credited the construction of the West Bank barrier and related fences (commonly described in media as about 500 miles when built and planned sections are combined) with roughly a 90% drop in suicide bombings and many other attacks since the early 2000s. Independent studies generally found large declines in attacks in areas protected by the barrier, though researchers also note other security measures and political factors contributed to the overall reduction.

claim: Metro Atlantans spend "over an hour every day" or "five hours a week" commuting, for a total of "260 hours a year."
rationale: Recent U.S. Census/American Community Survey and transportation reports show average one-way commute times in the Atlanta metro are roughly 30–33 minutes, which implies about an hour (or slightly more) round trip per workday. Multiplying roughly 5–5.5 hours per workweek by 52 weeks yields about 260–286 hours per year, so the cited figures are reasonable approximations.

claim: Since he took office as Milwaukee County executive, "we have never raised" bus fares and "this year there’ll be a million route-miles more than there were five years ago."
rationale: The claim bundles two specific, checkable assertions (no fare increases since he took office; an extra million route-miles this year vs five years ago) that depend on precise dates and transit-agency accounting. Public transit fares and service levels frequently changed during and after the pandemic, and without looking at Milwaukee County Transit System (MCTS) official fare histories and annual route-mile statistics the combined claim cannot be verified and is unlikely to be strictly true as stated.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden "doesn’t wear a mask on a plane."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified without the actual photo, its timestamp, and context; many circulated images of public figures are miscaptioned or cropped to mislead. President Biden has been photographed both with and without a mask depending on setting, timing, and whether he was eating or speaking, so a bare assertion that a photo shows him not wearing a mask on a plane is unsubstantiated as presented.

claim: "We’re spending tremendous amounts of money to educate our kids. In the world, we're No. 1 per pupil by a factor of four."
rationale: The U.S. does spend a lot per pupil and is often near the top in international rankings, but reliable international data (OECD/UNESCO/World Bank) do not show the United States spending four times as much per pupil as other countries.
