claim: "African-Americans are more likely to be arrested by police and sentenced to longer prison terms for doing the same thing that whites do."
rationale: Multiple government data sets and peer-reviewed studies show Black Americans are arrested at higher rates than white Americans and, controlling for offense severity and criminal history in many analyses, receive longer or harsher sentences for comparable crimes. Disparities have been documented by the U.S. Sentencing Commission, Bureau of Justice Statistics, DOJ reports, and academic research.

claim: "Missouri has one of the highest rates of uninsured children in the country."
rationale: National data from sources that track health insurance by state (e.g., Census American Community Survey and KFF summaries) show that states like Texas, Oklahoma, and several Southern states have some of the highest child uninsured rates; Missouri's child uninsured rate has generally been near or modestly above the national average, not among the very highest. Therefore the statement that Missouri has one of the highest rates is not supported by typical state rankings.

claim: "Last year we spent more than $40 billion on highways. And Lord knows we need that. But that's more than we spent on Amtrak in its entire 40-year history."
rationale: While annual federal highway outlays in some years have been around $40 billion, the claim that this exceeds what the U.S. spent on Amtrak over its first 40 years is incorrect. Amtrak was created in 1971 and received regular federal operating and capital support averaging roughly a billion dollars or more per year plus larger capital grants in some years, so cumulative federal support over four decades exceeds $40 billion. Therefore the comparison is misleading and false.

claim: Ché Guevara "wrote extensively about the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent."
rationale: Che Guevara did not publish extensive writings claiming the superiority of white Europeans over people of African descent. While some of his private diaries and early travel notes contain occasional derogatory or ethnically insensitive remarks, his public and political writings emphasize anti-imperialism, class struggle, and internationalism rather than racial hierarchy.

claim: "Breaking: Santa Fe killer expresses his love for Obama."
rationale: No credible contemporary reporting or official statements about any Santa Fe school shooter include an expression of love for former President Obama. Major news coverage of the Santa Fe (Texas/New Mexico) shootings documented motives, social-media posts and evidence, and none reported the quoted sentiment; the claim appears to be a fabricated/viral assertion.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: This claim is false. There is no known White House order that blanketly removes the public or press's right to photograph President Biden climbing stairs; the First Amendment protects photographing public officials in public settings. While specific restricted or secure areas can lawfully limit photography for safety or security, an across-the-board ban announced by a White House spokesman would be unprecedented and legally dubious, and no credible reports confirm such an order.

claim: Says Mark Zuckerberg invented the word "BFF," and if it doesn’t appear green after you type it in a Facebook comment, your account has been hacked.
rationale: The acronym "BFF" (best friends forever) was in common use and printed in media well before Facebook, so Mark Zuckerberg did not invent the word. Facebook has no security feature that turns the literal string "BFF" green to indicate an account hack; color/links in comments result from tagging, formatting, platform changes, or browser extensions, and the claim is a viral hoax.

claim: The president's health care proposals will cause "most Americans to have their premiums increased, not decreased, and hundreds of millions of people lose their current insurance coverage."
rationale: The claim is implausible and not supported by available evidence: saying "hundreds of millions" would lose coverage implies a majority of the U.S. population and far exceeds prior nonpartisan estimates of policy impacts. Analyses of major health-plan changes (e.g., CBO/JCT and academic studies) have projected changes in coverage affecting millions to tens of millions under dramatic scenarios, and premium effects vary widely by plan, income, and state rather than uniformly increasing for "most Americans."

claim: "By the word religion in the First Amendment, the founders meant Christianity."
rationale: The First Amendment was drafted to prohibit a federal establishment of religion and to protect free exercise generally, not to define 'religion' as only Christianity. Founding-era actions (e.g., Madison's Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom), correspondence (Jefferson's church-state letters), and later judicial interpretation treat the term broadly and reflect the founders' aim to protect diverse religious beliefs.

claim: "Mitt Romney’s pledged to protect (oil companies') record profits – and their billions in special tax breaks, too."
rationale: During his 2012 campaign Romney repeatedly opposed eliminating oil industry tax preferences and said he would not raise taxes on energy companies, and his stated energy policies (expanding drilling, opposing subsidy cuts) were broadly protective of industry profits and tax breaks. While he did not use the exact phrasing “I will protect their record profits,” his pledges to preserve tax preferences and favor policies that boost producers would effectively do so.

claim: Says "Scott Brown’s carrying some big oil baggage" because he "collected over $400,000 in campaign contributions."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that Scott Brown personally 'collected over $400,000' specifically from oil companies; publicly available campaign finance summaries show he received some energy-sector donations but not a documented $400,000+ from oil alone. The claim conflates a political attack line with an asserted precise dollar figure without specifying timeframe or source documentation.

claim: Starbucks executive "believes white men are the root of all evil."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting up to mid-2024 that a Starbucks executive publicly stated 'white men are the root of all evil.' Viral social-media claims like this are commonly misattributions, taken out of context, or originate from non-executive employees or parody accounts rather than verified company leadership. Without reliable sourcing, the allegation should be treated as false.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton and Tim Kaine "want to shut down shale, and shut down natural gas."
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. During the 2016 campaign neither Hillary Clinton nor Tim Kaine called for shutting down shale or the natural gas industry nationwide; both advocated stronger regulation, methane controls, and leaving certain decisions to states or supporting local moratoria in specific circumstances rather than an across-the-board shutdown.

claim: "The country is now in a manufacturing recession."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it names no country or time period. Whether a country is in a "manufacturing recession" depends on recent manufacturing output indicators (e.g., industrial production, manufacturing value added, or PMI) showing sustained contraction; without those data the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: The newly drawn congressional district map in Arkansas "keeps communities together."
rationale: While proponents described the new Arkansas congressional map as ‘‘keeping communities together,’’ independent reporting and analysis found the map splits major population centers and counties (for example, portions of Little Rock/Pulaski County are divided among districts) and was criticized for dividing communities of interest. That pattern undercuts the literal claim that it preserves community cohesion.

claim: "The Biden administration is engaging in human trafficking because they are enabling this to happen" at the southern border.
rationale: The claim alleges the Biden administration is actively 'engaging in human trafficking' by enabling it at the southern border. There is no credible evidence that U.S. government officials are participants in human trafficking; documented trafficking across the border is carried out by criminal smuggling and trafficking networks, and law enforcement investigates and prosecutes such crimes. Policy decisions can affect migration flows but do not constitute the government itself committing trafficking.

claim: "The Clintons' foundation took millions from foreign governments" including United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
rationale: Publicly available tax filings and donor records show the Clinton Foundation accepted donations from foreign governments and government-related entities, and those contributions cumulatively amounted to millions of dollars. News reporting and the Foundation's own disclosure lists include donors from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia among others. The receipts were to the Foundation and related philanthropic entities, not direct personal payments to the Clintons.

claim: Hillary Clinton wants to "wave the white flag of surrender and set a date for withdrawal."
rationale: Hillary Clinton has not advocated ‘waving the white flag of surrender and setting a date for withdrawal.’ In her public statements and policy positions (notably in the 2008 and 2016 campaigns) she opposed arbitrary fixed withdrawal dates and favored conditions-based or phased approaches, so the claim misrepresents her stance or reverses the context of remarks criticizing others who supported a set date.

claim: "In 2017, we had more marijuana possession arrests in our country than all other violent crimes combined."
rationale: The claim is misleading and likely false for typical interpretations (e.g., the United States). 2017 FBI Uniform Crime Report data show hundreds of thousands of marijuana possession arrests but arrests for violent crimes (murder, rape, robbery, aggravated assault) in aggregate do not appear to be fewer than marijuana possession arrests. The statement is also ambiguous about which country and whether it counts arrests versus offenses.

claim: "In the last 29 months, our economy has produced about 4.5 million private-sector jobs."
rationale: The statement gives a 29-month total but does not specify the start or end dates, so it cannot be verified as written. Official private-sector job totals are reported monthly by the BLS (establishment survey) and cumulative gains depend entirely on the exact 29-month window chosen. Without precise months and a cited data source, the claim is uncheckable and therefore treated as false.

claim: Says Quaden Bayles committed suicide.
rationale: Claims that Quaden Bayles committed suicide are false. Family members and multiple reputable news outlets have publicly denied such reports and previous social-media announcements of his death were debunked.

claim: "60 percent of the jobs lost in the 2008 recession were living-wage jobs. Of the jobs we’ve gotten back, only 40 percent are living-wage."
rationale: The statement presents precise percentages using the undefined term “living-wage” that are not supported by standard labor statistics. Government data and independent analyses show the 2008 job losses and subsequent gains were concentrated in different wage tiers and that recoveries skewed toward lower‑paid work, but the 60% lost / 40% recovered split depends on a particular, nonstandard living‑wage definition and time window and is not a robust, widely corroborated fact.

claim: Says Tony Thurmond was "Reprimanded by the Obama Administration for failing to address widespread sexual harassment and assault in district schools."
rationale: There is no reliable public record that the Obama Administration formally reprimanded Tony Thurmond for failing to address widespread sexual harassment and assault in district schools. Federal education enforcement (Office for Civil Rights) generally issues findings or resolutions against school districts, not political figures, and searches of contemporary reporting and agency actions do not show a reprimand of Thurmond. The claim appears to conflate possible district-level investigations or criticisms with a personal reprimand.

claim: Says Donald Trump "spent the least amount of money of any of the competitive primary contenders that he beat so badly."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and cannot be confirmed as written because it does not specify which primary cycle or which opponents count as 'competitive.' While Donald Trump notably relied on earned media and spent less than several rivals in the 2016 GOP primary, that does not prove he spent the absolute least of every competitive contender across cycles or by all spending measures. Without a specific year and roster of opponents, the claim is unverifiable and therefore judged false.

claim: Two photos show climate change "is a hoax."
rationale: Two photos cannot demonstrate that climate change is a hoax because climate is defined by long-term global trends, not isolated local weather events or images. Extensive, independently verified evidence — global temperature records, melting ice, sea-level rise, and atmospheric composition changes — supports that human-driven climate change is real, so cherry-picked photos do not refute it.

claim: Says 13 Texas universities "have announced or implemented a $10,000 degree."
rationale: I cannot verify that exactly 13 Texas universities have both announced or implemented a $10,000 bachelor’s-degree program. Reporting on Texas’s “$10K degree” initiative has named various institutions and the list has changed over time; some schools announced pilot programs while others only considered proposals. Because the number cited appears to be a moving target and no single authoritative source consistently confirms exactly 13 completed implementations, the specific claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "Last year we had the eighth fastest-growing economy in the country in West Virginia."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no specific year or metric and I cannot confirm a reliable ranking showing West Virginia was the eighth fastest-growing economy in the most recent year. State economic growth rankings (by real GDP or other measures) are published annually and vary year to year; without a clear year and data source the assertion is unsupported. Given the ambiguity and lack of corroborating evidence, the claim is classified as false.

claim: Said President Barack Obama "said he was going to stop (signature strikes)."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable public statement in which President Obama explicitly and categorically said “I am going to stop” signature strikes. The Obama administration did tighten and clarify rules (Presidential Policy Guidance) and said it would constrain the use of so‑called signature strikes, but it did not make a simple, unequivocal public pledge to stop them entirely. Reporting shows policy changes and limits rather than a flat, one‑line promise to end signature strikes.

claim: In New York, "Average college debt - $30,000 per student."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and not reliably true as written: reported student loan figures vary by year, by whether they measure mean vs median, by whether they count only borrowers or all students, and by institution type. While a roughly $30,000 average debt is near some national figures for graduates in recent years, New York-specific averages differ across datasets and years, so the blanket claim that average college debt in New York is $30,000 per student is unsupported without a specified year and methodology.

claim: Says Burisma admitted in a Ukrainian court to paying Joe Biden $900,000.
rationale: There is no credible record or verified Ukrainian court ruling showing Burisma admitted paying Joe Biden $900,000. Multiple reputable news organizations and fact-checkers have found no court documents or official admissions to support this claim, and Joe Biden's public financial disclosures and tax records do not show such a payment.

claim: "The coronavirus has officially reached Milwaukee County."
rationale: The claim gives no date or context, so as stated it is ambiguous and cannot be verified. In fact, Milwaukee County reported confirmed COVID-19 cases beginning in March 2020, so historically the coronavirus has been detected there; without a timestamp the claim cannot be judged as a current official update.

claim: The federal government "now tells us which light bulbs to buy."
rationale: The federal government does not literally tell consumers which brand or exact bulb to buy. It issues energy-efficiency and labeling standards (which have phased out many inefficient incandescent bulbs), so manufacturers and retailers must sell only compliant products while consumers still choose among approved types.

claim: President Obama was "raised Muslim."
rationale: Barack Obama's father was Muslim and Obama spent part of his childhood in Indonesia where he was exposed to Islam, but he was primarily raised by his mother and maternal grandparents in Hawaii without a religious affiliation, briefly attended a Catholic school, and as an adult was baptized as a Christian. Therefore the simple claim that he was "raised Muslim" is inaccurate.

claim: Mt. Hood Community College is No. 1 on average and top faculty pay and benefits.
rationale: The claim provides no source or clear comparator (state, region, or national) and there is no widely recognized ranking that lists Mt. Hood Community College as #1 for average faculty pay and benefits. Faculty compensation varies by state and district and must be shown with specific, up-to-date salary/benefits data; absent such evidence the assertion is unverifiable and likely incorrect.

claim: "The cost-of-living increase in Social Security is tied to wage inflation."
rationale: Social Security's annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is calculated from changes in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), a measure of price inflation, not from wage inflation. Wage growth is used elsewhere in Social Security rules (for example, indexing past earnings when computing initial benefits), which likely causes confusion but does not determine the COLA.

claim: "There was never a single shred of evidence presented to anyone" that the attacks in Benghazi, Libya, were "spontaneous, and in fact, the CIA themselves understood that early on."
rationale: The claim is too absolute and contradicts the record: U.S. officials and intelligence talking points initially presented assertions tying the Benghazi violence to spontaneous protests, and those talking points were publicly circulated. Multiple later reviews (congressional committees, intelligence and inspector general reports) found that assessments evolved and that the attack had organized militant involvement, so the notion that there was “never a single shred of evidence” for spontaneity and that the CIA uniformly understood it as spontaneous early on is inaccurate.

claim: Red-flag laws have been "shown to reduce the number of suicides by firearms."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed evaluations of state extreme-risk protection orders (red-flag laws), notably in Connecticut and Indiana, have reported associations with reductions in firearm suicides and estimated numbers of averted suicides when firearms were removed. These studies are observational and limited in scope, but they consistently support the conclusion that ERPOs can reduce firearm suicides.

claim: The 9-9-9 plan "does not raise taxes on those that are making the least."
rationale: Independent analyses at the time (notably the Tax Policy Center and many economists) concluded Herman Cain's 9-9-9 plan would likely raise net federal taxes on many low-income households. The plan replaced progressive income and payroll taxes with a flat income rate plus a national sales/consumption tax, which is regressive and was estimated to hit lower-income earners harder unless substantial offsets were added.

claim: President Obama has "stopped using the phrase 'war on terror.' "
rationale: This is inaccurate as an absolute claim: the Obama administration deliberately moved away from the phrase and Obama rarely used it, but he did not categorically stop using the words or the concept in all contexts. News coverage and his speeches show a shift in vocabulary (favoring terms like 'terrorism' or 'overseas contingency operations') rather than an outright ban on the phrase.

claim: Old photograph shows a group of women in KKK attire holding a sign that reads "Women of the Democrat Party."
rationale: The photograph has circulated with altered captions, but the original historic image does not show a sign reading "Women of the Democrat Party." Contemporary fact-checking and archival evidence show the photo depicts members of the Ku Klux Klan (women in KKK attire) and the sign in authentic versions refers to the Klan or is otherwise different; modern versions have been digitally relabeled to target the Democratic Party.

claim: Says Rep. Kyrsten Sinema supported a bill that is "essentially encouraging child trafficking."
rationale: The claim that Rep. Kyrsten Sinema supported a bill that is 'essentially encouraging child trafficking' is unsupported by available evidence. There are no credible reports or legislative records showing she backed legislation intended to or characterized by reputable sources as promoting child trafficking; such an extraordinary claim would require clear, specific evidence which is not provided here.

claim: Says Donald Trump "himself has a financial stake in the French company that makes the brand-name version of hydroxychloroquine."
rationale: The brand-name hydroxychloroquine product (Plaquenil) is produced by the French company Sanofi, but there is no credible evidence or disclosure showing that Donald Trump personally owned stock or had a direct financial stake in Sanofi. Public financial disclosures and contemporary fact-checking reporting did not document any such personal holding by Trump. The claim appears to conflate corporate makers of the drug with an alleged personal investment that is unsupported by the record.

claim: "The Doherty Campaign, unlike the Cicilline Campaign, is funded mostly by individual donors -- not the big PACs that Cicilline relies on."
rationale: The claim names two campaigns but provides no election cycle or first names, and I cannot verify a clear-cut contrast that Doherty is funded mostly by individuals while Cicilline 'relies on' big PACs. Public campaign finance records (FEC/state filings) show funding mixes vary by cycle; David Cicilline has taken both individual contributions and PAC money, and without checking specific filings for the Doherty referenced it is not supportable to assert the asserted funding split. Because the statement is specific but unverified, it should be treated as false unless substantiated with recent FEC data.

claim: Says "Ron Johnson calls Social Security a Ponzi scheme and wants to privatize the program."
rationale: The claim bundles two strong assertions. While Senator Ron Johnson has repeatedly called Social Security unsustainable and supported major reforms (including support for private accounts or changes to benefits), there is not a clear, consistent record that he plainly and repeatedly labeled the program a 'Ponzi scheme' or that he advocates full privatization of Social Security. Framing both statements as categorical assertions is therefore misleading.

claim: "The stock market has hit record numbers, as you know. And there has been a tremendous surge of optimism in the business world."
rationale: The statement is time‑dependent and vague: whether the stock market has hit record numbers and whether there is a 'tremendous surge' of business optimism depends on which market, which indices, and what time period is meant. Without a specific date, index (e.g., S&P 500, Dow, Nasdaq) or objective measures of business sentiment, the claim cannot be verified and so cannot be treated as a factual blanket assertion. Historical data show markets and business sentiment fluctuate, sometimes hitting records and sometimes not, so the claim as stated is not verifiable.

claim: "Atlanta just lost 75% of its police force"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official reporting that the Atlanta Police Department recently lost 75% of its officers. While APD has faced retirements, resignations and staffing shortfalls at times, those have not amounted to a three‑quarters reduction in its sworn force.

claim: In President Barack Obama’s 2015 State of the Union address, "the words ‘al-Qaida’ were never used, the first time those words have not been used in a State of the Union address since February 2001."
rationale: It is true that President Obama did not use the words "al-Qaida" in his 2015 State of the Union; however the claim that this was the first State of the Union since February 2001 to omit those words is incorrect or at least ambiguous. Public transcript checks and contemporary fact-checking noted the omission in 2015 but show discrepancies in the asserted February 2001 benchmark and how earlier addresses are counted.

claim: "The bulk of the people who are shot with a weapon — other than these drug gangs taking on one another — end up being shot with their own weapon."
rationale: The statement that most people shot (aside from drug-gang violence) are shot with their own weapon is not supported by criminological evidence. Available data and firearm-tracing research indicate victims are typically shot by someone else using that shooter's weapon or a third party's gun; while some shootings involve a victim's own gun (e.g., during a struggle or suicide), these are not the majority in most jurisdictions.

claim: In "the past four or five" presidential elections, "people who poll high at the beginning are not the people who end up being the nominees."
rationale: This generalization is inaccurate: while some early front‑runners have lost (e.g., Hillary Clinton led early in 2008 Democratic polling but Barack Obama won), several recent nominees were early high pollers — Mitt Romney was an early GOP front‑runner in 2012, Hillary Clinton was an early leader and won the 2016 Democratic nomination, and Joe Biden led early Democratic polling and became the 2020 nominee. The pattern is therefore inconsistent rather than uniformly true over the last four or five cycles.

claim: "I've either balanced every budget or we turned back a surplus."
rationale: The sentence is an absolute claim about budget outcomes but gives no identity, jurisdiction, or timeframe, so it cannot be verified as stated. Proving someone 'balanced every budget or turned back a surplus' would require complete, year-by-year official budget and audit records; absent those specifics the claim is not supportable.

claim: "Some of the wealthiest Americans are African-American now."
rationale: There are currently African-American individuals who rank among the wealthiest Americans — for example, people such as Oprah Winfrey, Robert F. Smith, Michael Jordan and Shawn "Jay-Z" Carter have been listed as billionaires or very high-net-worth individuals. Their reported net worths place them within the upper tiers of U.S. wealth rankings, so the statement that some of the wealthiest Americans are African-American is correct.

claim: California Republican gubernatorial hopeful Meg Whitman "contributed to, and campaigned, for" Democratic Sen. Barbara Boxer.
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that Meg Whitman both contributed to and actively campaigned for Democratic Senator Barbara Boxer. While Whitman has a history of bipartisan small donations and occasional support for some Democrats in the past, public records and reporting do not substantiate the specific claim that she campaigned on Boxer's behalf.

claim: A BP oil executive named Brice Cromwell blamed the Biden administration for high gas prices.
rationale: There are no widely reported instances of a BP executive named Brice Cromwell publicly blaming the Biden administration for high gas prices. Major coverage of BP and its U.S. leadership through mid-2024 does not show that name or quote; BP statements typically attribute price rises to global supply/demand and geopolitical factors rather than directly blaming the Biden administration.

claim: "Biden took down Dr. Seuss and Mr. Potato Head."
rationale: The claim is false: neither President Biden nor his administration 'took down' Dr. Seuss or Mr. Potato Head. Dr. Seuss Enterprises chose to cease publication of several Dr. Seuss titles in 2021, and Hasbro independently rebranded Mr. Potato Head (dropping the 'Mr.') as a corporate decision; these were private-company actions, not government removals.

claim: Says Mitt Romney’s investments created zero jobs.
rationale: The categorical claim that Mitt Romney’s investments 'created zero jobs' is demonstrably false. Romney led Bain Capital, which invested in many firms—some of those companies expanded and hired workers while others reduced staff—so the impact was mixed rather than uniformly zero job creation.

claim: "I never called for a partition" of Iraq.
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it does not identify who 'I' refers to or when the statement was made. Numerous public figures and commentators have at times proposed partitioning or federalizing Iraq, so a blanket denial cannot be confirmed without a specific speaker, date, and context. Therefore the broad claim is judged false for lack of verifiable specificity.

claim: Henry Kissinger "said that we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Henry Kissinger uttering that exact line. While Kissinger has long advocated pragmatic engagement with adversaries in many contexts, the specific quoted phrase appears to be a modern paraphrase or misattribution rather than a documented Kissinger quotation.

claim: "No Bridge to Nowhere could occur."
rationale: The absolute claim that a 'Bridge to Nowhere' could not occur is false: such projects have happened and can happen again given political incentives and pork-barrel earmarks. The term 'Bridge to Nowhere' was applied to the proposed Gravina Island Bridge in Alaska and similar wasteful infrastructure proposals have been recorded in multiple jurisdictions. It is not possible to categorically rule out future occurrences of similar projects.

claim: It was President Obama's "inaction that caused over three weeks to go by before he even approved the governor's plan to protect our marsh."
rationale: The claim provides no date, governor, or specific marsh, so it cannot be independently verified. Presidential approvals of state requests vary by incident and timeline; while there were disputed response timelines in events like the 2010 BP spill, I find no specific, verifiable record in this claim that Obama’s "inaction" caused a three‑week delay without additional context. Given the missing details, the assertion is unverified and therefore treated as false for now.

claim: "We don't know anything about Hillary in terms of religion. Now, she's been in the public eye for years and years, and yet there's no — there's nothing out there."
rationale: Hillary Clinton's religious affiliation and some expressions of faith are publicly known: she has long been associated with the United Methodist Church, attended the Chappaqua United Methodist Church with her family, and has discussed faith in interviews and on the campaign trail. Therefore the claim that there is 'nothing out there' about her religion is incorrect.

claim: "The administration raises revenue for nationalized health care through a series of new taxes, including a light switch tax that would cost every American household $3,128 a year."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any administration has proposed a literal 'light switch tax' that would charge every American household $3,128 per year. The specific dollar figure appears to be a misleading arithmetic division of aggregate projected program costs across households or a fabricated example used in political attacks; fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar claims. While administrations may propose new taxes to fund expanded health coverage, this particular tax and amount are not supported by documented proposals or policy texts.

claim: "Since 2010, Republicans have won unaffiliated voters in every general election."
rationale: The claim is too broad and incorrect as stated: unaffiliated/independent voters have not consistently favored Republicans in every general election since 2010. Exit polls and national results show independents have swung between parties across cycles (for example, many elections including 2012 and several midterms favored Democrats among independents).

claim: Obamacare premiums "have gone up 160 percent in West Virginia in 4 yrs."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While individual-market premiums in West Virginia did rise substantially in some years after the ACA’s implementation, the size of the increase depends on the specific plan (metal level), the benchmark used, and whether figures are before or after premium tax credits; independent analyses (KFF/HHS/CMS) do not support a general, across-the-board 160% rise in premiums over a four‑year span. Some benchmark or nongroup plans saw large increases in certain periods, but the claim presents a single omnibus percentage that overstates and simplifies the evidence.

claim: Since being elected in 2002, Scott Walker has "given back over $370,000 of his salary to the county."
rationale: Independent fact-checking and contemporary news coverage report that during his tenure as Milwaukee County Executive (first elected in 2002) Walker waived raises and returned portions of his pay, and the total reported amount he returned to the county exceeded $370,000. The figure matches the totals reported by multiple outlets and was a noted part of his public record and campaign messaging.

claim: "Jamaica has not recorded any case of the coronavirus."
rationale: This is false. Jamaica reported its first confirmed COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) cases in March 2020 and has publicly reported many cases and deaths since then through its Ministry of Health and international health agencies.

claim: The United States "is the only major country that taxes its own exports."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: the U.S. Constitution forbids federal export taxes, and the federal government does not levy an export duty. Many other major countries do impose explicit export taxes or duties on certain commodities (for example resource-exporting countries have used export taxes), so the U.S. is not uniquely taxing exports. The statement likely arises from confusion with corporate income taxes or indirect taxes that affect exporters rather than a direct export tax.

claim: Facebook users can avoid "problems with your Facebook going against community standards" by changing your settings.
rationale: Platform settings (privacy, audience restrictions, filters) can limit who sees your posts but do not exempt content or behavior from Facebook’s community standards. Enforcement is based on the content and activity itself, and Facebook can remove or penalize posts and accounts that violate policies regardless of a user’s settings. Therefore changing settings is not a reliable way to avoid problems with standards violations.

claim: Says "46 percent of people believe major national news organizations fabricate stories about me."
rationale: The statement gives a precise percentage (46%) about people believing national news organizations 'fabricate stories about me' but provides no source, poll, population, or identified referent for 'me.' While surveys show substantial media distrust among certain groups, there is no verifiable, widely cited poll that matches this exact claim about a specific individual. Without a clear source and context the claim cannot be confirmed and is treated as false.

claim: Video shows Ukrainian soldiers saying goodbye to loved ones amid Russia’s 2022 invasion.
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify that the referenced video actually depicts Ukrainian soldiers saying goodbye during Russia’s 2022 invasion. Without the original file, upload history, timestamps, or independent verification (geolocation, metadata, corroborating sources), the clip could be unrelated, misdated, or repurposed footage. Standard fact‑checking requires concrete provenance before confirming such a claim.

claim: "The Affordable Care Act is the single largest tax increase in my lifetime."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included several specific revenue provisions (e.g., higher Medicare payroll tax on high earners, the net investment income tax, and various fees), but those increases were limited in scope and magnitude and are not generally considered the single largest tax increase compared with other major tax changes in recent decades. Whether a law is the "single largest" tax increase depends on how you measure it (annual vs. cumulative revenue, who is affected, and the speaker's lifetime), and available budget analyses do not support the categorical claim.

claim: "Every time the weight of that vehicle is reduced by a hundred pounds, your chances of dying are going to go up by about 5 percent. Peel three hundred pounds off – you’re 15 percent more likely to die in that car."
rationale: The statement presents a universal rule (5% higher chance of death per 100 lb lost) but that effect size is not a general law. Some empirical studies have found that, in certain datasets and crash types (especially older two-vehicle crashes), lighter vehicles have higher occupant fatality risk relative to heavier ones by a few percent per 100 lb, but the magnitude and applicability vary widely by vehicle class, crash partner, model year, and safety features; modern crashworthiness and active safety systems further change the relationship.

claim: Says Miami Congressman Carlos "Curbelo supports drilling offshore" and "repeatedly voted against President Obama's ability to fight pollution and combat climate change."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Curbelo, a Republican, has sometimes supported conventional energy development positions, he is also a well‑known proponent of congressional climate action — he co‑founded the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus and sponsored the Market Choice Act to put a price on carbon. That mixed record makes the blanket statement that he "supports drilling offshore" and "repeatedly voted against President Obama's ability to fight pollution and combat climate change" inaccurate without specific votes cited.

claim: After J.D. Hayworth "was voted out of Congress, he became a registered lobbyist" who was "paid thousands by a Florida corporation to lobby the very committee he used to serve on."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that J.D. Hayworth registered as a federal lobbyist after leaving Congress or that he was paid by a Florida corporation to lobby a committee he formerly served on. Publicly known post-congressional activities for Hayworth include work as a talk-radio host and later political campaigns, and searches of lobbying registration records do not show a matching registration tying him to such corporate lobbying on a former committee.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "shows up in Broward County" and had a private meeting with elections supervisor Brenda Snipes.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Hillary Clinton 'showed up in Broward County' to hold a private meeting with Broward elections supervisor Brenda Snipes. The claim appears to stem from social-media rumors and has not been substantiated by reputable news outlets, official schedules, or public records.

claim: "The chances of being killed by a refugee committing a terrorist act is 1 in 3.6 billion."
rationale: The claim gives an exact probability without a cited source and is not supported by available public data or academic studies. While deaths from terrorist acts committed by refugees are extremely rare in many countries, no credible dataset or peer-reviewed analysis produces the precise figure 1 in 3.6 billion; such a number is almost certainly the result of flawed or opaque arithmetic and unstated assumptions.

claim: Photos show Ukrainian citizens destroying two Russian tanks with Molotov cocktails in Kyiv.
rationale: There is no verified evidence that the specific photos purportedly showing Ukrainian citizens destroying two Russian tanks with Molotov cocktails in Kyiv actually depict that event. Images and videos from that conflict were frequently miscaptioned or taken elsewhere, and open-source verification did not corroborate tanks being destroyed in Kyiv by Molotovs. Additionally, Molotov cocktails are unlikely to reliably destroy modern tanks, making the claim implausible without strong primary evidence.

claim: Says he "never supported" federal health care individual mandate.
rationale: The claim as given is unverified because it names no individual, time, or source; without attribution it cannot be evaluated as true. Many politicians have at times supported and later denied supporting a federal individual mandate, so the blanket statement is likely misleading without specific evidence.

claim: "President Barack Obama (is) the first president in history to cut Medicare by $700 billion."
rationale: The statement is misleading: the Affordable Care Act included roughly $700–720 billion in projected Medicare savings over a decade, but those were projected spending reductions and payment-rate changes scored by the CBO and enacted by Congress, not a one-time direct benefit cut by the president. Presidents are not singularly the first/only actors to produce Medicare payment reductions—Medicare payment reforms and reductions have occurred under multiple administrations and through legislation before and after Obama.

claim: It's a good sign for Obamacare that in California, "the proportion of kids who are signing up is the proportion of kids in the population."
rationale: The statement bundles a factual claim and an opinion but lacks supporting data: there is no clear evidence that California exchange enrollments had children represented exactly in proportion to their share of the population, and even if children signed up at population parity that would not necessarily be a strong indicator for Obamacare’s risk pool. In practice children are often already covered by Medicaid/CHIP and the critical metric for exchange stability is turnout among uninsured young adults, not children under 18.

claim: Says GOP recall challenger Kim Simac "was delinquent paying her property taxes eight of the last nine years."
rationale: I could not find credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting showing Kim Simac was delinquent on property taxes in eight of the last nine years. Property tax delinquency is a matter of public county records and such a persistent pattern would be documented; no reliable sources or public-record summaries corroborate this claim up to my knowledge cutoff.

claim: "Seventy-six percent of the American people support us passing the DREAM Act … with citizenship and legalization as part of it all. … More than 60 percent of Republicans support that."
rationale: While many polls show broad overall support for protecting DREAMers, the specific claim that 76% of Americans back passage of the DREAM Act 'with citizenship and legalization' and that 'more than 60% of Republicans' support that level of relief is not borne out by major surveys. Reputable polls typically show strong overall sympathy for allowing Dreamers to stay or receive legal status, but support for full citizenship is lower and Republican support for citizenship rarely exceeds 60% and depends heavily on question wording and timing.

claim: Says "Karen Handel’s office budget increased a whopping 42 percent."
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or specific office and I am not aware of an authoritative budget record showing a 42% increase tied to Karen Handel. Budget changes depend on the specific office (state secretary of state, congressional office, etc.), fiscal year, and whether one counts operating vs. programmatic funds, so the claim appears to be an unsupported, likely cherry-picked percentage rather than a verified fact.

claim: Says "President Obama’s proposed oil tax would cost consumers 24 cents a gallon."
rationale: The claim is too specific and not generally true: no single "President Obama’s proposed oil tax" universally carried a definitive, unavoidable consumer cost of 24 cents per gallon. Different Obama-era proposals (tax changes, cap-and-trade/carbon proposals, or royalty changes) were modeled by different groups and produced a wide range of estimated retail impacts; some partisan analyses produced ~24¢ estimates for particular proposals and assumptions, but that number is not an objective fact applicable to all proposals.

claim: "(Ronald Reagan) raised taxes a billion dollars in his first year as governor of California."
rationale: While Governor Reagan did sign tax increases early in his 1967–68 administration to close budget shortfalls, there is no clear evidence that he raised taxes by exactly $1 billion in his first year in office. The budget and revenue changes were spread over fiscal years, and commonly cited dollar figures vary depending on which taxes and which years are counted.

claim: "Jeff Greene can buy anything" ...  he owns two mansions.
rationale: The statement 'Jeff Greene can buy anything' is an absolute, hyperbolic claim that is not literally true—no individual has unlimited purchasing power nor can they legally acquire everything. While Jeff Greene is a wealthy real-estate investor who owns multiple luxury properties, the specific assertion that he 'can buy anything' is unverifiable and implausible; the claim that he 'owns two mansions' is a narrower factual assertion that may be roughly true but is not sufficient to prove omnipotent purchasing ability.

claim: As a result of Roe vs. Wade, "America’s maternal mortality rate dropped dramatically."
rationale: Legalization of abortion after Roe v. Wade did lead to a large decline in deaths from unsafe, illegal abortions, but the claim that America’s overall maternal mortality rate "dropped dramatically" solely as a result of Roe is an overstatement. Maternal mortality had been falling for decades due to improvements in obstetric care, antibiotics, and prenatal care, and multiple factors — not just Roe — influenced trends in the 1970s.

claim: "If you earn $100 and pay $33 income tax you’re left with $67. You then buy $67 worth of fuel and in doing so pay a 48% fuel tax (fuel tax = $32.16 + $6.70 GST). This means that the government just got $71.86 tax from your hard earned $100."
rationale: The claim miscalculates how GST and fuel excise are applied and double-counts taxes. GST is not 10% of the final quoted price but is 1/11 of a GST-inclusive price (so on a $67 sale GST would be about $6.09), and fuel excise is typically a fixed cents-per-litre levy rather than a 48% slice of the pump price. Because the claim adds an arbitrarily large "48% fuel tax" plus a wrongly computed GST on top of income tax, the $71.86 figure is incorrect and misleading.

claim: Photo shows "people coming from California to Washington DC" to protest election results.
rationale: No photograph or supporting metadata is provided that links the pictured people specifically to California or to travel to Washington, D.C., and a single image cannot reliably establish origin, destination, or intent. Claims about where people came from and why require corroborating evidence (geolocation, timestamps, travel records, or credible reporting), which is absent here.

claim: Says Daniel Radcliffe has the coronavirus.
rationale: Daniel Radcliffe publicly announced in March 2020 that he had tested positive for COVID-19, reporting mild symptoms and later recovery; this was widely reported by reputable news outlets at the time. The claim that he 'has the coronavirus' is true with respect to that documented past infection.

claim: "Right now, we are about 4% behind the (census) response rate where we were in 2010. But for Black and Latino and Native American communities, they’re behind by 10%."
rationale: The claim gives no specific date or source and therefore cannot be verified as stated. Census Bureau response-rate snapshots vary over time and by metric (self-response, mail, combined), and while there were documented gaps for Black, Latino, and Native American communities during the 2020 enumeration, the exact figures (4% overall and 10% for those groups) are not a reliably verifiable statement without a timestamp and source.

claim: The United States paid for a 274-mile wall between Jordan and Syria, "approved by the Dems in the house and senate," in order "to keep ISIS out."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the United States paid for a 274‑mile wall between Jordan and Syria or that Congress — specifically Democrats in the House and Senate — approved full payment for such a project. Jordan built and reinforced barriers on its Syrian border in the mid‑2010s to keep militants out, and while the U.S. provided limited security assistance and training to Jordan, that is not the same as funding a 274‑mile wall approved as a Democratic congressional project.

claim: Quotes Kamala Harris as saying: "After we impeach, we round up the Trump supporters."
rationale: There is no credible record of Vice President Kamala Harris saying "After we impeach, we round up the Trump supporters." The line circulated on social media in manipulated and out-of-context clips but has been debunked by fact-checkers and reviewed transcripts of her remarks do not contain that statement.

claim: "Greg Casar passed paid sick leave."
rationale: The claim as stated is misleading. While Greg Casar helped author and advance a paid sick leave ordinance as an Austin City Council member, he has not enacted a new federal paid sick leave law as a U.S. Representative, so saying simply that he 'passed paid sick leave' is inaccurate without specifying the jurisdiction and time.

claim: Says "Former President Barack Obama arrested for ESPIONAGE."
rationale: There are no credible reports, official statements, or public records indicating that former President Barack Obama has been arrested for espionage. Such an event would be major national news covered by mainstream media and government channels, and no reputable outlet has reported it. The claim appears to be misinformation or a hoax.

claim: "The unemployment rate for Wisconsin workers has reached historic lows. It’s never been this low before, ever, ever, ever."
rationale: The claim is an absolute historical statement but lacks a defined time window and is unlikely to be true. State unemployment series are only consistently available back to the mid-1970s and Wisconsin has had similarly low unemployment months in prior decades, so saying it has 'never been this low... ever' is not supportable.

claim: "IDC members also get tons of campaign money from real estate, charter school, and health care lobbyists, some of whom are Republicans with connections to Trump"
rationale: Reporting and campaign finance records show the Independent Democratic Conference members accepted significant contributions from real estate developers, charter-school advocates, and health-care industry donors. Investigations also found overlap between some of those donors and Republican-aligned contributors, including individuals and groups who gave to or had ties with Trump-era Republicans. The wording is broad and imprecise, but the core claim about major donations from those sectors and some GOP-connected donors is supported.

claim: Says President Donald Trump is one of "only three people that won the Ellis Island Award for their work within the black community."
rationale: Donald Trump did receive an Ellis Island Medal of Honor (in the 1980s), but the award is given annually to many recipients from diverse backgrounds and is not restricted to work "within the black community." There is no basis for the claim that he is one of only three people to win the medal specifically for work in the black community; far more individuals have received the award for varied kinds of community service and heritage contributions.

claim: Gina Raimondo "paid 70 million in taxpayer dollars to millionaire hedge fund managers."
rationale: The claim as phrased is misleading. Public reporting has noted that Rhode Island's public pension funds paid tens of millions in fees to outside investment managers while Gina Raimondo was governor, but those were institutional pension payments (not Raimondo personally writing checks), the exact $70 million figure and characterization as paid to 'millionaire hedge fund managers' are unsupported without a specific timeframe or source. Media accounts vary on the amount, recipients, and period, so the blunt assertion is not verifiable as stated.

claim: Says former Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said that "if the workers are more insecure, that's very healthy for the society" because "they'll serve the masters gladly and passively."
rationale: There is no credible record in Alan Greenspan's speeches, books, congressional testimony, or reputable fact-checking sources of him making this quoted statement. The phraseology and tone are inconsistent with his documented public remarks and the quotation appears to be a misattribution that has circulated on social media. Without a primary source citation, the claim should be treated as fabricated.

claim: The health care law was "a 2,733-page bill! . . . No amendments!"
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: page counts for the Affordable Care Act vary by printing and whether the separate reconciliation bill is included, so the specific '2,733 pages' figure is misleading. Also the law was changed by the subsequent Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act and was produced by amending an existing bill in the Senate, so it was not passed with 'no amendments.'

claim: Says North Carolina "hospital beds are typically 85% full across the state."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and unlikely to be true as a general, steady-state fact. Hospital bed occupancy varies by time, hospital type, and whether one counts licensed vs staffed beds; historical and national-level data typically show lower average occupancy (often in the 60–75% range) and state figures fluctuate, with short-term surges above 85% possible but not 'typical' across an entire state. Without a specific date range and bed definition, the blanket claim that North Carolina beds are 'typically 85% full' is unsupported.

claim: "A grant for $5,000 [from the Governor’s Workforce Board] went to teach an employee at a company that makes ornamental business card holders how to use Facebook and Twitter."
rationale: This specific allegation is unverified and implausible as stated: state workforce boards typically document and publicize grants and training outcomes, and there is no readily available supporting record or reputable reporting tying a $5,000 Governor’s Workforce Board grant to training an employee at a maker of ornamental business card holders in Facebook/Twitter use. While workforce funds can be used for small-business or employee digital-skills training, the precise claim appears anecdotal and lacks corroboration.

claim: Says he can be on the ballot for Congress while serving time in jail.
rationale: Under the U.S. Constitution the qualifications for serving in the House are age, citizenship, and residency; it does not automatically disqualify someone because they are incarcerated. State election laws control ballot access and in practice many jurisdictions allow candidates to appear on ballots even if imprisoned, though practical barriers (petitioning, campaigning) may exist. There are narrow exceptions (e.g., 14th Amendment disqualification for insurrection) and some state-level restrictions that could apply.

claim: Barack Obama wants to "restore" the estate tax that George W. Bush "repealed."
rationale: Barack Obama supported reinstating the estate tax after the Bush-era tax cuts phased it down and produced a temporary repeal in 2010. While the claim's wording is slightly blunt, Obama did advocate restoring estate taxes on large inheritances that were eliminated by the Bush tax-law schedule.

claim: "Phoenix is already one of the kidnapping capitals of the world."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence or international rankings showing Phoenix is among the world’s top cities for kidnappings. Global and national crime reports and media coverage typically identify other cities and regions (parts of Latin America, Africa, and Asia) as kidnapping hotspots, while Phoenix’s crime statistics do not place it at that extreme internationally. The claim appears to be an exaggerated or politicized statement rather than a supported fact.

claim: Says the majority of candidates in Texas’ 25th Congressional District live outside the district.
rationale: The statement is presented without a specific election cycle or list of candidates, so it cannot be verified as a factual general claim. Whether a majority of candidates live outside a given congressional district depends on the specific race and year and requires checking the official candidate filings and public addresses. Without that context or supporting evidence, the broad assertion is unsubstantiated and therefore treated as false.

claim: "Trump bailed out Wall Street, but not Main Street."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification. During the Trump administration the CARES Act and related actions provided large-scale support for financial markets and corporations but also included direct relief for Main Street—most notably the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP), expanded unemployment benefits, and grants/loans for small businesses—though access and distribution were uneven. Critics are correct that Wall Street and big firms received large backstops and that small businesses sometimes struggled to get timely relief, but it is inaccurate to say Main Street received no bailout.

claim: Says Pope Francis "was arrested Saturday in connection with an 80-count indictment of charges including possession of child pornography, human trafficking, incest, possession of drug paraphernalia and felony fraud."
rationale: There are no credible reports from major news organizations or official Vatican communications that Pope Francis has been arrested or is subject to an 80-count indictment alleging those crimes. Such an event would be globally major news and widely documented; the claim matches patterns of social-media hoaxes and misinformation.

claim: Says that "18 children died while in custody of Border Patrol" during the Obama administration.
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes the tally. Fact-checks and official DHS reporting show the commonly cited figure of 18 conflates deaths across different agencies, timeframes, and some deaths that occurred after release or while in the care of other offices (e.g., HHS/ORR), whereas far fewer children died while actually in U.S. Border Patrol custody during the Obama administration.

claim: Says state budget deal between Texas House and Senate leaders "funds nursing homes, our public schools and universities and provides financial aid for college students."
rationale: Texas biennial budget agreements between House and Senate leaders commonly include appropriations for K–12 public schools, public universities, and state student financial aid programs, and they typically fund long‑term care/nursing home services through Medicaid or state health budgets. While the exact amounts and whether funding was increased or cut depend on the specific deal and year, the general claim that such a budget deal funds those categories is accurate.

claim: "In fact, the data coming in from some states that have legalized marijuana is that they actually see a decrease in use over time, particularly among young people."
rationale: Multiple state-level surveillance reports and peer-reviewed studies have found that in several states that legalized recreational marijuana, adolescent use rates have remained flat or declined over time rather than increased; some analyses specifically report decreases among youth in the years following legalization. However, findings are heterogeneous across states, age groups, measures (past-month vs. lifetime), and study designs.

claim: "In Chesterfield (Va.), the Southside precinct is infamous for having over 100% of the vote count…"
rationale: There is no reliable, specific evidence that Chesterfield County’s Southside precinct is legitimately “infamous” for having over 100% of the vote as a standing fact. Reports of turnout above 100% typically result from misinterpreting raw feeds, using the wrong denominator (e.g., comparing votes to an outdated registered-voter figure), or including absentee/provisional ballots, not from systematic fraud at a precinct.

claim: "When I was born, defense spending was 60 percent of the budget. It's now 17 percent."
rationale: As stated the claim is misleading and likely incorrect: defense spending has not been 60% of the total U.S. federal budget in recent decades, and wartime peaks (WWII) produced defense shares of federal outlays around 40–50%, not 60%. Today defense constitutes roughly 15–20% of total federal spending, and the share is different if one looks only at discretionary spending. Without specifying the birth year and whether 'budget' means total or discretionary spending the quoted percentages are unsupported.

claim: Says Judge Gonzalo Curiel "is a member of a club or society, very strongly pro-Mexican."
rationale: The phrase is not an accurate direct quotation and lacks context or attribution. Public reports from 2016 show Donald Trump criticized Judge Gonzalo Curiel by referencing his Mexican heritage and suggesting community ties that could create bias, but there is no clear record of the precise wording 'member of a club or society, very strongly pro-Mexican.'

claim: Says "I was part of the second class to integrate Berkeley, California, public schools."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks a speaker identity, dates, or documentary evidence tying a specific individual to being in the "second class" to integrate Berkeley public schools. Without a named person and timeframe, there is no way to confirm enrollment records, contemporaneous news, or school district documentation that would support the claim. Given the ambiguity, I treat the unverified assertion as false until corroborating details are provided.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: The claim is an absolute universal statement that is not supported by evidence. While some campaigns do tighten late because of undecided voters, final events, or momentum, many races remain steady or even widen toward the end; there is no rule that 'they always have' tightened.

claim: Before COVID-19, "Iowa had one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country, and many employers were scrambling to find qualified employees to fill their job openings."
rationale: In the months immediately before the COVID-19 downturn (late 2019–early 2020) Iowa's unemployment rate was below the national average and ranked among the lower state rates, and employers across the state and nation reported difficulty filling open positions. State workforce reports and news coverage from that period documented labor shortages and hiring challenges for skilled and lower-skilled roles.

claim: A new Republican litmus test "would have resulted in (the GOP) kicking out Ronald Reagan."
rationale: The claim is a counterfactual assertion without evidence — it asserts that an unspecified "new Republican litmus test" definitely would have caused the GOP to reject or expel Ronald Reagan. Reagan was a leading conservative figure whose core positions aligned with mainstream Republicanism of his era, and whether a hypothetical, ill-defined modern test would have led to his ouster cannot be proven.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "took away $1.6 billion from schools and handed it off as over $2 billion in tax breaks to the rich."
rationale: The claim presents precise cumulative dollar figures as if they are uncontested, but those totals depend on the chosen time period, accounting conventions, and whether one counts shifting costs to local property taxpayers. Independent fact‑checks and budget analyses found school-aid reductions and multi-year tax cuts under Walker, but not the straightforward one-to-one $1.6 billion removed from schools and over $2 billion given solely as 'tax breaks to the rich' as stated. The assertion mixes categories and income-targeting in ways that are not supported by consistent state budget accounting.

claim: "Taxpayers earning $1 million pay an effective tax rate that is about four times what taxpayers earning $100,000 pay."
rationale: Typical data show taxpayers with about $100,000 in income face effective federal income tax rates in the mid-teens percent, while taxpayers with about $1 million face effective rates in the mid-20s to low-30s percent — roughly twice, not four times, as large. The exact ratio varies by filing status, mix of ordinary vs. capital gains income, and which taxes (federal income, payroll, state) are counted, but a 4x difference is inconsistent with published estimates.

claim: "Death penalty opponents like Roy Cooper and Josh Stein have imposed a de-facto moratorium on capital punishment."
rationale: Governor Roy Cooper has publicly refused to authorize executions while in office and Attorney General Josh Stein has declined to pursue or has limited use of the death penalty in many cases, and their combined executive discretion has effectively halted executions in the state. That practical stoppage of executions is commonly described as a de-facto moratorium.

claim: The FBI lost Hunter Biden’s laptop.
rationale: There is no verified evidence that the FBI "lost" Hunter Biden’s laptop. Reporting and public statements indicate the laptop and/or images of its drive were in the possession of the Delaware repair-shop owner, were copied, and the FBI subsequently obtained devices and images; claims that the agency misplaced the device are unsubstantiated and rooted in partisan accusations rather than confirmed chain-of-custody loss.

claim: As Florida secretary of state, Kurt Browning "allowed 1,800 illegal voters to register in Florida."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Kurt Browning personally "allowed" 1,800 illegal voters to register. Public reporting and official checks show the 1,800 figure stems from imperfect database matches and miscategorizations, not verified instances of 1,800 noncitizens being legally registered and permitted to vote, and election officials routinely flag and remove suspect records. The secretary of state oversees elections administratively and does not individually approve each registration.

claim: "California has more kids in poverty ... than virtually any other state."
rationale: On an absolute-count basis, California typically has the largest number of children living in poverty of any U.S. state because it has the nation's largest child population and substantial poverty. Multiple data sources (Census SAIPE and Kids Count) have reported California at or near the top in number of children in poverty in recent years.

claim: Says Joe Biden said, "the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor."
rationale: There is no credible record or mainstream reporting that President Joe Biden said ‘‘the Germans bombed Pearl Harbor.’’ The attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 was carried out by the Japanese, and such a mistake by a high-profile politician would have been widely documented; no reliable transcripts or news outlets corroborate this quote. Claims circulating online appear to be misquotes, satire, or misinformation.

claim: Between 2008 and 2014, "criminal aliens accounted for 38 percent of all murder convictions in the five states of California, Texas, Arizona, Florida and New York."
rationale: The 38% figure is misleading: it came from an analysis limited to offenders who were identified as removable/noncitizen and encountered by federal immigration authorities, not from all murder convictions in those five states. When the denominator is all statewide murder convictions, noncitizen/removable-offender convictions represent a much smaller share, so the claim overstates and mischaracterizes the original statistic.

claim: Says Emma Gonzalez, a survivor of the Parkland school shooting, ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Emma González ripped up a copy of the U.S. Constitution. Viral posts that claimed she did were debunked by fact-checkers and based on misidentified footage or unrelated incidents; González did not publicly rip a Constitution at March for Our Lives or other verified events.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden’s license plate says "THEBIGGUY."
rationale: The claim is false. The viral photo was misattributed/manipulated and there is no verified evidence that President Biden owns or was photographed driving a vehicle with a vanity plate reading "THEBIGGUY." Presidential and Secret Service vehicles use official or cover plates, and reputable fact-checkers have debunked the circulated image as not showing Biden with such a plate.

claim: "1776 flag flying over White House!" in January 2021. "Revolution Signal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a flag marked '1776' was raised on the White House flagpole in January 2021. Photographs and official accounts from that period show the U.S. flag continued to fly over the White House, and news fact-checkers reported that social media posts claiming a '1776' or 'Revolution Signal' flag flew there were false or misleading.

claim: California’s Prop 55 "prevents $4 billion in new cuts to our schools."
rationale: This statement is misleading. Nonpartisan analyses at the time estimated Prop 55 would raise roughly on the order of $4 billion in its initial year, but that was an estimate of additional revenue, not an automatic or legally guaranteed prevention of exactly $4 billion in school cuts—actual budget outcomes depend on overall state revenues and legislative choices.

claim: Says "John Loughlin voted to let people accused of domestic violence keep their guns."
rationale: I cannot confirm any reliable record that a politician named John Loughlin cast a vote specifically to let people accused of domestic violence keep their guns. The name matches multiple public figures and no clear, attributable roll-call or bill text supporting this exact claim is known to me. Given the ambiguity and lack of verifiable voting record tied to this precise statement, the claim should not be accepted as factual.

claim: The Foundation for Government Accountability, which supported a Florida law requiring drug testing of welfare recipients, is a "Koch brothers affiliated group."
rationale: The Foundation for Government Accountability (FGA) is an independent conservative policy shop that backed Florida's welfare drug‑testing measure, but it is not a formal arm of the Koch brothers. Reporting shows FGA operates within the same free‑market/state policy network and has received funding from donors and donor‑advised funds that overlap with Koch‑aligned philanthropy, but it is not directly a Koch organization.

claim: Says Section 1325 of U.S. immigration law was "put into place in 1929, by a segregationist."
rationale: The modern criminal provision codified at 8 U.S.C. § 1325 (improper entry by an alien) is the product of multiple earlier statutes and later recodifications (notably the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952) rather than a single 1929 enactment credited to one identifiable 'segregationist.' While parts of the U.S. immigration code have roots in early 20th-century laws and reflected xenophobic and racist attitudes of the era, the specific claim that Section 1325 was "put into place in 1929, by a segregationist" is not supported by the legislative history as a precise literal statement.

claim: "There are only about 10 people in the United States Senate who have any real business experience."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and imprecise: far more than about ten U.S. senators have private‑sector or business experience. Many current and recent senators served as CEOs, founders, bankers, small‑business owners, or executives (for example, Mitt Romney, Mark Warner, Rick Scott, Ron Johnson, David Perdue, and others), so the number with business backgrounds is substantially higher than ten.

claim: "In (Sen. Marco) Rubio's state of Florida alone, Social Security lifts more than -- count it -- a million people out of poverty."
rationale: State-level analyses based on Social Security Administration and Census data show that Social Security benefits prevent well over one million Floridians from falling below the poverty line. Florida's large population of retirees and beneficiaries means the program's poverty-reduction impact in that state exceeds the one‑million mark.

claim: The number of children in seven countries "missing so far this year" range from 20,000 to 460,000.
rationale: The statement provides no source, no named countries, and no clear definition or timeframe for “missing,” so it cannot be verified. Very large counts like 20,000–460,000 for multiple countries would normally cite official police, government, or international agency data and would be widely reported; without that context the claim appears unsubstantiated and possibly conflates different measures (e.g., displaced, unregistered, or otherwise unaccounted-for children).

claim: The city of Richmond "built the second richest team in the NFL a $14 million stadium."
rationale: There is no record that any city named Richmond built a $14 million stadium for an NFL franchise, and no NFL team is based in Richmond. NFL stadiums and franchise facilities typically cost hundreds of millions to over a billion dollars, and team valuations (per Forbes) show the richest teams are in major markets—not Richmond.

claim: "The reality is when you look at the Biden plan, it reads an awful lot like what President Trump and I and our task force have been doing every step of the way."
rationale: The claim asserts Biden’s plan 'reads an awful lot like' the Trump administration and task force approach, which overstates the similarity. While there are some overlaps (e.g., support for vaccine development and some economic relief ideas), Biden’s plan emphasized a different federal role, stronger nationwide public‑health mandates, larger testing/tracing investments, and different funding priorities, so the two are not essentially the same. The statement is therefore misleading.

claim: Patrick Rose "voted to explore a state income tax."
rationale: There is no clear legislative record showing Patrick Rose cast a vote specifically to “explore a state income tax.” Claims like this have appeared in campaign ads that conflate votes on broadly worded budget or committee measures with an explicit vote to study an income tax. Without a specific bill or roll-call showing he voted to authorize an income-tax study, the assertion is misleading.

claim: "As the election tracker FiveThirtyEight has reported, whoever wins Pennsylvania will be our next President."
rationale: FiveThirtyEight typically publishes probabilistic forecasts and occasionally names a 'tipping-point' state for a given model, but it does not categorically claim that whoever wins a single state will always be the next president. Whether winning Pennsylvania would determine the presidency depends on the specific electoral map and year; winning PA alone does not guarantee the presidency in general.

claim: Under President Barack Obama’s jobs bill, states would no longer have to lay off teachers, firefighters and police officers.
rationale: President Obama’s proposed American Jobs Act included federal aid intended to help states avoid layoffs of teachers, police and first responders, but it did not guarantee that states "would no longer have to" lay off such workers. The proposal was limited in size, required passage by Congress, and could not override state budget shortfalls or employment decisions.

claim: Says 89 members of Congress "hold dual citizenship with Israel."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that 89 members of the U.S. Congress hold Israeli citizenship. Such a large number would be a notable fact widely reported and verifiable; instead, lists claiming this figure have circulated without substantiation and often rely on dubious inference. The claim appears to conflate other attributes (e.g., positions on Israel or Jewish heritage) with actual dual citizenship.

claim: "The RI Board of Elections has heard official testimony from Providence residents who claim to have witnessed known illegal aliens voting in local elections."
rationale: There is no public record or credible news reporting showing that the Rhode Island Board of Elections formally received testimony from Providence residents asserting they had witnessed 'known illegal aliens' voting in local elections. While election boards sometimes receive anonymous complaints or unverified allegations, I found no documented official testimony or verified evidence supporting this specific claim.

claim: "Rosalyn Dance voted against President Obama’s Medicaid expansion."
rationale: Rosalyn Dance, a Democratic Virginia legislator, did not vote against Medicaid expansion; she supported the state-level Medicaid expansion enacted in Virginia during the 2018 legislative actions. The claim is incorrect because Medicaid expansion under the ACA was implemented by state legislatures, and Dance was not among those blocking the Virginia expansion vote.

claim: A video clip from the Notre Dame cathedral fire shows a man walking alone in a tower of the church "dressed in Muslim garb."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers and French authorities concluded the viral clip was misinterpreted and provided no evidence that it showed a man in "Muslim garb" walking alone in a Notre-Dame tower. Officials reported no suspicious person linked to the fire and noted many workers, journalists, and emergency personnel were present and could appear in footage, so the claim is unverified and misleading.

claim: "Crisis actor in Germany forgets he’s filming on TV."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting supporting a verified incident of a 'crisis actor' in Germany being caught on TV forgetting he was filming. Claims like this typically circulate on social media as part of conspiracy narratives and are routinely debunked when source video, context, and timestamps are examined. Without a specific, verifiable event or reliable sources, the claim is unsubstantiated.
