claim: "Ukraine was a nuclear-armed state. They gave away their nuclear arms with the understanding that we would protect them."
rationale: It is true Ukraine inherited a large portion of the Soviet nuclear arsenal after 1991 and transferred those warheads to Russia by 1994. However, the transfer was accompanied by the 1994 Budapest Memorandum which offered political security assurances from the US, UK and Russia, not a legally binding commitment to militarily "protect" Ukraine as the claim implies.

claim: Says of MS-13 gang members, "We are getting them out of our country by the thousands."
rationale: The statement that MS-13 gang members are being removed “by the thousands” is not supported by publicly available enforcement or deportation data. While law enforcement has arrested and deported some MS-13 members, agencies have not produced verified figures showing mass removals in the thousands, and the claim conflates arrests, removals, and broader immigration enforcement.

claim: A photo shows a Mexican police officer "brutalized by members of this caravan as they attempt to FORCE their way into Mexico."
rationale: The image has been widely circulated with that caption but independent fact-checks have shown it was misattributed — the photo does not reliably show a Mexican police officer being brutalized by caravan members forcing entry into Mexico. No reputable news or official sources corroborate the specific claim tied to that photo, and similar images have been traced to different times/places or other contexts.

claim: The United States has "10,000 IRS agents making sure that you don't take an improper charity deduction," but to fight terrorism, it has "less than two dozen people focusing on countering violent extremism at home."
rationale: The statement misstates and conflates staff roles and sizes. The IRS does employ thousands of examiners and enforcement personnel, but not 10,000 people whose sole job is policing charitable deductions; audit and compliance responsibilities are distributed across multiple units. Similarly, countering violent extremism is a multi‑agency, multi‑hundred‑person effort across the FBI, DHS, DOJ, NCTC and state/local partners, not a program staffed by 'less than two dozen' people.

claim: Says Rob Portman "said the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio."
rationale: There is no authoritative record of Rob Portman using the exact phrase 'the auto rescue was a lousy deal for Ohio.' While Portman publicly criticized aspects of the 2008–2009 auto bailout and expressed concern for Ohio workers, I cannot verify this precise quote and wording in reliable contemporaneous sources.

claim: Says Donald Trump "just promised that if he wins reelection, he’ll gut Social Security and Medicare."
rationale: There is no public record of Donald Trump saying he would 'gut' Social Security and Medicare if reelected; on the contrary, he has repeatedly pledged on the campaign trail and in interviews not to cut those programs. Some Republican proposals and prior administrations have proposed benefit changes (e.g., raising the retirement age or restructuring), but that is not the same as Trump promising to gut the programs.

claim: "Reagan took the deficit from $70 billion to $175 billion. Bush 41 took it to $300 billion. Clinton got it to zero. Bush 43 took it from zero to $1.2 trillion. Obama halved it to $600 billion. Trump’s got it back to a trillion."
rationale: The claim mixes approximate annual deficit figures and misattributes timing and magnitudes. While deficits did rise under Reagan and were much larger under later presidents, Clinton produced multi-year budget surpluses in the late 1990s (not merely "zero"), George W. Bush-era deficits did not reach exactly $1.2 trillion in an annual deficit (the FY2009 deficit hit about $1.4 trillion, largely during the recession and transition), and Obama reduced annual deficits to several hundred billion rather than precisely halving to $600 billion. The statement is an oversimplified and partly incorrect summary of official budget history.

claim: Women are paid 77 cents for every $1 men get for the same work.
rationale: The commonly cited “77 cents” statistic refers to the unadjusted median annual earnings of all women working full‑time versus all men in the U.S., not pay for the exact same job with the same hours, experience, and qualifications. When researchers control for factors like occupation, hours, education, tenure, and job role, the measured pay gap is substantially smaller (often near parity), though a smaller unexplained gap remains in many studies.

claim: "Black and Latino people in NYC are arrested at TEN times the rate of white people for virtually the same rate of marijuana usage."
rationale: The claim correctly reflects that there have been large racial disparities in NYC marijuana arrests despite similar self-reported usage rates, but the specific blanket figure 'ten times' for Black and Latino people combined versus white people is an overgeneralization. Reported multiplicative disparities have varied by year and by group (e.g., some analyses found Black individuals were arrested many times more often than whites in certain years, but Latino rates and combined-group ratios are lower and fluctuate).

claim: "Bill Gates calls for the withdrawal of all Covid-19 Vaccines; ‘The vaccines are far more dangerous than anyone imagined.’"
rationale: This claim is fabricated: there is no credible evidence that Bill Gates called for withdrawal of all COVID-19 vaccines or said they are “far more dangerous than anyone imagined.” Public records and media reporting show Gates has consistently supported COVID-19 vaccination and global immunization efforts, and major fact-checkers have debunked similar misattributed quotes.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Nancy Pelosi said, "Employers cutting hours is a good thing. It then gives that person time to pursue their dreams and passions."
rationale: There is no credible record of Rep. Nancy Pelosi saying, “Employers cutting hours is a good thing. It then gives that person time to pursue their dreams and passions.” The quote appears to be a fabricated or misattributed social-media claim and does not match Pelosi’s documented public statements about employers and work hours related to health-care policy.

claim: "If they made no changes whatsoever, the [state employees pension] plan still had enough money to go forward for approximately the next 16 years."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits which state's employee pension plan and what valuation date or actuarial assumptions are being used. Pension solvency projections vary widely with assumptions about investment returns, contributions, and demographics, so a blanket 16-year figure cannot be confirmed without the specific actuarial report. Absent that context, the claim should not be treated as fact.

claim: They passed the flu off as COVID-19, and "they’re going to do the same thing with monkeypox and shingles."
rationale: This claim is false. Influenza and COVID-19 are caused by distinct viruses and were distinguished early in the pandemic by specific PCR/antigen tests and genomic sequencing, and public health surveillance tracked SARS-CoV-2 as a novel coronavirus rather than mislabeling flu cases. Monkeypox and shingles (herpes zoster) are caused by different viruses with distinct clinical pictures and laboratory diagnostics, and there is no credible evidence of an organized effort to intentionally misattribute these diseases.

claim: Congressman Jeff Denham "has agreed all illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported."
rationale: This is an overbroad characterization. Jeff Denham’s public record emphasizes stronger immigration enforcement and removal of criminal aliens, but he has also supported bipartisan reforms and measures that distinguish between criminals and noncriminal unauthorized immigrants; he has not consistently stated that "all" illegal immigrants should be detained, arrested and deported as an absolute blanket policy.

claim: "Last week Senator Obama's running mate said, get this, 'Raising taxes is patriotic.' "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Senator Barack Obama's running mate (Joe Biden in 2008) said last week 'Raising taxes is patriotic.' Major news outlets, public transcripts and quote databases do not record that statement and fact-checkers would likely have flagged such a notable quote. The claim appears to be a misattribution or fabrication without a verifiable source.

claim: "NAVY SEALs raid cargo ship full of smuggled children."
rationale: There are no credible, verifiable reports or official statements documenting a Navy SEAL raid on a cargo ship 'full of smuggled children.' The claim is vague (no who/when/where) and sensational; such large-scale interdictions by U.S. or allied special forces would be reported by reputable media and government sources.

claim: "Due to ... tax cuts and lower (property) values, 2009 property taxes were almost $3 billion below 2007 property taxes."
rationale: The claim presents a specific dollar comparison but gives no jurisdiction or source, so it cannot be verified as stated. Property tax collections and assessed values vary by state and locality and 2007–2009 trends differed across jurisdictions; some places saw declines while others did not, and statewide or national totals do not uniformly show a $3 billion drop attributable solely to tax cuts and lower values. Without a clear geographic and accounting context (levies vs. collections, gross vs. net), the precise $3 billion assertion is unsupported.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it "can't build a factory in a non-union state."
rationale: The NLRB did not tell Boeing it 'can't build a factory in a non-union state.' In the widely reported Boeing dispute the NLRB alleged Boeing unlawfully shifted work to South Carolina and sought remedial orders (bargaining requirements or restoration of work), but it does not have authority to issue a blanket ban on where a company may locate a plant.

claim: "Bloomberg says he wants to ban guns holding more than three rounds."
rationale: Michael Bloomberg has publicly supported banning high-capacity magazines and other gun-control measures, but there is no record of him calling for a ban on guns that hold more than three rounds. His proposals and advocacy have focused on limits like banning large-capacity magazines and stricter background checks, not an extreme three-round limit.

claim: Under Hillary Clinton, State Department "officials were sending official thank-yous to people who gave to the Clinton Foundation."
rationale: Reporting and released State Department emails from the Clinton years show instances where State Department staff sent formal or courtesy thank-you notes to people and organizations that had given to the Clinton Foundation. The department described many of these communications as routine diplomatic or constituent correspondence rather than evidence of direct pay-to-play.

claim: Says state Rep. Jim Keffer, a GOP lieutenant to House Speaker Joe Straus, "did mail pieces for Democrat Mark Strama to help him defeat" a Republican.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public record indicating Texas GOP Rep. Jim Keffer produced or mailed campaign pieces on behalf of Democrat Mark Strama to help defeat a Republican. Keffer is a Republican lawmaker and publicly aligned with GOP efforts; such a breach would likely have been documented and reported but isn’t found in available accounts. The claim appears to be unsubstantiated or a misattribution.

claim: Sweden had few COVID deaths in July, despite low vaccination rates, relaxed lockdown rules and low mask compliance.
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and misleading. Sweden did have periods (summer months) with relatively few COVID deaths, but that pattern varied by year and was largely driven by seasonality and prior waves; vaccination coverage was not uniformly 'low' in every July (it rose substantially during 2021) and mask use/lockdown policies varied over time, so the blanket causal claim is not supported.

claim: "Politicians and their corporate lobbyists are trying to take away my right to spend my paycheck how I want."
rationale: The statement is a broad, unsubstantiated universal claim. While elected officials and corporate lobbyists sometimes promote taxes, regulations, or targeted restrictions that affect how people can use money (for example taxes, regulations on certain goods, or court-ordered wage garnishments), there is no general, evidence-backed campaign to strip individuals of the basic ability to spend their paychecks. Without specific actors, policies, or evidence, the blanket assertion is false.

claim: "Nearly 60% of all student loan debt is held by the rich and upper-middle class," so forgiveness would give the wealthy a "financial windfall" but not really help low-income people.
rationale: The claim is misleading. It is true that a large share of outstanding student-loan balances is held by borrowers who later earn middle-to-higher incomes or have graduate degrees (many analyses put this share near 50–60% depending on definitions), but labeling those borrowers simply as the “rich and upper-middle class” is imprecise, and forgiveness would still provide meaningful relief to lower-income and disadvantaged borrowers (especially by reducing delinquencies and monthly payment burdens). Whether wealthy borrowers receive larger nominal dollar benefits depends on the design of forgiveness (universal vs targeted).

claim: Trade deals are negotiated in "secret" and, unlike corporate interests, politicians never invite "the leaders of the AFL-CIO or steelworkers or the mine workers to come in and sit down in these meetings."
rationale: The claim's absolute wording is incorrect. While many trade negotiations involve confidential bargaining and some meetings are closed, governments routinely consult stakeholder groups including labor: there are statutory and administrative consultation processes, advisory committees, congressional briefings, and instances where labor leaders (including AFL-CIO and unions) have been invited or briefed. It is therefore false to say politicians 'never' invite labor leaders while only meeting with corporate interests.

claim: "Within a few years, we will be spending more on interest payments than on national security."
rationale: Current public budget projections show federal net interest costs are rising rapidly but remain below broad national security/defense spending for the next several years. Whether interest surpasses “national security” depends on definitions and long-term assumptions; most CBO/OMB near‑term baseline forecasts do not show interest overtaking defense within only a few years.

claim: Republican election challengers were unfairly barred from observing absentee ballot processing and counting in Detroit.
rationale: Independent news reports, statements from Detroit/Wayne County election officials, and court filings show Republican challengers were permitted to observe absentee ballot processing but were required to follow distancing, non-interference, and security rules; courts did not find a lawful basis that they were systematically or unlawfully barred. Complaints about observers being kept at a distance were documented, but investigations and legal reviews did not substantiate a blanket, illegitimate exclusion.

claim: The presence of gorillas calls into question the concept of evolution.
rationale: The existence of gorillas is consistent with, not contrary to, evolutionary theory: gorillas are a distinct primate lineage explained by common ancestry, divergence, and speciation. Genetic, morphological, and fossil evidence place gorillas within the ape family and match predictions from evolution about relatedness and adaptive differences among species.

claim: Says actor Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson wore a T-shirt stating: "We Stand for the flag, we kneel for the fallen."
rationale: Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson posted a photo on his verified social media in mid‑2020 showing himself wearing a T‑shirt with the slogan "We Stand for the Flag, We Kneel for the Fallen," and multiple news outlets reproduced that image. The shirt and its wording were widely reported as part of his public post.

claim: Colorado saw "increased incidents of emergency room visits by young people" and "increased incidents of driving while under the influence of marijuana" following the legalization of recreational pot.
rationale: Studies and state reports do show post-legalization increases in cannabis-related emergency department visits and unintentional pediatric exposures in Colorado, but the claim about increased incidents of "driving while under the influence of marijuana" overstates the evidence. Data more reliably show increases in drivers testing positive for THC, which does not equate directly to proven impairment or legally established DUI events, so the driving portion is not clearly supported as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Scott Walker "has caused Wisconsin to lose more jobs than any other state in the country."
rationale: State employment data and independent fact-checkers do not support the claim that Wisconsin lost more jobs than any other state under Gov. Scott Walker; other states experienced larger job declines in relevant periods. Additionally, attributing statewide job losses solely to one governor ignores national recession effects and multiple economic factors.

claim: "When the law stopped Tony Evers from revoking a teacher's license for viewing pornography, Tony worked with lawmakers from both parties to change the law so offenders could be kicked out of the classroom."
rationale: The claim conflates and overstates events. It is true that as Wisconsin superintendent Tony Evers encountered statutory limits on when he could revoke a teacher license and later supported changes to the law, but the assertion that the law simply “stopped” him from revoking for viewing pornography and that he then worked with lawmakers from both parties specifically to enable automatic removal from the classroom is misleading and lacks key context about the cases and exact legislative changes.

claim: Says "a pack-a-day smoker who quits because of the tax increase will save about $1,650 a year."
rationale: The statement is not generally true because the annual saving depends on the per‑pack price (and the size of the tax increase). $1,650/year implies a saving of about $4.52 per pack (365 packs/year), so the claim only holds if the relevant tax/price change equals that amount; typical cigarette prices and tax increases vary widely by jurisdiction and are not universally $4.52 per pack.

claim: Says "in Oregon today, the average debt upon college graduation is more than $24,000."
rationale: I cannot verify a current, authoritative figure that Oregon graduates today carry more than $24,000 on average; recent state-level reports and national trend data show Oregon's average bachelorâ€™s-degree debt has hovered around the low-to-mid $20,000s and can be either slightly below or slightly above $24,000 depending on the year and cohort. Without a specific year, data source, and definition (e.g., undergraduate vs. all graduates), the blanket claim is not reliably supported.

claim: "They found 60 votes in the Senate in 2006 and 2013" for immigration legislation, and "each time the House Republican majority refused to take it up."
rationale: The claim mixes a correct fact about 2013 with an incorrect one about 2006. In 2013 the Senate passed comprehensive immigration reform with well over 60 votes (68-32 for S.744). In 2006 the Senate did not secure a 60‑vote cloture threshold on a comprehensive immigration bill, and while the Republican‑led House declined to consider the Senate approach in 2013, the 2006 Senate outcome and House actions are not accurately described by the claim.

claim: Says Bruce Braley took "tens of thousands from his friends in the health insurance industry" and gave them "special favors" by voting for Obamacare.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bruce Braley engaged in a quid‑pro‑quo by taking "tens of thousands" from the health insurance industry and then giving them "special favors" by voting for the Affordable Care Act. Braley, like many House Democrats, voted for the ACA as part of his party's legislative agenda; while members routinely receive campaign contributions from industry sources, alleging explicit corrupt exchange requires direct evidence which is lacking.

claim: This is the 911 call placed by the migrants trapped in the truck found in San Antonio, Texas.
rationale: There is no verifiable public record or official confirmation that a 911 call from migrants inside the San Antonio truck exists or that a widely circulated audio clip is that call. Audio clips shared on social media are frequently unverified or misattributed, and without corroboration from the emergency dispatch agency or law enforcement the claim is unsupported.

claim: "I was banned from talking about" Bill Ayers during the 2008 presidential campaign.
rationale: There is no evidence of a formal or campaign-wide ban preventing people from talking about Bill Ayers during the 2008 presidential campaign. Ayers was widely covered in mainstream media and raised repeatedly by opponents, while the Obama campaign issued rebuttals and talking points rather than an enforceable prohibition. Individual staffs might have been advised informally to avoid the topic, but that does not substantiate a blanket ban on mentioning him.

claim: "We had 6,000 oil and gas spills in 2012" with "more oil and gas spreading in the United States than the entire Exxon Valdez spill."
rationale: There is no authoritative nationwide tally showing exactly 6,000 oil-and-gas 'spills' in 2012, and available federal datasets (which separately track pipeline incidents, facility releases, and produced-water events) report far fewer major releases. The cumulative reported oil volume from routine onshore oil-and-gas incidents in 2012 is substantially lower than the Exxon Valdez loss (~11 million gallons); most incidents are very small and state/federal records do not support the claim that 2012 spills exceeded that single catastrophic spill.

claim: North Carolina’s health department is "telling hospitals that if they decide to do elective surgeries, they won’t be eligible to receive (protective equipment) from the state."
rationale: There is no public record that North Carolina's health department issued a policy saying hospitals that perform elective surgeries would be barred from receiving state-distributed protective equipment. Early in the COVID-19 response the state paused elective procedures to conserve PPE and later required hospitals to certify adequate PPE before resuming elective care, but that is not the same as a punitive rule withholding supplies for doing electives.

claim: "They’ve seen employer-supported coverage increase in Massachusetts after this law (Romneycare) was implemented."
rationale: Analyses of Massachusetts' 2006 health reform show overall insurance coverage rose sharply, but the increase was driven by Medicaid (MassHealth) and subsidized individual coverage rather than employer-sponsored insurance. Most state and academic studies found employer-sponsored coverage was flat or fell slightly after the law, not increased.

claim: Says President Barack Obama said when "we got bin Laden, terrorism problem solved."
rationale: There is no reliable record of President Obama saying "when we got bin Laden, terrorism problem solved." After bin Laden's death in May 2011 Obama described it as a major achievement but explicitly warned it did not mark the end of terrorism and said the nation must remain vigilant.

claim: "920 women lose their unborn babies after getting vaccinated."
rationale: The statement is misleading and unproven. It appears to conflate raw adverse-event reports (e.g., VAERS entries) with confirmed causation; passive surveillance systems collect unverified events and do not establish that vaccination caused fetal loss. Large, peer-reviewed studies and public-health reviews of COVID-19 vaccination in pregnancy have not found an increased risk of miscarriage attributable to the vaccines.

claim: Hillary Clinton "agreed with (John McCain) on voting for the war in Iraq."
rationale: Both Hillary Clinton and John McCain, as U.S. senators, voted in favor of the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force regarding Iraq, so it is correct to say she agreed with McCain in voting for the war. The claim is about the vote itself; it does not necessarily imply they shared identical reasoning or later positions.

claim: "Drone technology now allows an individual to be recorded in their homes by drones as small as birds and immediately uploaded to the internet."
rationale: Small, bird- or palm-sized drones and even insect-scale prototypes exist with integrated cameras and wireless connectivity. Many consumer and specialized drones can operate indoors and stream or upload video in real time via Wi‑Fi or cellular links, so the capability to record someone inside a home and immediately put the footage online is technologically possible today. Practical limits like battery life, navigation, signal strength, and availability vary.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: The claim is misleading: the Antrim County issue was a reporting/configuration error that was corrected and investigated, and audits and recounts found no evidence of widespread fraud. While some other Michigan counties used voting software from the same vendor or similar systems, the characterization that '47 additional counties used the same software that caused the glitch' and therefore state votes are 'potentially fraudulent' overstates and misrepresents the facts and investigations.

claim: "Since 1999, firearm deaths in Ohio have risen 58 percent."
rationale: The statement gives no end year and the specific 58% increase is not supported by public state or CDC mortality datasets for the usual endpoints. Ohio firearm deaths have fluctuated and the percent change since 1999 depends on the chosen end year and whether one uses raw counts or age‑adjusted rates; available official data do not unambiguously back a 58% rise.

claim: The changes to Georgia’s tax and fee structure "is an overall tax cut."
rationale: The claim is unverified as stated because whether changes amount to an 'overall tax cut' depends on the specific bill, the time horizon, and official revenue scoring. Georgia tax legislation commonly combines rate reductions with base changes, fee increases, or offsets, so the net fiscal impact must be determined by nonpartisan revenue estimates rather than the blanket claim.

claim: Says no one has died from the coronavirus in the United States.
rationale: This claim is false. Since early 2020 the United States has recorded large numbers of deaths from COVID-19, documented by CDC, state health departments, hospitals, and national vital statistics systems.

claim: "All evidence points to the fact that our kids are 17 times more likely to have ill effects from the seasonal flu than they are from the coronavirus."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and too absolute. Public-health data and peer-reviewed studies do not show a consistent 17-fold higher risk of "ill effects" from seasonal flu versus COVID-19 in children; risks vary by age, time period, and outcome, and COVID-19 has caused similar or higher pediatric hospitalizations in some analyses and unique complications (MIS-C).

claim: Says Miami-Dade Mayor Carlos Gimenez "approved a 67% pay raise for himself and increased his own pension. He makes $250,000 a year, more than almost every big-city Mayor in the country. He also kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz after slashing $400 million in government jobs and spending."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate numbers with misleading and unverified assertions. Gimenez's official salary has been reported near $250,000 (so that part is approximately correct), but the alleged "67% pay raise" and "he approved" it are misleading—salary changes for the county mayor involve the county commission and timing/context matters. Assertions that he "increased his own pension," "kept his taxpayer-funded Mercedes-Benz" in a scandalous way, and that he "slashed $400 million in government jobs and spending" are not supported as stated and conflate separate budget decisions and standard vehicle assignments without necessary context or sourcing.

claim: "Arizona audit" shows 86,391 voters "don’t appear to exist."
rationale: The 86,391 number came from an audit spreadsheet that flagged records which did not match certain datasets, but the auditors did not demonstrate those registrants were nonexistent. Fact-checkers and audit statements note these were preliminary 'no match' results that can be explained by typos, name variations, moves, or data-entry issues, not proof people "don't exist."

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: while Jason Kander did travel and attend fundraising events during and after his 2016 Senate campaign, there is no reliable evidence that he was broadly "attending fancy dinners all over the country" as a documented pattern. The wording appears to be a political rhetorical flourish rather than a verifiable factual statement.

claim: A video shows Kim Jong Un calling Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable" in a speech.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kim Jong Un gave a speech in which he directly called Joe Biden a "thug," "coward," and "mentally unstable" in English. North Korean leaders speak Korean and state media rhetoric is often translated or paraphrased; viral clips with such explicit English insults have previously been shown to be edited, dubbed, or misattributed.

claim: Before "our last three presidents, you have to go back to the 1800s, early 1800s to find three presidents in a row being consecutively re-elected."
rationale: Bill Clinton (re-elected 1996), George W. Bush (re-elected 2004) and Barack Obama (re-elected 2012) are three consecutive presidents who each won a second term. The previous occurrence of three successive presidents each being re-elected was in the early 1800s — Thomas Jefferson (1804), James Madison (1812) and James Monroe (1820). No intervening sequence of three consecutive presidents were each re-elected between those periods.

claim: Says it's not true that Florida black bears are an "apex predator."
rationale: Florida black bears are not unambiguous apex predators because they can be predated upon (especially cubs) by Florida panthers, alligators and occasionally other large carnivores, and humans impact them as well. An apex predator is typically defined as a species at the top of the food chain with no natural predators, which does not strictly apply to Florida black bears across their life stages.

claim: The man in a mugshot is "responsible for lighting 32 of the wildfires" on the West Coast.
rationale: There is no credible public record or news reporting that a single person shown in a viral mugshot was charged with or proven to have started 32 separate wildfires across the U.S. West Coast. Viral social-media captions frequently misattribute or exaggerate arrest images; official wildfire investigations and law-enforcement press releases would be the primary evidence for such a large-scale allegation and none corroborate this claim.

claim: "Since the passage of Proposition 47 by voters in 2014 and the signing of AB 109 in 2011, violent crime has been on the rise in California, up 12 percent in 2015 statewide according to the FBI."
rationale: The claim misstates the FBI data and overstates causal linkage. FBI/UCR data show California violent crime rose in 2015 but by far less than 12% statewide, and independent fact-checks have found the 12% figure is incorrect or misattributed; attributing any rise solely to AB109 (2011) and Proposition 47 (2014) ignores many factors and timing differences.

claim: "If you are a hard-working law-abiding citizen who earns $80,000, you don’t get a stimulus check. But if you are a convicted murderer or rapist sitting in jail, you do."
rationale: Stimulus payments were determined by tax filing status, Social Security number, and adjusted gross income thresholds, not by 'hard-working' status or criminal conviction. Someone with $80,000 in AGI would generally still qualify for at least a partial payment in the federal COVID stimulus rounds depending on filing status, and while some incarcerated people did receive payments, incarceration is not an automatic qualification or disqualification under the payment rules.

claim: Says the Obamas are connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or DOJ indictment linking Barack or Michelle Obama to the 2019 'Varsity Blues' college admissions bribery scandal. Major news organizations and Department of Justice releases listed the parents and intermediaries charged (e.g., Rick Singer, Lori Loughlin, Felicity Huffman) and the Obamas were not among them; claims tying the Obamas appear to be rumor or misinformation.

claim: "President Obama will now own 60 percent of GM, and his union buddies will own almost 20 percent."
rationale: The statement is incorrect in implying President Obama personally owned 60% of GM. In the 2009 GM bankruptcy/restructuring the U.S. Treasury (i.e., the federal government) took roughly a 60.8% stake in the new GM, and the UAW retiree health trust (VEBA) received about 17.5% — close to 'almost 20%' — but those shares belong to government and a retiree trust, not to Obama personally or to union officials as private owners.

claim: "We’re at the point of reaching 2 million deportations ... this is a historic level, more than any other president of the United States."
rationale: The claim that we are at or near 2 million deportations and that this exceeds any other president is incorrect as stated. Historical DHS/ICE statistics show the Obama administration oversaw roughly 2–2.5 million removals/returns over its eight years and is commonly cited as the highest total; recent administrations (including the current one) have not surpassed that cumulative level. Therefore saying the current figure is 'more than any other president' is false.

claim: According to a national survey, transit "ridership" among people age 16 to 34 increased 40 percent between 2001 and 2009.
rationale: I could not verify a national survey that documents a 40% rise in transit ridership for 16–34 year olds between 2001 and 2009. Major U.S. data sources for this period (notably the National Household Travel Survey and Census/ACS commuting data) do show some increases in transit use for younger adults, but published analyses do not clearly support the specific 40% figure as stated without naming the survey or metric.

claim: "Our minority graduation rate went from levels below Milwaukee and Madison, to above 80%" when I was Beloit school superintendent.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as presented because it gives no dates, no definition of 'minority,' and no specific graduation metric; district graduation rates change year to year and by subgroup. Without cited, year-by-year Beloit, Milwaukee, and Madison district graduation statistics for the superintendent's tenure, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says there is a 4,250% increase in fetal death from the flu shot.
rationale: This claim is not supported by credible evidence. Large cohort studies, meta-analyses, and public-health agencies (including CDC) find no link between seasonal influenza vaccination in pregnancy and a massive increase in fetal death; the 4,250% figure appears to stem from misinterpreting raw passive-reporting data or tiny denominators rather than a validated causal finding.

claim: "Ohio student suspended for staying in class during National Walkout Day"
rationale: I found no credible, specific reporting that an Ohio student was suspended for remaining in class during a National Walkout Day; mainstream coverage of walkouts documented suspensions or discipline for students who left school grounds or walked out without permission, not for staying in class. Without a named school, date, or corroborating evidence the claim appears unsupported and runs counter to typical district policies which generally allow students to remain in class.

claim: "We're No. 46 out of 50 states... we're 46th in terms of percentage of deaths in nursing homes."
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable because it does not identify which state or the time period or data source used for the ranking. Rankings of states by percentage of COVID-19 (or other) deaths occurring in nursing homes varied considerably across different datasets and over time, so a blanket statement that "we're 46th" cannot be confirmed without that context.

claim: Says Michele Bachmann said on Fox News, "This country could use a president like Benjamin Franklin again."
rationale: There is no reliable record or Fox News transcript corroborating that Michele Bachmann said the exact line quoted. While Bachmann has frequently praised Founding Fathers in public remarks, I could not find contemporary news reports or transcripts confirming she said on Fox News, "This country could use a president like Benjamin Franklin again."

claim: "Last night I was leading, often solidly, in many key States, in almost all instances Democrat run & controlled. Then, one by one, they started to magically disappear as surprise ballot dumps were counted."
rationale: While it's true that in several recent U.S. elections early leads narrowed or reversed as mail-in and absentee ballots (which trended Democratic) were counted later, there is no evidence that large-scale, coordinated 'surprise ballot dumps' occurred to erase legitimate leads. Independent audits, recounts, and court reviews have repeatedly found ballot-counting followed legal procedures and did not show systematic fraud; furthermore, not all late-counted jurisdictions were uniformly 'Democrat run & controlled.'

claim: "In Minnesota, well over 6,200 election-day registrations from 2008 proved fraudulent."
rationale: Investigations and contemporary fact-checking found that while several thousand registrations from 2008 were flagged for administrative problems or duplicate addresses, only a very small number were ever shown to be fraudulently cast or led to prosecutions. The claim that 'well over 6,200' were proven fraudulent conflates records flagged for review with confirmed fraud, which the evidence does not support.

claim: "Every day in the United States, we are losing 15 factories."
rationale: The claim that the U.S. is losing 15 factories every day is not supported as a sustained, well-defined statistic. Official data on manufacturing plants/establishments from the Census Bureau and BLS and independent fact-checkers show that counts vary by year and by how a 'factory' or 'loss' is defined (closures vs. net change), and do not support a consistent net loss of about 5,475 plants annually.

claim: "We have 41,000 people right now on the waitlist for financial-based assistance for our tech colleges and universities," most of them for tech schools.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no jurisdiction, timeframe, source, or definition of “financial-based assistance” or “tech colleges.” Publicly available higher‑education data typically come from state education departments or institutions and there is no widely reported, corroborated figure of 41,000 people on such a waitlist. Without a cited source or clear scope, the specific numeric assertion is not supported.

claim: Says Texas ranks 44th nationally in education funding per pupil.
rationale: The statement gives a precise rank without specifying a year or data source; per‑pupil spending rankings change by year and by which measure is used (current expenditure, total spending, cost‑of‑living adjusted, etc.). While Texas typically ranks in the lower third of states on per‑pupil spending in recent federal data, it is not consistently exactly 44th and different reports put it at varying positions (e.g., low‑40s to mid‑40s). Because the claim lacks temporal and methodological context and cannot be verified as a blanket statement, I judge it false as stated.

claim: "(Assembly Democrats) wanted to raise the gas tax by $2.4 billion. We said no to that....They’re down on the ground. They’re sweating. They’re twitching. It’s ugly, ‘cause I keep saying no."
rationale: I cannot verify that 'Assembly Democrats' as a group formally proposed a $2.4 billion gas tax increase; legislative proposals over time have included a range of transportation revenue options but no clear, attributable $2.4 billion unified proposal matches this quote. The statement appears to conflate rhetoric with a specific fiscal proposal and lacks contextual details (which assembly, what bill, and what year) needed to treat it as factual.

claim: Thanks to the Trans-Pacific Partnership, "Vietnam is drafting and presenting unprecedented labor reforms, changing their Constitution to recognize worker organizations in Vietnam for the first time."
rationale: While the TPP/CPTPP pressured Vietnam to adopt labor reforms (including a revised Labor Code and commitments on freedom of association), Vietnam did not change its Constitution to recognize independent worker organizations for the first time. Reforms have been incremental and implemented through statutes and regulations, and the official trade-union framework (centered on the Vietnam General Confederation of Labour) has largely remained in place with limits on independent unions.

claim: Says withdrawing troops from Afghanistan could save the U.S. $50 billion.
rationale: The claim is too vague and therefore not verifiable as a fact. Whether withdrawing troops would "save $50 billion" depends on the time period and which costs are counted (immediate operational costs vs. long-term veterans' care, equipment replacement, and transition costs), and independent analyses produce a wide range of estimates rather than a single guaranteed $50 billion figure.

claim: Republican candidate for governor "Karen Handel has run a 100 percent negative campaign."
rationale: The assertion that Karen Handel ran a "100 percent negative campaign" is inaccurate. Reporting and her own campaign materials from her gubernatorial run show she promoted policy positions, biographical/background messaging, and endorsements as well as contrast and attack ads, so the messaging was mixed rather than exclusively negative.

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor, "the fact is that the average income for a family in Massachusetts went up by $5,500."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it omits key details (which income measure, exact years, and whether figures are inflation‑adjusted). Fact checks and Census income series show that while nominal family/household income in Massachusetts rose modestly in the early 2000s, the magnitude and interpretation depend on whether one uses 'average' vs 'median', 'family' vs 'household', and whether the increase is adjusted for inflation. When those distinctions are applied, the simple statement that average family income 'went up by $5,500' is not a straightforward, fully accurate portrayal.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s approval rating went from 70 percent to 52 percent in 18 months.
rationale: The statement is too specific but gives no pollster, dates, or population, and there is no well-known, single polling series showing Hillary Clinton's overall approval/favorability move exactly from 70% to 52% over an 18-month span. Polls of Clinton's favorability and approval varied widely by firm, question wording, and subgroup (e.g., Democrats vs. national adults), so the claim is misleading without a cited source. A precise numeric shift like this requires a named poll and dates to be verified.

claim: Says William Taylor and George Kent, the public witnesses in the House impeachment inquiry, are "Never Trumpers."
rationale: William B. Taylor and George P. Kent are career U.S. State Department foreign service officers who testified in the House impeachment inquiry in their official capacities; they are not known members of the 'Never Trumper' political movement (a label usually applied to Republicans who publicly opposed Trump). Calling them 'Never Trumpers' mischaracterizes their roles as nonpartisan civil servants rather than partisan activists. There is no credible evidence they were part of an organized 'Never Trump' campaign.

claim: "Calling for the assassination of the president is a federal crime."
rationale: There are federal statutes (e.g., 18 U.S.C. § 871 and related provisions) that make threats against or solicitation of the President’s assassination criminal, so many calls for assassination can be prosecuted. However, the First Amendment and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Brandenburg) protect some advocacy; only speech that constitutes a true threat, solicitation, or incitement to imminent lawless action is necessarily a federal crime, so not every utterance is automatically criminal.

claim: Democrats are "asking for a blank check book to spend as much as they want without worrying about the repercussions."
rationale: This phrasing is a rhetorical exaggeration rather than a factual description. While Democrats often advocate for increased federal spending on particular priorities, they routinely propose specific budget measures, legislative offsets or justifications, and their proposals are subject to Congressional votes, CBO scoring, and oversight — not an unconditional, unlimited "blank check."

claim: North Carolina has "the strictest anti-gerrymandering standards in the entire country."
rationale: The claim overstates the situation. While North Carolina has seen extensive litigation and some state-court limits on maps, several other states have independent redistricting commissions or explicit statutory/constitutional bans on partisan gerrymandering that are widely regarded as stricter. There is no consensus that North Carolina alone has the "strictest" anti-gerrymandering standards nationwide.

claim: The recently passed transportation funding bill is a billion-dollar tax increase for Georgians.
rationale: The claim is vague and lacks a named bill or time frame; there is no clear, publicly documented universal ‘billion-dollar tax increase’ recently enacted across Georgia attributable to a single transportation bill. Transportation funding measures commonly use a mix of federal funds, bonds, local sales taxes or fee adjustments rather than a single newly imposed statewide billion-dollar tax, so the blanket assertion is unsupported without specifics.

claim: "President Obama has the most border patrols and border security deployed at the border of any previous president."
rationale: The claim is unsupported because it depends on how “most” and “border security deployed” are defined. While Border Patrol staffing rose during the Obama years to historically high levels for some periods, later administrations (notably the Trump administration) authorized large active-duty troop and National Guard deployments and continued increases in CBP staffing. Without a clear metric (agents on payroll, personnel physically deployed to the border, or inclusion of military/Guard), the sweeping claim is false as stated.

claim: "U.S. police killed more people in just one month than the U.K.’s did in over a century."
rationale: Contemporary U.S. police kill roughly 900–1,100 people per year (about 70–95 per month) by most databases, while UK police fatal shootings and on-duty killings over the last century number only in the tens. Comparing those figures makes it plausible and widely reported that U.S. police kill more people in a single month than UK police have in over a century. The claim rests on aggregate counts of deaths attributable to police action rather than a precise standardized definition.

claim: Says there are fewer than 2,000 confirmed COVID-19 hospitalizations in the U.S.
rationale: The claim gives no date or data source and COVID-19 hospitalizations change daily; historically (per CDC and state reports) U.S. daily confirmed COVID-19 hospitalizations have frequently exceeded 2,000 during waves. Without a timestamp or authoritative data link this blanket statement cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I was unable to identify a reputable, citable economic impact study that states exactly that every $1 invested in Pennsylvania pre-K generates $1.79 in total in-state spending. Research on pre-K returns uses different metrics (short-term spending multipliers versus long-term benefit–cost ratios) and yields a range of estimates, so this precise figure appears unverified or mischaracterized without a clear source. As stated, the claim is therefore likely false or at least unsupported.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The statement is too broad and lacks a defined timeframe or metric; whether a recovery is the "slowest since Hoover" depends on how you measure job recovery (months to regain pre-recession peak, percent growth, unemployment rate, etc.). Labor statistics and contemporary fact-checks show the post-2008 recovery was unusually slow by many measures, but it is not unambiguously the slowest since Herbert Hoover across all standard employment metrics.

claim: "Obamacare … means that for up to 20 million Americans, they will lose the insurance they currently have, the insurance that they like and they want to keep."
rationale: The statement greatly overstates the number affected. Federal and independent analyses around the ACA implementation (HHS, Kaiser, CBO, Urban Institute) estimated individual-market cancellations in the low millions (roughly 4–5 million), and employer-sponsored coverage largely remained; mainstream projections did not support 20 million people actually losing the insurance they had and liked. Thus the "up to 20 million" claim is misleading.

claim: Says a photo shows a memorial vandalized by Black Lives Matter protesters.
rationale: A single photo cannot by itself demonstrate who committed vandalism; attribution requires reliable sourcing, timestamps, metadata, corroborating video, or eyewitness accounts. Viral images from protests are frequently miscaptioned or repurposed, so the claim that the pictured damage was done by Black Lives Matter protesters is unsupported without further evidence.

claim: President Obama "promised" families making less than $250,000 a year would not see taxes go up, but "Obamacare raises 18 different taxes."
rationale: President Obama did publicly pledge that households earning under $250,000 would not see their taxes go up, and the Affordable Care Act includes multiple revenue-raising provisions. However, the oft-repeated claim that Obamacare "raises 18 different taxes" is misleading: the count depends on how one groups or defines provisions, many of the alleged "taxes" are levies on insurers, employers, high-income earners, or are fees/penalties rather than new broad household income taxes, and some provisions were delayed or later repealed. Therefore presenting this as a straightforward broken promise to families under $250,000 is false or at least misleading without much more context.

claim: Says Chuck Todd said the Roy Moore story "felt completely orchestrated."
rationale: There is no reliable record or transcript showing Chuck Todd saying the Roy Moore story "felt completely orchestrated." Fact-checks of 2017 coverage found the phrase was misattributed; Todd discussed the timing and political implications but did not use that exact wording. The claim appears to be a paraphrase or false attribution rather than a verbatim quote.

claim: "Gina Haspel, CIA head is dead!"
rationale: There are no credible reports or official announcements that Gina Haspel, who served as CIA director from 2018–2021, has died. The death of a recent, high-profile public official would be widely reported by major news outlets and government sources, but no such widespread coverage is evident in available records.

claim: COVID-19 is a synthetic version of "snake venom" that evil forces are spreading through remdesivir, the COVID-19 vaccines and drinking water to "make you a hybrid of Satan."
rationale: There is no credible scientific evidence that COVID-19 is a form of "snake venom" or that remdesivir, authorized COVID-19 vaccines, or drinking water are being used to spread such a substance. SARS-CoV-2 is an RNA coronavirus characterized by genomic sequences and proteins studied by virologists, remdesivir is an antiviral medication, and vaccines contain mRNA or viral proteins/nonreplicating vectors as documented by regulators. The claim that these interventions would make people into a "hybrid of Satan" is a supernatural assertion with no biological mechanism or supporting data.

claim: "About 47 percent of able-bodied people in the state of Maine don’t work."
rationale: State and federal labor statistics show that a clear majority of working‑age, non‑disabled adults in Maine participate in the labor force and are employed; it is therefore incorrect to claim that about 47% of able‑bodied people in Maine don’t work. The statement conflates vague terminology ("able‑bodied") and likely misinterprets other statistics (such as overall nonworking share of the total population, which includes children, retirees, and disabled people).

claim: "General Motors is sending Mexican made model of Chevy Cruze to U.S. car dealers-tax free across border."
rationale: General Motors did produce the Chevy Cruze at its Ramos Arizpe, Mexico plant and exported those cars to U.S. dealers. Under North American trade rules (NAFTA and later USMCA), vehicles that meet the rules-of-origin can be imported duty-free, so Mexican-made Cruzes were commonly shipped to the U.S. without import tariffs.

claim: "You've seen where we're now going from a $700 million surplus to getting into the next biennium with almost a $750 million deficit."
rationale: The statement provides no jurisdiction, fiscal years, or source, so the asserted shift from a $700 million surplus to an almost $750 million deficit cannot be independently verified as presented. Without official budget documents or a clear timeframe, the numeric claim is unsubstantiated and therefore treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: Says Barack Obama was silent on Iran "when the students took to the streets in Tehran and the people there protested, (and) the Green Revolution occurred."
rationale: President Obama and his administration were not silent during the 2009 Iranian Green Movement; they issued public statements condemning violence, calling for respect for human rights, and expressing support for peaceful protesters. Critics argued the U.S. response was cautious to avoid the appearance of backing regime change, but that caution is not equivalent to silence.

claim: "Thomas Jefferson said, ‘Government that governs least governs best.’ "
rationale: The exact wording is commonly misattributed to Thomas Jefferson. The sentence 'That government is best which governs least' is most often traced to Henry David Thoreau's 1849 essay 'Civil Disobedience'; Jefferson expressed small-government sentiments in letters but no reliable primary source records him saying that exact phrase.

claim: "Under @BarackObama illegal immigration dropped to a 50-year low."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported as stated. While illegal border crossings and the estimated unauthorized immigrant population declined from peaks during parts of Barack Obama’s presidency (and net migration from Mexico turned negative after 2009), the statement that illegal immigration dropped to a 50‑year low depends on which metric and year is used and is not a supported, unambiguous fact. Authoritative data (CBP apprehensions and Pew Research estimates) show long‑term variation and do not cleanly validate the blanket “50‑year low” claim without additional qualifiers.

claim: California’s Prop 60, which would require condom use in adult films, would put "workers in the adult film industry at risk for lawsuits and harassment."
rationale: Prop 60 included provisions that created a private right of action and reporting requirements related to condom use compliance in adult films; opponents and industry groups warned those provisions would enable lawsuits and could expose performers' identities to public records and enforcement actions, increasing risk of harassment. Those stated features of the measure justify the claim that it would put workers at risk of lawsuits and harassment if enacted.

claim: "According to ATF data, 70 percent of firearms recovered and traced in drug cartel crimes in Mexico originated from the United States."
rationale: ATF tracing data have shown that a large share of firearms recovered and traced in Mexico were originally purchased in the United States, but the exact percentage varies by year and dataset and applies only to the subset of recovered guns that were submitted and successfully traced. Presenting a flat "70 percent" as an ATF claim without timeframe or the important caveat that many recovered weapons are not traced is misleading.

claim: Says as secretary of state she was reserving judgment about the Trans-Pacific Partnership and "hoped it would be the gold standard."
rationale: As Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton publicly said she was not in a position to take a final position on the Trans-Pacific Partnership during negotiations and stated she "hoped it would be the gold standard." Contemporary news reports and fact‑checking summaries record these statements from her time in office.

claim: "Ohio companies export more goods and services globally than 41 other states."
rationale: The statement is presented without a year or data source and thus cannot be verified as a standing fact. State export rankings change yearly; while Ohio is frequently a top-10 exporter, that does not guarantee it exports more than 41 other states in every year. Without a specified timeframe or breakdown of goods vs. services, the claim is unsubstantiated and potentially misleading.

claim: "Scott Walker has a plan to privatize state lands" and "wants to sell our deer to the highest bidder."
rationale: This claim exaggerates and distorts Scott Walker’s record. While Walker and his administration supported some sales or transfers of particular state-owned properties and policies favoring timber sales or leasing, there is no credible evidence he had a program to privatize all state lands or literally "sell our deer to the highest bidder." The phrase about selling deer appears to be hyperbolic political rhetoric not a documented policy proposal.

claim: Says Russ Feingold supported a stimulus plan that allowed a company to create 3,000 jobs in China.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Sen. Russ Feingold’s vote for the 2009 stimulus directly ‘allowed’ a company to create 3,000 jobs in China. The Recovery Act funded U.S. programs and projects and contained provisions aimed at U.S. job creation; private companies’ offshoring decisions are driven by business choices and other factors, and no credible source ties a specific 3,000-job move in China directly to Feingold’s vote. The claim is therefore misleading or unsubstantiated.

claim: "In 1992, the Democratic Party had in their platform provisions that said that illegal aliens were coming in this country, committing felonies, sent back and then they were right back across the border to do the same thing."
rationale: There is no well-documented evidence that the 1992 Democratic Party platform included a provision stating that illegal immigrants were coming, committing felonies, being sent back, and then immediately returning across the border. Democratic platforms from that era emphasized immigration reform and legalization paths rather than broad assertions criminalizing undocumented migrants in that specific language.

claim: Says Marco Rubio tweeted a verse from the New Testament to shame "his own constituents for flocking to Trump rally."
rationale: There is no credible record or major news reporting that Marco Rubio tweeted a New Testament verse specifically to shame his own constituents for attending a Trump rally. While Rubio has occasionally quoted Scripture publicly, the specific claim that he tweeted a verse in that context appears to be a misattribution or fabricated.

claim: "White busses marked ‘Soros Riot Dance Squad’ spotted in Michigan: It’s official, the riots are staged."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that buses labeled 'Soros Riot Dance Squad' were legitimately operating in Michigan or that such signage proves riots were staged. Similar claims rely on doctored or miscaptioned images and a long-running, unsubstantiated 'Soros' conspiracy narrative; independent reporting and law enforcement have not corroborated this allegation.

claim: "Romney signed government-mandated health care with taxpayer-funded abortions."
rationale: Romney did sign Massachusetts' 2006 health reform that included an individual mandate, but it did not establish broad "taxpayer-funded abortions." The law (Chapter 58) included restrictions on using public funds for elective abortions; while private plans could cover abortion, public subsidies were generally prohibited from directly paying for elective abortion services.

claim: Says Steve Jobs said, "I realize that all my recognition and wealth that I have is meaningless in the face of imminent death."
rationale: That exact sentence is not a documented verbatim quote from Steve Jobs. Jobs did express very similar sentiments about fame, wealth and mortality (notably in his 2005 Stanford commencement address and later interviews after his cancer diagnosis), but reputable sources do not attribute this precise wording to him.

claim: "There have been some estimates that if you deported everybody who is in Texas illegally," it "would create an economic recession for the state."
rationale: Multiple economic analyses and commentaries have modeled scenarios in which removing all undocumented immigrants from Texas would substantially reduce labor supply, consumption, and tax revenue and have concluded such shocks could push the state economy into contraction. The claim only asserts that 'there have been some estimates' of a recessionary effect, which is supported by published estimates and expert commentary.

claim: "Woman set to testify against Clintons blown up in home explosion."
rationale: No credible evidence supports that a woman scheduled to testify against Bill or Hillary Clinton was killed in a home explosion. Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar viral claims, which lack verifiable names, dates, locations, or official confirmation and originate from unverified conspiracy sources.

claim: "8% of the votes cast" in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary, 864 mailed ballots, came from dead voters. "NOTHING TO SEE HERE!!!"
rationale: The claim misrepresents the data and context. Even if 864 mailed ballots were associated with deceased registrants, that number is a tiny fraction of statewide primary turnout and does not equal 8% of votes cast; additionally, ballots addressed to people who died after ballots were mailed or clerical mismatches are often identified and not counted. Official election officials in Michigan repeatedly clarified such reports were misleading and did not indicate systemic fraud.

claim: Says Kanye West got 40,000 votes in the presidential election in Kentucky.
rationale: Official Kentucky election returns do not show Kanye West receiving 40,000 votes; in the general election he received only a few thousand votes in Kentucky, far short of 40,000. The claim overstates his support in that state by a large margin.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda "will cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion"
rationale: There is no widely accepted, nonpartisan analysis showing Hillary Clinton’s energy agenda would 'cost the U.S. economy over $5 trillion.' Estimates that large typically come from partisan or selective studies with long, unspecified time horizons and disputed assumptions; mainstream sources (CBO, DOE analyses, and independent policy analysts) did not publish corroborating $5 trillion-plus figures. Without a specific timeframe, metric (GDP loss, compliance costs, etc.), or credible methodology, the claim is not supported.

claim: "The collective net worth of Americans has taken a $5.5 trillion hit ... mainly due to plummeting home values."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable and likely misleading because it gives no timeframe or source. Changes in U.S. household net worth do occur, but official data (e.g., Federal Reserve Flow of Funds) show that large swings are often driven by stock market movements as well as housing, and a $5.5 trillion drop attributable 'mainly' to plunging home values is not a general fact without a specific period and citation.

claim: Says he "helped to draft parts of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street reform bill."
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who "he" is or provide supporting evidence. Major legislation like Dodd-Frank was drafted by named congressional authors, committee staff, and agency lawyers and contributions are publicly documented; without a named person or corroboration this assertion cannot be confirmed. Therefore it should be treated as unverified and likely false until specific, verifiable evidence is provided.

claim: Says Oregon canned blueberries will be cheaper in South Korea thanks to a trade agreement.
rationale: The claim definitively states Oregon canned blueberries will be cheaper in South Korea due to a trade agreement, but that outcome depends on the specific agreement’s tariff cuts, rules of origin, shipment costs, and whether savings are passed to retail. Without a named agreement and evidence that it lowers tariffs on canned blueberries and will reduce consumer prices, the claim is unproven.

claim: "Twitter is completely stifling FREE SPEECH" by adding a fact-check label to Trump’s tweet.
rationale: Adding a fact-check label to a tweet is a moderation action that provides context and can reduce amplification but does not equate to 'completely stifling' free speech. Twitter labeled (and in some cases limited visibility of) specific Trump tweets in 2020 but did not erase all of his or others' speech on the platform. Moreover, the First Amendment restricts government censorship, not content-moderation choices by private companies.

claim: An app called Talking Angela asks children personal questions and takes their photo.
rationale: The Talking Angela app contains scripted chat prompts that can ask for personal details (name, age, etc.) and includes a camera/selfie feature that can take a photo. However, it does not secretly take photos—camera use requires the user to tap the camera and grant permission, contrary to the viral hoax claims that it surreptitiously photographed children for predators.

claim: Says county parties representing more than half the state’s Republican voters approved resolutions "demanding changes" in Texas House leadership.
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable evidence that county GOP organizations representing a majority (>50%) of Texas Republican voters collectively approved resolutions demanding changes in Texas House leadership. While numerous county parties did pass resolutions criticizing or calling for leadership changes, those were primarily from many smaller counties and did not demonstrably add up to a majority of registered Republican voters in the state. Determining such a majority would require a county-by-county tally of registered Republican voters and the specific resolution votes, which has not been substantiated.

claim: Measures taken by my administration "have saved taxpayers $1 billion."
rationale: The claim is unverified because no administration, timeframe, or supporting documentation is provided; dollar-savings assertions require independent, audited budgetary evidence. While administrations sometimes report savings from reforms, such figures often depend on accounting choices (projected vs. realized, one-time vs. recurring) and need third-party confirmation, so the statement as presented is unsubstantiated.

claim: "The CDC has the power to extend the eviction moratorium."
rationale: While the CDC invoked public-health statutes to issue a temporary eviction moratorium during the COVID-19 pandemic, courts—including rulings in 2021—found that those statutes do not authorize a blanket, nationwide, open-ended eviction ban. Therefore it is incorrect to state generally that the CDC has the power to extend the eviction moratorium without new congressional authorization or a different legal basis.

claim: "For the month of February, Illinois has been the vaccination leader among the 10 most populous states in the country."
rationale: The claim is vague about which year and which vaccination metric is meant. Available public vaccination data from relevant periods do not show Illinois clearly leading all of the ten most populous states for a February; larger states (e.g., California, New York, Florida) generally reported higher totals or comparable per‑capita rates. Without a specific month/year and metric, the assertion is not supported.

claim: "The national unemployment rate has been above 8 percent for a record 36 months."
rationale: The claim is not supported by official monthly unemployment series for the United States. Modern BLS data do not show a consecutive 36‑month period with the national unemployment rate above 8%; stretches above 8% in recent recessions were shorter, and truly prolonged multi‑year episodes of >8% are only seen in much earlier, non‑comparable historical periods (e.g., the Depression era).

claim: Says "under our current sentencing laws, about 75 percent of all convicted felons in Oregon do not go to prison."
rationale: The claim overstates the share of convicted felons who avoid prison in Oregon. While many felony convictions result in probation, diversion, suspended sentences, or locally-administered sanctions, publicly reported Oregon sentencing and corrections data do not support a clear-cut figure that three out of four convicted felons nationwide or in Oregon avoid prison; the actual rates vary by year, offense type, and measurement method and are lower than a uniform 75% claim. Without a precise definition or recent statewide breakdown, the blanket 75% figure is misleading.

claim: "Even Fairfax County doesn’t pay the kind of (school administration) salaries that Richmond is paying right now."
rationale: The statement is a broad, unsupported comparison and therefore cannot be treated as fact. School administrator pay varies widely by exact title, experience, and district budget; Fairfax County Public Schools is a large, well-funded district with competitive pay scales, so it is unlikely that Richmond uniformly pays higher administrative salaries across the board without specific job-by-job data.

claim: Says "city leadership is threatening to lay off police and emergency services personnel to balance the budget."
rationale: The claim as given is unverifiable because it names no specific city, timeframe, or source and provides no evidence that any particular city leadership made such a threat. While municipalities sometimes propose layoffs to close budget gaps, this generic statement cannot be confirmed without a cited statement or official document.

claim: "Every day, a black name resume is 50 percent less likely to get responded to than a white name resume."
rationale: A landmark 2004 field experiment found resumes with Black-sounding names received about 50% fewer callbacks than identical resumes with White-sounding names, but the claim that this is true 'every day' is an overgeneralization. Subsequent audits show racial differences in response rates do occur but vary by time, place, occupation and methodology, so the absolute universal wording is false.

claim: "7 out of 10 Oregon families living in poverty have at least one parent who works."
rationale: State and federal survey data and Oregon policy analyses have repeatedly reported that about seven in ten families or children in poverty in Oregon live in households with at least one employed parent. Wording in reports often refers specifically to children in poor families and varies by year, but the claim matches commonly published estimates around 70%.

claim: "Mass media destroyed! Blackout for mass arrests event!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reports from reputable news organizations that mass media outlets have been destroyed or that a coordinated communications blackout has been implemented to enable mass arrests. An event of that scale would be widely observable and verifiable; the claim appears sensational and unsubstantiated.

claim: Protest vandalism in Richmond "all started two weeks ago when Mayor Stoney’s police gassed - tear gassed - a peaceful crowd of protesters, moms and children, at 7:30 p.m. sharp."
rationale: Contemporary reporting confirms Richmond police used crowd-control measures during protests, but the claim’s specific framing—that all subsequent vandalism “all started two weeks ago” when Mayor Stoney’s police tear-gassed a peaceful crowd of “moms and children” at exactly 7:30 p.m.—is not supported. Multiple accounts show a more complex timeline, varying times, and disputed descriptions of the crowd and causes of later vandalism, so the causal, precise-timing assertion is inaccurate or unproven.

claim: Says his plan to end the toll on Ga. 400 fulfills his campaign promise to commuters.
rationale: The statement asserts that someone said their plan to end the GA‑400 toll fulfills a campaign promise, but no speaker, source, date, or supporting evidence is provided. Without attribution or corroborating reporting or direct quotes, the claim cannot be verified as true and should be treated as unsubstantiated.

claim: "No Republicans voted for" recent hikes in the income tax, payroll tax, capital gains tax, dividend tax and estate tax. "These taxes were all passed under … Obamacare."
rationale: Only some of the listed levies — notably the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax on investment income (capital gains, dividends) and the 0.9% Additional Medicare payroll tax on high earners — were enacted as revenue provisions in the Affordable Care Act, which passed with no Republican votes. However, broader income tax rate changes and estate-tax changes were enacted in other legislation (e.g., post-2010 tax acts) and were not part of Obamacare, so the blanket claim that all those tax hikes were passed under Obamacare and that no Republicans voted for them is misleading and incorrect.

claim: "As a state rep, I was considered the fourth-most conservative in the Legislature."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no specifics (which state, which legislative session, who did the ranking or by what metric). Rankings like "fourth-most conservative" depend on a particular dataset or scoring method and require a cited source; without that evidence the assertion cannot be confirmed. Treating the claim as false is appropriate until supporting documentation is provided.

claim: Says Joe Biden has a medical device implanted in his skull so he can hear someone give him answers to questions.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Joe Biden has a surgically implanted device in his skull that feeds him answers. Close-up footage, medical transparency about the President, and multiple independent fact-checks have found this claim to be baseless and likely a conspiracy-motivated misinterpretation of normal campaign/stage aids. The claim is biologically and operationally implausible given surgical, security, and logistics constraints.

claim: Dr. Anthony Fauci has not spoken or appeared publicly for several weeks.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as a general statement: Dr. Anthony Fauci has continued to make public statements and appearances (interviews, op-eds, podcasts, and public talks) on an ongoing basis. There have been documented media engagements in recent weeks rather than a total absence of public activity.

claim: "Right to Work states have: faster private sector employment growth"
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While some studies report that Right-to-Work states have experienced faster private-sector job growth on average, the empirical literature is mixed and the association often disappears or weakens once one controls for preexisting differences (industry mix, population growth, and other policies); there is no clear, consistently demonstrated causal effect.

claim: Will Hurd "tends to have a 96 percent straight Republican, straight party voting record."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Public party-unity statistics and bipartisan rankings show Will Hurd was generally more bipartisan than many House Republicans and did not consistently vote with his party at a 96% rate across his tenure; yearly measures varied and were typically lower than a steady 96% figure.

claim: Says Julie Parrish "voted to divert $160 million from public schools to private for-profit schools."
rationale: There is no clear record that Julie Parrish cast a vote to directly divert exactly $160 million from public schools to private for‑profit schools. She has supported some school choice measures, but the cited $160 million figure appears to be an inflated or mischaracterized aggregation and funding for private schools in Oregon is not solely directed to for‑profit institutions. Legislative budget decisions are complex and no single documented vote matches the claim as stated.

claim: Says Joe Biden called ANTIFA "courageous Americans."
rationale: There is no credible public record or verified transcript showing Joe Biden explicitly called ANTIFA "courageous Americans." Biden has at times praised peaceful protesters or condemned violence, and several fact-checkers have debunked social posts that conflated or misattributed his remarks to ANTIFA. The claim appears to be a misattribution of praise for protesters more broadly, not for ANTIFA specifically.

claim: It is a "myth" that "per-student funding only rose by 47 cents this year."
rationale: I cannot confirm the blanket claim that it is a "myth" without knowing which state, jurisdiction, or exact funding measure and year are being referenced. Per‑student funding changes depend on whether figures are reported nominally or inflation‑adjusted, and whether federal, state, or local sources are included; those choices can make a small nominal increase (e.g., cents) look very different in real terms. Because the statement lacks crucial context and cannot be verified as universally false, I rate the meta‑claim as false pending more specific data.
