Isolated operational transfers of migrants or politically motivated moves by particular state officials do occur, but they do not establish a general federal rule of sending refugees only to Republican-governed states.

claim: "Since December 2010 Florida has created 540,000 new jobs."
rationale: This claim is false. Bureau of Labor Statistics and Florida state employment reports show cumulative job gains since December 2010 far exceed 540,000 — the increase is on the order of hundreds of thousands to millions depending on the exact end date, not merely 540,000.

claim: Says Joe Biden "helps build Afghanistan’s pipeline."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Joe Biden personally "helped build" any pipeline in Afghanistan. Major pipeline proposals (for example the Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India pipeline) were long‑running projects that were never completed during Biden's time in office, and Biden did not play a direct construction role in any Afghan pipeline project.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi said, "Building a wall will violate the rights of millions of illegals." ​
rationale: There is no reliable record of Nancy Pelosi using that exact phrasing; she has publicly opposed building a border wall on humanitarian and policy grounds but does not typically use the term "illegals." The quoted sentence appears to be a fabricated or paraphrased attribution circulated online rather than a verifiable direct quote.

claim: Democrats "want to tax your retirement funds to pay for their new trillion dollar power grab."
rationale: The claim is a broad and misleading characterization. Democrats do not have a unified proposal to broadly "tax your retirement funds" to pay for a single "trillion dollar power grab"; while some Democratic proposals have suggested limiting tax-preferred retirement benefits for high earners or closing specific loopholes, mainstream bills do not call for confiscatory taxes on ordinary retirement accounts. Without a specific bill text, the blanket assertion is inaccurate.

claim: Says scientists predict "sometime in the future, an event that will kill … somewhere between 80 and 90 million people."
rationale: There is no broad, authoritative scientific consensus that a specific future event will kill precisely 'somewhere between 80 and 90 million people.' Scientists produce scenario-based models (for pandemics, nuclear war, climate impacts, etc.) that can include very high death tolls under particular assumptions, but these are conditional projections, not categorical predictions that such an event will occur. Framing this as a generalized prediction by 'scientists' misrepresents how risk modeling and scientific consensus operate.

claim: A photo shows a helicopter rescue mission in Afghanistan where wounded men were loaded onboard.
rationale: There is insufficient information to verify that the pictured scene is a helicopter rescue in Afghanistan loading wounded men. Without original source, date, metadata, or independent reporting, images like this are frequently miscaptioned or originate from training exercises, other countries, or earlier conflicts. Therefore the claim as stated cannot be confirmed and should be treated as false/unverified.

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: This is false. The federal government — through the Department of Justice under many presidents — has a long history of suing states to enforce federal law (for example during Reconstruction, the civil rights era, and on environmental and voting-rights issues). Presidents prior to Obama oversaw administrations that authorized such suits, so he was not the first.

claim: Says Novak Djokovic said of Simone Biles: "Pressure is a privilege, my friend. ...If you are aiming to be at the top of the game you better start learning how to deal with pressure…"
rationale: There is no reliable record that Novak Djokovic specifically said that quoted remark about Simone Biles. Djokovic has indeed used variants of 'pressure is a privilege' in general, but the specific phrasing and context attributing it to comments about Biles appear to be a social-media misattribution rather than a verified quote in contemporary news coverage.

claim: "This year, Eric Cantor has received more money from oil companies than any other member of Congress."
rationale: The claim is time-specific but gives no year and therefore cannot be verified as stated. Campaign contributions from the oil industry fluctuate year to year and are tracked by FEC/OpenSecrets; while Eric Cantor has been a significant recipient in some cycles, he has not been consistently the single largest recipient across Congress. Without a specific year and definition of which receipts are counted (direct campaign, leadership PACs, etc.), the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: "Cincinnati is already one of the biggest cities in the country to run 100 percent on clean energy."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Cincinnati has announced steps to procure renewable electricity for city operations, there is no clear evidence the entire city (all retail electricity or all energy use) already runs 100% on clean energy; such claims are typically limited to municipal operations or achieved via purchased renewable energy credits. Saying it is “one of the biggest cities” to run 100% clean energy ignores these important qualifiers and overstates the situation.

claim: A statewide poll showing 76 percent support and other surveys are a "strong indicator" of  broad public support in Milwaukee County for a $10.10 minimum wage
rationale: A statewide poll showing 76% support demonstrates broad support across the entire state but does not necessarily prove the same level of support within a specific county. Polls must have adequate, representative subsamples of a locale (or a separate county-level poll) to be a reliable indicator of local opinion. Without evidence that the statewide survey included a sufficient, representative Milwaukee County sample or that the other unspecified surveys were county-representative, the claim overstates what the data show.

claim: Says Ron Johnson justifies his support of trade agreements by saying the U.S. has the Trade Adjustment Assistance program for displaced workers, but then he "voted to eliminate it."
rationale: Ron Johnson has publicly cited the Trade Adjustment Assistance program as a rationale for supporting trade agreements, while congressional voting records and reporting show he backed GOP budget measures and votes that would have cut or eliminated TAA funding. That creates an inconsistency between his stated justification and his votes.

claim: "We will have more people enter our country illegally than were born in this country in one year."
rationale: The claim is vague and implausible as stated: it gives no country or timeframe. In most countries annual births number in the hundreds of thousands to millions, while documented unauthorized entries or apprehensions are typically far lower. Without a specific country and clear definitions of "enter illegally," the generalized prediction is not supported.

claim: "Bill Gates talked about using vaccines to control population growth" in an "unedited 2010 TED Talk video"
rationale: In his 2010 TED talk Bill Gates explicitly said that improving vaccines, health care and reproductive health could lower future population growth (he gave an estimate of about 10–15 percent). He framed this as a consequence of reducing child mortality leading to smaller family sizes, not as a statement about using vaccines as a covert tool to forcibly reduce population.

claim: "There are more pain clinics in Broward County than there are McDonald's in Broward County."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it lacks a date and depends on how "pain clinic" is defined. Publicly available counts show McDonald's has dozens of locations in Broward County, while the number of pain clinics has varied over time and fell after regulatory crackdowns; there is no reliable current evidence that pain clinics outnumber McDonald's in the county. Given the uncertainty and shifting counts, the broad claim is not supported.

claim: Says unsuccessful Texas abortion legislation "was supported by a majority of" Texans.
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because public opinion in Texas on abortion is mixed and depends heavily on question wording, timing, and the specifics of a bill; there is no general evidence that a majority of Texans supported every unsuccessful Texas abortion measure. Without naming a specific failed bill and citing contemporaneous polls using the same question wording, the assertion that a majority supported it cannot be verified.

claim: "There are precious few religions that actually say you cannot" get vaccinated.
rationale: Most major world religions do not formally prohibit vaccination and many religious leaders and institutions have explicitly endorsed vaccines; only a small number of sects or faith-based groups discourage or forbid medical interventions generally, which can include vaccines. Opposition to vaccination is more often cultural, political, or based on individual interpretation rather than an explicit doctrinal ban across whole religions.

claim: Of six Rhode Island tax-credit programs worth about $35 million, "three companies got 90 percent of that -- CVS and two companies not even located in the state of Rhode Island."
rationale: The statement is a very specific, numerical claim about a particular set of six tax-credit programs and distribution of $35 million; I cannot corroborate those precise figures or the assertion that three firms (CVS plus two out-of-state firms) received 90% without a primary source. CVS is headquartered in Rhode Island, so the phrasing about “two companies not even located in the state” is ambiguous and likely misleading without a clear timeframe or list of the six programs and recipients. Specific fiscal-claim verification requires contemporaneous state reports or news coverage, which are not provided here.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
rationale: While NFL TV ratings and in-person attendance have fluctuated and declined in some seasons, they are not uniformly or dramatically "WAY DOWN" across the board, and long‑term attendance remained relatively strong pre‑pandemic. The claim's causal assertion—that many fans are staying away "because they love our country"—is unsupported: there is no credible evidence showing a large, patriotism‑motivated boycott driving audience declines. Observed declines are better explained by multiple factors (streaming/cord‑cutting, scheduling, competition, COVID impacts, and occasional political controversy) rather than a single patriotic motive.

claim: "Smallville star confesses she sold children to Rothschilds and Clintons."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that any cast member of Smallville confessed to selling children to the Rothschilds or the Clintons. The allegation mirrors common, debunked conspiracy narratives that target public figures without verifiable proof. Given the absence of corroboration from reliable news outlets or law enforcement, the claim is false.

claim: "8 years of the Clintons, major losses for Democrats across the nation."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While Democrats suffered major losses in the 1994 midterms (the Republican Revolution), they recovered in the 1998 midterms when Democrats gained seats, and overall the Clinton years saw mixed results rather than uniform nationwide major losses across the full eight years.

claim: "Switzerland (where the government) issues every household a gun . . . has the lowest gun related crime rate of any civilized country in the world!!!"
rationale: The statement is inaccurate: the Swiss government does not issue every household a gun. While Switzerland has a militia tradition in which many conscripts historically kept service rifles at home, not all households receive government guns and rules and ammunition storage have changed. Also, Switzerland’s gun-related crime/homicide rate is relatively low but is not uniquely the lowest — countries such as Japan, Singapore and several others report lower gun homicide rates depending on the metric and year.

claim: "Exit polls indicate that Democrats get over 70 percent of LGBT votes in federal elections."
rationale: Multiple national exit polls and surveys in recent federal elections (presidential and congressional) have consistently shown LGBT voters favor Democratic candidates at roughly the 70–80% level. While exact percentages vary by year and poll methodology, the general pattern of Democrats receiving over 70% of LGBT votes is supported by repeated polling results.

claim: Says Paul Ryan's budget relies on the same $700 billion in savings from Medicare that Mitt Romney and other Republicans have been attacking Democrats about.
rationale: Paul Ryan's budget proposals included roughly $700–720 billion in Medicare savings over a ten-year window, and the same ~$716 billion figure was the focus of Republican attacks on Democrats (notably over the Affordable Care Act). Thus it is correct that Ryan's plan relies on savings in the same dollar range that Romney and other Republicans had been criticizing Democrats about. The policies and labels differ (payment-rate reductions, structural reform vs. offsets in the ACA), but the headline dollar amount is the same.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s book "The Art of the Deal" advises: "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated."
rationale: The specific sentence quoted does not appear verbatim in The Art of the Deal. The book does promote tough negotiating tactics and projecting confidence rather than admitting defeat, so the claim is a paraphrase or summary of theme rather than a literal citation.

claim: "Newgard owed more than $13,000 for unpaid taxes on his $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating evidence that a person named Newgard owed more than $13,000 on a $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex. Property tax delinquencies are public records and typically reported if tied to a public figure, but I found no reliable reporting or records confirming this specific claim.

claim: While in Congress, Nathan Deal was a leader when it came to protecting our borders.
rationale: The claim overstates Deal's role: while Nathan Deal supported immigration enforcement and voted for measures to strengthen border security during his time in the House, he was not widely recognized as a national congressional leader on border protection or the primary architect of major border-security legislation. His record shows votes and some sponsorships in line with Republican enforcement priorities, but not leadership prominence relative to lawmakers best known for border-security initiatives.

claim: Sen. Kamala Harris "may have broken laws" when she visited a voting site in Ohio
rationale: There is no clear, cited evidence that Senator Kamala Harris committed any election-law violations by merely visiting a voting site in Ohio. Visiting or observing at a polling location is not inherently illegal; electioneering or interference within restricted zones would be required to establish a legal violation, and public reporting does not show she engaged in such prohibited conduct. Without specific, corroborated facts about prohibited actions, the claim that she "may have broken laws" is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Las Vegas shooting witnesses report multiple gunmen dressed as security guards."
rationale: Official investigations by the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department and the FBI concluded the attack was carried out by a single shooter, Stephen Paddock, firing from a Mandalay Bay suite. While some witnesses initially reported hearing shots from different directions or seeing people in security-type clothing, these accounts were unverified and no credible evidence of multiple gunmen disguised as security guards was found.

claim: "We're flying 1987 planes with 1987 technology."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsupported generalization. Modern air forces operate aircraft introduced after 1987 (for example F-22 and F-35 generations) and many older airframes have been retrofitted with modern avionics, sensors, and weapons through routine upgrade programs, so it is incorrect to say universally that "we're flying 1987 planes with 1987 technology."

claim: "By 2006, the American people were overwhelmingly against the Iraq War."
rationale: By 2006 a clear majority of Americans had turned against the Iraq War and many called it a mistake, but polls generally showed mid-50s to low-60s percent opposition rather than an "overwhelming" consensus. Saying the American people were overwhelmingly against the war overstates the size and uniformity of opposition.

claim: "Nancy Pelosi, Adam Schiff, and the rest of the corrupt Democrats made a promise to their crazy left-wing base that they would impeach me even BEFORE I took office."
rationale: There is no evidence that Nancy Pelosi, Adam Schiff, or House Democratic leadership made a public promise to impeach the claimant before he took office. Pelosi publicly resisted immediate calls for impeachment after the 2016 election, and Adam Schiff’s prominent role in impeachment came years later during formal House investigations and votes in 2019–2020. Impeachment of a president is a House vote that in practice occurred while the person was in office, not beforehand.

claim: "America owns 3 percent of the world’s oil but consumes 25 percent of its global reserves."
rationale: The claim mixes stock (reserves) and flow (consumption) metrics and is inaccurate. The United States holds roughly 2–3% of proven global oil reserves, but it consumes about 18–22% of global oil consumption in recent years—not 25% of global reserves. Saying the U.S. "consumes 25 percent of its global reserves" is misleading and incorrect.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Casten has held numerous "invite-only" town halls.
rationale: Available reporting and public schedules indicate Rep. Sean Casten has held a mix of open public town halls, virtual town-hall style calls, and some RSVP-based or constituent-only meetings, but there is not clear evidence that he has repeatedly held numerous strictly "invite-only" town halls as a regular practice. Describing his events as numerous "invite-only" is misleading without specifying event types or time frame.

claim: A photo shows ex-Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin wearing a "Make Whites Great Again Hat."
rationale: Independent fact-checkers found the circulating photo was digitally altered to add the "Make Whites Great Again" slogan. Reverse-image searches and image-analysis traced the picture to originals that do not show Chauvin wearing such a hat and show the slogan was added later.

claim: "Bill Nelson voted for higher taxes 150 times."
rationale: The specific claim that Bill Nelson "voted for higher taxes 150 times" is unsupported and misleading. There is no authoritative tally showing 150 distinct votes explicitly to raise taxes; similar numeric claims typically come from partisan tallies that conflate many different votes and definitions of "tax increases."

claim: Tim Tebow used to "kneel in prayer and the NFL complained."
rationale: Tim Tebow famously knelt in prayer after plays (the so-called 'Tebowing'), but the NFL did not formally complain or penalize him for kneeling; the league largely allowed the gesture while public discussion and some criticism occurred. Individual commentators, opponents, or team figures sometimes criticized the act, but that is not the same as an official NFL complaint.

claim: "Dark money is paying for over 80 percent of (Kavanaugh’s) ads."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that over 80% of ads supporting Brett Kavanaugh were paid for by so-called 'dark money.' Reporting and campaign-spend analyses from that period show a mix of spending by disclosed PACs, interest groups, and nonprofit groups, but not a documented figure that dark-money sources funded more than four-fifths of the ads. The claim overstates the documented role of nondisclosing groups.

claim: Bath and Body Works products are not recommended during pregnancy because they are suspected of "damaging fertility or the unborn child."
rationale: There is no broad medical or regulatory advisory that Bath & Body Works products as a whole are contraindicated in pregnancy for causing infertility or fetal harm. Some individual cosmetic ingredients (certain phthalates, fragrances, or preservatives) have been flagged by agencies such as California's Prop 65 or studied for potential reproductive effects, and a few products may carry localized warnings, but that does not justify a blanket recommendation against all Bath & Body Works products.

claim: Says proposed teacher contract "would layer on more restrictive rules."
rationale: The assertion is unverified because no specific contract text, jurisdiction, or authoritative analysis is provided to show it would "layer on more restrictive rules." Whether a proposed teacher contract adds restrictions depends entirely on its language and context, so the broad claim cannot be confirmed. I treat the statement as false pending supporting evidence.

claim: "Granite Staters who hold individual policies from Anthem...can indeed renew their policies and keep their current doctors and hospitals" in 2014.
rationale: The statement is misleading: while some Anthem individual policies were allowed to be renewed in 2014 under transitional policies or if they were grandfathered, many individual plans were cancelled because they did not meet Affordable Care Act requirements and could not simply be renewed. Even when renewals were permitted, continuity of specific doctors and hospitals was not guaranteed because provider networks and plan benefits often changed.

claim: NASCAR eliminated the national anthem at races.
rationale: NASCAR publicly announced it would stop including the traditional national anthem as part of its standard pre-race ceremonies, a change widely reported in news coverage. The move removed the anthem from routine pre-race lineups, though it does not necessarily mean the song is banned at every single event or special occasion.

claim: Says an appointed board created under Obamacare "will have the ability to come between you and your doctor in determining the best treatment options for you!"
rationale: This is a misleading exaggeration. The ACA created bodies like the Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) and PCORI, but IPAB's statutory mandate was limited to recommending Medicare cost‑saving measures and it was prohibited from recommending changes that would ration care, restrict benefits, or alter eligibility; PCORI funds comparative effectiveness research and does not dictate individual treatment. Those entities could influence policy or payments indirectly, but they do not have direct authority to come between a patient and their doctor to determine specific treatment choices.

claim: "State revenue projections have missed the mark month after month."
rationale: The statement is a broad, categorical claim but gives no state, timeframe, or definition of "missed the mark," making it unverifiable as stated. While individual states and months frequently show forecast errors, accuracy varies by state, revenue source, and period, so it is unlikely that every state's projections have missed month after month without additional context or evidence.

claim: Says that "the way to reach ‘herd immunity’ is for >70% of the population to get vaccinated."
rationale: This statement is an oversimplification. The herd immunity threshold is not a fixed >70% for all pathogens or situations; it depends on the pathogen's basic reproduction number (R0), vaccine effectiveness at preventing transmission, prior immunity in the population, and waning immunity. For example, early COVID-19 estimates around 60–70% were based on initial R0 estimates, but more infectious variants and vaccines that do not fully block transmission raise the required coverage (or shift reliance to hybrid immunity).

claim: "The price tag amounted to nearly $4,200 for every man, woman and child in the state."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written because it omits the specific state, the item or project described by 'the price tag', and the time period. Verifying a per‑person figure requires the total cost and the state's population; without those values the statement cannot be confirmed. Because of this missing context the assertion cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Says Marsha Blackburn "voted against the Reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which attempts to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and date rape."
rationale: Marsha Blackburn, while serving in the U.S. House, voted against the 2013 reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which is legislation intended to protect victims of domestic violence, stalking, and sexual assault. Contemporary roll-call records and news reports documented her 'no' vote and objections to certain expanded protections in that reauthorization.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We need to repeal Daylight Savings Time as a primary measure to decrease the rate of climate change. Less hours of sun shine equal less heat hitting Earth’s surface."
rationale: There is no credible record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez making that statement, and the factual claim in the quote is incorrect: Daylight Saving Time changes clock hours, not the total amount of sunlight or heat the Earth receives. Repealing DST would not reduce solar energy input and thus is not a primary climate-change mitigation measure.

claim: Oregon Rep. Tina Kotek, D-Portland, has "never held a job nor run a business"
rationale: This is incorrect: Tina Kotek has held paid public office for many years (she served as an Oregon state representative and as Speaker of the Oregon House) and has had prior paid and nonprofit leadership roles. Saying she has "never held a job nor run a business" contradicts the public record of her employment and public-service positions.

claim: The state contributed $80 million for the new Bucks arena, but new income tax revenue from basketball events alone "is estimated to be probably over $600 million over the life of the lease."
rationale: While Wisconsin did provide an $80 million state contribution toward the Bucks' Fiserv Forum, the claim that new income tax revenue from basketball events alone will “probably” exceed $600 million over the life of the lease is unsupported. That $600M figure traces to optimistic projections used by the team/developers and media summaries; independent analyses and fiscal watchdogs have characterized those projections as speculative and reliant on generous multipliers, not a conservative estimate of income-tax receipts from basketball events alone.

claim: "98 percent of small businesses make less than $250,000" and would not see a tax increase under Barack Obama's plan.
rationale: The statement is misleading. While Obama and his allies repeatedly said that most small businesses would not see tax increases because the proposal targeted individual incomes above $250,000, the "98 percent" figure depends on how "small business" is defined and counts tax returns rather than firms. Independent analyses and fact-checkers noted many small-business owners report individual incomes above the threshold or receive income through pass-through entities, so the simple claim that 98% of small businesses make less than $250,000 and would not face higher taxes is inaccurate without stronger qualification.

claim: "13 percent of Americans, the lowest ever, are without health care."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because the U.S. uninsured rate has been lower than 13% in recent years; U.S. Census and other health surveys recorded a record-low uninsured rate around 8.6% in 2016 (and rates in the high single digits thereafter). Saying '13 percent ... the lowest ever' contradicts established historical data on the uninsured rate.

claim: "Gov. Scott Walker (is) more than halfway to (his) 250,000 jobs goal."
rationale: The claim is underspecified and cannot be verified as stated: Walker did pledge a 250,000 jobs goal, but whether he was "more than halfway" depends on the date and which job metric is used (private payroll jobs, total nonfarm jobs, household employment, net job change). Without a specific timeframe or definition, the statement is not verifiable and therefore should be treated as false in its absolute form.

claim: "Biden says he doesn’t need voters to get elected."
rationale: There is no credible record that President Biden has asserted he does not need voters to get elected; on the contrary, his public campaigning consistently asks for votes and support. Claims that he said he "doesn’t need voters" appear to be misquotes or out-of-context excerpts of remarks (e.g., rhetorical asides) rather than a literal policy or admission.

claim: The "Buffett rule" "raises virtually no money, maybe a day and a half of our borrowing per year."
rationale: Contemporary estimates of the proposed 'Buffett rule' put additional revenue at roughly $40–50 billion over ten years (about $4–5 billion per year). At the time annual federal borrowing/deficit ran roughly $1.2–1.4 trillion (≈$3–4 billion per day), so $4–5 billion equates to roughly a day to a day-and-a-half of borrowing — meaning the claim that it 'raises virtually no money, maybe a day and a half of our borrowing per year' is accurate in scale.

claim: Says Marco Rubio believes the earth is 9,000 years old and that humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction; says  Rand Paul believes the earth is 10,000 years old and God removed dinosaurs "to make space for humans."
rationale: There is no credible record of Marco Rubio publicly asserting the Earth is 9,000 years old or claiming humans hunted dinosaurs to extinction, nor of Rand Paul saying the Earth is 10,000 years old and that God removed dinosaurs "to make space for humans." Both politicians have at times expressed skepticism or uncertainty about aspects of evolutionary timescales, but the specific age figures and the quoted assertions about humans or God removing dinosaurs are not supported by reliable sources.

claim: "794 law enforcement officers have fallen in the line of duty since B.H. Obama took office, with no special recognition from the White House."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate and misleading. Counts of line-of-duty deaths depend on the source and timeframe and do not universally match the figure 794, and the Obama White House did issue formal recognitions (proclamations, statements, flag orders and observances like National Police Week) honoring fallen officers. Therefore the blanket assertion that 794 officers fell since Obama took office and received "no special recognition" is false.

claim: "What were the old annual deficits under Republicans have now become the monthly deficits under Democrats."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsupported comparative statement and is too vague to be true as written. U.S. federal deficits are reported annually and monthly cash flows vary; while recent monthly deficits under Democratic administrations have sometimes been large, they do not generally equal entire prior annual deficits from Republican administrations except in isolated months during extraordinary periods (e.g., pandemic relief). Reliable budget data show variability by year, policy, and economic conditions, so the blanket statement is not accurate.

claim: "Senator Obama has, in fact, never had a serious Republican challenger."
rationale: False — in the 2004 Illinois Senate race Obama faced Republican Jack Ryan, a well-funded and initially serious contender who withdrew amid scandal; the GOP then tapped Alan Keyes, a national figure who mounted a late and weak campaign. Saying he 'never' had a serious Republican challenger ignores Ryan's initial candidacy and the fact that Republicans contested the seat.

claim: "I have a record on the environment of creating green energy ... taking trash and turning it into cash."
rationale: The statement is a first-person assertion of a record converting trash into green energy but provides no identifiable subject, dates, projects, or independent evidence. Without verifiable documentation (project records, contracts, media coverage, or third‑party verification) the claim cannot be confirmed as factual.

claim: "Because of my policies, Black Unemployment has just been reported to be at the LOWEST RATE EVER RECORDED!"
rationale: The claim combines two assertions — that Black unemployment is at the "lowest ever recorded" and that this is due to "my policies". Without a specific date and data series, the "lowest ever" claim is ambiguous (BLS race-specific unemployment data go back decades and have shown different historical lows), and the causal attribution to a single person's policies is not established by the statement itself. Given the missing context and the difficulty of proving causation, the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "DirecTV cancels OAN after Joe Biden orders media outlets and tech giants to banish voices that deviate from the regime’s official narrative."
rationale: There is no evidence President Biden issued any order directing media outlets or tech companies to "banish" dissenting voices, and the White House lacks legal authority to command private carriers to drop channels. While administration officials have urged platforms to address misinformation, those were requests and guidance, not binding orders; any decision by DirecTV to change carriage would be a private business decision, not a presidential directive.

claim: New food safety legislation will regulate backyard gardening.
rationale: As stated, the claim is too general and misleading: there is no broad, new food safety law that universally imposes regulations on private backyard gardening. Most recent food-safety legislation and agency rules target commercial production, processing, distribution, and retail (supply-chain actors), not individual home gardeners. Without a specific bill or jurisdiction named, the blanket assertion that 'new food safety legislation will regulate backyard gardening' is unsupported.

claim: Through the Clinton Foundation, "the Clintons are now worth in excess of $100 million."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation is a nonprofit whose funds are used for charitable programs and operating expenses, not personal enrichment; public tax filings and reporting do not show the foundation making the Clintons personally worth over $100 million. While some estimates of Bill and Hillary Clinton’s combined net worth from all sources (speeches, book deals, investments) approach or exceed $100 million, that wealth is not shown to have come "through the Clinton Foundation."

claim: A video shows Joe Biden lost and confused on stage.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because no specific video, date, event, or unedited source is provided; descriptions like "lost and confused" are subjective and cannot be confirmed from an unspecified clip. While there are viral short clips showing pauses or hesitations by President Biden, such moments are often edited or lack full context and do not by themselves prove he was objectively "lost and confused" on stage.

claim: A list shows over 14,000 dead people voted in Wayne County, Michigan.
rationale: Investigations by Michigan officials and independent fact-checkers found the circulated '14,000 dead people voted' claim for Wayne County arose from poor list-matching, duplicates, and inclusion of historic death records, not verified ballots cast by thousands of deceased people. Officials and audits found only isolated, explainable mismatches and no evidence that more than a handful (certainly not 14,000) of deceased individuals actually cast votes in Wayne County.

claim: "As chair of the Senate Education Committee, I led the charge to restore most of the education cuts from last session."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits key details (which senate, which session/year, and the specific cuts restored). Whether someone “led the charge” and whether “most” cuts were restored requires checking public legislative records, committee actions, appropriation bills, and roll-call votes for that specific jurisdiction and session. Without those specifics I cannot confirm the claim and must treat it as unproven.

claim: A "majority in every state favors path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants."
rationale: While many national polls find a majority of Americans support a pathway to citizenship, state-level polling varies and there is no consistent evidence that over 50% in every single state favor such a policy. Some states, especially more conservative ones, have shown lower support or narrow margins in state-specific surveys. Therefore the blanket claim that a majority in every state favors a path to citizenship is not supported.

claim: Says CNN and other news organizations tweeted that a journalist was executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters.
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that CNN and multiple reputable news organizations tweeted that a journalist was executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters. Major outlets typically avoid publishing such definitive claims without confirmation, and in chaotic situations social-media posts are often unverified or later corrected. Because the claim is specific but lacks a date, named journalist, or source, it appears to be unverified or false as presented.

claim: "Through competition as governor, I got agreements to build a nearly $40-billion natural gas pipeline."
rationale: There is no evidence that any U.S. governor secured agreements for a nearly $40 billion natural gas pipeline through a gubernatorial 'competition.' Typical large pipeline projects are far smaller (single-digit billions) and widely reported; a $40 billion pipeline would be unprecedented and notable but no such agreements or announcements are documented. The claim is vague about which governor, what 'competition' means, and which pipeline is referenced, and available cost benchmarks do not support the figure.

claim: Says Jeff Wentworth was the only Republican to vote against the Texas measure requiring women to have a sonogram before receiving an abortion.
rationale: The claim is unverified and likely incorrect because the statement lacks a specific bill or year and public roll-call records for Texas ultrasound/sonogram measures show multiple votes and some GOP opposition or abstentions across different sessions. Without a precise reference, it is not supportable that Jeff Wentworth was the single Republican to oppose such a measure.

claim: The Paul Ryan budget proposal would "privatize Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan's budgets proposed replacing Medicare's guaranteed defined-benefit structure with a 'premium support' or voucher-like system that would give future beneficiaries a fixed subsidy to buy private plans or traditional Medicare. That design would substantially shift Medicare from a primarily government-administered entitlement toward purchases of private insurance, which is commonly described as privatization, though current beneficiaries were generally grandfathered in many proposals.

claim: "Last year we lost $500 billion on trade with China."
rationale: If “we” refers to the United States, official annual trade statistics in recent years show a trade deficit with China in the low-to-mid hundreds of billions of dollars, not a $500 billion single-year 'loss.' Also, characterizing a trade deficit as a direct 'loss' is misleading: a deficit reflects net imports exceeding exports, not a cash loss equal to the deficit amount.

claim: "We’ve still had more deaths to the flu this year than we've had COVID-19."
rationale: Across national and global datasets for recent years, COVID-19 has caused substantially more deaths than seasonal influenza. Public health agencies (e.g., CDC, WHO) report COVID-19 fatalities in the hundreds of thousands to millions cumulatively, whereas typical annual U.S. influenza deaths are usually in the tens of thousands; therefore the blanket statement that "we've still had more deaths to the flu this year than we've had COVID-19" is incorrect in the usual understood contexts.

claim: "We've had two members engage in a Democrat-led persecution of ordinary citizens who engaged in legitimate political discourse."
rationale: The statement is a broad, specific claim that cannot be verified as true without identifying who the “two members” are, what actions they took, the victims, and the alleged Democrat-led coordination. In the absence of named incidents or credible evidence, the claim appears to be political rhetoric rather than a documented fact.

claim: Says Michelle Obama said Florida shooting "is clearly our president’s fault."
rationale: There is no credible record or reporting that Michelle Obama said the precise line 'is clearly our president’s fault' about a Florida shooting. While she has spoken about gun violence and criticized leadership more generally, the specific quoted allegation appears to be a misattribution circulated on social media rather than a verified public statement.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because no source, timeframe, or poll is cited. Rick Scott has not been Florida governor since 2019 (he is a U.S. senator), and I have no verifiable polling data showing a clear upward trend in his approval; without specific, recent poll results the assertion that his approval ratings are 'up' cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says there's a "100-year-old international norm not to use chemical weapons."
rationale: There has long been an international prohibition on the use of chemical weapons: the 1899 Hague declarations restricted asphyxiating gases and the 1925 Geneva Protocol explicitly banned use of chemical (and biological) weapons in war, with the Chemical Weapons Convention later codifying a comprehensive ban. Describing this as a roughly 100-year-old international norm is therefore accurate, though the norm has been violated at times.

claim: Tide gauges measuring sea level in Rhode Island since 1930 have risen "maybe about 10 inches since that time."
rationale: NOAA tide gauge records for Rhode Island ports (e.g., Providence, Newport/Brenton Point) show multi-decadal sea level rise rates on the order of ~2.5–3.5 mm/year. Over the ~90–95 years since 1930, that rate corresponds to roughly 8–12 inches of rise, so "maybe about 10 inches" is a reasonable summary of observed relative sea level change there.

claim: Four state Assembly Democrats "scored a death blow to northeast Wisconsin’s economy" by killing hundreds of jobs at a potential Bass Pro Shops near Green Bay.
rationale: There is no substantiated evidence that four state Assembly Democrats alone ‘scored a death blow’ to northeast Wisconsin’s economy by single‑handedly killing a Bass Pro Shops project and hundreds of jobs. Large retail developments are typically decided by the company, local governments, financing arrangements and multiple legislative steps; blaming four legislators is an oversimplification and hyperbolic without specific documented votes or direct causation.

claim: Graduation rates in Buffalo’s school district, which were "around 48 percent are now up to 64 percent" since Say Yes Buffalo launched.
rationale: The precise claim ties a rise from “around 48%” to “64%” directly to the launch of Say Yes Buffalo, but public graduation-rate reports for Buffalo vary by year and cohort and do not unambiguously support that exact baseline-to-current jump or sole attribution. While Buffalo’s graduation rate did improve in the years after Say Yes launched, the baseline year, the end year, and the degree to which the improvement is attributable to Say Yes (versus other district and state policy changes) are disputed. Because the claim states a specific before-and-after percentage increase and implies causation without that clear, corroborated linkage, it is not fully supported.

claim: The United States has "the highest corporate tax rate in the free world."
rationale: This is not currently true. The U.S. federal corporate tax rate was cut from 35% to 21% by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, and even after adding typical state corporate taxes the combined U.S. rate is below the top rates among developed countries. The U.S. was among the highest before 2017, but that context is essential.

claim: "We haven't yet taken out a negative ad."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it provides no information about who "we" refers to, the campaign or timeframe, or what counts as a "negative ad." Without those specifics one cannot confirm the absence of any negative ad; moreover, negative advertising is common in politics so the blanket assertion is unlikely. Given the ambiguity I judge the claim more likely false than provable true.

claim: Alison Alter "has exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars to fund her campaign."
rationale: I find no reliable, verifiable evidence that Alison Alter exploited a campaign finance loophole to obtain over $64,000 in public dollars. Public financing and matching-fund programs do exist in some jurisdictions, but claims about an individual 'exploiting a loophole' and a precise dollar amount require specific, documented investigation which is not supported by widely reported sources.

claim: "We’re second only to Boston in college students per capita."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and cannot be verified as written because it does not identify which place 'we' refers to and lacks a clear metric or timeframe. Rankings of college students per capita vary widely depending on whether you use city limits, metro area, and which enrollments are counted, and many smaller college towns and cities (e.g., Cambridge, Amherst) have higher student-per-capita ratios than Boston. Without a specified location and definition, the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Perry is "by far and away the highest-paid state employee on an hourly basis."
rationale: Texas governors receive a fixed annual salary (around $150,000 in recent years), but many other public employees — notably university presidents and high-profile public university coaches — have annual pay that exceeds the governor’s by large margins. Even when adjusting for hours worked, those multi‑hundred‑thousand- or million‑dollar contracts produce a higher hourly rate than the governor’s compensation, so the claim that Perry is "by far and away the highest‑paid" is incorrect. The statement also glosses over how "hourly basis" and "state employee" are defined.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation folded."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation has not ceased to exist; it continues to operate programs, accept donations, and file nonprofit reports. While it has scaled back some activities and leadership changes have occurred, there is no credible evidence that the organization completely folded or shut down.

claim: "They talk about this problem with binding arbitration. It doesn’t make a lot of sense to me to have somebody from Los Angeles fly into Zanesville and impose a wage settlement on you ... and then they’re on the plane back to Los Angeles."
rationale: The quote describes a common and factually accurate aspect of binding arbitration: parties often use neutral arbitrators drawn from regional or national panels rather than local residents. Those arbitrators can travel to hearings, issue a binding wage decision, and then leave, so the scenario described is plausible and consistent with typical arbitration practice.

claim: Under Gov. Tom Corbett, "Pennsylvania ranks 49th in job creation."
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute fact but lacks a specific time period and metric. While Pennsylvania had relatively weak job growth during parts of Gov. Tom Corbett’s 2011–2015 term and ranked very low in some short intervals, it was not uniformly 49th in job creation across his entire tenure—the rank varies by year and by whether one measures absolute job gains, percent change, or private-sector jobs.

claim: "President Trump marshalled the full resources of our federal government from the outset. He directed us to forge a seamless partnership with governors across America in both political parties."
rationale: While the Trump administration implemented measures (travel restrictions, a Coronavirus Task Force), independent reporting and many governors' public statements show the federal government did not deploy 'full resources from the outset' and relations were not 'seamless.' Governors across states — including high-profile complaints about testing, PPE and ventilator shortages and inconsistent federal guidance — documented disputes and requests that were not immediately met or were handled unevenly.

claim: Says "all my grandparents" immigrated to America.
rationale: The statement is a specific personal claim about an individual's family and cannot be verified from the information provided. Without documentary evidence (birth certificates, immigration or naturalization records, or other primary sources) the claim is unproven; per conservative fact-checking practice I treat unverifiable specific claims as false.

claim: "Donald Trump to issue an executive order to ban Facebook across U.S."
rationale: There is no evidence that Donald Trump has issued or announced an executive order to ban Facebook nationwide. Past actions by the Trump administration focused on apps like TikTok and WeChat and were publicly reported and legally contested; a nationwide ban on Facebook would face major legal and constitutional barriers and would have been widely covered in reliable media.

claim: "In two terms in the Missouri General Assembly, Jason Kander passed ZERO bills that were signed into law."
rationale: This statement is false. Contemporary fact-checking and Missouri legislative records indicate Jason Kander sponsored or saw provisions he authored enacted during his two terms in the Missouri House; the assertion that he passed "zero" laws conflates primary authorship with co-sponsorship and measures adopted via amendments. Misleading phrasing about what counts as a bill becoming law likely produced the claim.

claim: Says Joe Biden wants to "defund the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has publicly and repeatedly stated he does not support 'defunding the police' and has rejected that slogan. His campaign and administration have promoted policing reforms and investments in community programs rather than eliminating police funding.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Faso "voted for an age tax on seniors."
rationale: There is no record that Rep. John Faso voted for a law that explicitly imposes an "age tax" on seniors (for example, raising the Medicare eligibility age or enacting an explicit age-based tax). Political ads sometimes label certain tax or health-policy votes as an "age tax" rhetorically, but the congressional record does not show Faso casting a vote to enact a statutory age-based tax on seniors.

claim: Says according to the FBI, more people are killed each year with hammers and clubs than rifles.
rationale: FBI Uniform Crime Report/Crime Data Explorer weapon-category tables show that deaths attributed to blunt objects (clubs, hammers) typically exceed deaths attributed specifically to rifles in recent annual data. Rifles represent a small fraction of firearm homicides compared with handguns, so the statement that more people are killed each year with hammers and clubs than with rifles is supported by FBI annual counts.

claim: Justice Antonin Scalia agreed for the Supreme Court to hear a case about whether Barack Obama is eligible to be President.
rationale: The Supreme Court never agreed to hear a merits case deciding whether Barack Obama was constitutionally eligible; petitions challenging his eligibility (the so‑called 'birther' cases) were denied certiorari and no oral-argument merits decision was reached. There is no record that Justice Antonin Scalia voted to grant cert in such a case; he publicly stated he believed Obama was born in the United States and did not place such a case on the Court's docket.

claim: Says proposal to boost teacher pension fund "puts no mandate on local government."
rationale: The statement cannot be verified without the specific proposal text; proposals to increase teacher pension funding often have fiscal implications for state or local budgets and frequently include statutory provisions that can require local cost-sharing. Absent the exact legislative language and fiscal analysis, it is not accurate to assert categorically that the proposal "puts no mandate on local government."

claim: Says David Rivera "allowed House Republican leaders to strip key provisions from the STOCK Act" that would crack down on insider trading by members of Congress.
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Rep. David Rivera individually 'allowed' House Republican leaders to strip key STOCK Act provisions. The STOCK Act's wording was altered through leadership-driven floor actions and amendments in 2012, and reporting and roll-call records attribute those changes to House leadership and specific amendments, not to a singular action by Rivera.

claim: Says Texas is "last in mental health expenditures."
rationale: The claim that Texas is "last in mental health expenditures" is not accurate as an absolute statement. While Texas ranks relatively low on some per‑capita mental‑health spending measures, multiple states often report lower per‑capita or per‑beneficiary behavioral‑health spending in available state comparisons; moreover Texas' total mental‑health outlays are large because of its population. Rankings also vary by year and by whether the metric is total dollars, per capita spending, or Medicaid behavioral‑health spending.

claim: Says there’s an 800 number you can call to track the status of your stimulus check.
rationale: There is no single official 800 number that the IRS set up for the public to simply call and track the status of stimulus checks; the IRS instead provided an online "Get My Payment" tool and limited phone support and repeatedly warned that scam numbers were circulating. Messages claiming a universal 800 number to track payments have been used in scams and misinformation.

claim: Says Tammy Baldwin's record includes "opposing harsher punishments for criminals who commit violent crimes near schools."
rationale: There is no clear record that Senator Tammy Baldwin specifically opposed harsher penalties for violent crimes committed near schools. Baldwin has supported school safety and child-protection measures, and while she has backed criminal-justice reform that critiques mandatory minimums, that is not the same as opposing enhanced penalties for crimes targeting schools.

claim: A photo shows three men on crosses who "feel like they’re being crucified by being required to stay at home."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a genuine news photo shows three men literally crucified as a protest about stay‑at‑home orders; similar images circulated during the pandemic were reused, taken out of context, or were staged/artistic rather than documentation of people being crucified. The claim conflates a dramatic visual with an asserted motive and situation that reliable reporting does not support.

claim: "I was totally against the war in Iraq, saying for many years that it would destabilize the Middle East."
rationale: The statement is a personal claim about past positions but gives no identity or supporting evidence. Without knowing who 'I' refers to, public statements, voting record, or documented repeated remarks, the assertion cannot be verified and thus is treated as false in this context.

claim: Says "Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated and confirmed 43 days before an election."
rationale: Ruth Bader Ginsburg was nominated to the U.S. Supreme Court by President Bill Clinton in June 1993 and confirmed by the Senate later that year; those actions did not occur 43 days before a general presidential or midterm election. The nomination came after the 1992 election and well before the next major federal elections, so the 43-day-before-election timing is incorrect.

claim: In the recent House special election in Florida, Democrats "got outspent in a Republican district."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify because it doesn't name which Florida House special election or date is meant, and spending patterns differ by race. I cannot confirm that Democrats were outspent in a specific recent Florida special election without identifying the district and consulting the race-by-race spending reports, so I mark the general statement as not supported.

claim: "President Obama has declared disasters in 48 of 50 states this year."
rationale: There is no evidence that Obama issued disaster declarations covering 48 of 50 states in any single year; presidential disaster declarations are public and far fewer states typically receive declarations in a given year. The claim likely confuses county-level or multiple separate declarations with unique state-level declarations or misstates the time period.

claim: "Dwayne 'The Rock' (Johnson) Has Officially Filed For The 2020 Presidential Campaign"
rationale: Dwayne Johnson publicly discussed the idea of running and said he was considering a 2020 bid, but he never filed official candidacy paperwork with the Federal Election Commission and did not enter the 2020 presidential race. Major news outlets and FEC records show no filing by Johnson for the 2020 election.

claim: Says President Barack Obama's parents were communists.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that either of Barack Obama’s parents were communists. Barack Obama Sr. was a Kenyan economist who worked for the Kenyan government and international institutions, and Ann Dunham was an American anthropologist focused on development work in Indonesia; reputable biographies and public records do not identify them as communists. The claim appears to be a baseless political rumor.

claim: "Covid-19 is now the leading cause of death in the United States."
rationale: Available U.S. mortality data through recent years shows heart disease and cancer remain the top causes of death nationally; COVID‑19 has not been consistently the leading cause and in most recent annual and multi‑month reports ranked below those two. COVID‑19 deaths can spike in short periods, but the claim as a blanket present-tense statement is not supported by typical national CDC tallies.

claim: "Since 2007 David Jolly has given almost $30,000 to keep Democrats in Congress!"
rationale: I am not aware of evidence that David Jolly, a Republican former member of Congress, has given nearly $30,000 specifically to "keep Democrats in Congress" since 2007. Public campaign‑finance records tracked by the FEC and organizations like OpenSecrets show donors' party-leaning patterns and Jolly's contributions have generally not been reported as large donations to Democratic incumbents. Without a specific source, the precise claim appears unsupported.

claim: Says detained immigrant parents separated from their children at the border are being charged "as much as $8 a minute to call their children."
rationale: This claim overstates documented per‑minute rates. Reporting and investigations about phone service in immigration and criminal detention have documented high fees and various connection and transaction charges, but reliable sources do not substantiate routine $8-per-minute charges for parents calling separated children; typical per‑minute rates reported were much lower and the costs were often a mix of per‑minute rates plus added fees. The claim appears to conflate or exaggerate fees rather than reflect standard billed per‑minute rates.

claim: "They were going to build the wall a while ago, not so long ago, like in '06. And they couldn't get environmental impact statements."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Congress passed the Secure Fence Act in 2006 authorizing large-scale border fencing, and agencies did conduct some environmental assessments; at the same time DHS had statutory waiver authority (from the Real ID Act of 2005) and used it in some cases so requirements were sometimes bypassed rather than simply 'unable to get' impact statements.

claim: "The U.S. is borrowing approximately $2.52 for every $1 of economic growth so far in 2012."
rationale: The quoted 2.52 figure is not supported by standard, consistently defined data for 2012; results vary widely depending on whether one uses calendar-year vs. fiscal-year borrowing, gross vs. net debt changes, and nominal vs. real GDP growth. Using commonly reported figures (fiscal-year 2012 deficit ≈ $1.0–1.1 trillion and 2012 GDP growth of roughly 2% on a ~$15 trillion economy, i.e., a few hundred billion dollars of growth) produces ratios that differ materially from exactly 2.52. The claim therefore overstates certainty and is misleading without precise definitions and timeframes.

claim: "Cities in notoriously ‘tough on crime’ states like Texas and Florida saw a more significant increase in violent crime than cities in NYS."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization and not reliably supported without a specified timeframe, list of cities, or data source. Violent‑crime trends vary widely by city and year (especially around the 2020–2022 period), with some Texas and Florida cities experiencing large increases and other New York State cities doing the same or worse. Because the claim asserts a blanket comparison across states without defining scope, it cannot be verified as true.

claim: "Republicans are attempting to remove Barack Obama from Georgia’s Presidential Ballot in 2012."
rationale: During the 2012 campaign there were legal challenges and activist efforts—largely from conservative and ‘birther’ critics aligned with or part of the Republican movement—to bar Barack Obama from state ballots, and Georgia saw at least one such challenge seeking removal. These efforts were unsuccessful and were driven by private plaintiffs and activists rather than being a unanimous action by the entire GOP establishment.

claim: In one year, the United Nations "did 24 resolutions and 20 of them were against Israel."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and does not match public records for any principal UN body in a single year. Different UN organs (General Assembly, Security Council, Human Rights Council) pass very different numbers of resolutions, and while Israel is frequently the subject of multiple Human Rights Council and General Assembly resolutions, there is no verified instance where a UN body passed exactly 24 resolutions in one year with 20 directed at Israel. Without specifying which UN body and which year the claim is unverified and likely an exaggeration.

claim: "Do this research … watch how much crime picks up if you take away [football]."
rationale: The claim presents a causal generalization that removing football will cause crime to increase, but there is no robust, universal evidence that eliminating a particular sport reliably raises crime rates. Empirical studies on sports and crime show mixed results and are often correlational—effects vary by context, age group, and other social factors—so the blanket causal statement is unsupported.

claim: "Every state that has put in a graduated income tax, the middle class always pays more."
rationale: The claim is false because a graduated (progressive) income tax imposes higher rates on higher income brackets but does not automatically or invariably increase middle‑class tax payments. Whether the middle class pays more depends on the specific rate schedule, bracket thresholds, deductions, credits, and the broader state tax mix, and there are examples of states where middle‑income liability did not rise after adopting graduated rates. The universal words "every" and "always" make the statement demonstrably incorrect.

claim: Says there have been no cases of wolves killing people in Rocky Mountain states.
rationale: This claim is incorrect because historical records and wildlife-agency reviews show that while wolf attacks on people are extremely rare, there have been documented attacks — including fatal ones — in parts of the broader Rocky Mountain region. The rarity of such events has led to public impressions that they never occur, but archival and incident reports contradict an absolute statement of "no cases."

claim: Photo shows Ice Cube and 50 Cent wearing Donald Trump hats.
rationale: The circulated photo is a digitally altered composite; the original source images of Ice Cube and 50 Cent do not show them wearing Donald Trump "Make America Great Again" hats. Independent image checks and the pattern of viral edits of celebrity photos indicate the hats were pasted on rather than actually worn by the artists in a single photo.

claim: "Surveys show that many of our citizens think we devote a full quarter or even a third of our federal budget to foreign aid."
rationale: Multiple national polls have repeatedly found that Americans greatly overestimate how much of the federal budget goes to foreign aid, with many respondents giving answers in the roughly 20–33% range. Thus the claim that many citizens think a quarter or a third of the budget goes to foreign aid is supported by survey evidence.

claim: President Barack Obama’s latest executive order "mandates the apprehension and detention of Americans who merely show signs of ‘respiratory illness.’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama issued an executive order that broadly mandates the apprehension and detention of Americans merely for showing signs of a respiratory illness. U.S. executive orders and public-health law provide limited quarantine/isolation authority for specific communicable diseases administered by public-health authorities, and reputable fact-checkers and legal analyses have debunked viral claims of a blanket detention order. Such a sweeping, indiscriminate mandate would also raise serious constitutional and due-process problems and thus is not consistent with how federal health and emergency powers are implemented.

claim: "The Obama-Clinton war on coal has cost Michigan over 50,000 jobs."
rationale: Michigan has never had a large coal-mining workforce; coal mining and coal-plant employment in the state have numbered in the hundreds to low thousands, not tens of thousands. National and state coal job declines during the Obama years were largely driven by market forces (cheap natural gas), plant retirements, automation and broader economic trends rather than an identifiable ‘‘Obama‑Clinton war’’ that eliminated 50,000 Michigan jobs, so the claim greatly overstates and misattributes the losses.

claim: Say Portland Public Schools' central administration makes up less than 4 percent of the staff.
rationale: I cannot verify the precise percentage from available general knowledge; whether central administration is under 4% depends on the district year, the staffing categories included, and the source. Portland Public Schools employs thousands of staff and different definitions (e.g., supervisors, principals, program managers) change the denominator, so the claim is unsubstantiated without current HR or budget data. Without a cited PPS report showing that figure, the statement should not be taken as proven.

claim: "America is one of the highest-taxed nations in the world."
rationale: The United States is not generally considered one of the highest-taxed countries when measured by overall tax burden: U.S. total tax revenue as a share of GDP (roughly mid-20s percent) is below the OECD average and well below high-tax countries like Denmark, France, Belgium, and Sweden, which often exceed 40% of GDP. While some Americans face high marginal income tax rates or high local taxes in certain places, on aggregate the U.S. tax-to-GDP ratio places it well down the list.

claim: Mitt Romney "said it was 'tragic' to end the war in Iraq."
rationale: There is no well-documented, verifiable quote in which Mitt Romney explicitly said it was "tragic" to end the war in Iraq. Romney repeatedly criticized rapid withdrawal and warned against leaving before the job was done, but available public records and news coverage do not show him using the exact language that ending the war itself would be "tragic."

claim: "The Katy Freeway, or Interstate 10 west of Houston, is the widest freeway in the world, with up to 26 lanes, including frontage road lanes."
rationale: The Katy Freeway (I‑10 west of Houston) does reach up to about 26 lanes in certain cross-sections when main lanes, managed lanes and parallel frontage roads are all counted. However, declaring it the undisputed "widest freeway in the world" is inaccurate: international comparisons depend on how lanes/frontage roads are counted and other roadways have been reported with comparable or greater lane counts, so the superlative is contested.

claim: McCain's energy plan is a "single-answer proposition" — new domestic oil drilling.
rationale: McCain’s 2008 energy platform included multiple components beyond expanding domestic oil drilling — for example increased fuel economy standards, support for nuclear power, renewable energy and biofuels, energy R&D, and conservation measures. While he emphasized opening some domestic areas to drilling and critics often framed drilling as a centerpiece, describing the whole plan as a “single-answer proposition” is inaccurate because the platform explicitly contained many other policies.

claim: "Obama administration kept illegal Mexican kids in detention camps as ‘experiment’"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama administration deliberately held Mexican children in detention camps as an "experiment." While the Obama years saw large numbers of unaccompanied minors and family detention—especially during the 2014 surge—and use of HHS/ORR shelters and private contractors, reporting and oversight describe enforcement and processing policies, not a secret experimental program targeting Mexican children.

claim: Wagon arriving at Detroit counting center after deadline "may have been a ballot box."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a wagon arriving at a Detroit counting center after a deadline in any recent election contained a ballot box. Election officials, chain-of-custody records, and post-election audits and reporting found no proof of unauthorized late ballots delivered in that manner; the suggestion remains speculative rather than established fact.

claim: Says Joe Biden was asleep and snoring during a TV interview.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable news reporting that President Joe Biden fell asleep and snored during a televised interview; viral clips claiming this have been shown to be edited or misinterpreted. Fact‑checking organizations and mainstream outlets did not verify any live interview in which he actually slept and snored on camera.

claim: "Fifteen years ago, the assets of the six largest banks in this country totaled 17 percent of GDP ... The assets of the six largest banks in the United States today total 63 percent of GDP."
rationale: Independent summaries of Federal Reserve/flow-of-funds data and banking analyses show the six largest U.S. banks held roughly the mid-teens percentage of GDP in the early 2000s (around 15–20%) and that their combined assets rose to roughly 60–65% of GDP by the late 2010s. The claim matches those reported magnitudes and reflects post‑crisis consolidation and asset growth at the biggest banks.

claim: Says state lawmakers have voted to "spend virtually all of the Rainy Day Fund four times" since the fund’s creation.
rationale: Since the creation of most state "Rainy Day" or Economic Stabilization funds (for example Texas' fund created in 1988), lawmakers have tapped the funds several times for shortfalls or emergencies, but they have not voted to spend "virtually all" of the fund on four separate occasions. Most withdrawals have been partial or for specific purposes; only a small number of episodes involved very large draws, and characterizing four distinct votes as spending nearly the entire fund is inaccurate or unsupported.

claim: "We've seen in this last year tremendous things happening, including our unemployment rate come down 2 percentage points."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it does not specify the country or the exact 12‑month period referenced; unemployment rates are reported by country and month and can rise or fall by different amounts. While some countries have seen ~2 percentage point annual declines at certain times, the blanket statement cannot be confirmed without those specifics.

claim: "Barack Hussein Obama will … force doctors to assist homosexuals in buying surrogate babies."
rationale: There is no evidence that President Barack Obama proposed or enacted any policy that would "force doctors" to assist same-sex couples in purchasing infants via surrogacy. While the Obama administration supported expanding LGBT rights and non-discrimination protections, medical practice and surrogacy law are primarily state-regulated and there was no federal mandate compelling physicians to facilitate commercial surrogacy.

claim: "Just passed into law today: You cannot go 5 miles over speed limit" in North Carolina.
rationale: There is no widely reported or legally documented North Carolina law that was enacted 'today' making it illegal to drive 5 mph over the posted limit. Traffic statutes already make exceeding the posted limit unlawful, but routine enforcement tolerance (e.g., officers not ticketing small overages) is a matter of practice, not a new law banning '5 over.' Claims framed as 'just passed into law today' about statewide speed-tolerance changes are inconsistent with how traffic laws are enacted and reported.

claim: "Ron Johnson pushed through a special tax loophole that benefited his own family's business … Then he cashed out of the company for $5 million … (he has) doubled his wealth since taking office."
rationale: The claim bundles several assertions that are not fully supported by public records. While Johnson supported the 2017 tax changes that included a broad pass-through deduction that could help family-owned businesses, there is no clear evidence he 'pushed through a special tax loophole' tailored to his family's firm. Reporting about him selling a stake in a business has appeared but the specific 'cashed out for $5 million' figure and the assertion that he has 'doubled his wealth since taking office' are not conclusively corroborated by public financial disclosures and vary across sources.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "just gave a speech a few weeks ago" and said "we should still have troops in Iraq."
rationale: There is no verifiable record of Mitt Romney giving a speech 'a few weeks ago' in which he is quoted saying exactly 'we should still have troops in Iraq.' While Romney has previously supported a limited U.S. military presence in the region to counter ISIS and Iranian influence, the specific recent speech and wording in the claim are not corroborated by available public reports.

claim: Blinken, Austin trip to Kyiv may have been staged
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Blinken–Austin visit to Kyiv was staged. Multiple independent news organizations, photos and videos, and confirmations from U.S. and Ukrainian officials documented the trip and the meetings with President Zelenskyy; no reliable source has produced evidence of fabrication. Claiming staging relies on conspiracy speculation rather than verifiable facts.

claim: An episode of "The Simpsons" showed Donald Trump in a coffin.
rationale: No canonical episode of The Simpsons depicts Donald Trump in a coffin. The show has parodied Trump (notably referencing a future President Trump in the 2000 episode 'Bart to the Future') but fact-checkers and episode guides show no scene of Trump in a coffin; viral images claiming this are altered or fan-made.

claim: "News report accidentally reveals doctors giving ‘banned’ COVID treatment to the Queen."
rationale: There is no credible reporting from reputable news outlets that doctors accidentally revealed giving any ‘banned’ COVID treatment to a queen. Major medical treatment of a high-profile royal would be widely reported and officially confirmed if true, and no such confirmation or verifiable evidence exists. Claims like this have circulated as misinformation in relation to disputed COVID therapies (e.g., ivermectin or hydroxychloroquine).

claim: Clips of Dr. Anthony Fauci show he "flip-flopped" on guidance for wearing masks, whether kids should be in school and whether people should change how they interact.
rationale: Public video clips do show Dr. Anthony Fauci making different public statements over time about mask use, school attendance and how people should interact; his recommendations changed as the pandemic evolved. Early in 2020 he and CDC guidance discouraged general public mask use (partly due to limited PPE and limited evidence of asymptomatic spread) and later recommended universal masking; guidance on schools and social interactions likewise shifted with accumulating data and changing risk assessments.

claim: Obama's budget plan would "take national debt up to about 80 percent of gross national product. ... Historically, it's been about 40 percent."
rationale: The claim blends different measures and timeframes. CBO/OMB projections around the Obama years did show federal debt rising substantially under certain scenarios, but whether it reached “about 80%” depends on whether one uses debt held by the public versus gross federal debt and which year is referenced. Likewise, the statement that it has 'historically' been about 40% is misleading: historical debt-to-GDP has varied widely (well above 40% after WWII and well below 40% in other decades), so a single 40% figure is an oversimplification.

claim: The omnibus bill "does not designate a single dollar for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The claim is misleading because omnibus appropriations typically do not direct funding to named private organizations, but they do fund federal programs (Medicaid, community health centers, etc.) that can reimburse or support Planned Parenthood. Some omnibus bills also include riders that restrict use of federal funds for abortions or explicitly bar funds to Planned Parenthood, but many do not explicitly name or 'designate a single dollar' while still allowing indirect federal funding. Without specifying the year/text of the omnibus bill the absolute statement is incorrect in general.

claim: "Our university campuses by federal law do not check the immigration status of their students just as our public schools don’t."
rationale: The claim is false because there is no federal law that universally prohibits universities from checking students' immigration status. A 1982 Supreme Court case (Plyler v.
