Sweeney, as Senate President, was one actor in a legislative process and cannot be solely credited with creating statewide tax levels, nor is there clear evidence that any NJ tax changes he supported directly "drove out" jobs given many factors affect employment and migration.

claim: Says Mark Kirk "called for the mass arrest of 18,000 African Americans" and "was apparently fine with Trump’s #StillTooRacist call for mass deportation."
rationale: There is no contemporaneous record or credible reporting showing Mark Kirk explicitly called for the mass arrest of '18,000 African Americans,' nor that he publicly endorsed a Trump 'mass deportation' tweet tied to the hashtag cited. The allegation appears to be a mischaracterization or conflation of other statements and political attacks rather than a documented quote or policy position by Kirk.

claim: Says Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Tammy Baldwin ranks "as the most liberal member of the House."
rationale: Tammy Baldwin was widely viewed as one of the most liberal House members, but she was not consistently ranked as the single most liberal member. Multiple common measures of ideology (DW-NOMINATE, ADA scores, and contemporary media rankings) typically placed other Democrats — e.g., Cynthia McKinney, Dennis Kucinich, John Conyers, or Barbara Lee — at the very top in various years. Because the claim asserts an absolute ranking without specifying the metric or year, it is inaccurate as stated.

claim: "Al-Qaida operatives, have said, 'Hey, we want you to use this loophole (for purchasing guns despite being on a watch list) to attack and kill Americans.'"
rationale: There is no publicly verifiable evidence or credible reporting that al‑Qaida operatives issued that exact quoted instruction. Extremist groups have broadly encouraged attacks and U.S. officials have warned that some watchlisted individuals could exploit information‑sharing gaps in background checks, but the specific quote and direct attribution to al‑Qaida appear unverified or misattributed.

claim: Says the estate tax is a threat to family farms.
rationale: As a general claim this is misleading: under current U.S. federal law most family farms fall below the estate-tax exemption and never owe federal estate tax. Additionally, tools like special-use valuation, installment payment rules, and valuation discounts further reduce the likelihood that an estate tax forces sale of a family farm, though isolated high-value or illiquid estates can be affected.

claim: "The biggest contribution" behind a decrease in U.S. unemployment "was 1.2 million people leaving the workforce"
rationale: The claim lacks a specified time period or data source and therefore cannot be verified as stated. Whether a 1.2 million drop in the labor force was the largest contributor to a decline in the unemployment rate is a month-by-month, data-dependent statement; BLS decompositions of changes in the unemployment rate typically cite specific employment, unemployment, and labor-force movements. Without a cited month and BLS seasonally adjusted figures showing a 1.2 million exit and that it was the dominant factor, the claim is not supported.

claim: "North Carolina spends $855 less per student than it did before the Great Recession, and we have one of the lowest per pupil spending levels in the nation."
rationale: The claim bundles a precise dollar decline with a broad ranking without specifying years or whether figures are inflation-adjusted. While North Carolina did cut K–12 spending after the Great Recession and its per-pupil spending has been below the national average in many years, the specific '$855 less per student than before the Great Recession' is not consistently supported across common datasets once you choose a baseline year and adjust for inflation; rankings likewise vary by measure and year. Because the statement lacks necessary context and precise, verifiable data, it cannot be accepted as stated.

claim: Says Wisconsin Manufacturers & Commerce’s "own 2014 survey revealed that just 15 percent of business executive respondents were in favor of Right-To-Work legislation."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Wisconsin Manufacturers & Commerce's 2014 survey showed only 15% of business executives supporting Right-to-Work. Reports from that period and WMC's own public positions indicate WMC did not publish a survey with such a low pro-RTW figure among business executives, and it would be inconsistent with WMC's advocacy to report results that strongly contradict its policy stance. The claim appears to misstate or fabricate the survey findings.

claim: "Recent data showed Nevada ranks 50th in the money received from" the stimulus bill.
rationale: The statement is implausible and unsupported as written. Federal COVID-era stimulus allocations (like CARES/ARP) were largely tied to formulas based on population and need, and Nevada, with a population of about 3 million (roughly mid‑30s by state population rank), would not rank last (50th) in total dollars received. No widely reported recent dataset shows Nevada as 50th in stimulus money without additional qualifiers.

claim: Says Joe Biden talked about eating wooden corn dog sticks.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or reliable transcript showing President Biden stating he ate wooden corn-dog sticks; viral claims appear to stem from misheard audio or out-of-context clips and have not been substantiated by reputable fact-checkers. The anecdote is more consistent with a garbled or joking remark about corn dogs rather than a literal admission of eating the wooden stick.

claim: Wisconsin's Lincoln Hills youth prison has a "66 percent recidivism rate," while "states like Missouri, that have more of a regional model -- 8 percent."
rationale: The claim mixes incompatible measures and overstates the comparison. Lincoln Hills has been reported to have a high recidivism rate by some measures (often cited in the range of ~60–70% for certain follow-up periods), but Missouri's widely cited low rates (single-digit numbers) refer to different cohorts, definitions, and timeframes; when measured comparably statewide, Missouri's juvenile recidivism is not as uniformly low as '8%.' Therefore the juxtaposition is misleading rather than a factual parity.

claim: "Thanks to President Trump and Republican leadership, the number of people collecting food stamps has declined by more than two million."
rationale: While SNAP (food stamp) participation did fall by more than two million in the years before the COVID-19 pandemic, attributing that decline solely to President Trump and Republican leadership is misleading. The drop reflected broader factors including a strengthening labor market, state-level policy changes and administrative actions; moreover the pandemic in 2020 reversed much of the decline.

claim: The Rev. Wright compared "the United States Marine Corps with Roman legionnaires who were responsible for the death of our Savior."
rationale: There is no credible record of Rev. Jeremiah Wright (the widely discussed Rev. Wright) explicitly saying the United States Marine Corps were like the Roman legionnaires who killed Jesus. Wright's publicly known sermons contain harsh criticisms of U.S. policy and historical analogies but not this specific comparison. Without a verifiable primary source for that exact quote, the claim appears to be a misattribution or distortion.

claim: "So that 2005 energy bill was a big step backwards on the path to clean, renewable energy. That's why I voted against it."
rationale: The statement mixes a subjective judgment about the 2005 Energy Policy Act and an asserted motive for a specific vote but provides no speaker or verifiable voting record. The 2005 law contained both renewable energy incentives and provisions benefiting fossil fuels, so calling it definitively a "big step backwards" is a partisan interpretation rather than an established fact, and the claimed vote cannot be confirmed from the claim alone.

claim: "More Americans receive food aid than work in (the) private sector."
rationale: U.S. private-sector employment is on the order of roughly 120–130 million people (BLS payroll data). By contrast monthly SNAP participation is roughly 40–50 million, and even when adding WIC, school meals, and other food programs the total of individuals receiving food aid is well below the size of the private-sector workforce. Therefore the statement that more Americans receive food aid than work in the private sector is incorrect.

claim: "They voted for (a border wall) in 2006. Then-Senator Obama voted for it. Sen. Schumer voted for it. Sen. Clinton voted for it."
rationale: In 2006 Congress passed the Secure Fence Act, which authorized construction of extensive fencing and related barriers along parts of the U.S.–Mexico border. Senate roll-call records show then-Senator Barack Obama, Senator Chuck Schumer, and Senator Hillary Clinton voted in favor of the bill. The law authorized fencing rather than a single continuous concrete 'wall.'

claim: "Tommy Thompson created the first school choice program in the nation, giving thousands of Milwaukee students the choice of where they go to school – no matter where they live or how much money their parents make."
rationale: Tommy Thompson championed and signed the 1990 Milwaukee Parental Choice Program, which is often cited as the first modern school voucher program in the U.S., but he did not unilaterally 'create' it and the program originally had residency and income eligibility limits. It therefore is incorrect to say it gave 'thousands' of Milwaukee students unrestricted choice 'no matter where they live or how much money their parents make.'

claim: "The nuclear test conducted in our nation this time is the Earth's 2,054th nuclear test. The five permanent members of the U.N. Security Council have conducted 99.99 percent of the total nuclear tests."
rationale: While the global total of nuclear tests is on the order of about 2,000, the specific figure of 2,054 for 'this' test is not independently verifiable from standard tallies, and the claim that the five permanent U.N. Security Council members conducted 99.99% of all tests is incorrect. Several non‑P5 states (notably India, Pakistan and North Korea) have carried out multiple confirmed nuclear tests, so they account for well more than 0.01% of the worldwide total. P5 states performed the majority of tests, but not virtually every single one as 99.99% would imply.

claim: "Six justices" on the U.S. Supreme Court have been "confirmed in presidential election years since 1912."
rationale: The specific numeric claim (exactly six justices confirmed in presidential election years since 1912) does not align with standard historical rosters of Supreme Court confirmations. Known examples (e.g., Louis Brandeis in 1916, Benjamin Cardozo in 1932) show confirmations occurring in election years, but a review of confirmations from 1912 onward does not support the precise count of six without additional specification. I could not find authoritative evidence that the total equals six.

claim: "Bicycle ownership drops by half while obesity in Rhode Island rises by 154 percent"
rationale: This claim is unsupported and likely misleading: no authoritative data shows bicycle ownership in Rhode Island fell by half while obesity concurrently rose by 154%. Public health surveillance (e.g., CDC BRFSS) reports gradual increases in obesity prevalence over decades but not such dramatic percentage changes in short periods, and bicycle ownership figures from Census/ACS do not show a one‑time 50% collapse without a specified timeframe. The statement also lacks source, dates, and clear definitions, suggesting a misinterpretation or conflation of unrelated statistics.

claim: "Bill Gates says you don't have a choice to be vaccinated or not."
rationale: There is no reliable record of Bill Gates explicitly saying that individuals have no choice about being vaccinated. Publicly he has strongly advocated for vaccines and broad uptake to control disease, and has discussed policy tools to increase coverage, but that is different from an outright statement that people are legally or morally stripped of choice. Claims that he said this are consistent with misquotes and misinformation spread out of context.

claim: Online voter registration is a "more secure" way of doing voter registration.
rationale: Whether online voter registration is "more secure" is not universally true — security depends on how the system is designed and operated. Online systems can reduce paper-handling errors and allow automated identity checks, but they also introduce cyber risks (hacking, data breaches, phishing, availability attacks) and require strong authentication, encryption, and auditing to be secure. Without those safeguards, online registration can be less secure than well-controlled traditional processes.

claim: President Obama, Sen. Harry Reid and Rep. Nancy Pelosi passed a "$1.2 trillion stimulus bill."
rationale: This is false. The major 2009 stimulus signed by President Obama was the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, commonly estimated at about $787 billion, not $1.2 trillion, and presidents do not 'pass' bills—Congress passes legislation and the president signs it. While Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and House Speaker Nancy Pelosi were congressional leaders who helped advance the measure, the $1.2 trillion figure is inaccurate without additional context.

claim: John McCain says he never supported the privatization of Social Security, even though video shows he did.
rationale: During the 2008 campaign McCain at times asserted he had not supported privatizing Social Security, but archival video and earlier campaign statements (notably around 2000) show him endorsing private/personal accounts as an option. Contemporary fact-checkers reported that those earlier statements contradicted his later denials.

claim: Claims Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said "she prefers the South African Constitution over the United States Constitution."
rationale: This claim overstates and misrepresents Justice Ginsburg's remarks. Ginsburg publicly praised certain features of South Africa’s constitution (notably its equality and dignity provisions) and said she admired aspects that differed from U.S. law, but she did not state that she prefers the entire South African Constitution over the U.S. Constitution. The claim is a simplified, misleading restatement of her nuanced comments.

claim: Says that during his eight years as Florida governor, "we created 1.3 million net new jobs -- more jobs created than Texas."
rationale: Although Florida officials have cited roughly 1.3 million private‑sector jobs added over an eight‑year gubernatorial term, independent BLS state employment data for the same period show Texas added more jobs in absolute terms. The claim’s core comparative statement — that Florida created more jobs than Texas — is not supported by contemporaneous federal employment statistics.

claim: Sherrod Brown "voted six times to raise his own pay."
rationale: There is no clear authoritative record that Senator Sherrod Brown explicitly cast six roll-call votes solely to raise his own congressional pay. Claims like this typically conflate votes on broad budget bills, cost-of-living or federal employee pay provisions, or procedural actions with an explicit personal pay raise, and omit that pay changes for members are constrained by the 27th Amendment and often take effect only after the next election.

claim: Gov. Rick Scott's sale of the state planes was "not proper."
rationale: There is no public record of a definitive legal or official finding that Gov. Rick Scott's sale of state aircraft was unlawful or formally ruled 'not proper.' While the sales drew political criticism and scrutiny in news coverage, critics' statements did not become formal determinations of impropriety.

claim: Says he "beat (President Barack) Obama at the Supreme Court, saving coal jobs."
rationale: The statement conflates a complex legal outcome and broad economic trends into a simple personal victory. The Supreme Court issued a procedural stay of the Obama administration’s Clean Power Plan in 2016 in response to petitions from multiple states and industry groups, not as a personal win credited to one individual, and the long-term decline in U.S. coal jobs has been driven largely by market forces (cheap natural gas and renewables) as well as regulations, so claiming a single person 'beat Obama at the Supreme Court, saving coal jobs' is misleading and incorrect.

claim: "Heitkamp has voted against Trump 68 percent of time."
rationale: The statement asserts a precise 68% rate but provides no timeframe or data source; public vote-alignment trackers report different percentages for Senator Heidi Heitkamp depending on the period and methodology, and there is no consistent, well-documented figure of her voting against President Trump exactly 68% of the time. Without a specified period or source the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says each of the past three years "has been the hottest on record."
rationale: The claim as stated, without a timeframe, is misleading. Only certain consecutive years (notably 2014, 2015, and 2016) each set new global temperature records; many other recent three-year spans do not have every year as a record-setting year (for example 2017 was cooler than 2016). A blanket statement that each of the past three years 'has been the hottest on record' is therefore false unless a specific three-year period that meets that condition is named.

claim: Says Tallahassee "is experiencing a five-year low in our crime rate."
rationale: The claim provides no timeframe, data source, or definition of "crime rate," so it cannot be confirmed as stated. Crime statistics are reported by local police and federal systems and can vary by category (violent vs. property) and by exact five-year window; without checking Tallahassee PD or FBI/NIBRS data the assertion is unsupported.

claim: The Keystone pipeline creates "35 permanent jobs" after construction, according to a government report.
rationale: The U.S. Department of State’s environmental review for the Keystone XL project estimated roughly 35 permanent U.S. jobs associated with pipeline operations after construction. This figure has been widely cited by fact-checkers and news reports as the government estimate for direct, long-term jobs.

claim: "In Ohio, more than half the providers of safe and legal abortion have had to shut down" since Gov. John Kasich took office in 2011.
rationale: I cannot verify the blanket claim that more than half of Ohio’s safe, legal abortion providers closed since Kasich took office in 2011. Public data (from state reporting, media coverage, and reproductive-health research groups) document a substantial decline in clinic numbers over the 2010s but do not consistently show a >50% drop nationwide in Ohio across every authoritative dataset, and different counts and definitions produce different totals. Because the claim is stated categorically without citing a data source, it overstates what the available evidence clearly supports.

claim: Photos show cemeteries and war memorials damaged during George Floyd demonstrations.
rationale: There is no reliable, widely corroborated evidence that photos showing cemeteries and war memorials being damaged are from the George Floyd demonstrations; many viral images were fact-checked and found to be misattributed or from other times/places. While some protests included vandalism of statues and monuments, the specific claim that photos show cemeteries and war memorials damaged during those demonstrations is not supported by verified reporting.

claim: About "1 percent of all the gun sellers are responsible for more than half of the guns that are used in crimes."
rationale: Multiple analyses of ATF trace data and academic studies have found that a very small share of licensed gun dealers — on the order of one percent — account for a disproportionately large share (often reported as more than half) of guns recovered and traced in crimes. The specific phrasing and exact percentage depend on the dataset and time period, but the core claim reflects documented patterns of a small number of sources supplying many crime guns. This finding is about traced/recovered guns and dealer-level concentration rather than all sellers or all firearms transfers.

claim: "Johns Hopkins University confirms: You can be vaccinated with a PCR test, even without knowing"
rationale: Johns Hopkins has not confirmed that a PCR diagnostic test can vaccinate someone. PCR tests collect samples (swabs) and use reagents to detect viral genetic material; they do not contain vaccine antigens or mRNA and have no mechanism to induce immunity. Vaccination requires delivery of a vaccine formulation by approved routes and doses, which diagnostic swabs and PCR reagents are not.

claim: "While fat-cat bureaucrats at the Department of Education are getting paid an average salary of $102,000 a year, teachers in Georgia are getting paid half of that."
rationale: The statement mixes and misrepresents figures: the often-cited $102,000 number for the Department of Education is misleading without a specified year or definition (mean vs median and whether benefits are included), and Georgia teachers’ average pay is not precisely half that — recent state data put Georgia teacher salaries in the low-to-mid $50,000s to low $60,000s depending on year and source. The claim uses inflammatory language and conflates different pay populations, making the comparison inaccurate.

claim: "Vern Buchanan. His old business was caught illegally funneling over $60,000 in campaign donations to Buchanan to influence his election."
rationale: Public reporting shows Vern Buchanan has been the subject of allegations and probes about campaign contributions tied to businesses and associates, but there is no definitive public record that his old business was legally found to have illegally funneled over $60,000 to his campaign. No criminal conviction or official enforcement finding confirming that exact scheme and amount has been established against Buchanan or his business in major news and legal records.

claim: "California Democrat Maxine Waters charged on 3 counts."
rationale: There is no credible public record or mainstream news reporting that U.S. Representative Maxine Waters has been criminally charged on three counts. Indictments of a sitting congresswoman would be widely reported and appear in Department of Justice filings, but no such charges have been reported as of mid-2024.

claim: Under the current procedure, if someone "on a terror watch list" tries to buy a gun, authorities are notified.
rationale: This claim overstates how the system works. Being on a terrorism watchlist does not automatically prevent a gun purchase nor universally trigger a notification to local authorities; NICS checks may return a “possible match” or delay that prompts further FBI review, but many watchlist entries are not sufficient to produce an automatic denial or routine notification. Historical reviews (GAO/DOJ reporting) have documented gaps and discretionary handling of watchlist matches.

claim: "I’m running the second-largest county district attorney’s office … at 1985 staffing levels."
rationale: The claim is a specific factual statement about current staffing compared to 1985 levels for the 'second-largest county district attorney’s office,' but no corroborating data or a named county is provided. Publicly available staffing and budget data for large county DA offices generally show net growth or significant changes since 1985, making an exact match to 1985 staffing unlikely without supporting evidence.

claim: "As chairman of the City Colleges, I cut millions in waste and we cut property taxes."
rationale: The claim mixes an unverified claim of cutting “millions in waste” with an assertion about cutting property taxes. Community college board chairs may oversee budgets and implement efficiencies, but they do not have unilateral authority to set or cut property tax rates—which are set by elected taxing bodies and through public levies. Without specific audited budget records and a named jurisdiction/timeframe, the combined claim is not supported.

claim: Wrote that in 2006, Nancy Pelosi said she didn’t think capturing Osama bin Laden "makes us any safer," but in 2011 called his killing "historic."
rationale: Contemporary news reports record that in 2006 Pelosi expressed skepticism that capturing Osama bin Laden "would make us any safer," and after the 2011 raid she publicly called bin Laden’s killing "historic." Both statements were widely reported and attributed to her in the respective years.

claim: Says a photo shows Adam Schiff and Jeffrey Epstein.
rationale: There is no credible, authenticated photograph showing Rep. Adam Schiff together with Jeffrey Epstein; viral images claiming this have been debunked as misidentifications or digitally altered. Major fact-checkers and image analyses have found the person pictured is not Schiff or the image has been manipulated.

claim: "From 2000 to 2016, every major drug that was introduced came out of" National Institutes of Health funding.
rationale: This is inaccurate. Although NIH-funded basic research has contributed to many therapies, it is not true that every major drug introduced from 2000–2016 'came out of' NIH funding. Many major new drugs in that period were discovered and developed primarily by private pharmaceutical or biotech companies without direct NIH funding, even if NIH-supported science occasionally informed later work.

claim: Says in 2000, Fox News broke the story of George W. Bush’s drunk driving arrest. "Who broke it? Fox News."
rationale: There is no evidence that Fox News was the outlet that 'broke' an alleged George W. Bush drunk driving arrest in 2000. Contemporary reporting and later fact-checks indicate the allegation circulated via local sources, opposition research, and gossip channels rather than a Fox News investigative scoop, and major outlets did not credit Fox with breaking such a story.

claim: I am the only U.S. Senate candidate who spoke out against bombing Syria, and who challenged Georgia’s governor and insurance commissioner over obstruction to the Affordable Care Act.
rationale: The claim asserts uniqueness across all U.S. Senate candidates for two separate positions, which is implausible and not verifiable without exhaustive, time-bounded evidence. Many Senate candidates and public figures have publicly opposed bombing Syria and many have criticized Georgia officials over Affordable Care Act implementation, so claiming to be the sole candidate is almost certainly incorrect. Without a specific election cycle, candidate name, and documented comparisons, the uniqueness claim fails.

claim: "We haven't had any legislation which took away one gun in the past 20 years from anybody in this country--not one."
rationale: False — in the past 20 years many jurisdictions have passed laws that authorize removal of firearms from individuals. Examples include state 'red flag' (extreme risk protection) laws and statutes requiring surrender of guns after protective orders or disqualifying convictions, which have resulted in courts or authorities ordering guns be turned over or seized.

claim: "750 days since Bill Nelson & the Democrats in the Senate passed a budget. How can this be justified?"
rationale: The statement is misleading and unsupported: a single senator (Bill Nelson) cannot by himself 'pass a budget,' and federal budgets are enacted by both chambers of Congress and the President. The claim's 750-day count and attribution to "the Democrats in the Senate" cannot be verified without a clear reference date or definition of "passed a budget" (budget resolution vs. appropriations), and recent years have seen a mix of appropriations bills and continuing resolutions rather than a single omnibus budget event that matches the claim.

claim: Says Texas routinely gets "a lot more federal spending" than it pays in taxes.
rationale: Whether Texas is a net beneficiary of federal spending varies by year and by how receipts and taxes are measured; it is not accurate to say Texas 'routinely gets a lot more' than it pays. State-level Treasury/BEA data show Texas often near parity or fluctuating between modest net recipient and modest net contributor depending on the fiscal year and what items (grants, contracts, retirement, etc.) are included, so the blanket claim overstates and oversimplifies the evidence.

claim: "Senator Cryin’ Chuck Schumer fought hard against the Bad Iran Deal, even going at it with President Obama, & then Voted AGAINST it! Now he says I should not have terminated the deal"
rationale: Senator Chuck Schumer publicly opposed the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement, engaged in a high-profile clash with the Obama administration over it, and supported congressional measures to disapprove the deal. After President Trump withdrew the U.S. from the JCPOA in 2018, Schumer criticized the unilateral termination and said the president should not have ended the agreement in that manner.

claim: Says CNN President Jeff Zucker ordered employees to downplay Bill Clinton’s relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and make it look like Epstein was "Trump’s partner in all of this."
rationale: There is no credible, publicly documented evidence that Jeff Zucker instructed CNN staff to downplay Bill Clinton’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein or to portray Epstein as ‘Trump’s partner in all of this.’ Major news outlets and independent fact-checkers have not substantiated such an order, and the claim appears to stem from partisan allegation rather than verifiable internal communications or reliable eyewitness testimony.

claim: "The price of soybeans has fallen 50% since 5 years before the election. A big reason is bad (terrible) trade deals with other countries."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about which election and five‑year window is meant, and there is no clear, general fact that soybean prices have fallen exactly 50% over every plausible five‑year period before an election. Moreover, attributing a large price move chiefly to vague "bad trade deals" is unsupported: soybean prices are driven by multiple factors (global supply/demand, weather, currency moves, crop yields, and specific trade disruptions), so a single causal attribution to unspecified trade deals is not justified.

claim: Says he has supported "George Bush more than I have Barack Obama."
rationale: The claim presents an unattributed quote with no speaker, time, or source. I cannot verify that any specific person said “I have supported George Bush more than I have Barack Obama” on the available evidence, so the statement is unverified and is treated as false under the instructions to prefer false when uncertain.

claim: "We've seen the increase of alcohol use for underage kids even though alcohol has been illegal ... for kids under 21."
rationale: Major national surveys show long-term declines in underage alcohol use in the United States rather than an overall increase. Reports from Monitoring the Future, the CDC Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System, and NSDUH indicate lower past‑month drinking and binge drinking among teens compared with past decades, so the blanket claim of an increase is not supported.

claim: Says the Georgia Dome would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting from the Atlanta stadium debate cited a consultant study and officials who said keeping the aging Georgia Dome would require up to about $350 million in work over the next five to seven years; that estimate was repeatedly used to justify replacing the Dome. The figure and timeframe were widely reported in local news and public agency discussions.

claim: "AIG insures the pension trust of the United States Congress!"
rationale: U.S. congressional pensions are federal retirement benefits administered under federal law (and typically processed by OPM or the Treasury) and are not insured as a private pension trust by AIG. There is no public evidence that AIG is the insurer backing the Members of Congress retirement system; government pension obligations are effectively backed by the U.S. government, not a private insurer.

claim: "I’ve been against that war in Afghanistan from the very beginning."
rationale: The statement is a first-person claim with no identified speaker or supporting evidence here, so it cannot be verified as true. Establishing it would require checking that individual's contemporaneous public statements, votes, or other records showing opposition at the time the Afghanistan war began, none of which are provided.

claim: Says Mitt Romney belittled middle-class tax cuts "as nothing more than 'little Band-Aids.' "
rationale: There is no clear, contemporaneous record of Mitt Romney using the exact phrase 'little Band-Aids' to belittle middle‑class tax cuts. Romney did criticize aspects of opponents' economic proposals during campaigns, but credible transcripts and fact‑checks do not substantiate this direct quote and it appears to be a paraphrase or attack‑ad framing rather than his wording.

claim: "Nationwide tuition at public universities is up almost 300 percent ... in the last 20 years."
rationale: National averages for public university tuition have risen substantially over the last two decades, but not by 'almost 300%' across the board. Most authoritative sources (NCES, College Board) show much smaller increases in average published tuition and fees—especially after adjusting for inflation—and large variation by state, campus, and whether in‑state or out‑of‑state rates are used. While some individual schools or categories (out‑of‑state or private) may have seen very large nominal increases, the nationwide average is far below 300% over a 20‑year span.

claim: Says PolitiFact reported that "95 percent of what (Donald Trump) says is a lie."
rationale: PolitiFact has not published a finding that "95 percent" of Donald Trump’s statements are lies. PolitiFact rates individual claims with categories (True, Mostly True, Half True, Mostly False, False, Pants on Fire) and while it has found a large share of Trump statements to be false or misleading, no official PolitiFact report uses the specific 95% figure. The 95% number appears to be a misattribution or an approximate claim from other analyses or commentators, not a PolitiFact conclusion.

claim: Says he is the "ranking member" of the House select committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol.
rationale: The statement as given is unverifiable because it omits who “he” is; without a named individual there is no way to confirm that person claimed to be the committee’s ranking member. Additionally, the title “ranking member” on the Jan. 6 select committee was politically disputed and required formal designation by House Republican leadership, so blanket claims need specific attribution. Because of missing context, the claim cannot be treated as a factual assertion about any particular person.

claim: "If your employer is mandating any pokes, do not quit. Make them fire you. That way you get unemployment benefits."
rationale: This is an overbroad prescription. Eligibility for unemployment benefits depends on jurisdiction and the reason for separation: many places deny benefits if you are fired for misconduct (which can include refusing a lawful workplace policy), while in other circumstances (e.g., termination for reasons beyond your control, or valid medical/religious exemptions not accommodated) you may be eligible. Quitting voluntarily also often disqualifies unless you had 'good cause' under local rules.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton sold 20 percent of America’s uranium to Russia and then "the Russian government gave $145 million to the Clinton Foundation." Former FBI Director and special counsel Robert Mueller "delivered it."
rationale: The claim misstates and conflates separate facts. In 2010 Rosatom acquired Uranium One, which at the time controlled interests representing about 20% of U.S. uranium production capacity, but that transaction was approved by the multi-agency CFIUS panel (not 'sold by Hillary Clinton' personally). There is no credible evidence that the Russian government paid $145 million to the Clinton Foundation as part of the deal, and Robert Mueller had no role in 'delivering' any such payment; subsequent reporting and reviews found no quid pro quo linking Clinton to the sale.

claim: "The richest 1 percent of America will get a bigger tax cut through this bill than the family income of the average family here in Central Texas."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it fails to identify which bill and what time period (annual vs cumulative) the tax cut refers to. Estimates of major recent tax bills show top-1% benefits that vary widely depending on whether amounts are measured per year or over multiple years, and local "average family income" for Central Texas also varies by definition and geography. Without a specified bill, timeframe, and locale definition the absolute comparison cannot be supported.

claim: "Bill Nelson voted for a ban on millions of commonly owned firearms, which included many popular hunting and target rifles."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. Bill Nelson was not in Congress for the 1994 federal assault weapons ban and did not cast a vote that banned “millions of commonly owned firearms,” and no later Senate action by Nelson banned widely owned hunting/target rifles. The 1994 law targeted certain newly manufactured semiautomatic models and cosmetic features and grandfathered existing guns rather than confiscating broadly owned hunting or target rifles.

claim: "New evidence ties COVID-19 creation to research funded by Fauci"
rationale: There is no credible new evidence showing SARS-CoV-2 was created with funding from Anthony Fauci. While NIH (including NIAID, which Fauci led) funded some coronavirus research via grants to organizations like EcoHealth Alliance, multiple investigations, public records, expert reviews, and intelligence assessments have not produced verifiable proof that those funds financed creation of the virus.

claim: "The president and vice president can't be from the same state."
rationale: The Constitution does not bar a president and vice president from being from the same state. The Twelfth Amendment restricts electors — it requires that at least one of the two persons voted for by a given state's electors not be an inhabitant of that state, which means electors from a shared-home state cannot cast both of their votes for candidates of their own state, but it does not forbid the candidates themselves from being from the same state.

claim: "All schools in Canada are closed for the rest of the school year, each family will receive $950 every two weeks for the next 15 weeks, banks were notif(ied) to suspend mortgage payments for at least 6 months, and student loans deferred."
rationale: The claim bundles several policies that were not universally implemented as stated. School closures during the COVID-19 period were decided provincially and were not uniformly closed for the rest of the school year across all provinces. The payment amount and schedule ($950 every two weeks for 15 weeks to each family) does not match federal emergency benefits (e.g., CERB was roughly $500/week to eligible workers), and banks generally offered mortgage deferral options on request rather than being ordered to suspend payments for everyone for at least six months. Federal student loan repayment was paused/interest-free for a limited period, but provincial loan policies and details varied.

claim: Says New Jersey Rep. Leonard Lance voted repeatedly "to let insurance companies charge more to people aged 50 and over."
rationale: Leonard Lance voted for House Republican health bills (notably the 2017 American Health Care Act and related repeal measures) that would have loosened age‑rating protections and replaced ACA subsidies with age‑tiered tax credits, measures that would let insurers charge older adults substantially higher premiums. Those votes were repeated across multiple repeal/replace legislative actions in the House, so the characterization that he voted repeatedly to allow insurers to charge more for people aged 50+ is accurate.

claim: Says Chris Christie was the "first governor in America to endorse" Mitt Romney.
rationale: Chris Christie did endorse Mitt Romney, but he was not the first governor to do so; Romney received gubernatorial endorsements before Christie's public endorsement. The claim lacks context (which Romney campaign and whether "governor" means sitting or former), and under ordinary readings it is inaccurate.

claim: "Eighty percent of the antibiotics in this country are fed to livestock."
rationale: The claim is overly broad and unqualified: antibiotic use by sector varies by country, year, and how use is measured. In some past U.S. reports a large share (around 70–80% by weight) of antibiotics sold were for food animals, but that depended on the year and included drugs not used in human medicine; many countries show very different shares. Without a specified country, timeframe, and definition of “antibiotics,” the blanket 80% statement is not reliably true.

claim: "Russ Feingold got a memo in 2009 that outlined veteran harm" at a Wisconsin VA facility "and nothing was done."
rationale: There is no reliable, contemporaneous reporting or documentation showing that Senator Russ Feingold received a 2009 memo describing veteran harm at a Wisconsin VA facility and that nothing was done. Major investigations of VA problems (including Tomah and Phoenix) from 2014–2015 do not corroborate a specific 2009 memo to Feingold, and Feingold left the Senate in 2011, making this particular claim unsubstantiated.

claim: "The vast majority of our public school students are receiving less state support than their private voucher peers."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and generally incorrect: in most U.S. contexts the total per-student funding that public school students receive (state plus local and federal dollars) exceeds the typical private-school voucher amounts, which are usually partial scholarships or fixed payments below average public per-pupil spending. While some jurisdictions or specific voucher programs may offer payments comparable to or higher than certain public allocations for some students, those are exceptions and do not support the blanket claim that the vast majority of public students receive less state support than voucher peers.

claim: Says the California congressional district he represents "has a higher GDP than Russia."
rationale: No individual California congressional district has a nominal GDP anywhere near the size of Russia's national GDP. Russia's economy in recent years has been on the order of roughly $1.5–2.5 trillion (nominal), while even the wealthiest U.S. metropolitan areas or congressional districts have GDPs measured in the hundreds of billions, not trillions. Therefore the statement that a single congressional district exceeds Russia's GDP is false.

claim: "Austin is the largest city in the U.S. or Texas with no geographic representation" on its city council.
rationale: Austin has a district-based city council (a 10-1 system: ten single-member geographic districts plus an at-large mayor), so it does have geographic representation and is not a largest-city exception. Larger U.S. and Texas cities (e.g., Houston, San Antonio, Dallas) also use district representation for council seats.

claim: There are "49 different federal job training programs that report to eight agencies."
rationale: I cannot confirm the specific claim that there are exactly '49' federal job training programs reporting to exactly eight agencies. Authoritative government reviews (GAO and Congressional Research Service) have reported different program and agency totals at different times, and counts depend on how programs are defined and grouped. Because reported totals vary and no single current authoritative source supports the precise 49/8 figure, the claim as stated is not reliably true.

claim: Tim Kaine "made Virginia the best state for business four years in a row."
rationale: The claim that Tim Kaine “made Virginia the best state for business four years in a row” overstates what is supported. While Virginia did receive high business rankings from publications in multiple years around Kaine's governorship, the phrasing credits Kaine with a four-year consecutive #1 ranking without specifying the ranking source or exact years, and available rankings do not clearly support an uncontested four-year streak attributable solely to his actions.

claim: The Senate Republican education plan is an unfunded mandate for local school districts.
rationale: The statement cannot be verified as true because “the Senate Republican education plan” is unspecified; whether a proposal constitutes an unfunded mandate depends on the actual bill text and accompanying appropriations. Some Republican education proposals include new requirements paired with funding or block grants, while others attach conditions to existing funds, so the blanket claim is not demonstrably accurate without identifying the specific legislation.

claim: Says Rick Scott "didn’t even come to his own education summit. But he did take time to go to the tea party convention the same week."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific assertion as stated — there is no clear, contemporaneous record identifying which 'education summit' and which 'tea party convention' are meant, nor reliable reporting confirming that Rick Scott skipped his own summit while attending a Tea Party event in the same week. Because the claim ties two specific attendance facts to the same timeframe without precise dates or sources, it cannot be confirmed and should not be accepted as factual as presented.

claim: Says Clint Eastwood called Joe Biden an "incompetent, lying, flip-flopping, insincere, double-talking, radical socialist."
rationale: There are no credible news reports, transcripts, or verified clips showing Clint Eastwood uttering that exact string of epithets about Joe Biden. The phrase reads like a composite of common political insults circulated online and appears to be a misattribution or fabrication rather than a documented quote.

claim: Says it was "a crime for Nixon to wiretap the Democrats at Watergate but OK for Obama to wiretap Republicans at Trump Tower."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Obama ordered wiretaps of Republicans at Trump Tower; the allegation (famously tweeted by President Trump in March 2017) was investigated and not substantiated by DOJ inspector general and congressional reviews. By contrast, Nixon-era wiretaps around Watergate were illegal and led to prosecutions, so the specific claim that it was a crime for Nixon but "OK for Obama" is unsupported.

claim: "We sell 40 percent of our guns without a background check."
rationale: The statement is a blanket claim with no context and overstates what is known. Federal law requires licensed firearms dealers to run background checks through NICS, and most retail sales are screened; while private sales (at gun shows, online, etc.) can occur without checks in some jurisdictions, reputable surveys and analyses generally report lower and variable rates than a uniform 40% nationwide. Therefore the unqualified claim is misleading and likely false.

claim: "Maxine Waters Is Getting Criminally Charged!"
rationale: There is no public record or credible reporting indicating Representative Maxine Waters has been criminally charged or indicted. High-profile criminal charges against a sitting Member of Congress would be widely reported by major news outlets and recorded in court filings; no such filings or credible reports existed through mid‑2024.
cited_knowledge: Knowledge of major news coverage, lack of DOJ or court indictment filings against Maxine Waters through mid‑2024, and standard legal procedures for criminal charging.
safety_notes: Claim lacks date or jurisdiction; if making this assessment after mid‑2024, please check current news and court records as circumstances could have changed.

claim: "We have an increase in murder within our cities, the biggest in 45 years."
rationale: The statement is too vague and not clearly supported as written. While many U.S. cities experienced large increases in homicides in 2020–2021, declaring a nationwide increase as 'the biggest in 45 years' depends on the exact country, timeframe, and whether one measures percentage change or absolute counts, and federal crime data do not unambiguously support that specific blanket claim. Historical homicide trends have fluctuated, so the claim is misleading without precise context and sourcing.

claim: Says Matt Wand has sided with anti-choice activists "to restrict access to reproductive health care services."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence in my available knowledge that a specific public figure named Matt Wand publicly sided with anti‑choice activists to restrict reproductive health access. The name is ambiguous and without corroborating reports, voting records, or public statements I cannot confirm the accusation. Given the lack of clear, attributable documentation, the claim should not be treated as established fact.

claim: "Estimates say individuals who escaped these high tax states have taken with them around $2 trillion in adjusted gross income."
rationale: The statement is unsupported and implausible as written: it gives no timeframe or named states and cites no source. Total U.S. adjusted gross income is on the order of $10–12 trillion, and IRS/state migration analyses and media reports indicate that AGI moved by taxpayers who changed state residency is much smaller than $2 trillion, not commensurate with the claim.

claim: Says Joe Biden’s website shows that he supports the Green New Deal, despite denials in debate.
rationale: During the 2019–2020 campaign Biden publicly said in debates that he did not back the Green New Deal resolution, yet his campaign climate plan and website endorsed many of the same goals and policies (net‑zero by midcentury, large clean‑energy investments, justice provisions). Multiple news fact-checks noted the discrepancy that he rejected the label while supporting core elements. Thus the website content supports the claim that he backed Green New Deal–style policies despite debate denials.

claim: A recall election for Wisconsin governor would cost "$7.7 million -- $7.7 million that may already be allocated to merit raises for teachers or health care for the poor or school books for your kids."
rationale: It is true that Wisconsin election officials estimated a gubernatorial recall would cost on the order of $7–8 million, but the claim's assertion that those exact dollars "may already be allocated" to teacher merit raises, health care for the poor, or schoolbooks is unsubstantiated and misleading. State election expenses come from general appropriations and budgeting is complex; there is no clear evidence that the estimated recall cost was specifically reserved for those particular programs.

claim: "Today, the United States has, sadly, one of the lowest voter turnouts of any major country on earth."
rationale: The United States does have relatively low turnout compared with many advanced democracies, but it is not universally one of the very lowest countries on earth. Turnout rankings depend on the metric (voting-age vs. voting-eligible population) and the type of election, and several major countries have similar or lower participation rates.

claim: The "top ten most unhealthy U.S. cities" are San Francisco; Seattle; Portland, Oregon; San Diego; Honolulu; Washington; Austin, Texas; Irving, Texas; Portland, Maine; and Denver.
rationale: Reputable city health and wellness rankings (based on metrics like obesity, smoking, access to care, and life expectancy) typically list San Francisco, Seattle, Portland (OR and ME), San Diego, Honolulu, Washington, Austin, Irving, and Denver among the healthier—not most unhealthy—U.S. cities. The stated list contradicts standard public-health indices and common-sense indicators of population health in those metro areas.

claim: "Republicans would give seniors a (Medicare) voucher that limits what's covered, costing seniors as much as $6,400 more a year."
rationale: The claim is an overbroad characterization. Some Republican proposals (so-called “premium support” or voucher plans) would replace traditional Medicare’s financing with fixed payments and could, according to nonpartisan analyses, lead some beneficiaries to face higher premiums or narrower plan choices; however, whether coverage is explicitly "limited" and whether seniors would pay "$6,400 more a year" depends entirely on the specific proposal, year, and modeling assumptions. The $6,400 figure appears to come from particular analyses or scenarios and is not a universal, across-the-board outcome of all Republican plans.

claim: Says 19,000 text messages exchanged between former FBI officials that were "purposely and illegally deleted ... would have explained (the special counsel investigation) hoax."
rationale: The DOJ Office of the Inspector General found that thousands of FBI text messages were not preserved because of device replacement and recordkeeping/technical failures, and it did not conclude they were purposely or illegally deleted. There is no evidence that the missing messages would have proven the special counsel investigation was a 'hoax' — that assertion is speculative and unsupported by the IG findings or subsequent public records.

claim: Says the state’s budget shortfall is "not that much different" than it was in 2003.
rationale: The statement is unverified and likely misleading because it gives no state or current year and compares nominal shortfalls across a 20+ year span. Budget shortfalls must be compared in real (inflation-adjusted) terms and relative to current budgets and populations; most states' fiscal positions have changed materially since 2003, so asserting they are 'not that much different' is unsupported without detailed, adjusted figures.

claim: Says Charlie Crist "was pro-life, pro-gun and vehemently anti-tax."
rationale: The statement is an oversimplification. While Crist, as a Republican governor, supported gun rights and campaigned on low-tax themes, his positions shifted over time (he later became a Democrat and publicly identified as pro‑choice), so describing him uniformly as “pro‑life, pro‑gun and vehemently anti‑tax” is inaccurate without a specific timeframe.

claim: "In the 2020 election, President Trump voted from behind the desk in the White House in Florida."
rationale: The statement is factually incorrect because the White House is in Washington, D.C., not in Florida, so one cannot have voted "from behind the desk in the White House in Florida." Donald Trump had established Florida as his primary residence by 2019 and cast his 2020 ballot as a Florida resident, but there is no evidence he voted from any Florida location described as the White House desk. The claim conflates locations and is therefore false.

claim: Shirley Sherrod "was forced to resign before anybody on Fox said a word about this."
rationale: The claim that Sherrod was forced to resign before anyone at Fox said anything is inaccurate. An edited clip posted by Andrew Breitbart sparked immediate coverage across conservative outlets including Fox affiliates and websites the same day USDA Secretary Tom Vilsack accepted her resignation; Fox commentators and Fox News-related sites reported on the controversy very quickly.

claim: Says Nancy Pelosi "made millions in coronavirus insider trading."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi personally engaged in illegal insider trading related to the coronavirus; fact-checks and reporting show the trades in question were executed by her husband as private investments and were publicly disclosed. Multiple independent fact-checkers and news organizations found no proof that Pelosi used nonpublic congressional information or was charged with wrongdoing.

claim: George Allen voted for budgets that increased the national debt by $16,400 for every second he served in the U.S. Senate.
rationale: The claim is a misleading attribution: it appears to divide total federal debt growth during Allen's Senate term by the number of seconds he served and assigns the entire amount to his votes. While total debt did rise by several trillion dollars in 2001–2007 (which yields a similar per‑second number when divided by seconds in six years), a single senator does not unilaterally cause that increase and the arithmetic depends on which dates and measures of debt are used.

claim: Republican challenger Bill Flores "has never once voted in a general election in our district."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute that Bill Flores never voted in any general election in a named district, but there is no publicly available evidence to support such a sweeping statement. Voter participation records (where public) and contemporary reporting about Flores — a long‑time resident and congressional candidate — do not substantiate that he never voted, making the absolute claim unsupported.

claim: Says a Congressional Budget Office report found low-income seniors in Florida will face "800 percent premium increases" under the American Health Care Act.
rationale: The CBO’s March 2017 analyses produced national estimates and scenarios about how premiums and coverage would change under the American Health Care Act, but it did not report a finding that low-income seniors in Florida would face “800 percent premium increases.” That figure appears to be a misinterpretation or extrapolation by others (often comparing a near-zero current subsidy to a much larger unsubsidized premium), not a specific CBO conclusion for Florida.

claim: Wisconsin bill "grants drug companies and medical device manufacturers immunity from injuries and deaths caused by their products."
rationale: There is no evidence that any recent Wisconsin bill creates blanket immunity shielding drug companies and medical device manufacturers from all liability for injuries and deaths caused by their products. Product liability is typically governed by longstanding state tort law and federal regulations, and when immunity has been granted in past measures it has been narrow and situational (for example limited pandemic-era or government-contracted actions), not an across-the-board exemption from lawsuits for harms caused by products.

claim: Says West Virginia is "down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working now because of addiction or conviction."
rationale: The claim that West Virginia is "down to around 50 percent of the adult workers who are actually working now because of addiction or conviction" is not supported by available labor and public-health data. State employment-population and labor-force participation rates are higher than the claim implies, and while West Virginia has elevated rates of opioid use and relatively high incarceration compared with some states, the combined numbers of people incarcerated or with substance-use disorders do not account for half of the adult population or explain a 50% working rate attributable solely to addiction/conviction.

claim: "The number of people who just got their voting rights restored in Florida is greater than the populations of Wyoming, Vermont, Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Delaware, Rhode Island, Montana, Maine and New Hampshire."
rationale: Florida’s 2018 Amendment 4 (and subsequent actions) affected roughly 1.3–1.5 million people whose rights could be restored, whereas the combined population of Wyoming, Vermont, Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Delaware, Rhode Island, Montana, Maine and New Hampshire is on the order of about 9–10 million. Therefore the number of Floridians whose voting rights were restored is far smaller than the total population of those ten states combined.

claim: As a senator, Hillary Clinton "has her name on three laws in eight years."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Counts of laws "having her name on" depend on whether one counts primary sponsorship, cosponsorship, or bills that merely reference a senator; fact-checkers have noted that Clinton sponsored or cosponsored many measures during her Senate tenure and the simple claim that she had her name on only three laws over eight years is an inaccurate simplification. Without a clear definition of what counts, the claim as stated is not reliably true.

claim: Says unlike Tim Kaine, who "invested" in education, Indiana Gov. Mike Pence "slashed education funding."
rationale: The statement is misleading: Tim Kaine, as Virginia governor, did oversee increases in education funding and teacher pay, but Mike Pence did not enact a blanket 'slashing' of education funding in Indiana. K–12 funding in Indiana was generally stable or modestly increased in several budgets under Pence, while higher education and certain programs saw cuts and Pence also expanded school choice/voucher policies — so calling it a simple 'slashing' overstates and conflates different categories.

claim: "Under ‘Trumpcare,’" domestic violence and sexual assault "could be considered pre-existing conditions."
rationale: Republican ACA-replacement proposals (commonly called 'Trumpcare', e.g., the 2017 AHCA) included state waiver options and plan designs that weakened uniform protections and allowed insurers greater leeway in underwriting and benefit limits. They did not specifically bar treating conditions stemming from domestic violence or sexual assault (such as PTSD, injuries, or related medical needs) as pre-existing, so such conditions could, in practice, be used to affect coverage or cost under those proposals.

claim: "About 95 percent of America’s production of ethylene is produced on the Gulf Coast in Texas and Louisiana."
rationale: The statement overstates the concentration. While a large majority of U.S. ethylene capacity and production is indeed clustered on the Gulf Coast (especially Texas and Louisiana), independent industry and government data indicate the share is substantially less than 95%. Estimates typically place Gulf Coast capacity/production well below that figure, depending on whether one counts only ethylene monomer, ethylene-equivalent streams, or downstream derivatives.

claim: Says Republican lawmakers delayed COVID-19 testing
rationale: The claim is an overbroad generalization. While actions by some federal and state Republican officials (and the Trump administration's early regulatory choices and the CDC's flawed test) contributed to delays in scaling COVID-19 testing, it is not accurate to say 'Republican lawmakers' as a whole delayed testing—responses and positions varied, and multiple actors and technical failures were involved.

claim: "On the pace that we're on with job creation in the last four months ... we will have created more jobs in this year than in the entire Bush Presidency."
rationale: The statement is misleading and cannot be affirmed without precise definitions and numbers. George W. Bush's presidency included large job losses during the 2008–09 recession, so comparisons depend on whether one means net jobs over the whole presidency or gross monthly hires, and on the specific year and four-month pace used for the projection. Extrapolating a short recent trend to claim it will exceed an entire presidency's job change is unreliable and likely inaccurate as stated.

claim: Says Donald Trump's first 17 Cabinet appointments "have a net worth of more than a third of America."
rationale: Public estimates put the combined net worth of President Trump's first 17 Cabinet appointees in the low billions of dollars, while total U.S. household/net worth is in the tens of trillions—so their combined wealth is a tiny fraction, not one-third, of national wealth. The claim therefore materially overstates their share of 'America' when read as one-third of the country's wealth.

claim: Says Google Earth blocked people from seeing the Suez Canal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Google Earth deliberately blocked public viewing of the Suez Canal. The canal is covered by publicly available satellite imagery on Google Earth and other map services; occasional low-resolution tiles, cloud cover, or delayed imagery updates can make it appear obscured but these are technical/update artifacts rather than intentional blocking.

claim: "Since that famous day in February where the governor campaigned with Barack Obama on behalf of the stimulus program, 211,000 Floridians have lost their jobs."
rationale: The claim gives a precise cumulative jobs-loss number tied to an unspecified February date and an unnamed governor but cites no data source or clear time window. Official employment series (monthly state nonfarm payrolls and household employment) tracked by the BLS and Florida agencies do not support accepting a specific 211,000 figure without a cited start and end month; such claims are frequently misstated or cherry-picked. Because the statement lacks verifiable sourcing and precise dates, it is not supported as presented.

claim: "We don't need a separate (prescription drug) database ... Pharmacies already have a database in place."
rationale: While individual pharmacies and pharmacy chains maintain internal electronic records of prescriptions they dispense, those systems are proprietary, fragmented, and do not provide a comprehensive, standardized dataset for regulators, public health, or cross-pharmacy monitoring. Many jurisdictions have separate prescription drug monitoring programs or centralized databases precisely because pharmacy systems alone do not meet needs for statewide surveillance, interoperability, or access control. Therefore the claim that a separate database is unnecessary because pharmacies already have one is misleading.

claim: "Under President Obama, U.S. security funding for Israel is at an all-time high."
rationale: The Obama administration negotiated and announced a 2016 10-year Memorandum of Understanding guaranteeing $38 billion in U.S. military assistance to Israel, the largest such security-assistance pledge in U.S. history. That commitment represented an all-time high level of U.S. security funding pledged to Israel compared with prior agreements.

claim: Says Measure 3-386 will cost a fortune for elections while Measure 3-388 will cost less.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because measure numbers are jurisdiction-specific and no supporting fiscal analysis or official cost estimates are provided. Whether one measure is dramatically more expensive than another depends on the specific text, implementation details, and the jurisdiction’s official fiscal notes, none of which are cited here.

claim: "We know mask mandates work. There’s enough evidence out there between counties that have done it and counties that haven’t."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed observational studies and public-health reviews comparing jurisdictions (counties/states) with and without mask mandates found reductions in COVID-19 case growth and transmission after mandates were implemented. While these are largely natural experiments rather than randomized trials, the aggregate evidence supports that mask mandates reduce spread when coupled with compliance.

claim: Federal money for Medicaid expansion "is guaranteed for a few years and then goes away."
rationale: Under current law (the ACA), federal payments for Medicaid expansion were 100% for newly eligible enrollees for the initial years and then phased down, reaching a permanent federal match of at least 90% by 2020. The federal share does not simply 'go away' after a few years; it remains a significant ongoing match unless Congress changes the law.

claim: "We saw the president of the United States engage American troops in a fourth conflict in a foreign land. This is historic."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify: it does not identify which president, what counts as a distinct 'conflict', or the time period. Numerous U.S. presidents have authorized or engaged American forces in multiple foreign operations across different administrations, so the unqualified claim that 'we saw the president ... engage American troops in a fourth conflict' cannot be confirmed as a factual, historically unique event. The characterization 'This is historic' is subjective and unsupported without context.

claim: "A portion of everything you pay A.A.R.P goes directly to the Democratic Party."
rationale: AARP is officially a nonpartisan organization and its membership dues are not automatically routed to the Democratic Party. AARP operates a separate PAC funded by voluntary member contributions, and PAC disbursements have gone to candidates of both parties. Membership fees primarily fund AARP's programs, services, advocacy, and operations rather than direct payments to a single political party.

claim: "Biden wants to end Shareholder Capitalism.. that's your 401k..your pensions.. your retirement.. are you voting for that???"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that President Biden has proposed abolishing “shareholder capitalism” or eliminating 401(k)s, pensions, or retirement accounts. His administration has supported corporate governance reforms, increased regulation and disclosure (including ESG-related policies), and measures to strengthen workers and retirees, but not a policy to end shareholder-owned markets or retirements tied to them. The claim conflates rhetorical critiques of shareholder primacy with a nonexistent proposal to abolish market-based retirement accounts.

claim: "I remember one of [Curt Schilling's] teammates said he painted his sock, the bloody sock."
rationale: There is no credible, contemporaneous reporting or reliable quote showing a Red Sox teammate publicly said Schilling 'painted' his bloody sock; the 2004 bloody-sock incident was widely documented (photos, medical treatment) and teammates publicly supported the authenticity. Claims that the sock was faked have circulated as rumor, but no verifiable source attributes that exact quote to a named teammate.

claim: Says that he’s responsible for Austin including Anderson Mill Road in the city's proposed transportation bond package.
rationale: The statement attributes sole responsibility to an unnamed individual for Austin including Anderson Mill Road in the proposed transportation bond, but municipal bond packages are typically developed by city staff and approved by a city council, not unilaterally by one person. Without a named individual or documentary evidence (e.g., council records, staff memos, or public statements) tying that person directly to the decision, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "If every house in Florida had a solar-heated water tank, that would eliminate consumption by 17 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading and cannot be accepted as true as written. Water heating typically represents roughly 15–20% of a household's energy use, so converting all homes to solar water heaters could reduce residential water‑heating energy use substantially, but it would not eliminate 17% of statewide energy or electricity consumption because much of Florida's load is air conditioning and nonresidential use; additionally not all homes use electric water heaters and solar systems do not supply 100% of demand year‑round.

claim: "150,000 (oil spill) claims have been filed by Floridians, but only 40 percent of them have been paid."
rationale: The claim is misleading: filings related to the Deepwater Horizon spill were in the hundreds of thousands across Gulf states, but Florida-specific filings were not accurately reported as exactly 150,000, and the share ultimately paid was higher than 40% once adjudications and settlements proceeded. Official BP/Gulf Coast Claims Facility and later settlement figures show a large portion of claims were approved or paid over time, and percentages vary by date and definition of 'paid.'

claim: Says an investigative report concluded Ken Cuccinelli "should have been prosecuted" for disclosure violations, but Virginia's law was too weak.
rationale: There is no widely reported investigative report that formally concluded Ken Cuccinelli 'should have been prosecuted' for disclosure violations while saying Virginia's law was too weak. Major news coverage documented ethical questions and criticism of his disclosures, and some opinion pieces argued enforcement was limited, but no authoritative investigative report made the explicit prosecutorial recommendation claimed.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: Recent state-level baby-name data for Texas show names like Liam ranking first in the most recent years, not Jose. While Jose is a common male name in Texas—especially in Hispanic communities—it has not been the statewide No. 1 male baby name in recent official SSA data.

claim: "Court orders Obama to pay $400 million in restitution."
rationale: There is no credible record or mainstream media reporting that a court ordered former President Barack Obama to pay $400 million in restitution. A judgment of that magnitude against a former U.S. president would be a widely reported public record, which does not exist. The claim appears to be fabricated or misattributed.

claim: "Foreign aid makes up about 1 percent of our entire budget."
rationale: If referring to the U.S. federal budget, annual civilian foreign aid is on the order of tens of billions of dollars versus total federal outlays of roughly several trillion dollars, which equates to about 1% (or slightly under) of the federal budget. Therefore the claim that 'foreign aid makes up about 1 percent of our entire budget' is broadly accurate in common usage.

claim: "Nobody’s invited us" to the Obama events in Atlanta.
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement but provides no context or evidence about who "us" refers to or which Obama events in Atlanta are meant. Without specification, it is not verifiable and unlikely to be literally true because large political events typically include invited guests, press, and public attendees, so a blanket "nobody's invited us" is unsupported.

claim: "When was the last time you saw a Chevrolet in Japan? It doesn’t exist, folks."
rationale: Chevrolet vehicles do exist in Japan, though they are uncommon. While General Motors' official retail presence in Japan has been limited or withdrawn at times, American models such as the Corvette and Camaro have been imported and registered in Japan both through official channels in some periods and via private/grey-market imports.

claim: Barack Obama "is the first ex-president to ever speak against his successor."
rationale: This is false — numerous former U.S. presidents publicly criticized their successors long before Barack Obama. Examples include John Adams criticizing Thomas Jefferson after leaving office, Theodore Roosevelt attacking William Howard Taft, and Herbert Hoover denouncing Franklin D. Roosevelt's policies.

claim: Requesting a chargeback is "a better way to get back at" GoFundMe.
rationale: Requesting a chargeback as a form of retaliation is not a reliable or legitimate way to "get back at" GoFundMe. Chargebacks are designed for bona fide payment disputes (fraud, non‑delivery) and abusing them can lead to reversal, fees, account penalties, or legal consequences rather than punitive impact on the platform. Additionally, payment processors and banks investigate disputes and may side with the merchant or donor if the chargeback is improper.

claim: In comparing mass shootings, "France had a higher casualty rate in one year than the entire two administrations of Barack Obama."
rationale: The claim is misleading: France’s worst single year (notably 2015 with the Charlie Hebdo and November Paris attacks totaling on the order of a few dozen to a couple hundred killed) did not exceed the cumulative U.S. mass‑shooting deaths across Barack Obama’s two terms, which include many high‑casualty events (Sandy Hook, Aurora, San Bernardino, Orlando, etc.). Summing U.S. mass‑shooting fatalities over 2009–2016 yields a larger toll than France’s single worst year. Therefore the statement as written is false.

claim: In the plot to kidnap Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, "the perps were ANTIFA and BLM anarchists."
rationale: Investigations and prosecutions by the FBI and Michigan law enforcement identified members of a far-right militia and allied individuals as the perpetrators and led to arrests and convictions of those men. Authorities found no credible evidence tying Antifa or Black Lives Matter activists to the Whitmer kidnap plot; claims attributing the plot to Antifa/BLM have been debunked as misinformation.

claim: "Same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. Still don’t believe the media is #fakenews?"
rationale: A single person cannot die multiple times in different countries; the claim conflates or reuses the same photo or story across reports. Such viral posts typically repurpose an image or misattribute a report, but that does not mean the same child actually died three times.

claim: "We're spending millions for each individual" held at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
rationale: Multiple government analyses and news reports have found that operating Guantanamo costs hundreds of millions per year while the detainee population is small, yielding an annual cost per detainee in the millions. Reported per-detainee figures have varied by year and accounting method but have often been in the multi-million-dollar range.

claim: "Our economy still has three people looking for every job (opening)."
rationale: The common labor-market metric is BLS's "unemployed persons per job opening." In recent U.S. data since the pandemic-era recovery, that ratio has been well below three (often under 1), so the statement that the economy "still has three people looking for every job" is not accurate for current U.S. conditions. Historical episodes (e.g., the 2009 recession) did see much higher ratios, but that is not the present situation.

claim: Says "we had to cut 13 billion dollars in state spending over two years."
rationale: The claim gives no identifying state or two-year period, so it cannot be verified as a general statement. State budgets vary widely and a $13 billion cut over two years would be true for only a few large states in specific fiscal years; without that context the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: Pennsylvania rejected 372,000 mail-in ballots
rationale: Official Pennsylvania election data and contemporary fact‑checks show far fewer than 372,000 mail‑in ballots were rejected; rejections were on the order of tens of thousands (not hundreds of thousands) and most were later cured or counted. The 372,000 figure appears to be a misrepresentation or conflation of different categories or totals, not the official count of rejected mail‑in ballots.

claim: Ukraine adopted "laws banning the Russian language."
rationale: This claim is false.
