Oregon’s food‑insecurity and child‑hunger rates have generally been lower than those top five states, so the blanket claim that it “remains among the top five hungriest” is not supported without a specific year or metric.

claim: The United States "spends more on potato chips than we do on ALL energy R&D."
rationale: The claim is misleading and false as stated. It conflates consumer spending on potato chips with ‘all energy R&D’ without defining the scope; when federal and private-sector energy research investments are summed they amount to many billions (and often tens of billions) annually, which is comparable to or larger than U.S. potato chip retail sales. Therefore the blanket statement that the U.S. spends more on potato chips than on all energy R&D is inaccurate.

claim: "In 2021, 65 people in Milwaukee have lost their lives due to reckless driving accidents, and more than 9,000 cars have been stolen, double the amount in 2020."
rationale: The statement mixes and overstates figures that aren’t supported as presented. Milwaukee did see a large increase in vehicle thefts in 2021 and higher traffic deaths versus 2020, but official city/county reports and news coverage show variation by jurisdiction and definition (stolen vehicles reported citywide range near several thousand, and traffic fatalities are reported differently when limited to 'reckless driving' cases), so the precise claim (65 reckless-driving deaths and 'more than 9,000' stolen cars being exactly double 2020) is not reliably supported.

claim: Says "FBI and Texas State Police are both confirming that Raymond Peter Littleberry, the man accused of shooting up a Texas church, was an avid atheist on the payroll of the Democrat National Committee."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official confirmation from the FBI or Texas law enforcement that a person named Raymond Peter Littleberry committed a Texas church shooting, was an 'avid atheist,' or was on the payroll of the Democratic National Committee. The claim also uses a non-existent agency name ('Texas State Police' — Texas law enforcement is typically the Texas Department of Public Safety), and such extraordinary allegations would have been reported by major news outlets and official statements but were not.

claim: Says Scott Walker is proposing to add 485 employees "in the category of supervisor and management" to his Department of Administration.
rationale: This claim misstates what Walker proposed. Public records and fact-checks show the cited figure referred to reclassifications or personnel changes across agencies (or budgeted position adjustments), not the creation of 485 new supervisor/manager jobs specifically added to the Department of Administration.

claim: "NASA confirms earth will go dark for 6 days in December 2020."
rationale: This claim is false. NASA never confirmed a six-day global blackout in December 2020 and publicly debunked similar viral hoaxes; additionally there is no plausible astronomical mechanism that would cause the entire Earth to go dark for six days without catastrophic, widely observed consequences.

claim: "At John Lewis funeral Obama told a room full of people that rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote."
rationale: There are no credible reports or transcripts that President Obama told attendees at a John Lewis funeral that 'rooms full of people is too dangerous so we must mail in vote.' Obama's public remarks at memorials focused on Lewis's life and legacy, and while Obama and other leaders did encourage voting by mail during the 2020 pandemic in other venues, this specific quoted statement at Lewis's funeral is a mischaracterization or conflation.

claim: "Why should you get a break for racehorses and not get a break for child care?"
rationale: The claim is a rhetorical question implying that governments universally give tax or other 'breaks' to racehorse owners while denying breaks for child care. In reality, treatment varies by jurisdiction: some places offer incentives to the horse-racing industry, while many countries and states also provide childcare tax credits, subsidies, or leave policies. Therefore the blanket implication is inaccurate.

claim: "Nearly 20% of our residents" are born abroad.
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it lacks any geographic area or time period for “our residents.” The share of foreign‑born residents varies widely between countries, cities, and years, so without context the claim cannot be confirmed and should not be presented as fact.

claim: "Tommy Thompson wanted to implant data chips in humans."
rationale: The claim misstates or overstates Thompson's positions. As U.S. HHS Secretary (2001–2005) Tommy Thompson promoted electronic health records and explored use of RFID technology for tracking medical supplies and patient information, but he did not formally propose implanting data chips into people; media reports and political opponents sometimes mischaracterized or exaggerated his comments about RFID and health IDs.

claim: Says the USMCA is the "biggest trade deal ever made."
rationale: The USMCA is a trilateral update to NAFTA between the United States, Mexico, and Canada, not an unprecedentedly large trade deal. Larger trade arrangements exist — for example the European Single Market/EU and broad multilateral frameworks (WTO) cover more countries, trade volume, and GDP than the USMCA. Calling USMCA the "biggest trade deal ever made" is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the company’s board.
rationale: There is no credible contemporaneous reporting or verifiable evidence that a Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland publicly resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the board. Major resignations tied to high-profile events like Musk joining Twitter's board received news coverage and this specific name does not appear in reputable accounts. The claim likely stems from an unverified or misattributed social-media post.

claim: "Almost 40% of borrowers with student loan debt didn't finish their degree."
rationale: The share of student-loan holders who did not finish varies by cohort, institution type, and the time window used; some analyses find noncompletion rates in the ~30–40% range for certain cohorts, but there is no single authoritative statistic that universally supports the blanket claim that 'almost 40% of borrowers' didn't finish. The statement is imprecise and can be misleading without specifying the population and time period.

claim: "The toxicity of COVID-Omicron is 5 times higher than that of the delta variant, and the mortality rate is also higher than that of Delta."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed studies and public-health assessments found Omicron to be more transmissible but generally less intrinsically severe than the Delta variant, with lower rates of hospitalization and death on average; there is no credible evidence that Omicron is "5 times" more toxic or has a higher mortality rate than Delta. The claim contradicts consensus findings that Delta caused more severe disease at the population level.

claim: Says Texas has so few gas-pump inspectors in the field, "the HEBs of this state, the Brookshires of this state, they're calibrating their own gas pumps. The (Texas Department of Agriculture) just sends them the stickers and they calibrate them."
rationale: The claim exaggerates and mischaracterizes how gas pumps are regulated in Texas. Retailers or licensed service agents often perform routine maintenance and calibration, but the Texas Department of Agriculture (TDA) maintains regulatory oversight, conducts inspections, and requires proper certification rather than merely mailing out stickers for self-calibration. While Texas has faced inspector staffing constraints at times, the depiction that chains like H‑E‑B and Brookshire’s simply calibrate pumps themselves and receive only stickers from TDA is misleading.

claim: Says President Dwight Eisenhower "moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants out of this country."
rationale: Eisenhower’s administration did carry out large deportation efforts (notably the 1954 'Operation Wetback'), but historians’ estimates of people removed or repatriated in that period are generally around one to about 1.3 million and include many voluntary returns; the specific claim of 1.5 million is an overestimate and simplifies complex counting. Framing it as Eisenhower having 'moved 1.5 million illegal immigrants' is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez took a "$10 million payout from Netflix."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or congressional financial-disclosure evidence that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez received a $10 million payment from Netflix. Such a large payment to a sitting member of Congress would be publicly disclosed and widely covered, and no trustworthy sources document it. The claim appears to be misinformation or a misattribution.

claim: "When the union says I want to eliminate tenure, that’s not true."
rationale: This statement is a denial of an allegation but lacks any identifying context (who, which union, what tenure policy). Without specific speaker, union, or evidence, I cannot verify the truth of the denial; therefore I treat it as unverified and default to FALSE. Confirming would require checking the person’s public statements, policy proposals, or voting record about tenure.

claim: Says Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T-shirt with progressive slogans on it.
rationale: There is no well-documented, verifiable instance in major news or reputable image archives showing Tom Hanks publicly photographed wearing a T‑shirt emblazoned with clearly identifiable progressive political slogans. Viral social‑media claims to that effect tend to be uncorroborated, miscaptioned, or show edited/isolated images without reliable provenance. Without a specific, verifiable photo and source, the claim is not supported.

claim: Says Charlie Crist rode on a jet that "belongs to a serial polluter with a history of environmental violations fined nearly $2 million for polluting water."
rationale: I found no credible reporting or public records tying a jet Charlie Crist flew on to an owner described as a "serial polluter" who was fined nearly $2 million for polluting water. While Crist has accepted flights on aircraft owned by donors or supporters, the specific allegation about a nearly $2 million water-pollution fine and a history of environmental violations is not substantiated by available news or enforcement records.

claim: "Just about everyone everywhere is spending more hours on the job, less time with their families, bringing home smaller and smaller paychecks, while they're paying more and more at the gas pump and the grocery stores."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization. While many people in some countries and groups have faced stagnant or falling real wages and periods of higher gas and grocery prices, hours worked and family time have not universally increased everywhere—trends vary by country, sector and time period. Available labor and price statistics show mixed results rather than the near-universal, continuous decline the claim asserts.

claim: U.S. military uniforms are manufactured in China.
rationale: The blanket claim is false: U.S. military uniforms are generally produced under U.S. defense contracts and domestic-sourcing rules rather than being manufactured in China. While there have been isolated reports of uniform components or commercial items sourced or made overseas (and contract suppliers/production locations can vary), the standard practice and legal requirements favor U.S.-based manufacture.

claim: "We've had 11,000 attempts to amend the Constitution since 1789."
rationale: Congressional records and scholarly counts show that well over 10,000 proposed amendments to the U.S. Constitution have been introduced since 1789; commonly cited tallies (from sources such as the Congressional Research Service and legislative records) put the total at about 11,000–11,600 proposals. Most of these were proposed in Congress and died in committee, so the large number reflects proposals/attempts rather than ratified amendments.

claim: "In the last decade, the average income of the bottom 90 percent of all working Americans actually declined. The top 1 percent saw their income rise by an average of more than a quarter of a million dollars each."
rationale: The claim overstates and is imprecise. Broad U.S. data sources (Census, CBO, IRS-based studies) show that over many recent 10-year spans the bottom 90% saw at best modest real gains or stagnation rather than a clear decade-long decline, and while the top 1% did see substantially larger gains, the headline "more than a quarter of a million dollars each" is not a generally supported uniform figure and depends on the exact decade, whether mean or median incomes are used, and whether households or individuals are measured.

claim: Says Chris Christie "vetoed equal pay for women 3 times. He only let the bill pass once it became a damaging campaign issue."
rationale: Public reporting and legislative records show Chris Christie vetoed at least one major equal-pay bill (notably in 2013), but there is no clear evidence he vetoed three separate equal-pay measures. The additional assertion that he only let a bill pass once it became a damaging campaign issue is speculative about motive and not supported by documented evidence.

claim: Claims Joe Biden said "coal is more dangerous than terrorists."
rationale: There is no credible record or reliable transcript showing Joe Biden uttered the exact claim 'coal is more dangerous than terrorists.' The phrase appears to be a misquote or viral paraphrase; while Biden has discussed coal industry safety and energy policy, reputable news outlets and fact‑checkers do not document him saying that sentence verbatim.

claim: Huckabee "was one of the highest taxing governors that we had in this country and rivaling Bill Clinton in terms of the Cato ratings."
rationale: This statement overstates Huckabee’s place in Cato’s governor rankings. Cato’s Fiscal Policy Report Cards rate governors year-by-year on tax and spending changes and give Huckabee mixed/mid-range scores across his tenure (he enacted some tax increases early and some cuts later) rather than consistently ranking him among the very highest-taxing governors; he is not commonly listed as rivalling Bill Clinton in Cato’s worst-on-taxes rankings without specifying years. The claim lacks a specific timeframe and appears to conflate isolated measures with an overall Cato ranking.

claim: A photo of Pete Buttigieg in a military uniform without visible patches shows that "he is a fraud."
rationale: A single photograph showing no visible patches does not prove someone is a fraud. Pete Buttigieg’s service in the U.S. Navy Reserve and deployment is documented, and missing insignia in images can be caused by angle, resolution, uniform configuration, authorized removal, or image editing rather than fabrication of service.

claim: The average Atlanta resident "spends an extra $924 each year in additional gasoline and wasted time."
rationale: The statement presents a precise per-resident annual cost without a cited source or year. Estimates of congestion-related extra fuel and time losses vary substantially by methodology and year, and most authoritative reports quote per-commuter (not per-resident) costs; some studies produce numbers in this general range but not reliably the exact $924 figure for the average Atlanta resident.

claim: Rob Cornilles is a Tea Party candidate.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rob Cornilles ran explicitly as a Tea Party candidate. Available information identifies him as a Republican or conservative local candidate in Washington at times, but not as a formally Tea Party-branded or widely recognized Tea Party-endorsed candidate.

claim: "By the way, I'm not raising tolls 50 percent....Jon Corzine did."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Jon Corzine enacted a one-time 50% toll increase while governor. Major toll hikes in New Jersey around that period were smaller, disputed, or occurred under different authorities or administrations, and a single 50% across-the-board toll hike attributable directly to Corzine is not documented.

claim: Image shows Donald Trump’s new Christmas card.
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence provided linking the image to an official release by Donald Trump; no provenance, metadata, or confirmation from his office or reputable news sources is included. Without such confirmation, an image circulating online could be edited or misattributed and cannot be reliably labeled as his 'new Christmas card.'

claim: "I believe in tax cuts. I believe in being a supply-sider. I cut the income tax I think it was 24 percent. We got 42 percent more revenues."
rationale: The claim mixes imprecise numbers and implies a causal link that is historically inaccurate. There was no clear-cut single “24%” income-tax cut that directly produced a 42% revenue increase; major U.S. tax cuts (e.g., Reagan-era and others) altered rates by different amounts and subsequent revenue changes reflect inflation, GDP growth, and other policy changes rather than a simple supply-side effect. Presenting those two percentages as a straightforward cause-and-effect is misleading.

claim: On tax inversions, the Wall Street Journal "surprisingly attacked this tax scheme."
rationale: The claim is framed as a surprising editorial stance but is vague and subjective. The Wall Street Journal has run both critical and supportive pieces about corporate tax inversions at different times (and its news reporting is separate from its editorial pages), so a blanket statement that it "surprisingly attacked this tax scheme" cannot be verified without a specific article or date. Without that context the assertion overstretches the available evidence.

claim: Vaccines "will remove parts of your DNA and replace it with GENETIC CODING (TECHNOLOGY)" that will "cause people to HAVE to cooperate with the New World Order."
rationale: This claim is false. Approved vaccines (including mRNA and most viral‑vector vaccines) do not remove or replace parts of your DNA; mRNA vaccines deliver transient messenger RNA that is translated in the cytoplasm and does not integrate into the genome, and commonly used vaccine vectors are engineered not to integrate. There is no credible biological mechanism or evidence that vaccines can implant 'genetic coding' to compel political behavior — that assertion is a conspiracy theory, not a scientific finding.

claim: "South Florida ranks No. 1 in the gap between wages and housing."
rationale: The statement is too vague and cannot be verified as a general truth: rankings of a "wage–housing gap" depend on the exact metric, geographic boundaries, and time period. Different analyses (housing wage, share of income to housing, affordability indices) often place West Coast metros or other large urban areas ahead of South Florida, and South Florida is not universally ranked No. 1 across reputable datasets.

claim: Says Peter DeFazio votes with Nancy Pelosi 86 percent of the time.
rationale: The assertion gives a precise 86% figure but provides no source or time period. Public 'votes with' percentages for members (from sources like FiveThirtyEight or GovTrack) vary by year and methodology, and DeFazio's alignment rate with Nancy Pelosi has changed over time, so the standalone 86% claim cannot be verified as generally true.

claim: "400 bills have my name on them either as a sponsor or a co-sponsor. You don’t get that done unless you work with folks on the other side."
rationale: The statement combines a verifiable numeric claim and a normative claim but gives no identity, timeframe, or jurisdiction; without checking that person's legislative sponsorship records I cannot confirm 400 bills bore their name. Such a total is plausible for a long-serving legislator but is not demonstrable from the claim alone, and the follow-up assertion that achieving that necessarily requires cross-party cooperation is a generalization that may be true in some cases but is not universally provable. Given the missing specifics, the safe determination is that the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: The Obama administration "raised discretionary spending by 24 percent from President George W. Bush's last full-year budget and will run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years."
rationale: The claim mixes incompatible measures and timeframes. Independent fact-checkers and budget data show that the “24%” figure depends on which discretionary items (one‑time stimulus, war funding, or base discretionary) are included and on whether you compare enacted vs. proposed budgets; using comparable baselines the increase is much smaller. Likewise, the assertion that Obama would “run up more debt by October than Bush did in eight years” misstates projections and conflates deficits, debt held by the public, and timing—Bush’s eight‑year increase was larger than the short‑term increase in the early Obama months.

claim: "Certainly we're going to be the most restrictive state in the land … in terms of who can get medical marijuana, how it will be prescribed and how it will be achieved in terms of moving it into the marketplace."
rationale: The claim asserts a definitive comparative outcome — that a particular state will be "the most restrictive" on medical marijuana — yet offers no supporting evidence and is not verifiable as an absolute statement. U.S. states have varied widely in qualifying conditions, prescribing rules, and market access, and several states historically had similarly or more restrictive regimes (e.g., CBD-only programs or physician-only recommendations). Without specific metrics, timing, and comparison to every other state's laws, the blanket assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Police are "20.8 times more likely to kill than be killed by a criminal."
rationale: The claim is misleading as stated because it gives a single ratio with no timeframe or jurisdiction. In the U.S. some years produce a similar figure (roughly ~1,000 people killed by police vs ~40–60 officers feloniously killed yields ~20×), but the numbers and the ratio vary year-to-year and depend on data sources and definitions. As a blanket statement it is not reliably true.

claim: "I can't sign money. That's illegal."
rationale: The statement is false as an absolute. In many jurisdictions (notably the United States) simply signing or autographing paper currency is not per se illegal; laws prohibit mutilation or defacement done with intent to render notes unfit for reissue or to commit fraud. Casual signatures are commonly permitted, though purposeful damaging or altering to deceive is prohibited.

claim: "Already, the Affordable Care Act is helping to slow the growth of (Medicare’s) health care costs."
rationale: Multiple government analyses found that Affordable Care Act provisions (reductions in Medicare Advantage overpayments, lower updates to provider payments, new value‑based programs such as ACOs and readmission penalties) reduced Medicare spending relative to prior law and helped slow per‑beneficiary spending growth in the 2010s. While other economic and secular factors also contributed to the slowdown, the ACA's payment and delivery‑system reforms are credited with a measurable portion of the reduction in Medicare cost growth.

claim: "3.8% of Wisconsin’s coronavirus funding has been spent."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it lacks necessary context (which pot of coronavirus funding and what date). Different COVID-19 funding streams (CARES Act state relief, federal programs, local allocations, FEMA, PPP) had very different spending rates, and reported percentages like 3.8% applied to specific funds at particular times rather than to all Wisconsin coronavirus funding overall. Without specifying the fund and date the claim cannot be treated as an accurate universal fact.

claim: "President Biden says he wants to ban handguns."
rationale: This is false. President Biden's public gun policy proposals and speeches have called for banning assault weapons, high-capacity magazines, ghost guns, and strengthening background checks and red flag laws, but he has not advocated banning handguns. Claims that he said he wants to ban handguns are mischaracterizations circulated by critics.

claim: "If it weren’t for me … (illegal immigration) wouldn’t even be a big subject."
rationale: The importance of illegal immigration as a public topic cannot reasonably be attributed to a single individual. Illegal immigration has been a significant political and social issue for decades, driven by economic conditions, demographic trends, foreign conflicts, and policy choices by many administrations and legislators. While a high-profile person can amplify attention, they are not solely responsible for making it "a big subject."

claim: Says Kurt Schrader voted to cut $500 billion from Medicare, threatening "thousands of Oregon seniors and their access to their current coverage."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Kurt Schrader cast a vote to cut Medicare by $500 billion; as a Democratic member he has generally opposed large cuts to Medicare and I am not aware of a specific roll call where he supported a $500B Medicare reduction. The claim appears to conflate or mischaracterize complex budget or reconciliation proposals or CBO scoring tied to other bills rather than a direct Schrader vote to slash Medicare benefits.

claim: "Not a single Republican candidate, announced or potential, is clearly and consistently supporting a path to citizenship. Not one."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that no Republican announced or potential candidate 'clearly and consistently' supports a path to citizenship; that is false. Historically and in recent years some Republicans (including senators and governors) have publicly supported immigration reforms that included paths to citizenship or legal status for Dreamers and other groups, and at least a few Republican figures often discussed as potential candidates have endorsed limited pathways. However, many leading 2024 GOP contenders oppose broad citizenship paths, which may be the basis for the claim.

claim: Oregon Health Plan rations "covered procedures under certain circumstances"
rationale: Oregon’s Medicaid program (the Oregon Health Plan) uses a prioritized benefits list, medical-necessity rules, and prior-authorization policies to determine when and whether particular procedures will be paid for, which effectively limits or "rations" coverage in certain circumstances. Historically the state explicitly ranked services to allocate limited resources, and current policy still imposes clinical and administrative restrictions on coverage.

claim: "Voted the ‘best specialty plate in America’"
rationale: The statement is given with no subject, date, or source and therefore cannot be verified. There is no single, universally recognized award called 'best specialty plate in America,' and rankings of specialty license plates vary by organization and year, so the unqualified claim is not supportable.

claim: Barack Obama is "the only candidate who doesn't take a dime from oil company PACs or lobbyists."
rationale: The statement is misleading and unprovable as written. Obama did pledge in 2008 to refuse money from oil-company PACs and from federal lobbyists, but other candidates made similar pledges at times, and his campaigns still received contributions from oil-industry employees and related interests and benefited from outside groups. Without specifying the election cycle and which opponents, the absolute claim that he was the "only candidate" is false or at least unsupported.

claim: Says under the Senate immigration bill, newly legalized immigrants will "pay every tax possible, but you don’t get a single benefit" for 10 years.
rationale: The claim is an overstatement. While some Senate immigration proposals have included multi-year waiting periods (often up to 10 years) before newly legalized immigrants can access many federal means-tested benefits, they are not barred from literally every benefit for a decade. Payroll taxes still apply and can lead to Social Security/Medicare eligibility once work‑credits are earned, and emergency medical care, certain state/local programs, education, and other services are not universally prohibited.

claim: Scott Walker "couldn’t get his own party" to back more than a 500-student increase in Milwaukee’s school choice program, but in Indiana, "Mitch Daniels’ voucher program is approaching 30,000 students two years after opening."
rationale: The statement mixes political characterization and numerical claims that are not fully supported. While Wisconsin Republicans did negotiate only a modest 500-seat increase to Milwaukee's voucher program in one budget compromise, the phrasing that Walker “couldn’t get his own party” to back more is a partisan interpretation and omits context about the legislative negotiations. The Indiana figure is also imprecise: Indiana’s Choice Scholarship enrollment did grow rapidly under Mitch Daniels’ administration, but reported counts and the exact timeline (e.g., “approaching 30,000 two years after opening”) vary depending on which program start-date and definition are used.

claim: Says Barack Obama had "huge majorities" in Congress during his first two years in office and "did nothing with them to create jobs in America."
rationale: While “huge” is subjective, Democrats held clear majorities in both chambers during Obama’s first two years (the 111th Congress). The Obama administration and Democratic Congress passed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (Feb 2009) and other measures (unemployment benefits extensions, auto rescue support, tax credits) intended to save and create jobs, so the claim that they “did nothing” is incorrect.

claim: President Barack Obama "has doubled the size of government since he took office."
rationale: The statement is false as a blanket claim because no common, objective metric of "size of government" actually doubled during Obama's presidency. Federal civilian employment was roughly flat or slightly lower, federal outlays rose but did not double, and while the national debt nearly doubled from ~$10.6T to ~$19.6T in that period, debt is not the same as overall government size and rose largely due to the financial crisis and stimulus measures.

claim: "Last year, we borrowed $1.4 trillion -- or 41 cents of every dollar we spent. Over half of this debt is held by foreign investors."
rationale: The claim mixes inconsistent figures. The U.S. did run about a $1.4 trillion deficit in FY2022, but that was roughly 24% (about 24 cents of every dollar) of total outlays, not 41 cents; the 41% ratio corresponds to a much larger deficit in a different year. Separately, less than half of U.S. federal debt is held by foreign investors—foreign holdings are on the order of about 20–30% of marketable Treasury securities, not over 50%.

claim: Says the Obama administration spent taxpayer dollars on electric cars in Finland (and) windmills in China.
rationale: This claim is misleading. The Obama administration did fund U.S. electric-vehicle and clean-energy programs (loans and grants) and some recipients or supply chains involved foreign-made parts, but the federal government did not directly spend taxpayer dollars to buy electric cars in Finland or to purchase windmills in China as the claim states. Reports of components or manufacturing ties abroad were limited exceptions and do not support the categorical assertion.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s "Make America Great Again" hats were made in China.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and physical product labels showed that many of the official 'Make America Great Again' hats sold by Donald Trump’s campaign were manufactured in China. Multiple investigations and fact-checks documented China as a principal source for campaign merchandise, although some later batches and other vendors produced hats domestically.

claim: Zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago.
rationale: There are no credible news reports or official confirmations that zoo animals were released during protests in Chicago; Lincoln Park Zoo and city officials stated animals remained secured. Viral photos and videos claiming releases were debunked or miscaptioned by fact-checkers.

claim: "The American people don't want us to raise taxes."
rationale: The claim asserts a uniform, timeless preference for all Americans, which is not supported by evidence. Public opinion on taxes is mixed and varies by tax type, income group, party affiliation, and timing — polls often show opposition to broad tax hikes but support for increases on the wealthy or for specific programs. Therefore the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: "While states used to have regulatory power over fishing, federal law now regulates down to the tenth of the inch the minimum size of fish that anglers can keep."
rationale: Federal law does not universally supersede state fishing regulation nor does it broadly mandate minimum retained-fish sizes specified to the tenth of an inch. U.S. federal fisheries (managed under the Magnuson–Stevens Act and by NOAA/Regional Fishery Management Councils) regulate particular marine and interstate fisheries in federal waters and for certain species, while states retain authority over many inland and inshore recreational fisheries. Where federal rules set minimum sizes they typically specify whole inches or defined measurement methods (e.g., total vs. fork length), and precision to a tenth of an inch is not a general nationwide standard.

claim: Says 100,000 are on waiting list to attend Texas charter schools.
rationale: Multiple reports from charter-school advocates and media coverage have cited roughly 100,000 students on waiting lists for Texas charter schools in recent years. State and charter-association data have repeatedly shown large, six-figure waitlists reflecting high demand for charter seats. The claim matches those widely reported figures.

claim: Says Jacob Blake "declared he had a gun in the car and was going to go get it" and was "brandishing" a knife
rationale: Publicly released dashcam and bodycam footage and official summaries do not show Jacob Blake clearly announcing he had a gun in the car and would go get it, nor do they show him actively brandishing a knife at officers at the time he was shot. Police reports noted a knife was involved earlier in the incident or found in the vehicle, but independent video does not corroborate the specific claim that he declared he would retrieve a gun and was brandishing a knife toward officers.

claim: "Matt Rosendale supports plans that don’t have to cover (pre-existing conditions)."
rationale: There is no clear, unambiguous evidence that Matt Rosendale has explicitly endorsed insurance plans that categorically do not have to cover pre-existing conditions. He has opposed the Affordable Care Act and promoted market-based alternatives, but in public statements he has also claimed support for protections for people with pre-existing conditions; his record is ambiguous rather than a straightforward endorsement of plans that deny such coverage.

claim: Says $6 billion projected to accumulate in the state’s rainy day fund is already used.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written because it omits which state and which projection period; budget projections that $6 billion would accumulate are estimates and are not automatically 'used' unless the state legislature or authorized officials have appropriated or transferred those funds. Without named state and official budget or treasurer statements showing the rainy day fund balance was fully spent, the assertion cannot be verified.

claim: "A gallon (of gasoline) delivered to the front lines for our troops in Afghanistan cost more than $400."
rationale: Multiple military reports and contemporary news investigations documented that the all-in cost to deliver fuel to remote forward operating bases in Afghanistan — when factoring in helicopter lift, convoy security and logistics — could reach or exceed roughly $400 per gallon in extreme cases. The figure refers to delivered cost in austere locations, not the retail price at a U.S. gas station or typical base fuel costs.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "paid only 14 percent in taxes — probably less than you."
rationale: Romney’s disclosed tax returns showed an effective federal income tax rate of roughly 13.9% in the year released, so the 14% figure for federal income tax is approximately correct. But the added claim that this rate is "probably less than you" is speculative and unverified — whether Romney paid a lower rate than a given person depends on that person’s income and which taxes (federal income only vs. payroll/state) are counted. Because the comparative statement is ambiguous and cannot be generally asserted, the overall claim is misleading/false.

claim: Rhode Island's unemployment insurance system "is the most expensive such system in the country."
rationale: The statement is an absolute superlative without a time frame or metric; Rhode Island has had relatively high unemployment insurance costs at times but is not unambiguously or consistently the most expensive system in the country. Rankings depend on measures (employer tax rates, benefit generosity, payroll tax burden, trust fund solvency) and vary year to year, with other states often ranking higher on some metrics.

claim: Says he was the first person to call for invoking the Defense Production Act.
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as presented because it names no individual or time period; without that context it cannot be verified. Historically the Defense Production Act has been suggested or invoked by many officials and advocates across different crises (including long before recent events), so claiming a single person was the first is unlikely and would require precise evidence.

claim: "In an interview with the Chicago Tribune's Editorial Board, Comptroller Leslie Munger says that in order to balance a budget, the state would have to 'cut social services completely.'"
rationale: I find no reliable record of Leslie Munger using the exact phrase 'cut social services completely' in an interview with the Chicago Tribune Editorial Board. While Munger did warn during the Illinois budget impasse that deep spending reductions would be required and spoke about potential cuts to services, the quoted absolute phrase appears to be a mischaracterization or paraphrase rather than a documented direct quote.

claim: The New York Times published an old stock photo of a young girl and claimed Israeli forces killed her during its recent war with Hamas.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that The New York Times itself published an old stock photo and falsely claimed Israeli forces killed the child in its recent coverage; images misattributed in that way circulated widely on social media, but fact-checkers traced those to user posts or other outlets rather than a NYT editorial claim. The Times typically credits photographers and agencies and issues corrections when captions are wrong; no verified correction from NYT matching this allegation has been documented.

claim: "Congressman Kasich wants to use our tax dollars to give secret bonuses to his corporate friends."
rationale: The statement asserts that a 'Congressman Kasich' advocated using taxpayer dollars to pay secret bonuses to corporate friends, but there is no public record showing John Kasich (the only widely known Kasich who served in Congress) proposed or supported such a plan. Kasich's documented legislative and gubernatorial record contains tax and economic policies but not proposals to fund undisclosed corporate bonuses with public money. Without a specific bill, quote, or credible evidence, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: In 2010, uninsured voters made up "about 5 percent of the electorate."
rationale: Data from 2010 show a much larger share of Americans were uninsured (roughly mid-teens percent), so uninsured adults or voters were far above 5%. Even accounting for voting likelihood differences, reputable sources (Census, KFF) indicate the uninsured portion of the population and of voting-age adults in 2010 was well above 5%.

claim: No openly gay man has ever been elected to the Georgia Legislature.
rationale: This claim is false. Sam Park, an openly gay man, was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives in 2016 (becoming the first openly gay man in the Georgia General Assembly), and other openly gay men such as Matthew Wilson have also been elected to the Georgia Legislature.

claim: "The VA negotiates prescription drug prices. Medicare doesn't do that."
rationale: The Department of Veterans Affairs has statutory authority and an established formulary and procurement process that lets it negotiate and secure discounted prescription drug prices. Historically Medicare as a federal program was barred from directly negotiating drug prices (Medicare Part D uses private plans that negotiate on beneficiaries' behalf). Newer law (the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act) creates a future Medicare negotiation program, so the claim is correct in the historical/current sense but time-sensitive.

claim: "The (health care) law does not demand that all of these cancellations go out."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act itself did not contain a provision that literally ordered insurers to send cancellation notices to enrollees. Instead the law imposed new coverage standards and limited grandfathering of prior plans; many existing plans failed to meet those standards and insurers or regulators therefore discontinued them. So in a narrow statutory sense the law did not explicitly "demand" every cancellation, though its requirements made many cancellations inevitable.

claim: "There are communities under Sharia law right now in our country. Up in Illinois. ... There’s Sharia law, as I understand it, in Illinois, Indiana -- up there. I don't know."
rationale: No U.S. state, city, or recognized community is legally governed by Sharia law; U.S. federal and state law are supreme. While some Muslim communities may use voluntary religious arbitration or informal mediation based on Islamic principles, those arrangements operate only by mutual consent and must comply with state law and can be overturned by civil courts.

claim: Milwaukee’s problems include "52 percent black male unemployment."
rationale: The statement is misleading: no standard labor-market measure shows a 52% unemployment rate for all black men in Milwaukee. The 52% figure has circulated as a different metric (for example, share out of the labor force or for a narrow age cohort or neighborhood) rather than the official BLS-style unemployment rate, so presenting it as a general unemployment rate for black males in Milwaukee is inaccurate.

claim: "U.S. deaths since 1/22 (2020): COVID-19: 27, flu, 4,700; abortion: 118,000."
rationale: The figure for COVID-19 deaths (27) is vastly inconsistent with official U.S. counts since early 2020, which are in the hundreds of thousands to over a million. The flu and abortion numbers are also incompatible with established estimates (seasonal flu deaths are typically in the thousands to tens of thousands per season, and annual induced abortions in the U.S. were on the order of hundreds of thousands pre-2020), suggesting the claim cherry-picks or misstates metrics and timeframes.

claim: Says the "only valid reason to oppose voter ID is that you plan to cheat," and "every Democrat in Congress opposes voter ID."
rationale: The claim is incorrect on both counts. Opponents of voter ID commonly cite legitimate policy concerns—such as disenfranchisement of low-income and minority voters, administrative burdens, and constitutional or legal objections—so it's false that the only valid reason to oppose it is an intent to cheat. Likewise, Democrats in Congress do not hold a unanimous position; while many oppose strict ID laws, some Democratic members have supported versions of voter ID with safeguards or voted for specific ID-related measures, so the universal statement that every Democrat opposes voter ID is false.

claim: Says 2010 was the "worst year ever for America's doctors" reimbursed by Medicare.
rationale: There is no clear evidence that 2010 was uniquely the "worst year ever" for physicians reimbursed by Medicare; Medicare payments have fluctuated over decades with multiple years of significant cuts or threats of cuts (often due to the SGR formula) and Congress frequently intervened. Saying 2010 was the single worst year is a qualitative and unsupported superlative without a defined metric or comparative data across years.

claim: "Infection rates in Allegany, Cattaraugus and Chautauqua counties have consistently been among the lowest in the state."
rationale: The claim is too broad and unqualified — it does not specify which infection or what timeframe. County-level infection rates (for example during the COVID-19 pandemic) have varied over time; Allegany, Cattaraugus and Chautauqua have been low relative to other New York counties at some points but have not been consistently among the lowest across the entire pandemic. Without a specified period and disease, the assertion of consistent lowest rates is not supported.

claim: John McCain and George Bush have "absolutely no plan for universal health care."
rationale: Neither John McCain (Senator and 2008 presidential nominee) nor President George W. Bush ever proposed or endorsed a policy to guarantee universal health care for all Americans. Their public health proposals focused on market-based measures (tax credits, HSAs, portability, Medicare Part D, SCHIP expansions) rather than a plan to achieve universal coverage.

claim: Says the Clintons "burst through their own self-pronounced guidelines" by accepting foreign donations. "There is a clip of Bill Clinton saying we're not going to take foreign donations."
rationale: The Clinton Foundation and related Clinton entities accepted donations from foreign governments and foreign-linked donors, and in 2015 the Foundation publicly pledged it would not accept foreign government contributions while Hillary Clinton served as secretary of state. Bill Clinton has been recorded saying the Foundation would not take foreign government donations. Critics have pointed to earlier foreign gifts and agreements as inconsistent with that pledge.

claim: Cannabis reform "is supported by the majority of the residents of our state, including a majority of Republicans."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it names no state, timeframe, or poll to show a majority of residents and of Republicans support cannabis reform. While national polling often shows a majority of U.S. adults favor cannabis legalization, Republican support varies by poll and state and is not consistently a majority. Without specific, recent state-level data the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: Bull sharks were released in an Arkansas river.
rationale: There are no widely reported, credible accounts that bull sharks were deliberately released into an Arkansas river. While bull sharks can tolerate freshwater and have been found in river systems connected to the Gulf, a claim of a release in Arkansas lacks substantiation in major news or agency reports.

claim: "We have pay equity. When you think about that wage gap, we all know it's 78 cents to the dollar. Well, in New York state it's 90 cents to the dollar."
rationale: The widely used, recent U.S. measure of the gender pay gap (median usual earnings of full-time, year-round workers) is about 80–83 cents on the dollar, not 78 cents, and estimates vary by year and data source. New York’s gap is somewhat smaller than the national gap and has been reported near the high-80s to low-90s cents depending on the year and definition, so stating flatly “78 cents” nationally and “90 cents in New York” is misleading without specifying the year and exact earnings measure.

claim: Says presidential candidate Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said, "Social Security must (be) expanded to illegal immigration, it’s their right."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said the quoted phrase endorsing expanding Social Security to 'illegal immigration.' Gillibrand has supported immigration reform and pathways to citizenship but has not been documented as advocating blanket extension of Social Security benefits to undocumented immigrants; Social Security eligibility typically requires eligible work credits and lawful status.

claim: "The deficit was on track to top $1 trillion the year I took office."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because the pronoun "I" and the specific year of taking office are not identified; whether the deficit was on track to exceed $1 trillion depends entirely on which administration and which fiscal or calendar year is meant. U.S. deficits exceeded $1 trillion in the COVID-era 2020–2021 period, but in other transitions (for example 2017) projections did not show a $1 trillion deficit that year. Without a named officeholder and date, the assertion cannot be confirmed.

claim: "In seven years that (nuclear) deal will have expired, and Iran is free to go ahead and create nuclear weapons."
rationale: This claim oversimplifies and misstates timelines. The 2015 Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) placed many restrictions with staggered expirations (so‑called 'sunset' clauses) at different intervals (commonly 10–15 years for key limits), not a single seven‑year cutoff, and Iran would still be bound by the Nuclear Non‑Proliferation Treaty and subject to IAEA safeguards and monitoring. While some limits expiring over time would shorten Iran's 'breakout' time to produce fissile material, it would not be an automatic, unconditional legal freedom to build nuclear weapons after seven years.

claim: A "majority of our students are trapped in" underperforming schools.
rationale: The statement is a broad, unsupported generalization: whether a majority of students are in "underperforming" schools depends entirely on the jurisdiction, timeframe, and how "underperforming" is defined. National and state/local assessment data vary widely, so the claim cannot be verified as true without specific data and definitions.

claim: "92 percent" of President Barack Obama's administration has "never worked outside government."
rationale: Independent fact-checks found the 92% figure is a misinterpretation or misapplication of a limited dataset and does not reflect the broader Obama administration. Many senior officials and appointees had prior private‑sector experience, and the claim conflates different personnel categories and timeframes to produce an inflated percentage.

claim: Says Rep. Justin Amash "votes more with the Democrats than with the Republicans."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about timeframe, but over the bulk of Justin Amash's House tenure he voted with House Republicans more often than with Democrats. He did break with Republicans on several high‑profile votes (and after leaving the GOP in 2019 he sometimes sided with Democrats), but roll‑call alignment data across his career do not show a persistent pattern of voting more with Democrats than with Republicans.

claim: Says photo of beaten woman is Aracely Henriquez, a pregnant woman who George Floyd assaulted during an armed robbery.
rationale: Independent fact-checks found no evidence that the photo shows someone named Aracely Henriquez or that George Floyd assaulted a pregnant woman by that name; the image has been misattributed and does not tie to Floyd. Public reporting and available criminal records do not corroborate the alleged incident or victim identity.

claim: "Cory Gardner is sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions right now."
rationale: This is false: Cory Gardner is not currently a member of Congress and therefore cannot be sponsoring federal legislation right now. While he supported and co-sponsored more limited abortion restrictions during his Senate term, there is no evidence he is sponsoring a bill to ban all abortions nationwide at the present time.

claim: Rick Perry is "taking money away from hurricane victims" and diverting it to "remodel the Governor's Mansion."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rick Perry diverted disaster relief funds earmarked for hurricane victims to pay for a Governor's Mansion remodel. Federal disaster aid (FEMA and HUD CDBG-DR) is administered under specific rules and oversight, and state budget transfers for a mansion renovation would require separate appropriations and public record; reporting about mansion repairs did not show diversion of hurricane-victim funds.

claim: "Hollywood celebs: We will go on ‘total strike’ if Trump does not resign."
rationale: There is no evidence that Hollywood celebrities collectively issued a formal, industry‑wide pledge to launch a 'total strike' unless Trump resigned. Major entertainment unions and mainstream news outlets did not report any unified strike demand; at most there have been isolated calls for protests, boycotts, or statements by individual celebrities. The claim thus overstates and misrepresents the situation.

claim: Dan McCready backed state legislation that raised consumers "$149 million a year in higher energy costs."
rationale: The claim misattributes passage of a specific state law and its projected $149 million cost to Dan McCready. McCready was not a state legislator and did not vote to pass state legislation that directly produced $149 million a year in higher energy costs; independent fact-checks found the ad’s attribution and framing misleading. The $149 million figure has been tied to disputed modeling and different policy proposals, not to a clear, direct vote by McCready.

claim: "You (Hillary Clinton) get a subpoena, and after getting the subpoena you delete 33,000 emails."
rationale: The claim that Clinton deleted 33,000 emails after receiving a subpoena is false. Clinton's lawyers said they reviewed and removed roughly 30,000–33,000 personal emails in early 2015 and produced about 30,000 work-related emails to the State Department before any congressional or FBI subpoena related to the email server was issued; multiple fact-checks and official timelines place the deletions prior to formal subpoenas or criminal process.

claim: BREAKING: Trump Just Ended Welfare For One HUGE Group For 5 Years!
rationale: The claim is vague and sensational with no specifics about which program or group; there is no credible evidence that former President Trump 'just ended welfare for one huge group for 5 years.' Major changes to federal benefit eligibility would require legislation or formal administration rulemaking and typically face legal and public scrutiny, and there has been no verified reporting of such a blanket five-year cutoff enacted by Trump. If the claim refers to a recent announcement, it is either inaccurate or missing essential context.

claim: "We have laws on the books where people can walk right up to our ports of entry, say ‘I have a credible fear of persecution,’ and we bring them in. We don’t send them back."
rationale: U.S. law requires screening for asylum claims (a "credible fear" interview) when someone at or between ports of entry expresses fear of persecution, but a positive credible-fear finding does not automatically allow permanent admission. Successful credible-fear claimants are placed into removal proceedings and may be released on parole or bond pending court, not simply "brought in" permanently, and people found not to have credible fear can often be returned. Policy exceptions (e.g., Title 42 expulsions at times) and enforcement discretion affect outcomes, so the claim's blanket assertion is inaccurate.

claim: Says Ron Johnson said Americans should go back to work, because "death is an unavoidable part of life."
rationale: Senator Ron Johnson publicly urged reopening and made comments characterizing death as an unavoidable part of life while arguing against prolonged shutdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic. Multiple news reports and video excerpts from his interviews quote him saying variations of "death is an unavoidable part of life" as part of his argument that Americans should return to work.

claim: "The fact is" the Clinton Foundation has "got about 80 percent in overhead and 20 percent of the money is actually getting into the places it should."
rationale: Independent audits, IRS Form 990 filings, and charity watchdog analyses show the Clinton Foundation typically reports a majority of its expenditures as program expenses (often in the range of roughly 70–90% in many years), not that 80% is overhead and only 20% goes to programs. The claim reverses the documented proportions and has been repeatedly debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: "I have always been focused on reining in the deficit."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim ('always') but no speaker, timeframe, or objective evidence is provided. Budget deficits and "focus" on them are measurable by specific policy actions and deficit trajectories, and many politicians who professed deficit-reduction goals nonetheless presided over rising deficits, so the unqualified claim cannot be verified as true without supporting records.

claim: "Since 2004, more than 2,000 suspected terrorists have legally purchased weapons in the United States."
rationale: The commonly cited "more than 2,000" figure refers to potential name-based matches between firearms background checks and terrorism watchlists, not confirmed terrorists who legally bought guns. Most of those hits were unconfirmed or resolved and did not establish that the purchaser was a terrorist; very few actual denials resulted from terrorism-related records.

claim: Abigail Spanberger "wants a tax increase of $32 trillion - that’s with a `T,’ to pay for her socialist health care plan."
rationale: Abigail Spanberger has not proposed a $32 trillion tax increase. She has been publicly positioned as a moderate Democrat who opposed Medicare-for-All-style single-payer plans; the $32 trillion figure is a widely circulated estimate of the gross 10-year cost of some single-payer proposals, not a tax increase she has advocated.

claim: "A law enforcement officer is more likely to commit a crime than a CWP (concealed weapons permit) holder."
rationale: There is no strong, consistent evidence that law enforcement officers as a group commit crimes at higher rates than concealed-weapons-permit (CWP) holders. Multiple studies and official statistics have found CWP holders have very low arrest/conviction rates relative to the general population, while police misconduct and criminality do occur but are not shown to be higher in aggregate than among permit holders. The blanket comparative claim is unsupported without careful, jurisdiction-specific analysis.

claim: "Disney stock is down more than 70% and attendance is down more than 55%! 10.1 million people canceled their Disney+ subscription."
rationale: The statement bundles several misleading claims. Disney's share price has not fallen more than 70% from recent multi-year highs and recovered substantially from pandemic lows; park attendance largely rebounded toward or above pre-pandemic levels by 2022–2023 rather than being down over 55%; and Disney's public quarterly reports do not show a single verified 10.1 million-person mass cancellation of Disney+—subscriber counts have fluctuated quarter to quarter but no authenticated one-time exodus of that magnitude was reported.

claim: "I went to the Olympics that was out of balance, and we got it on balance."
rationale: The statement is vague and contains no verifiable specifics (which Olympics, when, who 'we' refers to, or what 'got it on balance' means). There are no identifiable public records or credible reports that match this phrasing, so it cannot be confirmed as a factual claim as presented.

claim: "To this day, (the Cuban government) is a regime that provides safe harbor to terrorists and fugitives."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While Cuba has in the past granted asylum to specific individuals wanted by the U.S. (for example Assata Shakur) and has hosted armed groups for negotiations, characterizing the current Cuban government as broadly providing safe harbor to terrorists and fugitives is not supported as a consistent, ongoing policy and is politically contested. Official U.S. designations and diplomatic relations on this issue have changed over time.

claim: Says that "all those who do not answer directly to the president, they've said (repealing Don't Ask, Don't Tell) is a terrible idea."
rationale: The statement asserts that everyone who does not report directly to the president said repealing Don't Ask, Don't Tell was a terrible idea. This is incorrect: public records from the DADT repeal debate show a mix of positions—some senior military and civilian leaders opposed repeal, but others (including top officials) publicly supported it, so it was not a unanimous 'terrible idea.'

claim: "States with the most gun laws tend to have the fewest gun deaths."
rationale: Multiple cross‑state analyses and summaries of CDC data show a general association: U.S. states that have enacted more and stronger gun‑safety laws tend to report lower firearm death rates per capita than states with fewer such laws. However, this is an observational correlation with notable exceptions and does not by itself prove causation — differences in suicide rates, urbanization, poverty, and enforcement also affect outcomes.

claim: Under New York's new abortion law, "If the baby was born alive, they would just let the baby expire."
rationale: New York’s recent abortion legislation (commonly the 2019 Reproductive Health Act) did not create any legal allowance to withhold care from infants born alive after an attempted abortion. Federal and state law and medical ethics require that a liveborn infant be treated as a person and receive appropriate medical care; the RHA removed abortion from the criminal code and expanded circumstances for later abortions to protect the patient’s health, but it did not legalize 'letting a baby expire.'

claim: "While (Chris Christie) talks about job creation, we don't see jobs being created in this state."
rationale: The statement is too vague to verify because it does not identify which state or what time period is meant; job creation is an empirical claim that requires specific state-level employment data. Without a defined jurisdiction and timeframe, the claim cannot be confirmed and therefore is judged false as presented.

claim: U.S. Senate candidate Michelle Nunn "earned as much as $300,000 running a nonprofit that had laid off 90 workers."
rationale: The claim mixes accurate and misleading elements. Michelle Nunn did earn a six-figure compensation as CEO of Points of Light, but her reported pay on nonprofit tax filings was generally below $300,000 in most years and did not clearly peak at the asserted $300,000 figure; furthermore the reported staff reductions around the 2010–2012 merger with the HandsOn Network involved affiliates and reorganizations rather than a straightforward single layoff of 90 employees directly attributable to Nunn’s nonprofit. Presenting both pieces together implies a direct causal and numerical link that the public records and news coverage do not support.

claim: "Thanks in part to our all-of-the-above strategy for American energy," the United States generates "more natural gas than anybody."
rationale: The United States has been the world’s largest producer of natural gas in recent years, driven by the shale-gas boom and increased production from tight gas and associated gas. Data from major energy statisticians (EIA, BP, IEA) show U.S. annual natural gas production exceeding that of other countries, including Russia, over the last several years.

claim: "Under Republicans, recessions happen four times as frequently as under Democrats."
rationale: This claim is not supported by standard measures: using NBER recession dates and attributing recessions to the party of the sitting president or Congress does not produce a result of Republicans having recessions four times as often as Democrats. Recessions have occurred under presidents of both parties and while there may be a modest partisan tilt in some post‑war periods, it is far smaller than a fourfold difference and sensitive to the chosen timeframe and attribution method.

claim: "We've seen 115,000 jobs created in the American auto industry since GM and Chrysler emerged from bankruptcy."
rationale: The statement is imprecise and cannot be verified as an accurate, standalone fact. Net job changes in the U.S. "auto industry" depend on the exact start/end dates and which BLS series are used (motor-vehicle and parts manufacturing vs. broader supply-chain or dealer employment), and prior fact-checkers have found the 115,000 figure to be a selective interpretation rather than a clear, verifiable total.

claim: The coronavirus "was constructed in the Wuhan Institute of Virology."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SARS‑CoV‑2 was deliberately constructed in the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Multiple peer‑reviewed genomic analyses report features consistent with natural evolution and identify close coronaviruses in bats (and some in pangolins); international investigations and mainstream scientific consensus have not found proof of genetic engineering. While hypotheses about a lab‑associated incident have been discussed, that is not the same as evidence the virus was constructed.

claim: "In eighth grade math, we’ve fallen to ninth place."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsupported by major international assessment results; recent TIMSS and PISA data show that rankings for eighth-grade/math-age cohorts fluctuate by year and country, and the United States has not been consistently reported as having 'fallen to ninth place.' Without a specified country, assessment, and year, the claim is misleading.

claim: Says Ohio Gov. John Kasich "got lucky with a thing called fracking," which "is why Ohio is doing well."
rationale: John Kasich has publicly credited shale gas development for helping Ohio's economy and used phrasing like being 'lucky' with fracking as a factor in the state's recovery. Media coverage and his own campaign/governor remarks record him making statements to that effect.

claim: "Probably one out of every two households in Oklahoma has a gun."
rationale: Most reputable state-level estimates and national surveys place household gun ownership in Oklahoma below 50% (typically in the mid-40% range), so the statement that "one out of every two households" is likely an overestimate. Survey results vary by year and method, but available data do not clearly support a 50% household ownership rate in Oklahoma.

claim: Refugees are throwing rocks and trying "to kill you."
rationale: This is a sweeping, unverified assertion about refugees as a group. While there have been isolated incidents of violent behavior at some border confrontations, there is no credible evidence that refugees generally are throwing rocks and trying to kill people; most refugees flee violence and are protected under international law.

claim: Undocumented immigrants "pay $12 billion a year into Social Security."
rationale: Multiple analysts and government-related studies have produced estimates that unauthorized or undocumented workers collectively contribute on the order of $10–13 billion per year in payroll taxes to Social Security; the commonly cited $12 billion figure falls squarely within that range. The number is an estimate rather than a precise tabulation because payroll tax records do not explicitly label workers by immigration status.

claim: "6,400 Ohioans ... lost manufacturing jobs in the month of September."
rationale: The statement omits a year and source, so it cannot be verified as presented. Monthly manufacturing job changes are reported by the BLS at the state level and can be positive or negative by thousands in different months and years, so the claim might be true for a specific September but is unprovable without that context.

claim: "Update: van full of illegals caught voting at multiple Alabama polling locations."
rationale: There is no credible or contemporaneous reporting from reliable news outlets or official election authorities documenting a van of noncitizens being caught voting at multiple Alabama polling places. Large-scale, coordinated noncitizen voting would almost certainly trigger immediate law-enforcement and election-official statements and widespread media coverage, which is lacking for this claim.

claim: Says he can’t release his internal affairs record because there are Attorney General guidelines in place protecting it.
rationale: The claim presents a blanket reason that an Attorney General's guidelines prevent release of an internal affairs file, but whether such guidelines bar release depends entirely on the jurisdiction and specific rules; many AG opinions and public-records laws allow disclosure or partial release while others restrict it. Without knowing the state, agency, or the exact guidance cited, the assertion that AG guidelines universally protect the record is misleading and cannot be verified as stated.

claim: "We won. We won in a landslide. This was a landslide."
rationale: In the context this phrase is commonly used (the 2020 U.S. presidential election), the certified results show Joseph R. Biden Jr. won 306–232 in the Electoral College and the popular vote by about 7 million votes (~4.5 percentage points), which is not generally characterized as a 'landslide.' State certifications, recounts, and court decisions upheld those results, contradicting the claim of a landslide victory for the opposing candidate.

claim: "More businesses are closing than opening in Virginia today."
rationale: There is no publicly available, real-time statewide data showing that more businesses are closing than opening in Virginia on any given day; openings and closures are typically reported over weeks or months via official filings and surveys. Without contemporaneous statistics from Virginia agencies or reliable trackers, the assertion that 'more businesses are closing than opening today' is unsubstantiated.

claim: "More people have watched ‘Morning Joe’ than CNN and HLN 5 years in a row."
rationale: The claim is not supported without a specified metric or timeframe. Morning Joe has at times outperformed CNN and regularly beats low-rated HLN in certain time slots, but Nielsen ratings fluctuate year-to-year and there is no clear evidence that Morning Joe has had more viewers than CNN and HLN for five consecutive years across a defined calendar metric.

claim: The Uvalde, Texas, school shooter was a "transsexual leftist illegal alien named Salvatore Ramos."
rationale: This claim is false. The Uvalde shooter was identified by law enforcement and major news outlets as Salvador Ramos (not 'Salvatore'), an 18-year-old local resident and U.S. citizen; there is no credible evidence he was an undocumented immigrant, transgender, or a 'leftist.' These specific personal and political labels were not supported by official reports or reputable reporting.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Perry is "spending Texans’ hard-earned money to live like Louie XIV."
rationale: The statement is a rhetorical exaggeration and not supported by evidence. Public records and mainstream fact-checking of Gov. Rick Perry's tenure show routine gubernatorial expenses (travel, security, official residence) but no documented use of Texans' money to fund an opulent, Louis XIV–style personal lifestyle. Criticisms of his spending typically point to specific items or standard official costs rather than evidence of monarchy-level personal extravagance.

claim: "The government will be infiltrating" personal text messages.
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsubstantiated prediction with no specified government, timeframe, or evidence. While some governments have the legal authority or technical programs to intercept or obtain access to some individuals' messages (usually via warrants, court orders, or targeted surveillance), there is no general, verifiable fact that governments will universally "infiltrate" all personal text messages.

claim: "He's the only candidate who's balanced budgets and brought jobs to Providence."
rationale: The claim is an absolute, exclusive statement that cannot be verified as true without naming the candidate, the time period, and objective measures of ‘balanced budgets’ and job creation. Multiple Providence officials and administrations have claimed or been credited with budget balancing and economic development over time, so asserting a single person is the only one is almost certainly false or at best unprovable.

claim: "Ukraine was the No. 1 donor to Hillary Clinton when she was running for president."
rationale: U.S. law forbids foreign governments from contributing to federal campaigns, and public campaign-finance records show Hillary Clinton's top donors in her presidential runs were U.S. individuals, PACs and industry groups (not the country of Ukraine). The claim likely confuses donations to the Clinton Foundation or contributions from individuals of Ukrainian origin with a sovereign-state "donor."

claim: "If we ban the practice of earmarks, we could save the American taxpayer anywhere between $15 (billion) to $20 billion dollars a year in pork-barrel spending."
rationale: The claim presents a precise annual saving range without supporting citation, but historical estimates of earmarks vary widely by year and definition and do not consistently show $15–$20 billion in net savings. Analyses by budget offices and watchdogs have produced lower or inconsistent figures, and banning earmarks would often reclassify or shift spending rather than automatically eliminate that full amount. Therefore the specific assertion is not reliably supported.

claim: "The pace of missile development between (Kim Jong Il and Kim Jong Un) has increased the testing about twenty-fold."
rationale: While missile testing in North Korea increased dramatically under Kim Jong Un compared with Kim Jong Il, the specific claim of an "about twenty-fold" increase is not reliably supportable without specifying dates and what counts as a test. Known reporting shows Kim Jong Il presided over only a handful of launches, whereas Kim Jong Un oversaw dozens to over a hundred launches depending on the end date, so the multiplier varies widely and is not a precise twenty-fold.

claim: "Actress Emma Stone: ‘For the first time in history we have a president that…"
rationale: The provided text is an incomplete, unattributed fragment and there is no reliable record of a widely reported political quote by Emma Stone beginning with that phrase. Without a full quote, date, or source, the statement cannot be verified and is likely a misattribution or invented fragment. I therefore treat the claim as false until a primary source is shown.

claim: In the infrastructure bill that just passed the House, "only 10% is actual infrastructure."
rationale: The claim is misleading: independent analyses of the recent bipartisan infrastructure package (and House-passed infrastructure proposals) show far more than 10% of the funding goes to traditional infrastructure categories — roads, bridges, transit, water, broadband, power grid, and resilience. The 'only 10%' figure reflects a narrow or selective accounting that excludes many commonly accepted infrastructure items and is contradicted by mainstream budget breakdowns and fact-checks.

claim: "Nonpartisan experts have consistently ranked Claire one of the most independent senators — right in the middle."
rationale: The claim is vague and not supported by consistent evidence: different nonpartisan measures (party unity scores, bipartisan index, and ideological placement) have placed 'Claire' at varying positions over time. While some metrics have put her near the center in certain years, others have not ranked her among the "most independent" senators, so it is inaccurate to say experts have "consistently" ranked her that way.

claim: Says Bill O’Reilly spoke 40 percent of the words in an interview with President Barack Obama.
rationale: I could not find authoritative, transcript-based evidence showing Bill O’Reilly spoke exactly 40% of the words in any specific interview with President Obama. Major fact-checkers and available transcripts do not corroborate that precise proportion, and such a specific percentage would require a published word-count analysis that is absent. Without a verified transcript analysis, the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: Florida Democrats "put my Social Security number and my wife's Employment Identification Number in a mail piece."
rationale: There is no verifiable, widely reported evidence that the Florida Democratic Party mailed a piece containing a private individual's full Social Security number and his wife's Employer Identification Number. A release of that magnitude of sensitive data would be broadly reported and legally notable; absent corroborating documentation or credible news coverage, the claim remains unsubstantiated and unlikely as stated.

claim: Says Mike DeWine "flip-flopped on the gun issue and has earned an F from the NRA."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable record that Mike DeWine has been given an overall ‘F’ rating by the NRA across his career; historically he has had a generally pro-gun record and received favorable NRA attention while serving in Congress and statewide offices. The phrase “flip‑flopped on the gun issue” is subjective and depends on which specific votes or statements are cited; while DeWine has supported some gun-safety measures at times, that alone does not prove a wholesale reversal or an official NRA ‘F’ grade.

claim: Putin beheaded bioweapon engineers in Ukraine.
rationale: There is no credible, independently verified evidence that Vladimir Putin personally beheaded anyone, nor verified reporting that Russian forces systematically beheaded 'bioweapon engineers' in Ukraine. Major fact-checkers and independent news organizations have debunked circulating claims about Ukrainian 'biolabs' and fatal executions as unverified or propaganda.

claim: "There will be several thousand dollars in payments going to families with six-figure incomes who’ve had no income interruption whatsoever."
rationale: The claim is presented as a broad, categorical statement but lacks context about which program and timeframe it refers to. Federal relief and tax-credit payments typically have income thresholds and phase-outs, so it is not generally true that 'several thousand dollars' will automatically go to all families with six-figure incomes and no income interruption, though specific programs or exceptions could allow some higher‑earning families to receive payments.

claim: ISIS sends out "90,000 social (media) messages a day."
rationale: The precise figure of 90,000 social-media messages per day is unverified and appears to be an exaggeration. Public estimates of ISIS online activity have varied widely across time, platforms, and reporting organizations, and no consistent authoritative source confirms a steady rate of 90,000 messages per day.
