claim: Under the Democratic health plan, families "will be forced to spend an additional $2,100 a year to keep their current health care."
rationale: The statement presents a blanket, precise dollar increase for all families without attribution or context; no authoritative analysis of major Democratic health reform proposals concluded that every family would be "forced" to spend an additional $2,100 per year to keep their current coverage. Independent and government analyses of different Democratic proposals showed widely varying effects depending on family income, current insurance status, subsidies, and which plan elements are adopted, so a universal $2,100 figure is misleading.

claim: "Already this calendar year, since January 1, we have had more than 20,000 people come across the border, apprehended, unauthorized."
rationale: The claim as stated omits the year and which border, so it cannot be independently verified. U.S. border encounter/apprehension totals often do exceed 20,000 in short periods in many recent years, so the assertion might be true in some contexts, but presented without a timeframe or source it is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Our governor proposed initially a 5% cut across the board of state government."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it gives no identifying details (which governor, which state, or when). Without those specifics I cannot confirm the proposal; while some governors have proposed across‑the‑board cuts in various years, this exact statement is unsubstantiated.

claim: The Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise"
rationale: The Buffalo Billion has been widely criticized and state audits and reporting found numerous promised jobs were not realized, but it is incorrect to say it is "still breaking every job promise". Some projects produced jobs or partial fulfillment while others failed or underdelivered, so the statement's absolute claim of universal ongoing failure is inaccurate.

claim: Says Mitt Romney is using "a million of his presidential campaign dollars to finance his Utah Senate race."
rationale: Campaign finance records and contemporary news reporting show Mitt Romney transferred $1,000,000 from his earlier presidential campaign account into his newly formed Senate campaign committee when he ran for the Utah Senate in 2018. That transfer constituted using presidential-campaign funds to help finance his Senate bid.

claim: President Barack Obama’s health care reform "slashed $500 billion from Medicare."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act included roughly $500 billion in projected Medicare savings over about a decade, but those were mainly reductions in future spending growth and lower payments to providers and Medicare Advantage plans, not a $500 billion cut to beneficiaries' benefits. Describing the law as having 'slashed $500 billion from Medicare' is misleading because it conflates projected spending reductions and payment-rate changes with direct cuts to Medicare benefits.

claim: "Lauren Boebert received a PPP loan for her restaurant."
rationale: Public PPP recipient records and contemporaneous news reporting identified Shooters Grill — the restaurant associated with Lauren Boebert — as having received Paycheck Protection Program funds in 2020. While there was some political messaging about whether she personally 'took' a loan, the documented loan went to the business she co-owned at the time.

claim: In the U.S. Constitution, "there’s a little section in there that talks about life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness."
rationale: The phrase "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" is in the Declaration of Independence (1776), not the U.S. Constitution (1787). The Constitution's preamble speaks of securing "the Blessings of Liberty," but it does not contain that exact phrase.

claim: Says that as president, Barack Obama has not gone to the Texas-Mexico border
rationale: The claim that Barack Obama did not go to the Texas–Mexico border while president is false. Obama made at least one official trip to the U.S.–Mexico border region during his presidency — he visited the El Paso/Juárez border area and met with local officials and border personnel, which was covered in White House schedules and news reports. Therefore saying he never went is incorrect.

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The statement asserts a specific, extreme character judgment about a named U.S. Representative but provides no verifiable incidents or evidence. There is no widely recognized member of the U.S. House currently serving named 'Steven Smith,' and claims that someone is a 'misogynist bigot of epic proportions' are subjective and require documented behavior or statements to substantiate.

claim: Proposition 2 on November’s Texas ballot "does not cost state taxpayers any money."
rationale: As an absolute statement, this is misleading. Texas constitutional amendments and ballot propositions routinely have fiscal notes and can create direct or indirect costs (administration, implementation, or litigation), so claiming categorically that Proposition 2 "does not cost state taxpayers any money" is not reliably true without reference to the specific year's official fiscal analysis.

claim: "Middle-class income rose to a record level in 2017 as the strong economy lifted the fortunes of more Americans."
rationale: U.S. government and news reports for 2017 showed real median household (commonly used as a proxy for middle‑class) income rose to a record high that year and poverty rates fell, and analysts attributed those gains in part to a stronger labor market. While the upward move is well documented, the statement's causal wording (“as the strong economy lifted the fortunes of more Americans”) is interpretive rather than a formal causal proof.

claim: "Phony" ballots "were printed without my name on it."
rationale: This specific assertion cannot be verified from the information given and no corroborating evidence is provided. Claims about ballots require documentary proof (photographs, chain-of-custody, official audit or court findings); absent that, the statement should not be treated as established fact.

claim: Says COVID-19 has killed more North Carolinians in a year than the flu has in 10 years.
rationale: The claim is not reliably true as stated because it lacks specific years and influenza seasons. CDC estimates show seasonal flu deaths vary widely year-to-year and, when scaled to North Carolina's population, a 10-year total of flu deaths can be similar to or exceed the number of COVID-19 deaths in a single year depending on which years are compared. Without a defined COVID year and defined 10-year flu window the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: Amanda Murphy has "two vacation homes around the world."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that a public figure named Amanda Murphy owns "two vacation homes around the world." Public financial disclosures and news coverage for known politicians or public personalities named Amanda Murphy do not list multiple international vacation properties, and no credible sources were found to substantiate the claim. Given the commonality of the name and absence of documentation, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "In Rick Perry's Texas, the governor threatens to leave, to secede from the greatest country in the" world.
rationale: Rick Perry, while governor of Texas, made provocative rhetorical comments about states' rights and sometimes invoked nullification or criticized federal actions, but he never officially threatened or took steps to secede Texas from the United States. Reporting and official records show political rhetoric and debate, not an actual gubernatorial secession threat or action.

claim: "Hydroxychloroquine cures this ‘virus.’ It just so happens this is the treatment used for radiation sickness!!"
rationale: Multiple randomized trials and health agencies have found hydroxychloroquine does not cure COVID‑19 or other viral infections and can cause significant side effects. Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial and immunomodulatory drug used for malaria and autoimmune diseases, and it is not an established treatment for radiation sickness (which is treated with agents like potassium iodide, Prussian blue, or DTPA depending on the contaminant).

claim: "Ten percent of violent deaths in the U.S. each year are due to strangulation."
rationale: Available national data on violent deaths (homicides and other assault-related deaths) show firearms and sharp instruments account for the largest shares; documented deaths from strangulation/asphyxiation are a small minority, not roughly 10%. Strangulation is more commonly reported among nonfatal intimate-partner assaults, but fatal strangulation deaths constitute only a small fraction of overall violent deaths in the U.S.

claim: Says Michael Kors said, "I’m tired of pretending I like blacks."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that Michael Kors ever made that statement; the quote has circulated on social media and meme sites but was not attributed in any reputable news outlets and has been debunked by fact-checkers. High-profile racist quotations attributed to public figures are typically traceable to interviews or recordings, which do not exist for this claim.

claim: "This is the only state in the country that bypassed the General Assembly to authorize [in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants]."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because multiple states have authorized in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants through non-legislative means (such as university boards, state higher-education agencies, executive actions, or court decisions), so no single state is uniquely the only one to have bypassed its legislature. Without a specific state and timeframe the statement cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Democratic Party created Planned Parenthood
rationale: Planned Parenthood traces its origins to Margaret Sanger and activists who founded the American Birth Control League in 1921 and later reorganized as Planned Parenthood; it was not created by the Democratic Party. While individual Democratic politicians have often supported Planned Parenthood, the organization’s founding was by private activists and reformers, not a political party.

claim: Heroin and prescription opioids are "the number one cause of accidental or preventable death in Wisconsin."
rationale: While heroin and prescription opioid overdoses have risen sharply and are a major contributor to unintentional injury deaths in Wisconsin, available state and CDC vital-statistics reporting does not consistently show them as the single top cause of accidental or preventable death statewide across all recent years. Other unintentional injury categories (notably motor vehicle crashes and falls) have historically been leading causes, and rankings can vary by year and age group.

claim: "Iowa's Republican caucus stopped mattering years ago. It in no way determines the party nominee."
rationale: The claim is too absolute. While Iowa's Republican caucus has not reliably predicted every eventual nominee in recent cycles (e.g., winners who did not become the nominee), it still influences momentum, media coverage, candidate viability, and delegate math early in the process. Saying it "in no way determines" the nominee misstates its continued, if variable, influence.

claim: "I became a Republican sooner in my life than" Ronald Reagan did in his.
rationale: The claim compares an unspecified speaker's timing of becoming a Republican to Ronald Reagan's, but no information is given about who "I" is or when they changed affiliation. Without the person's birthdate and date of party change (and a clear definition of "became a Republican"), the statement cannot be established as true. Ronald Reagan is generally known to have switched to the Republican Party in the early 1960s, so a concrete comparison requires more data.

claim: "Under the ruling of the Supreme Court, any lobbyist could go into any legislator and say, if you don't vote our way on this bill, we're going to run a million-dollar campaign against you in your district."
rationale: Supreme Court rulings (e.g., Citizens United and related decisions) allow independent political spending by corporations and groups but do not authorize lobbyists to directly coordinate or legally threaten legislators. Directly telling a legislator "vote our way or we'll run a million-dollar campaign against you" would be coercion or extortion/bribery in many circumstances and coordination rules and criminal laws still apply.

claim: "Congress files charges against Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: There is no record that Congress has "filed charges" against Nancy Pelosi. In the U.S. system criminal charges are brought by prosecutors (state or federal), while Congress can only pursue impeachment (articles in the House) or disciplinary actions; no impeachment or criminal indictment of Pelosi has been reported through mid-2024.

claim: Quotes Andy Borowitz as saying "stopping Hillary is a short-term solution. The long-term solution — and it will be more difficult — is fixing the educational system that has created so many people ignorant enough to vote for Hillary."
rationale: There is no reliable record or credible archive attributing this explicit quote to Andy Borowitz. Borowitz is a known satirist whose work is published under the Borowitz Report; that archive and mainstream fact-checking resources do not contain this wording, making the attribution likely fabricated or misattributed.

claim: Under David Dewhurst’s leadership, the Texas "Senate passed an expansion of in-state tuition and free health care to illegal immigrants."
rationale: The claim mixes facts and timing incorrectly. Texas did enact a 2001 law allowing certain undocumented students to qualify for in-state tuition, but that law passed before David Dewhurst became lieutenant governor and did not create free health care for undocumented immigrants. Texas has not passed a broad expansion providing free health care to undocumented residents.

claim: President Barack Obama "is the first president to keep a dog-trainer on retainer for $102,000 a year at taxpayer expense."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate. Previous administrations had government-paid handlers or animal-care staff for presidential pets, and reporting by independent fact-checkers found the $102,000 number was a mischaracterization (attributing routine Secret Service or staff pay or contract costs to a supposed unique annual private retainer). No evidence supports that Obama was the first president to have a taxpayer-funded dog trainer on a $102,000-a-year retainer.

claim: "You have 200,000 to 400,000 military veterans on the street in this country on any given day."
rationale: Recent U.S. point-in-time counts and VA data show roughly 30,000–40,000 veterans experiencing homelessness on a single night, not 200,000–400,000. The claim greatly overstates the number of veterans 'on the street' on any given day based on authoritative homelessness counts.

claim: Hillary Clinton "has already said she's going to wipe out the Second Amendment. She doesn't believe in the First Amendment. And, she also believes in big government, which flies in the face of the 10th Amendment"
rationale: The statement bundles several exaggerated claims. Hillary Clinton has advocated gun-control measures (universal background checks, some bans/restrictions) but has not stated she will 'wipe out the Second Amendment' or seek repeal of it. She has not publicly declared disbelief in the First Amendment and has defended free speech in many contexts, and while she supports an active federal role on many issues, labeling that as literally 'flying in the face of the 10th Amendment' is a political interpretation rather than a factual claim about her statements or constitutional intent.

claim: A photo shows "brave women of the Red Cross" arriving in Normandy on D-Day to help injured troops.
rationale: This attribution is commonly debunked: contemporary records and historians note that Red Cross volunteer women did not land with the initial D‑Day assault waves, and frontline medical care on the beaches was provided by military medics, corpsmen and ship‑borne/hospital units. The photo circulating with that caption is miscaptioned or from a different time/place (other volunteer groups or later arrivals), not women arriving on the Normandy beaches on D‑Day itself.

claim: Former Gov. Pat McCrory appointed liberals to the North Carolina Textbook Commission, which "mandated textbooks" pushing critical race theory.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the North Carolina Textbook Commission (or subsequent adoption actions) 'mandated' K–12 textbooks that push critical race theory. While Gov. Pat McCrory made appointments to state education bodies during his term, those appointments were not broadly characterized or documented as a scheme to install 'liberals' who then forced CRT into adopted textbooks. The textbook-adoption process in NC involves reviews and recommendations and CRT is an academic legal framework not present as a mandated K–12 curriculum in state-adopted textbooks.

claim: "By registration fewer than 20 percent of Florida voters are Independents."
rationale: Florida’s official registration categories show that voters registered with No Party Affiliation (commonly called Independents) have comprised more than 20% of registered voters in recent years. Thus the statement that fewer than 20% are Independents is inconsistent with recent state registration data.

claim: The 2020 election is in "recount territory" and "I’ve seen elections change as a result of" recounts.
rationale: Most 2020 presidential state margins exceeded typical statutory recount thresholds, and only a small number of states (notably Georgia) were close enough to prompt recounts; those recounts and audits confirmed the original outcome with only trivial changes. Although recounts can and occasionally have changed the outcome of extremely narrow contests in rare historical cases, that did not happen for the overall 2020 presidential result.

claim: In Afghanistan, "over 100 billion dollars spent on military contracts."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and cannot be verified as stated. While total U.S. war-related spending for Afghanistan over two decades is in the many hundreds of billions (and some estimates including long-term obligations run into the trillions), published figures for what counts specifically as "military contracts" in Afghanistan vary by source and timeframe and do not conclusively show a single verified, standalone tally of over $100 billion without additional context.

claim: David Beckham’s proposed soccer stadium at Miami’s Port "threatens the 207,000 jobs and $27 billion economic impact tied to the cargo and cruise industries."
rationale: The cited figures (about 207,000 jobs and $27 billion) echo economic-impact numbers publicized for PortMiami, but there is no credible evidence that Beckham’s stadium proposal would directly eliminate or ‘threaten’ the entire cargo and cruise industries that produce those totals. Beckham’s later stadium plans shifted to a different site (the Melreese golf course / Freedom Park proposal), and independent analyses do not show the stadium would wipe out the full port employment and economic output cited. The claim thus overstates and conflates port-wide economic figures with an asserted, proven causal threat from the stadium.

claim: Officials "recommend that women who get one of these (COVID-19) shots should absolutely not get pregnant for at least the first two months after they’ve been injected."
rationale: Major public-health agencies did not issue a blanket recommendation that women must avoid pregnancy for two months after receiving a COVID-19 vaccine. Organizations such as the CDC, WHO, and obstetrics professional societies have stated there is no need to delay pregnancy after vaccination and that the authorized COVID-19 vaccines are not live vaccines and have not been shown to cause infertility.

claim: The Keystone XL pipeline "doesn’t even have any oil for America."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Keystone XL was designed to carry Canadian crude to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries, so it would deliver oil into the U.S. refining system and not "none for America." While access to the Gulf makes it easier for some oil or refined products to be exported, significant volumes would be refined in the United States and could supply domestic fuel markets.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no credible record of Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez making this statement; major fact-checkers and a review of her public statements and social media show the quote is fabricated and circulated as a meme. The language and sentiment praising an ISIS-linked individual as 'more of a hero than our veterans' is inconsistent with AOC's known public positions and would have prompted documented responses if true.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: This quotation is widely circulated on social media but there is no record of Keanu Reeves saying it in any verified interview, speech, or publication. Reputable fact-checkers and searches of archival interviews find no original source, and the language and context do not match Reeves's known public statements.

claim: The people who want President Barack Obama impeached "are all white, they're all older, and guess what, they're in the far right wing of the Republican Party."
rationale: The statement is an overgeneralization: while many prominent calls to impeach President Obama came from older, white, conservative and Tea Party-aligned Republicans, it is not true that everyone who wanted him impeached fit that description. Public records and media coverage show a majority of proponents were Republican conservatives, but there were exceptions in age, race, and political labels and the phrase "all" is inaccurate.

claim: The minimum wage "in real terms right now is below where it was when Harry Truman was in office."
rationale: The federal minimum wage during Truman’s presidency (1945–1953) ranged in nominal terms roughly between $0.40 and $0.75 depending on the year; when converted to modern dollars using CPI-type inflation adjustments those amounts are roughly comparable to or slightly below today’s federal minimum of $7.25 in many year-to-year comparisons. Multiple historical series of the federal minimum wage show that the current real (inflation‑adjusted) federal minimum is not uniformly below the levels seen during Truman’s years, so the blanket claim is inaccurate without specifying a particular year and inflation series.

claim: Says Texas high school graduates must pass Algebra II to be eligible for automatic admission to state's public universities.
rationale: Texas law granting automatic admission (the "top‑10%" rule) requires students to complete the state's college‑preparatory/recommended high‑school curriculum to be eligible, and that curriculum includes Algebra II (or an approved equivalent). While the state's general high‑school graduation rules were modified by HB5 to allow some substitutes, automatic‑admission eligibility still depends on completing the college‑prep/recommended curriculum, which effectively requires Algebra II in most cases.

claim: "Under Terry McAuliffe (there was a) record investment in education."
rationale: Terry McAuliffe did push for and secure notable increases in education funding (pre-K expansion, teacher pay increases, K–12 spending boosts) during his 2014–2018 term, but the blanket claim of a “record investment in education” is ambiguous and not unambiguously supported across standard metrics (total spending, per‑pupil, or year‑over‑year increases). Some statements from his administration called certain budget items "record" for specific programs, but there is no clear, single authoritative measure showing an all‑around record investment for the state under his tenure.

claim: "Last year, 36 million Americans didn’t have a prescription filled because they couldn’t afford it."
rationale: Multiple recent national surveys and analyses (for example by Kaiser Family Foundation and other health-policy organizations) have reported that roughly 35–36 million U.S. adults did not fill a prescription in the prior year because of cost. The figure is based on self-reported survey responses and is commonly cited in that range for the most recent year measured.

claim: "The average homeowner spends more than $2,000 each year on energy costs – more than on either real estate taxes or homeowners insurance."
rationale: While combined household energy bills can approach or exceed $2,000 in some years, typical U.S. owner-occupied households on average pay more in property taxes annually (often several thousand dollars) than they do for energy. Homeowners insurance premiums are generally lower than $2,000, so the claim is half-true (energy can exceed insurance) but incorrect overall because energy does not typically exceed real estate taxes.

claim: "Trump’s daughter works at the White House. Her husband works at the White House. Rudy’s son works at the White House. Barr’s son-in-law works at the White House. Barr’s daughter works at Treasury. Trump’s sons do foreign business. Trump’s daughter is getting Chinese patents and Saudi grants."
rationale: Parts of the claim are true: Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner served as Senior Advisors in the White House during the Trump administration, and Andrew Giuliani (Rudy Giuliani’s son) worked on White House staff. However, the assertions about William Barr’s daughter or son‑in‑law working at the White House or Treasury are not supported by public personnel records or reliable reporting, and the final phrase about Ivanka “getting Chinese patents and Saudi grants” is vague and misleading (she and her brand pursued foreign trademarks/registrations and there were foreign investments linked to Trump‑related businesses, but the claim as stated is unsupported). Because the statement mixes verified facts with unverified or false assertions, the overall composite claim is false.

claim: "Amazing fact: Senate has already voted on more amendments in 2015 than Reid allowed ALL YEAR last year."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported: it compares an unspecified early period of 2015 to all of 2014 under Majority Leader Harry Reid without providing counts. Public roll-call activity for the Senate is recorded and there is no clear, widely reported evidence that the Senate had already held more amendment votes in 2015 than Reid 'allowed' during the entire prior year. Without specific dates and numeric counts the statement is misleading and cannot be verified as true.

claim: "It's just outrageous that under President Bush, the National Institutes of Health have been basically decreased in funding."
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated: under President George W. Bush the NIH's nominal appropriations did not decrease overall and were higher than at the start of his term. However, after early increases growth largely stalled and in inflation-adjusted terms NIH purchasing power fell and grant success rates declined, so saying funding was "basically decreased" without qualification is misleading.

claim: "When Marcy Kaptur brought home $42 million for new manufacturing jobs, Dennis Kucinich voted 'no'."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that Dennis Kucinich specifically voted ‘‘no’’ on a bill or amendment that directly corresponds to Marcy Kaptur ‘‘bringing home $42 million’’ for new manufacturing jobs. Kucinich’s record shows mixed votes on stimulus and appropriations measures and he sometimes opposed bills for broader policy reasons, but the claim ties a specific $42 million earmark to a single ‘‘no’’ vote without identifying the bill or date, so it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: Estimated annual COVID-19 deaths in the U.S. totals 27,530, after you subtract those who died "with, not from" COVID-19, not in nursing homes and who didn't have four or more comorbidities.
rationale: The claim appears to be a heavily filtered and arithmetic reduction of official counts that misinterprets how COVID-19 deaths are recorded. CDC provisional and vital statistics data show many more annual deaths attributed to COVID-19 even after excluding nursing-home residents and accounting for comorbidities; the distinction “with, not from” is not supported by death-certificate practice and cannot validly reduce national counts to a single figure of 27,530. The specific number seems to result from cherry-picking subsets and applying unsupported exclusions rather than a defensible national estimate.

claim: "The Pentagon itself says that we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable Pentagon statement that unambiguously says “we could eliminate 20 percent of U.S. bases.” The Department of Defense has at times discussed base consolidation, BRAC processes, and studies estimating possible reductions or savings, but the broad one-line claim as stated lacks supporting attribution, timeframe, or definition (domestic vs. overseas) and therefore is not supported as presented.

claim: Says Trump ties are made "in China, not Colorado. Trump suits in Mexico, not Michigan. Trump furniture in Turkey, not Ohio. Trump picture frames in India, not Wisconsin."
rationale: Reporting and product-label evidence show many Trump‑branded consumer goods have been manufactured overseas rather than in the U.S.; for example, ties and other apparel labeled under the Trump name have been produced in China, suits and apparel in countries including Mexico, home furnishings sourced from places such as Turkey, and framed goods or decor imported from India. The quoted line accurately reflects a common factual point about the Trump licensing business model: brand goods were often made abroad, not in the specific U.S. states named.

claim: Video footage from Georgia shows suitcases filled with ballots pulled from under a table and illegally counted after election observers were told to leave.
rationale: Independent fact-checks and statements from Georgia election officials establish the viral footage was misleading: the items described as “suitcases” were ballot transfer/secure ballot bags and the clips were cropped or shown out of context. There is no credible evidence that ballots were pulled from under a table and illegally counted after observers had been ordered to leave.

claim: "Hillary Clinton invented ISIS with her stupid policies. She is responsible for ISIS."
rationale: ISIS was not "invented" by Hillary Clinton; it grew from a mix of factors including the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq, the collapse of Iraqi institutions, the Al-Qaeda in Iraq insurgency led by Abu Musab al‑Zarqawi, and the Syrian civil war. While U.S. and other foreign policies (including actions during and after Hillary Clinton's tenure as Secretary of State) affected regional dynamics, assigning sole responsibility to Clinton is historically inaccurate and unsupported by the record.

claim: "Every four minutes, another American home or business goes solar."
rationale: This statement is a time-dependent industry slogan rather than a stable fact. Solar industry reports have used different rates (for example claims of every X minutes) in different years, so without a specified timeframe and definition of "goes solar" (new installations, systems energized, customers), the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: A video shows an animal chip scanner detecting a microchip where a woman was vaccinated.
rationale: There is no evidence that vaccines contain injectable microchips, and consumer animal/RFID scanners pick up implanted glass capsule transponders much larger than any vaccine dose would contain. Videos claiming a scanner 'detects a microchip' at a vaccination site are consistent with false positives from external metal, nearby electronics, the scanner itself, or deliberate manipulation, not proof of a vaccine-embedded chip. Therefore the claim as stated is misleading and false.

claim: "Julia Roberts claims ‘Michelle Obama isn’t fit to clean Melania’s toilet’ "
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that actress Julia Roberts made this statement; the alleged quote appears to originate from satirical or fake-news sources and viral social-media misattributions. Reputable fact-checkers and mainstream outlets have not corroborated the claim, making it highly unlikely to be genuine.

claim: Says "there have been some job gains in the McMansion State since Mr. Christie took office, but they have lagged gains both in the nation as a whole and in New York and Connecticut, the obvious points of comparison."
rationale: State and federal labor data show New Jersey experienced net job gains after Chris Christie took office in January 2010, but the pace of job growth in New Jersey was slower than the national average and slower than neighboring New York and Connecticut over the same recovery period. Contemporary analyses of BLS state employment series during Christie's early years documented these relative lags.

claim: Quotes Anthony Fauci as writing, "I reject the notion that it’s ‘just a virus’ and we’ll all get it eventually. What a careless, lazy, heartless stance."
rationale: There is no credible record of Anthony Fauci writing that exact sentence, and major fact-checkers and news archives do not attribute this quote to him. While Fauci did publicly reject the idea of letting COVID-19 spread unchecked and made similar arguments in interviews and statements, this specific phrasing appears to be a misattribution or fabricated quotation.

claim: "On average, women make 77 cents for every dollar men make."
rationale: The '77 cents' number is an oversimplified, often outdated headline that depends on which year and which measure of pay is used. More precise measures (median hourly pay for full-time workers, or pay adjusted for occupation, hours, experience, and demographics) produce different ratios and the exact gap has changed over time, so the claim as stated without context is misleading.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The statement is too general to verify: whether an election is "unusually close" depends on which election, the metric used (popular vote margin, electoral college margin, number of contested races), and historical baselines. Without specifying the election and the comparative data, the claim cannot be supported. To assess closeness one must compare the actual margin to historical distributions for that office or jurisdiction.

claim: "Mitt Romney: ‘Trump has some very serious emotional problems, he must resign before we…’"
rationale: There is no reliable record of Senator Mitt Romney making the specific statement quoted or explicitly demanding that Trump 'must resign before we…' while using those words. Romney has publicly criticized Trump's behavior and actions on multiple occasions, but fact-checking of similar viral posts shows this exact quote appears fabricated or taken out of context.

claim: "Every day, 34 Americans are murdered with guns."
rationale: The claim as stated is not reliably true for all recent years. Annual CDC/FBI data show firearm homicides vary year to year (roughly ~11,000–15,000 in recent years), which corresponds to about 30–41 firearm homicides per day; 34/day is within that historical range for some years but is not a fixed daily count and omits year-to-year variation and definitional differences.

claim: "The same federal government that offers some money for a program is walking away from another health care program."
rationale: The claim is too vague to verify as stated: it names no programs, dates, agencies, or actions. While it is possible for a federal government to fund one program and discontinue another, that general possibility does not make this specific assertion true without concrete details or evidence.

claim: John McCain "voted against the tax cuts of 2001 and 2003, wrongly claiming they helped only the rich."
rationale: McCain did vote against the major Bush-era tax bills in 2001 and 2003 and criticized them as favoring high earners, but the statement that he was 'wrongly claiming they helped only the rich' is inaccurate: the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts provided tax reductions to households across income groups even though benefits were skewed toward higher-income taxpayers. Saying they helped 'only' the rich is an overstatement of their incidence.

claim: Tax rates were significantly higher "in the '40s, the '50s, and the '60s."
rationale: Statutory federal top marginal income-tax rates were much higher in the mid-20th century (peaking around 94% in the mid-1940s and about 91% through much of the 1950s and early 1960s), so saying tax rates were significantly higher in the '40s–'60s is accurate in that common sense. However, headline statutory rates overstate what most taxpayers actually paid, since exemptions, deductions, and lower effective rates applied to most taxpayers.

claim: "Sixty percent of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid patients."
rationale: There is no credible, widely cited evidence that exactly 60% of New Jersey doctors refuse Medicaid patients. Medicaid acceptance rates vary by specialty, practice type, and year, and available state and national physician-survey data do not support a single uniform 60% non-acceptance rate for New Jersey.

claim: Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp "mandates restaurants reopen"
rationale: Gov. Kemp issued executive orders in spring 2020 that allowed restaurants to reopen at limited capacity and barred localities from fining or penalizing businesses that did so, but he did not issue an order forcing or mandating restaurants to reopen. Businesses were permitted to remain closed at their own discretion and there was no statewide requirement that they must reopen.

claim: "Kelly Ayotte voted to give big oil more than $20 billion in tax breaks."
rationale: There is no single roll-call vote by Sen. Kelly Ayotte that unambiguously 'gave big oil more than $20 billion.' While she supported some tax provisions and extenders that benefited the oil and gas industry, the $20+ billion figure is a misleading aggregation or attribution to a specific Ayotte vote and overstates what any one recorded vote enacted. Fact-checks have found the claim conflates multiple measures/timeframes and misattributes total estimated costs to a single Ayotte vote.

claim: "NYT is correcting their lies..Trump paid $1M in 2016 & $3.8M in 2017-18..THEY LIED..AGAIN. INFO ON TWITTER THIS AM."
rationale: There is no public evidence that the New York Times issued a correction stating Trump paid exactly $1 million in 2016 and $3.8 million in 2017–18, and the claim mixes unspecified payments and accuses the paper of lying without supporting documentation. Major reporting on Trump’s taxes and reimbursements does not substantiate these precise figures or an NYT correction that would confirm the allegation.

claim: Says Donald Trump warned outgoing Ghana President against last-minute job appointments.
rationale: There is no widely reported or verifiable record up to mid‑2024 of Donald Trump publicly warning an outgoing Ghanaian president about last‑minute job appointments. Such a statement about a foreign leader would likely have been covered by international media and archived in Trump's known public statements, but no credible sources corroborate the claim.

claim: "Under the federal Controlled Substance Act, marijuana is listed in the same Schedule I as heroin," even though "marijuana is not a killer drug like heroin."
rationale: Under the federal Controlled Substances Act both cannabis (marijuana) and heroin are listed as Schedule I substances. Public-health evidence shows heroin (an opioid) is strongly associated with fatal overdoses, whereas cannabis does not produce fatal overdoses via direct pharmacologic toxicity and is not implicated in the same kind of overdose deaths.

claim: "After World War II, we tried, convicted, and, in some cases, executed Japanese soldiers for war crimes that included charges of waterboarding."
rationale: After WWII Allied military and international tribunals prosecuted many Japanese servicemen for war crimes, including torture and mistreatment of prisoners. Contemporary trial records and prosecutions in places like the Philippines and elsewhere include convictions for torture methods described as 'water treatment' or similar forced drowning techniques comparable to what is now called waterboarding, and some defendants were executed for their crimes.

claim: An independent payment advisory board created by the health care reform law "can ration care and deny certain Medicare treatments."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act's Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) was explicitly barred from making recommendations that would ration care, restrict benefits, raise premiums, or limit eligibility. Its statutory role was to propose cost-saving changes in Medicare payment and delivery, not to directly deny specific treatments, though opponents argued some recommendations could indirectly affect access. Therefore the claim that it 'can ration care and deny certain Medicare treatments' is misleading under the law's explicit prohibitions.

claim: Says Jim Renacci ran against the Washington establishment in the election, but is now "hypocritically embracing it with big money, special interest fundraisers."
rationale: The statement mixes a verifiable claim — Renacci has framed himself as an outsider in prior campaigns — with an unverified and subjective charge that he is now 'hypocritically embracing' the Washington establishment via 'big money, special interest fundraisers.' I am not aware of specific, corroborated evidence showing he currently organizes such fundraisers or that his donor activity meets that description, so the accusatory part is not supported as stated.

claim: "Human meat found in McDonald’s meat factory"
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reputable reporting that human meat was found in any McDonald’s meat processing facility. Such claims are recurring urban legends and would have prompted regulatory, criminal, and media investigations if true. McDonald’s supply chain is subject to inspections and auditing that make this extremely unlikely.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's Iran nuclear deal "lined the pockets of the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism with your money."
rationale: The 2015 nuclear agreement (JCPOA) did provide sanctions relief that allowed Iran access to previously frozen assets and greater oil revenues, but those were Iran's own funds or commercial receipts rather than direct payments from U.S. taxpayers. Also, the deal was negotiated by the Obama administration and the P5+1, not solely by Hillary Clinton, though she expressed support. Framing it as Clinton having her deal 'lined the pockets ... with your money' is therefore misleading.

claim: The Strategic Petroleum Reserve has "been mostly empty" for decades.
rationale: The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve has held hundreds of millions of barrels for much of its history and was not "mostly empty" for decades. While large releases in 2022–2023 substantially reduced inventories, those drawdowns are recent and do not support the claim of decades-long emptiness.

claim: Says Ted Budd "voted to gut protections for pre-existing conditions … letting insurance companies deny coverage for (necessary) treatment."
rationale: Ted Budd voted for the 2017 House GOP health bill (the American Health Care Act) that would have let states obtain waivers from ACA rules on essential health benefits and limited community-rating protections, and it allowed higher premiums after coverage gaps. Policy analysts and independent fact-checkers concluded those provisions would have substantially weakened protections for people with pre-existing conditions and could let plans exclude or limit coverage for needed treatments. Thus saying he "voted to gut protections" and enable insurers to deny necessary treatment is a fair characterization.

claim: U.S. Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison "voted to continue Roe v. Wade."
rationale: Kay Bailey Hutchison was a Republican senator with a consistently pro‑life voting record and supported legislation restricting abortion (for example she backed partial‑birth abortion bans and other limits). There is no clear, specific roll‑call showing she voted to "continue Roe v. Wade," and the vague phrasing lacks a concrete vote that would support the claim.

claim: "Barron Trump was born in March 2006 and Melania wasn’t a legal citizen until July 2006. So under this executive order, his own son wouldn’t be an American citizen."
rationale: Barron Trump was born in New York in March 2006 and is a U.S. citizen by birth under the 14th Amendment; an executive order cannot strip birthright citizenship guaranteed by the Constitution. The claim's assertion about Melania's status is also wrong—the timing cited (July 2006) is incorrect, as she was naturalized in 2006 earlier in the year.

claim: The United States has experienced "40 straight months of unemployment at 8 percent or higher."
rationale: U.S. monthly unemployment (the standard U-3 series) did rise above 8% during the Great Recession, but historical BLS data do not support a continuous 40-month stretch at or above 8%. The rate moved above and below that threshold over time, so the blanket statement of 40 straight months is inaccurate.

claim: "State Rep. Kathleen Peters has a 100 percent pro-abortion voting record – even voting against a ban on sex-selection abortions."
rationale: Kathleen Peters, a Republican lawmaker, does not have a 100% 'pro-abortion' voting record; her legislative history includes votes in favor of some abortion restrictions and other votes that fact-checkers have described as mixed. Claims highlighting a single vote (for example opposing a particular sex‑selection ban) omit context — she has supported other pro‑life measures and her overall record is not uniformly pro‑abortion.

claim: "Congressman Cicilline, when he was the mayor of Providence, espoused a sanctuary city."
rationale: While David Cicilline as mayor promoted immigrant-friendly policies and resisted local enforcement of federal immigration law, there is no clear evidence he formally declared Providence a "sanctuary city" or launched an official sanctuary-city ordinance during his mayoralty. Describing him as having "espoused a sanctuary city" overstates the case; he supported protections for immigrants but Providence did not adopt a formal sanctuary-city declaration under his administration.

claim: "Hate crimes against American Muslims and mosques have tripled after Paris and San Bernardino."
rationale: There were documented short-term spikes in anti-Muslim incidents after the Paris and San Bernardino attacks reported by advocacy groups and media, but authoritative national datasets (e.g., FBI hate-crime reports) do not support a broad, across-the-board statement that hate crimes against American Muslims and mosques 'tripled' overall. Whether an increase of that magnitude is true depends on the specific time window, geographic scope, and data source, which the claim does not specify.

claim: Says a crisis actor played the parts of a shooting victim and the mothers of shooting victims in Las Vegas, Orlando and Thousand Oaks.
rationale: The claim that a single 'crisis actor' played a shooting victim and the mothers of victims in the Las Vegas, Orlando, and Thousand Oaks attacks is false. Official reports, victim lists, obituaries, and credible news investigations identify different, documented victims and family members in each incident, and fact-checkers have repeatedly debunked similar 'crisis actor' assertions as misidentifications and manipulated images. No reliable evidence supports one person appearing in those distinct roles across unrelated events.

claim: Joe Biden "wants to get rid of something called ‘stepped up basis’" that reduces inheritance taxes.
rationale: President Biden has proposed limiting or eliminating the "step-up in basis" treatment for inherited assets as part of his tax plans, which would require unrealized capital gains at death to be taxed for high-value estates. This change is aimed at reducing a common way heirs avoid capital gains tax, though proposals have generally targeted wealthy estates rather than a blanket repeal for all inheritances.

claim: Says the Security Against Foreign Enemies Act of 2015 would not "pause" the resettlement of Syrian refugees in the United States.
rationale: Contemporary analyses and fact-checks found the Security Against Foreign Enemies (SAFE) Act would have imposed new certification and vetting requirements and conditions that had to be met before Syrian refugees could be admitted, which in practice would have halted or sharply curtailed resettlement until those requirements were satisfied. Although the bill did not use the single word "pause," its provisions would effectively have prevented normal refugee admissions from Syria until certification occurred.

claim: Fifty-three percent of graduates from liberal arts colleges these days can’t find jobs.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 53% of liberal-arts college graduates are unable to find jobs. Official labor statistics and graduate-employment surveys show overall unemployment for recent college graduates is much lower, and while some liberal-arts majors face higher rates of underemployment, that is not the same as 53% being jobless. The claim is also vague about timeframe, country, and what 'can’t find jobs' means.

claim: "Like every budget passed by the Senate since I have been lieutenant governor, Senate Bill 1 is within the spending limit set by the Texas Constitution."
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that every Senate budget since the speaker became lieutenant governor complied with the Texas constitutional spending limit. Whether a particular bill (like SB1) is within the limit is determined by the Texas Comptroller's certification, and I cannot verify that every single Senate-passed budget in that entire span received such certification. Because the claim is sweeping and unverified here, it is likely false without specific comptroller certifications for each budget referenced.

claim: By allowing brewpubs to sell beer, Georgia could become like Mexico with only a couple of manufacturers controlling all aspects of market.
rationale: The claim is speculative and unsupported. Mexico’s beer market has historically been concentrated in a few large firms due to past consolidation and distribution control, but allowing brewpubs to sell beer tends to increase local competition and direct-to-consumer options, not produce a market dominated by only a couple manufacturers controlling all aspects. There is no clear mechanism by which permitting brewpub retail sales would recreate Mexico-style national-level concentration in Georgia.

claim: Says over 1,000 mail in ballots were found in a dumpster in California.
rationale: There are no credible, contemporaneous reports from election officials or major news outlets confirming that over 1,000 mail-in ballots were found dumped in a California dumpster. Fact-checkers have traced viral social-media claims to mischaracterized or much smaller incidents, and large-scale ballot dumps of that magnitude would have been widely reported and investigated.

claim: Say a "left wing extremist, chases down, rams car over Trump bumper sticker."
rationale: There is no verifiable, credible reporting or evidence provided to support the specific claim that a 'left wing extremist' chased down and rammed a car over a Trump bumper sticker. The statement is vague, unsourced, and uses a politically charged label without substantiation, so it cannot be confirmed as fact.

claim: "Texas has lost the most law enforcement officers in the line of duty of any state in America."
rationale: By cumulative historical totals reported by law-enforcement memorial organizations, Texas has the largest number of line-of-duty deaths of any U.S. state. The state's large population and many law enforcement agencies contribute to the higher absolute count, though totals vary by source and definition.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or data source, so it cannot be verified as a universal truth. State and federal labor statistics do separate private- and public-sector job gains, and while the private sector often supplies the majority of net job growth in Virginia, the exact share varies by period and is not reliably or universally 90% without a specified date range.

claim: "There are parks in Southeast Raleigh that still don’t have air conditioning in the gym"
rationale: This is a specific, time-sensitive local claim about facility conditions that I cannot verify with available information. I found no authoritative, up-to-date data confirming that any parks in Southeast Raleigh currently lack air conditioning in their gyms, so the claim is unverified and thus treated as false for fact-checking purposes. It may be true in some cases, but that requires local inspection or confirmation from the city parks department.

claim: Says "roughly two-thirds of (state) corporations didn’t pay any income tax in Virginia."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because it gives a blanket "roughly two-thirds" figure without specifying the year, the data source, or how "corporations" are counted. Whether a corporation pays Virginia corporate income tax depends on entity type (C‑corp vs pass‑through), credits, losses, and the specific tax year; a large share of business entities (e.g., S‑corporations and LLCs taxed as pass‑throughs) do not owe corporate income tax, but that does not validate the precise two‑thirds figure for Virginia without citing a particular dataset. State tax reports show varying percentages by year and by how filers are counted, so the claim is not verifiably true as stated.

claim: Says Rick Scott took $200,000 in campaign contributions from a company that "profited off pollution."
rationale: The claim as stated is not verifiable because it does not identify the company, time period, or source for the $200,000 figure. Campaign contributions are a matter of public record (FEC/state filings), so a specific allegation about amount and donor can be checked; without those details there is no confirmed evidence that Rick Scott took $200,000 from a company that ‘profited off pollution.’

claim: "Quite frankly, it was during the Bush years of spending, multiplied now by the Obama years that we have this mess."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplified causal statement. While deficits did grow during the Bush years (tax cuts, wars) and Obama approved large near-term stimulus and safety-net spending during and after the 2008 crisis, Obama also inherited a severe recession that drove deficits up through automatic stabilizers and then oversaw declining deficits later in his presidency; attributing 'this mess' solely to Bush spending 'multiplied' by Obama is inaccurate.

claim: "One out of every five people that the federal government charges with murder is an illegal alien."
rationale: The claim is unsupported: most murder prosecutions are handled by state and local authorities, not the federal government, and DOJ/FBI reporting does not show that one-fifth of federal murder defendants are undocumented. Prior fact-checking and general statistics about jurisdiction indicate the 20% figure is not backed by reliable federal data and appears to be fabricated or misinterpreted.

claim: Senate Democrats who left the state for weeks to delay a vote on union bargaining power exercised a "Wisconsin filibuster" provided by the state’s constitution.
rationale: While Democratic state senators fled Wisconsin in 2011 to deny a quorum and thereby delay a vote on limits to collective bargaining, that tactic relied on the state's quorum requirement for fiscal bills rather than a constitutionally provided 'filibuster.' The Wisconsin constitution does not create a filibuster mechanism; a filibuster normally refers to extended debate under legislative rules, not legislators leaving to break quorum.

claim: Says his administration balanced "two budgets with over $13 billion in deficits without raising taxes."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which administration, which budgets (federal, state, local), or which years are meant; without those specifics the statement cannot be confirmed. Additionally, claims of balancing large deficits “without raising taxes” are commonly achieved through one‑time transfers, accounting changes, spending cuts, or fee increases, so the phrase is often misleading.

claim: "Trump's campaign manager, Paul Manafort, commits bank and tax fraud and gets 47 months. A homeless man, Fate Winslow, helped sell $20 of pot and got life in prison."
rationale: The first part is accurate: Paul Manafort, who managed Trump’s campaign, was convicted of bank- and tax-related fraud and received a federal prison sentence of about 47 months. However, I find no reliable corroboration that a homeless man named 'Fate Winslow' received a life sentence for helping sell $20 of marijuana; such an extreme punishment for a single small marijuana sale would be highly unusual absent extensive prior-felony enhancements or different charges. Because the second claim is unverified and likely false or misreported, the combined statement is false.

claim: "They're saying that 40 percent of the traffic that goes over [the Sakonnet River Bridge is from] out of state."
rationale: There is no publicly available traffic study or authoritative data showing that 40% of vehicles crossing the Sakonnet River Bridge are from out of state. Regional traffic counts and typical commuter patterns indicate the bridge primarily serves local Rhode Island traffic with some Massachusetts traffic, but not a documented 40% share. Absent a cited source for that percentage, the claim is unverified and likely incorrect.

claim: Says that in 1770 "British parliament banned lipstick, saying it had the power to seduce men into marriage, which was classified as witchcraft."
rationale: There is no historical evidence that the British Parliament passed a law in 1770 banning lipstick or declaring makeup to be 'witchcraft.' While cosmetics were morally criticized in the 18th century, legal action against alleged magic was governed by the Witchcraft Act of 1735 (which targeted people claiming supernatural powers), not by any statute banning lipstick. The claim conflates social stigma or anecdotal moralizing with formal parliamentary legislation.

claim: "Never mind that no red light camera, no speed camera, nor any radar gun has ever stopped one accident from occurring."
rationale: The claim asserts that no red light camera, speed camera, or radar gun has ever prevented a single accident, which is contradicted by empirical evidence. Multiple peer-reviewed evaluations and agency reports show automated enforcement and speed/radar policing reduce speeding, red-light running, and overall collisions and injuries, indicating these tools have prevented accidents. While effects vary by setting and implementation, the absolute statement is incorrect.

claim: "Nobody applies to the United States for refugee status. They apply to the United Nations."
rationale: The United States processes refugee and asylum claims through its own agencies: people can apply for asylum at ports of entry or from within the U.S., and refugees overseas are vetted through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program. While the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) often registers displaced people and may refer candidates for resettlement, applicants do not simply 'apply to the United Nations' in place of U.S. authorities — U.S. screening, decisions, and approvals are carried out by U.S. government bodies.

claim: "Illegal immigration and the crime rate are as low as they’ve been in decades."
rationale: The statement conflates two distinct trends and is inaccurate. U.S. illegal border crossings and border encounters were at historically high levels in recent years, not at multi-decade lows, and violent crime/homicide rates rose in 2020–2021 and in many measures remain above late‑2010s levels (even though long-term crime since the 1990s is much lower). Saying both are "as low as they’ve been in decades" is therefore misleading and false without a specific timeframe or jurisdiction.

claim: Al Sharpton went to Ferguson, Mo., and is "declaring as a matter of fact that ... Michael Brown didn't use any deadly force or posed no deadly threat to the officer."
rationale: Rev. Al Sharpton traveled to Ferguson in August 2014 and publicly spoke about the Michael Brown shooting, characterizing Brown as unarmed and arguing the shooting was unjustified. In speeches and press appearances there he and his organization asserted as fact that Brown did not present a deadly threat or use deadly force against the officer.

claim: Jason Carter supports using Georgia tax dollars to promote Obamacare
rationale: This claim is misleading. Jason Carter supported Medicaid expansion and state-facilitated enrollment outreach for the Affordable Care Act, but he did not explicitly call for using Georgia general tax revenues to run partisan promotions of “Obamacare”; much outreach is funded through federal ACA grants and navigator programs, and opponents’ ads overstated his position.

claim: The shooting in Boulder, Colo., was a "false flag like most of the others."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Boulder, Colorado, shooting was a "false flag." Authorities identified, arrested, and charged a named suspect and reporting and investigations attribute the attack to that individual rather than to any government-orchestrated operation. Labeling it a "false flag like most of the others" is a conspiracy claim not supported by available official records or reliable reporting.

claim: "In 1968, a full-time worker earning minimum wage, could actually support a family of three above the poverty line. Today, that same worker would earn less than the poverty line for a family of two."
rationale: In 1968 the federal minimum wage was $1.60/hour, or about $3,328/year for a full-time worker; the Census poverty threshold for a three-person family in 1968 was slightly below that level, so a full-time minimum-wage worker would be just above the poverty line. Today the federal minimum is $7.25/hour (annual full-time $15,080), which is below recent U.S. poverty thresholds for a two-person household (roughly $17k–$18k in recent years).

claim: "If we use (Tax Increment Financing) funding, that's going to take funds from the general fund for Pinellas County, as it will take funds from the general fund for the city of St. Pete."
rationale: This claim overstates how tax increment financing (TIF) works. TIF/CRA mechanisms divert only the incremental increase in property tax revenue above a base year and typically only from taxing jurisdictions that are part of the TIF arrangement; some TIFs capture only the municipal portion while county participation often requires agreement or is governed by state/local rules. Therefore it is not automatic that using TIF will take funds from Pinellas County just because it would reduce the City of St. Petersburg's incremental receipts.

claim: "While all COVID-19 news has been going on, the U.S. Government has been sneakily trying to remove end-to-end encryption" which means "the government will be able to see all of your messages and listen to all of your calls."
rationale: This is misleading and false as stated. While U.S. law enforcement and some lawmakers have publicly advocated for ways to access or limit end-to-end encryption and there were bills and debates during 2020, there has been no secret nationwide removal of end-to-end encryption that lets the government automatically read all messages or listen to all calls. End-to-end encryption by design prevents providers from seeing plaintext unless companies build deliberate backdoors, users' devices are compromised, or data is surrendered under lawful process.

claim: "I helped win one of the biggest private lawsuits against Medicare fraud in history. The government declined to pursue the case, so my firm did, and we recovered $324 million for taxpayers."
rationale: I cannot find independent, verifiable public records tying a declined-government qui tam case to a private firm recovery of exactly $324 million among the largest Medicare fraud recoveries. Major False Claims Act recoveries of that size are typically documented in DOJ press releases and public settlement databases and usually involved government intervention; a $324 million recovery of that prominence with the described facts would be publicly traceable but is not shown in available records. Without a named case, date, or parties this specific claim is not verifiable and is therefore assessed as likely false.

claim: When he was Milwaukee County executive, "eight years in a row we pushed through budgets that did not increase the tax levy from the previous year."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Independent fact-checks have noted that while several Milwaukee County budgets under Walker avoided raising the property tax levy in some years, there were exceptions and the apparent 'no increase' record relied on accounting shifts and one-time revenues rather than sustained year-to-year levy freezes for eight consecutive budgets.

claim: Says Melania Trump’s dress at Mount Rushmore speech was designed from "drawings of several young victims of sex trafficking."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Melania Trump's Mount Rushmore dress was based on drawings by young victims of sex trafficking. Independent fact-checkers and available reporting found the claim originated on social media and was not corroborated by the designer, the First Lady's office, or reputable news outlets.

claim: "Of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents, three are in Florida. … We rank No. 1 in the country in staged auto accidents."
rationale: There is no authoritative, consistent national data publicly available that confirms three of the top five cities for staged automobile accidents are in Florida or that Florida ranks No. 1 overall. Media and industry summaries sometimes highlight particular Florida cities in certain years, but the precise, nationwide ranking claimed is unsubstantiated without a named source and timeframe.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: This is false: Louisiana does receive money tied to Gulf of Mexico offshore oil. The state benefits from federal revenue‑sharing under laws such as GOMESA, collects state severance/production taxes and lease revenues from state waters, and has received large payments related to the Deepwater Horizon settlements and RESTORE Act distributions.

claim: "When I took office, the deficit was nearly 10 percent of our economy. Today, it's approaching 3 percent."
rationale: When the office was assumed in January 2021, the federal deficit (driven by COVID relief and economic contraction in 2020) was substantially larger than 'nearly 10%' of GDP — on the order of roughly 14–15% of GDP for 2020. More recent deficits have fallen from that peak but have generally remained above 3% of GDP (in the mid-single-digit percent range in the latest fiscal years), so the two-part numerical claim is inaccurate.

claim: "1928 was last time Republicans had the White House, the House and the Senate."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: Republicans have held the presidency and both chambers of Congress since 1928 on multiple later occasions. Notably, Republicans controlled the White House and both the House and Senate after the 2002 elections (during George W. Bush's presidency) and again after the 2016 election (during Donald Trump's presidency).

claim: David Perdue did not support the 2014 farm bill that U.S. Sens. Isakson and Chambliss did.
rationale: The claim implies a direct contrast in votes or clear public support/opposition; Isakson and Chambliss did vote for the 2014 farm bill in the Senate, but David Perdue was not a U.S. senator at the time and therefore cast no Senate vote. Perdue may have expressed opinions about the bill as a candidate, but he did not have a Senate vote opposing it in 2014, so the assertion as stated is misleading.

claim: "If we had been on 'Obamacare' and a bureaucrat was trying to tell me when I could get that CAT scan, that would have delayed my treatment."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act (commonly called 'Obamacare') primarily expanded access to private insurance through marketplaces and Medicaid expansion rather than creating a single government program in which a government bureaucrat schedules imaging. While insurers (public or private) sometimes require prior authorization that can delay imaging, that is an administrative insurer practice and not a universal consequence of being covered under the ACA or a government official personally dictating timing.

claim: Says Donald Trump has written 10 checks to Hillary Clinton "and four of those checks were not to her Senate campaign. … It was to her presidential campaign."
rationale: Public campaign finance records and contemporary fact-checks do not support the specific claim that Donald Trump wrote 10 checks to Hillary Clinton with four directed to her presidential campaign. Trump has made some donations to Democrats and to committees in past decades, and there are occasional small donations linked to Hillary-related committees, but the precise numbers in the claim are not corroborated by FEC and historical reporting.

claim: "So far, out of 175 arrested in Kenosha, 102 were not from Kenosha. Rioting has become its own industry."
rationale: The numeric claim cannot be confidently verified without a contemporaneous official source: arrest totals and residency status during the Kenosha unrest varied by reporting date and by how 'from Kenosha' was defined. The second clause, 'Rioting has become its own industry,' is a subjective characterization or metaphor, not a factual statement that can be proven true or false. Because the factual component is time‑specific and unsourced and the rest is opinionated, the overall claim is labeled false for lack of reliable evidence.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: Available, reputable estimates do not support a current figure of 8 million jobs held by undocumented immigrants in the U.S.; most government and research sources place the number of undocumented workers lower (commonly in the roughly 4–6 million range). The total undocumented population is often cited around 10–11 million, but not all are employed, and methods and definitions vary, so the flat claim of 8 million jobs is misleading.

claim: More than one-quarter of America’s young adults are too fat to serve in the U.S. military
rationale: Multiple government and research summaries have estimated that roughly 25–30% of Americans aged about 17–24 exceed military weight/body‑fat standards and are therefore ineligible without a waiver, so the statement that more than one-quarter are too fat to serve is accurate in broad terms. The exact percentage varies by service branch, age window, and measurement method, but central estimates commonly cited are around 27%.

claim: The snow is government-generated or fake.
rationale: Snow is a natural form of precipitation formed when atmospheric water vapor freezes in clouds and falls as snowflakes; meteorological processes and temperatures explain observed snowfall. While humans can and do produce artificial snow for ski resorts using specialized snowmaking machines, that is localized and requires equipment and water, so the broad claim that snow is government-generated or fake is unsupported.

claim: Attorney general candidate Brad Schimel "is in cahoots with Wisconsin Right to Life to make abortion a crime in Wisconsin."
rationale: There is no public, verifiable evidence that Brad Schimel secretly coordinated with Wisconsin Right to Life to enact a plan to make abortion a crime in Wisconsin. Schimel is publicly pro‑life, has taken legal positions defending restrictions and has accepted support from pro‑life groups, but that is different from documented clandestine collusion to criminalize abortion.

claim: "The last major oil spill from a drilling accident in America happened over 40 years ago in 1969."
rationale: This is false. While the 1969 Santa Barbara blowout was a major drilling spill, there have been later and larger drilling-related disasters in U.S. waters — most notably the 2010 Deepwater Horizon blowout in the Gulf of Mexico that released millions of barrels. Therefore the last major drilling accident was not in 1969.

claim: The typical elementary school teacher pays $7,239 in federal income taxes, and firefighters pay $5,328, while Donald Trump paid $750.
rationale: The claim mixes a specific reported figure (Donald Trump reportedly paid $750 in federal income tax in 2016) with broad, unsigned ‘typical’ tax numbers for elementary teachers and firefighters that are context-dependent. Reported teacher/firefighter averages vary by year, source, and whether mean or median is used, so the blanket figures cited are misleading without a stated data source and time frame. Even if Trump did pay $750 in a particular year, the three-number comparison as presented is not reliably supported.

claim: "In the last year, Wisconsin ranked third in Midwest job growth."
rationale: The claim gives no data source or precise 12‑month period, and I cannot confirm a specific recent ranking that places Wisconsin third among Midwest states for job growth. Job‑growth rankings vary by data source (BLS payrolls vs. household survey), time window, and which states are counted as the Midwest; without a clear citation the assertion is not verifiable. Because of that ambiguity I treat the claim as unsubstantiated and therefore false.

claim: "Right now, women are able to access an abortion in the later stages of their pregnancy under certain conditions with approval of their medical doctors. I’ve done nothing to change that."
rationale: The statement is misleading as an absolute claim. While later‑term abortions can still be provided in many places for serious maternal health risks or severe fetal anomalies with clinician approval, access is not universal and many U.S. states now restrict or ban abortions at various gestational ages. Whether any particular officeholder “did nothing to change that” depends on which jurisdiction and actions by that official, so the blanket assertion is false without qualification.

claim: Quotes incoming U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez as saying "under capitalism, man oppresses man. Under socialism, it’s the other way around."
rationale: The pithy line is a longstanding aphorism that predates Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and is frequently misattributed; there is no reliable evidence or transcript showing she authored or was quoted saying that exact phrasing. Searches of her public statements and contemporary fact-checking do not support the attribution to Ocasio-Cortez.

claim: After a "major water main break," Georgia election workers counted "18,000 ballots, all for Biden" that they pulled from suitcases and with no election observers present.
rationale: Multiple official statements and independent fact-checks found no evidence that 18,000 ballots were pulled from suitcases and counted 'all for Biden' with no observers after a water-main break. Ballots were moved in sealed containers due to a plumbing incident in Fulton County, observers were allowed or present per chain-of-custody records, and audits/recounts did not support the claimed 18,000 uniform pro-Biden ballots.

claim: "Trump Management was charged with discriminating against African-Americans and breaking federal law."
rationale: In 1973 the U.S. Department of Justice sued Trump Management, Inc. (and Donald J. Trump) alleging they discriminated against Black rental applicants in violation of federal civil rights/fair housing laws. The case was resolved by a 1975 consent decree requiring nondiscriminatory practices; the company settled without admitting liability.

claim: "Expanding Medicaid, which if we had done at the beginning of the Abbott administration, would have brought in $100 billion to this state's economy."
rationale: The statement is unsubstantiated as written: Medicaid expansion does bring substantial federal dollars and economic activity to states, but claims of exactly "$100 billion" depend on unspecified assumptions (time period, whether it counts cumulative federal spending, economic output, or budgetary effects). Public analyses for Texas and other non‑expansion states typically project tens of billions over a decade under certain scenarios, not a single verifiable $100 billion figure tied to the start of the Abbott administration. Without a cited study and timeframe the precise $100 billion claim is not supported.

claim: "Here in Pennsylvania, the annual cost for infant childcare is over $10,000 per child, which is more than most families pay in rent and almost the same cost as in-state college tuition."
rationale: While center-based infant childcare in Pennsylvania commonly exceeds $10,000 per year, the statement overreaches by claiming it is "more than most families pay in rent" and "almost the same cost as in-state college tuition." Median rents in Pennsylvania are roughly $1,000–$1,200 per month (about $12,000–$14,400/year), so many households pay comparable or higher rent. In-state college tuition varies widely (community colleges are much cheaper; four-year public tuition can be lower or higher), so the "almost the same" comparison is not generally accurate without more detail.

claim: Says Nevada state Sen. Michael Roberson "forced Common Core for Nevada schools."
rationale: Nevada's adoption of the Common Core State Standards was a multi-step process led by the Nevada State Board of Education around 2010 and by state education agencies, not the unilateral action of one state senator. A single senator, including Michael Roberson, would not have been able to "force" the standards statewide by himself; legislative and board actions and prior administrative decisions drove adoption and implementation.

claim: "The total (state) payroll has gone down. The total amount of the number of workers in the state has gone down. I like the fact that the bulk of that is just by retirements."
rationale: The claim gives no specific state or time period and therefore cannot be verified as stated. State payroll totals and employee headcounts vary by jurisdiction and year—some states have seen declines driven by layoffs or privatization, others have seen increases—and attributing the 'bulk' of any reduction to retirements requires detailed personnel and retirement data that are not provided.
