claim: Says GOP primary opponents Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham cast a "compromise vote that cost $788 million" in higher electricity costs.
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative evidence tying a single “compromise vote” by Glenn Grothman and Joe Leibham to exactly $788 million in higher electricity costs. Attributing a precise dollar amount to one or two lawmakers is misleading because cost estimates depend on modeling choices, timeframes, and many other votes and actors. Without a specific bill, time period, and credible source for the $788 million figure, the claim is unverified and likely false.

claim: On Syria, "a lot of the allies signed on. At the last minute, Obama backed off."
rationale: The claim overstates the situation. In 2013 several U.S. allies publicly supported a punitive response to Syria’s chemical attack (France, Turkey, some Gulf states), but key partners did not commit forces (the UK Parliament voted against military action) and there was no large-scale coalition that "signed on" to join a strike. President Obama ultimately did not order an immediate strike after Syria agreed to a Russia-brokered deal to relinquish chemical weapons, which is better described as a diplomatic de-escalation than simply "backing off."

claim: Hillary Clinton "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her."
rationale: The statement is presented without a timeframe or a source and is therefore misleading. While Hillary Clinton’s unfavorable or opposed ratings did hover in the mid-40s in some national polls around 2015–2016, poll results varied by pollster and over time, so a blanket statement that she “starts off with 47 percent of the country against her” is not a solid factual claim without specifying which poll, metric (unfavorable, opposition, or vote intention), or date.

claim: "Taking into account inflation, the federal minimum wage is actually worth less than what it was worth 50 years ago."
rationale: When adjusted for inflation, the purchasing power of the federal minimum wage today is lower than it was about 50 years ago. The federal minimum has been $7.25 since 2009, and historical CPI-adjusted calculations show minimum wages in the late 1960s/early 1970s were worth substantially more in constant dollars than $7.25 is today.

claim: "The state's unemployment rate is fifth-highest in the country, a full point above the nationwide rate and higher than all of our...neighboring states."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not name which state or which time period is referenced, and unemployment rankings change month to month. Without a specific state and date, the assertion that it is fifth-highest, a full point above the national rate, and higher than all neighboring states cannot be confirmed.

claim: "Not even Tim Kaine is willing" to say he trusts Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Tim Kaine was Hillary Clinton’s 2016 vice presidential running mate and repeatedly expressed confidence in and defended her publicly during the campaign and afterward. The blanket statement that “not even Tim Kaine is willing” to say he trusts her is incorrect without a specific time or interview to support it.

claim: "At least 450,000 ballots in the key states ... miraculously only have a mark for Joe Biden on them, and no other candidate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 450,000 ballots across unspecified 'key states' contained only a mark for Joe Biden and no other candidates. State election officials, audits, recounts, and independent fact-checkers have not reported any anomaly of that magnitude and would have investigated and publicized such a clear pattern. Claims of large numbers of identical single-candidate ballots have been repeatedly debunked in relation to recent U.S. elections.

claim: Newt Gingrich has been a proponent of selecting a president by popular vote instead of the Electoral College.
rationale: Newt Gingrich has not been known as a proponent of replacing the Electoral College with a national popular vote; historically he has defended the Electoral College and has not campaigned as an advocate for its abolition. While he has made occasional remarks about accepting popular-vote outcomes, there is no clear record of him actively promoting a switch to direct popular-election selection of presidents.

claim: Poll shows that men are more likely to do chores than women in U.S. households.
rationale: Multiple nationally representative surveys and polls show that, on average, women spend more time on unpaid household chores and are more likely to perform routine domestic tasks (cooking, cleaning, laundry) than men. Men are more likely to do some specific tasks (repairs, yard work), so a blanket statement that polls show men are more likely to do chores is misleading and not supported by mainstream data.

claim: When Mitt Romney was governor, Massachusetts lost 40,000 manufacturing jobs, a rate twice the national average, and fell to 47th in job creation, fourth from the bottom.
rationale: The claim mixes and exaggerates statistics. Massachusetts did lose manufacturing jobs during Romney’s 2003–2007 term, but independent analyses found the loss was smaller than 40,000 on the specific term window used by critics, the decline was not clearly twice the national rate once different baselines and industry classifications are used, and the state did not reliably rank as low as 47th in job creation over the standard timeframes — the ranking depends heavily on the exact months and metrics chosen and was misleadingly presented.

claim: Regarding the surgery that saved Jimmy Kimmel's son, "Medicaid has stopped providing this kind of service."
rationale: There is no evidence that Medicaid has universally stopped covering the type of life‑saving pediatric surgery Jimmy Kimmel's son received. Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program generally cover medically necessary inpatient and surgical care for eligible children, although individual denials or state policy differences can affect access.

claim: Says Gov. Evers "has refused to identify or discipline the staff member who secretly taped" a conversation with GOP leaders.
rationale: Public reporting around the incident indicates Gov. Evers' office declined to publicly name the staff member who made the recording and did not announce any formal discipline, but there is no clear evidence that Evers explicitly 'refused' to identify or discipline the staffer. Saying he 'has refused' implies a decisive, public denial of responsibility or action, which is not supported by available reporting.

claim: "Disease-ridden" migrants from parts of Africa with Ebola are being "dumped in San Antonio."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that migrants with Ebola are being intentionally 'dumped' in San Antonio; local and federal public-health authorities and major news outlets have not reported Ebola cases tied to migrant arrivals there. Migrant flows to San Antonio primarily come through the U.S.–Mexico border and any infectious-disease cases would be investigated and publicly reported, so this appears to be an unsubstantiated and sensational claim.

claim: "Fox Sports cancels all NFL broadcasts ‘until players respect the flag.’ "
rationale: There is no evidence or credible reporting that Fox Sports has cancelled all NFL broadcasts; Fox continues to air NFL games under existing broadcast contracts. The assertion appears to be a social-media hoax or misattribution rather than a factual corporate action.

claim: "Roy Cooper won't say how he will pay for ‘free’ college tuition."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Roy Cooper has publicly discussed funding for higher-education initiatives (including scholarship expansions, budget allocations, and proposals to support community colleges) and included related items in state budgets; while he may not have provided a single exhaustive line-item for a universal 'free college' pitch in every forum, he has not categorically refused to say how he would pay for such measures.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders once said, "Instead of removing the conditions that make people depressed, modern society gives them antidepressant drugs."
rationale: I cannot find a verifiable primary source or reliable transcript showing Bernie Sanders uttered that exact sentence. While the statement matches Sanders' known critiques of socioeconomic causes of distress and his skeptical comments about pharmaceutical fixes, the precise phrasing appears to be an unattributed or paraphrased internet quote rather than a documented quotation.

claim: There are 86 languages spoken at Miami Dade College.
rationale: I cannot confirm the precise claim that exactly 86 languages are spoken at Miami Dade College. Institutional diversity figures for MDC are reported inconsistently (often described as 'over 80 languages' or a similar rounded figure) and may change over time, so asserting the exact number 86 without a current official source is not supportable.

claim: Says murder is the chief cause of death for pregnant women.
rationale: The claim is overly broad and inaccurate: globally and historically the primary causes of death in pregnancy are obstetric complications such as hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, and sepsis, not murder. It is true that in some specific settings (for example certain U.S. studies and CDC reports for particular years) homicide has been identified as a leading cause of death among pregnant and postpartum women, but that finding is context- and time-specific and does not support the blanket statement.

claim: Says Russian President Vladimir Putin "calls me brilliant."
rationale: There is no publicly verifiable record that Vladimir Putin told the unnamed speaker he 'calls me brilliant.' Similar reported claims (for example by U.S. politicians) have appeared in media reports but have not been independently confirmed by the Kremlin or other reliable sources. Without corroboration, the assertion should be treated as unverified and likely false.

claim: "Americans work way more than an average of industrialized countries around the world."
rationale: OECD and other labor statistics show U.S. workers do record somewhat higher annual hours than the OECD average, but the difference is modest rather than dramatic. Many industrialized countries have similar or higher hours and differences depend on measurement (full‑time only, hours per worker, or including part‑time and leave), so 'way more' overstates the gap.

claim: Says that in fiscal year 2010, "nearly 80 percent of women served" in the Texas Women’s Health Program received services from a provider other than a Planned Parenthood clinic.
rationale: I could not find authoritative, reproducible data showing that in fiscal year 2010 nearly 80% of Texas Women’s Health Program clients were served by providers other than Planned Parenthood. WHP provider-share figures are reported at varying levels (by county, clinic type, and by service) and publicly available summaries do not unambiguously support the precise 'nearly 80 percent' claim without additional context or citation.

claim: Americans "bought into climate change" in 2004-06, but then most "began wandering away from this issue."
rationale: Polling does show an increase in U.S. public belief and concern about climate change in the mid-2000s, but it is inaccurate to say most Americans then "began wandering away" from the issue. Subsequent years saw fluctuations and growing partisan polarization (declines in concern among some groups, especially after the financial crisis), not a uniform mass abandonment by the majority.

claim: "We’re already bombing seven countries."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and cannot be verified as a current factual claim without specifying who “we” refers to and what time period or definition of “bombing” is used. Public records show that U.S. and allied forces have conducted airstrikes in several countries (examples include Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Somalia, Yemen, Libya and historically Pakistan), but the exact number of countries being bombed at any given time varies and is often fewer than seven in recent public reporting. Because the claim gives no timeframe or actor, it cannot be reliably confirmed as stated.

claim: ABC News recently banned reporters from wearing American flag lapel pins on air.
rationale: This claim overstates and mischaracterizes reporting about an internal ABC News dress/appearance guidance. In late 2023 ABC circulated guidance asking reporters to avoid overt partisan or advocacy symbols on-air and to be mindful of perceived bias, but there was no widely corroborated, formal network ban specifically targeting American flag lapel pins. Media coverage described the memo as guidance and sparked debate, which some outlets framed as a "ban."

claim: "One percent of the American people make over 21 percent of all the income in America. That wasn’t the way before George Bush became president."
rationale: Income-share data show the top 1% captured roughly 21–23% of U.S. income in the mid-2000s (around 2006–2007), so the numeric statement is accurate for that period. Historical series indicate the top 1% share was substantially lower before George W. Bush took office in 2001, so it is correct to say that was not the case before his presidency.

claim: "We have 25 million Americans out of work."
rationale: The claim as stated (with no date or definition) is misleading. At its COVID-19 peak in spring 2020 the official BLS count of unemployed persons was on the order of ~23 million, and recent official unemployed totals have been much lower; claiming a current 25 million out of work is not supported without a specific timeframe or definition.

claim: Says Anthony Fauci "wants Americans to get 4 shots per year."
rationale: There is no verified record of Dr. Anthony Fauci explicitly stating he 'wants Americans to get 4 shots per year.' He has discussed that future COVID-19 booster frequency could depend on variant evolution and population immunity and has mentioned possibilities like periodic or annual boosters, but he did not advocate a blanket four-shots-per-year requirement for everyone.

claim: Once people become citizens under the DREAM Act "and turn 21, they can sponsor their illegal immigrant parents for legalization."
rationale: While U.S. citizens aged 21 or older can generally petition to sponsor parents, the DREAM Act itself does not automatically legalize parents. Many DREAM Act proposals would give eligible youth a path to conditional permanent residence and eventual citizenship, but parents who entered or stayed unlawfully face inadmissibility bars and usually must undergo consular processing and obtain difficult waivers — sponsorship by a child is not an automatic legalization.

claim: "If you take into account all the people who are struggling for work, or have just stopped looking, the real unemployment rate is over 15 percent."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it gives no country or time period. In the U.S. the broader unemployment measure (U-6), which counts marginally attached workers and those working part time for economic reasons, did exceed 15% during the 2009–2010 Great Recession, but in normal recent periods the U-6 rate has been well below 15%. As a blanket present-day statement it is false without additional context.

claim: Stay-at-home orders "actually are the law of these states."
rationale: Stay-at-home orders are typically executive or public-health emergency orders issued under state statutes or health codes, not statutes passed by state legislatures. While they can have legally enforceable effects and be backed by existing law, calling them 'the law of these states' conflates emergency orders with enacted legislation and ignores judicial review and statutory limits.

claim: "We have one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" from COVID-19.
rationale: The claim is too vague and cannot be confirmed as stated: whether a jurisdiction truly had "one of the lowest mortality rates in the world" depends on which country, which time period, and which metric (case fatality rate, infection fatality rate, or deaths per capita). Public health data show wide international variation and many countries have had lower COVID mortality by some metrics; differences in testing, age structure, and reporting make blanket claims unreliable.

claim: The media has "a lower approval rate than Congress."
rationale: The claim is overly general and unsupported as stated: public approval of "the media" and of Congress varies by poll, question wording, and time period. In some polls and years media approval has been lower than Congress, while in others Congress's approval is lower; there is no universal, time-independent fact that the media always has a lower approval rate than Congress.

claim: "90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless."
rationale: The statement gives a specific number without a year or source, so it cannot be confirmed as presented. Official point-in-time (PIT) counts and HUD reports are the usual sources for unsheltered homelessness and their totals for California vary by year and methodology; recent PIT counts and statewide estimates do not consistently match the standalone claim of 90,000. Because the claim lacks context and does not align reliably with available annual counts, it is not verifiable as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim money to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws."
rationale: I am not aware of any credible reporting or documentary evidence that Gov. Greg Abbott offered the uncle of a Uvalde shooting victim money specifically to say "we don’t need stronger gun laws." Media coverage documented outreach by Abbott's office and political actors to some family members and public statements by certain relatives, but no verified report shows a direct paid offer for that quoted line.

claim: Ezekiel Emanuel, one of President Obama's key health care advisers, "says medical care should be reserved for the nondisabled. So watch out if you're disabled."
rationale: This statement misrepresents and exaggerates Emanuel's views. Ezekiel Emanuel wrote controversially about lifespan, resource allocation, and not pursuing aggressive life-extending interventions indefinitely (notably in a 2014 Atlantic essay), but he did not state that medical care should be reserved only for the nondisabled or call for denying care to disabled people. The claim quotes him out of context and attributes a sweeping prescription he never endorsed.

claim: Says Donald Trump "was one of the people who rooted for the housing crisis. He said back in 2006, ‘Gee, I hope it does collapse because then I can go in and buy some and make some money.’ "
rationale: There is no reliable record or mainstream fact-check reporting that Donald Trump said the specific 2006 line quoted here. Fact-checkers have not found a verifiable source for the exact phrase; while Trump has at times said he likes to buy during market downturns, the precise quoted wording ('Gee, I hope it does collapse...') is not documented in credible archives.

claim: Twenty million Americans are "out of work."
rationale: The claim is presented without a date or definition of "out of work," so as a blanket statement it is misleading. U.S. labor statistics vary over time and "out of work" could mean unemployed, not in the labor force, or those filing initial unemployment claims — numbers have reached roughly 20 million in specific moments (notably early in the COVID-19 shock) but it is not a timeless fact.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: I cannot verify that any congressional Banking Committee formally voted a 1,336-page bill 'out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments' and with a pre-agreed bipartisan deal; that combination of precise page count, 21-minute vote, and no amendments is unlikely and is not supported by standard committee practice or public records I know. Committees typically hold longer markups, allow and record amendments, and produce a transcript/markup that would show such a rapid, amendment-free action if it occurred.

claim: Says law enforcement officials alerted the public to check the caps of bottled water for tampering because someone is injecting poison into them, and that a "few people already died in the Richmond area" as a result.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official advisories that law enforcement issued a public warning about people injecting poison into bottled-water caps nor any verified reports of a few deaths in the Richmond area from such tampering. Media fact-checks and statements from local police and public-health agencies have repeatedly debunked similar viral posts as hoaxes rather than confirmed incidents.

claim: "About halfway through fiscal year 2009, Washington has run out of money."
rationale: There is no evidence that 'Washington' (either the U.S. federal government or the State of Washington) completely exhausted funds about halfway through fiscal year 2009. The federal FY2009 (Oct 1, 2008–Sep 30, 2009) was funded through appropriations and temporary measures and did not experience a shutdown or an official declaration of running out of money mid‑year; state budget shortfalls did occur but were not described as a total depletion of funds at that time.

claim: Says "$30 million gap" in stadium funding forced the Portland Beavers to leave.
rationale: Contemporary news coverage and statements from the team's ownership reported an approximate $30 million shortfall in public funding for a replacement ballpark, and the failure to close that funding gap and secure a new stadium was the proximate reason the Portland Beavers were relocated. The team left after negotiations over a new stadium failed, with the cited $30M shortfall commonly reported in coverage of the move.

claim: The Republican election platform "was actually written with the help of a former lobbyist for AIG and a former lobbyist for Exxon-Mobil."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as stated: public records and reporting on recent Republican national platforms do not support a definitive assertion that the entire platform “was actually written” with the help of a former AIG lobbyist and a former ExxonMobil lobbyist. Platform drafting is typically done by party committees with input from many advisors and outside groups, but there is no clear, attributed, verifiable evidence naming both former AIG and former ExxonMobil lobbyists as authors of a party platform. The statement is vague about year and individuals and therefore cannot be verified as fact.

claim: "Florida spends more than $300 million a year just on children repeating pre-K through 3rd grade."
rationale: Multiple analyses of Florida Department of Education data and state funding formulas have produced estimates of roughly $300–$340 million per year attributable to students being retained in early grades. Commonly cited figures (around $330 million) refer to the cost of students held back in K–3 and are consistent with news and policy analyses using state per‑pupil funding and retention counts.

claim: Clicking on this link in a text message lets sex traffickers track you.
rationale: Clicking a random link in a text message does not automatically enable sex traffickers specifically to track you. A clicked link can reveal technical information (IP address, browser/device fingerprints) or deliver malware if the site is malicious, and if criminals control the link they could use those capabilities to try to identify or target you. However, tracking in a robust way typically requires more—malware installation, permission to access location, or additional personal information—so the claim as an absolute statement is misleading.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to get rid of the federal minimum wage."
rationale: Donald Trump has publicly stated he is "not a believer in the minimum wage" and has said the issue should be left to states rather than set federally. Those campaign and public remarks indicate he favors eliminating or rolling back a federal minimum wage in favor of state-level control.

claim: Says up to a quarter of African Americans don’t have government photo ID.
rationale: Multiple reputable analyses of voter ID and identification access have produced estimates that a substantially higher share of African Americans lack government-issued photo ID, with some studies and state-level analyses citing figures around one quarter. However, estimates vary by definition of ID, year, and state, so 'up to a quarter' is a plausible summary of published findings.

claim: Pepsi admitted an employee contaminated its products with AIDS.
rationale: This claim is false. Pepsi has not admitted that an employee contaminated its products with AIDS; the story is a long‑running hoax that the company and public health authorities have debunked. Moreover, HIV is not transmitted through sealed beverages and does not survive in soda, making the alleged mode of transmission scientifically implausible.

claim: "Live cats have holes drilled into their skulls," posts put into their heads and coils put into their eyes, and some have had their ears cut off or are intentionally deafened or starved at UW-Madison labs that do research to improve hearing in humans.
rationale: Auditory neuroscience has long used cats and the invasive procedures described — skull openings/craniotomies, implanted head posts, implanted or attached eye coils, and surgical or chemical deafening — are standard methods documented in the literature and in animal-welfare investigations of university labs including UW–Madison. Claims that ears were physically removed or animals were deliberately starved are less precisely worded but align with reports of ear surgeries to access the auditory apparatus and of disputed food-restriction practices cited in past inspections and news coverage of UW–Madison research. Because the statement mixes well-documented standard procedures with emotive wording, it is judged substantially true overall but context matters.

claim: Says 15,000 IRS employees "have to be added to administer ‘ObamaCare’ and look at the tax implications."
rationale: There is no authoritative evidence that the Affordable Care Act legally requires adding 15,000 IRS employees; independent IRS estimates and budget requests around implementation envisioned far smaller, incremental staffing increases over several years to handle new tax provisions and enforcement. The '15,000' figure appears to be a political exaggeration rather than a statutory or documented IRS staffing requirement.

claim: "I've been here almost every day."
rationale: The assertion "I've been here almost every day" is not verifiable as stated because it omits who is speaking, what location "here" denotes, and the relevant timeframe. Without independent evidence (attendance logs, timestamps, witness corroboration) the statement is unsubstantiated and cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Georgia spends fewer tourism advertising dollars than any other state in the South.
rationale: The claim is unlikely to be true—Georgia operates multi‑million dollar tourism marketing programs and is not generally lowest among Southern states; many smaller or less tourism‑focused Southern states typically have smaller advertising budgets. The statement also provides no year or metric (total vs. per‑capita), so it cannot be verified as written.

claim: Says last year "13 million (health insurance) rebates went out, in all 50 states. Another 8.5 (million) rebates are being sent out this summer, averaging around 100 bucks each."
rationale: I cannot find authoritative evidence that exactly 13 million health-insurance rebates were issued last year and that another 8.5 million rebates averaging about $100 each are being sent this summer. Public reporting on ACA Medical Loss Ratio rebates and insurer rebate distributions gives varying totals by year and by insurer, and the precise figures in this claim do not match widely reported official summaries. Without a clear source or year, the specific numbers and average amount are unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "When you sanction the Iranian central bank, that will shut down (Iran's) economy."
rationale: Targeting Iran's central bank can severely disrupt foreign payments, access to reserves, and trade, causing sharp contractions, high inflation, and shortages, but it has not historically 'shut down' the economy completely. Iran has continued economic activity via domestic markets, barter/alternative payment channels, exemptions for humanitarian goods, and informal financial networks despite heavy central bank sanctions.

claim: Says Russ Feingold said that with Obamacare, "we could keep our doctors and our plans, it was rated as the Lie of the Year."
rationale: I cannot find verified evidence that former Sen. Russ Feingold specifically said the quoted line attributing 'we could keep our doctors and our plans' as 'rated as the Lie of the Year.' While fact-checkers (notably PolitiFact) did label President Obama's 'you can keep your plan' promise as their 2013 Lie of the Year, the specific attribution to Feingold appears unverified and likely misattributed without a clear source.

claim: "So Trump comes to Nashville to oversee damage from the tornado. He flies into the area in a helicopter to get there without further traffic problems in the city. He writes PERSONAL checks to those in need, with his personal accountant in tow."
rationale: Contemporary reporting about presidential disaster visits typically documents official travel and any aid given; there are no credible reports that Trump personally wrote checks to tornado victims in Nashville or that he brought his personal accountant to distribute funds. While a president may travel by helicopter to reach affected areas, the specific claim that he flew in to avoid traffic and wrote personal checks to those in need is unsupported and implausible given that disaster relief is normally handled through FEMA and other official channels.

claim: Says she couldn't take stimulus money because it required "universal building codes."
rationale: There is no blanket federal requirement that accepting stimulus funds mandates adopting a single "universal building code." While some federal grant programs (especially disaster mitigation or construction grants) require funded projects to meet certain building standards or encourage use of model codes, those are program-specific conditions and not a universal precondition that would categorically prevent someone from taking stimulus money. The claim misstates how federal grant conditions and local/state code adoption actually work.

claim: Says he never told anyone he hated the U.S. Senate.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it does not identify who 'he' is, when or where the statement was made, or provide a source. Without a specific speaker and attributable quote or record, it's not possible to confirm that any particular person asserted they never told anyone they hated the U.S. Senate. Because of this missing context, the claim as presented is effectively unprovable and treated as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: The projected revenue from the Mayweather/Pacquiao fight is "larger than the annual GDP of 29 different countries."
rationale: Reported projected revenue for Mayweather–Pacquiao (commonly cited around $600–700 million) would exceed the annual nominal GDPs of a number of very small countries, but the precise claim that it is larger than the GDP of exactly 29 countries depends on which revenue total and which year/source of GDP data you use. Independent checks show the count varies by dataset and year, so the unqualified statement is not reliably supported.

claim: Wisconsin voter turnout jumped from 67% in 2016 to 89% in 2020.
rationale: Wisconsin turnout did rise from about 67% in 2016 (voting-eligible population) but 2020 turnout was roughly in the low-70s percentage points, not 89%. The 89% figure is much higher than the widely reported 2020 turnout measures and likely arises from a different denominator or misreporting.

claim: The balanced-budget amendment once came within one vote of passing Congress but was defeated because of the no vote from a top Senate Republican, and Rick Santorum says he "stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship."
rationale: The claim mixes inaccurate specifics. Constitutional amendments require two‑thirds votes and historical balanced‑budget amendment efforts failed by margins larger than a single decisive "no" from one top Republican in Congress; there is no clear record that a BBA "came within one vote of passing Congress" and was defeated solely by a single top Senate Republican. I also could not verify the attributed Santorum quote or that he publicly 'stood up and called for him to resign his chairmanship' in connection with such a single‑vote defeat.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: The claim that Barack Obama's birth certificate is fake is false. The State of Hawaii and its Department of Health confirmed and released a certified long-form birth certificate for Obama in April 2011, and contemporaneous Hawaiian newspaper birth announcements and multiple independent fact-checks corroborate his Hawaii birth. Repeated investigations and official statements have found no evidence that the certificate was fraudulent.

claim: Japan's "interest on its own debt" is "25 percent of its national budget"
rationale: The statement greatly overstates Japan's debt service burden. In recent years interest payments on Japan's central government debt have been a single-digit percentage of the national budget (typically well under 10%), aided by very low nominal interest rates and central bank policies, not 25% of the budget.

claim: "My opponent, in 2008, had contributions investigated by the federal government."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify who "my opponent" is or what specific contributions were allegedly investigated in 2008. Federal investigations of campaign contributions are specific, documented events involving agencies such as the DOJ, FBI, or FEC and would normally be publicized; without a named individual or sources, there is no basis to support the assertion.

claim: Says opponent David Dewhurst is a "career politician."
rationale: David Dewhurst has spent multiple decades holding and seeking public office in Texas, including long tenures as Texas Land Commissioner and as Lieutenant Governor, so describing him as a "career politician" is a reasonable characterization. His professional life has been dominated by elected and statewide political roles rather than a single nonpolitical career.

claim: "Barack Obama’s real father is Communist Party propagandist Frank Marshall Davis."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Frank Marshall Davis was Barack Obama’s biological father. Contemporary documents (including Obama’s birth certificate), biographical records, and Obama’s own memoirs identify Barack Obama Sr. as his father, and major fact‑checking organizations have debunked the Davis paternity rumor. Davis was a family friend and mentor to Obama’s maternal relatives, not his father.

claim: Kathryn Starkey "aided and abetted the continued taxation on residents’ properties over 70 percent of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific assertion that Kathryn Starkey 'aided and abetted' continued property taxation over 70% of the time by seconding motions and voting to keep the millage rate the same. The claim is a precise numeric allegation about vote behavior that would require examination of official roll-call votes and minutes for a named governing body and time period; I have no verifiable records in my training data confirming that percentage. Without those records, the claim should not be treated as established fact.

claim: "666,000 teachers have been laid off already since March."
rationale: The claim gives a precise large number without specifying country or timeframe and no authoritative national or state reports support that 666,000 teachers have been laid off since March. In the U.S., for example, there are roughly 3.5–4 million public school teachers, so 666,000 would imply an implausibly large share (~15–20%) and would have been widely documented; reported layoffs and furloughs during recent crises have been much smaller. The lack of corroborating data and ambiguous scope make the claim unreliable.

claim: A 50-50 public-private split for paying for a new Milwaukee Bucks arena would "be much better -- in terms of the portion of the public financing -- than most of the other arena projects done around the country."
rationale: A claim that a 50/50 public-private split would be "much better" than most other arena projects implies that most projects have a larger public share. In fact, many recent NBA and NHL arena projects have been majority privately financed or used mixes that put less than 50% on the public coffers, while the largest public shares tend to be in some high-profile NFL stadium deals. Therefore a blanket claim that 50/50 would be much better than most arena projects is misleading.

claim: "Ten years ago, John McCain offered a bill that said he would ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists."
rationale: There is no record that John McCain introduced a bill specifically stating "he would ban a candidate from paying registered lobbyists." McCain was a prominent advocate of campaign finance reform (e.g., McCain-Feingold) and supported restrictions on lobbyist gifts and the revolving door, but the precise claim as stated appears to conflate or misstate those reforms and is not supported by known legislation.

claim: Virginia "is home to more veterans per capita than any state in America."
rationale: Virginia has a large absolute veteran population, but it does not have the highest number of veterans per capita. Census and VA data consistently show states such as West Virginia, Alaska, Maine, and Montana with higher veteran share of their populations than Virginia.

claim: The administration has issued rules for "$1 abortions in ObamaCare" and "requires all persons enrolled in insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage to pay" an abortion premium.
rationale: The administration's rule required that insurance plans that include elective abortion coverage must show and collect a separately-stated premium or rider for that coverage and keep separate accounting so federal premium tax credits do not subsidize abortion. It did not mandate “$1 abortions” nor require all enrollees to pay an abortion premium; only those who buy plans or riders that include elective abortion coverage would be charged the separate premium. The '$1' phrasing is a misleading simplification of a possible low monthly surcharge in some markets, not a government-set price per abortion or a universal charge on all enrollees.

claim: "Shakespeare said: ‘I always feel happy. You know why? Because I don’t expect anything from anyone. Expectations always hurt. Life is short. So love your life. Be Happy. & Keep smiling."
rationale: This wording and punctuation are modern and no passage in Shakespeare's plays, sonnets, or known letters contains this quote. It is a common internet-era aphorism frequently misattributed to famous authors like Shakespeare.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: The term "hidden" in website code is a technical HTML/input attribute that hides data from page display, not a legal clause that causes users to waive privacy rights. Legal waivers require explicit language in terms of service or a privacy policy and user assent; a field named "hidden" in the code does not by itself effectuate such a waiver. While healthcare.gov has privacy and monitoring statements, equating a code label with a legal relinquishment of privacy is incorrect.

claim: "It has been estimated that only 12% of workers in businesses that are likely to stay open during this crisis are receiving paid sick leave benefits as a result of the second coronavirus relief package."
rationale: I found no authoritative estimate that exactly 12% of workers in businesses likely to stay open gained paid sick leave from the second U.S. coronavirus relief package. Analyses of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act noted limited coverage (private employers under 500 employees, exemptions for some employers and health care workers), and estimates of who gained leave varied by definition of 'likely to stay open' and were not centered on a single 12% figure.

claim: A photo taken on Jan. 6, 2021, at the United States Capitol riot was "doctored to look as if the Capitol was on fire."
rationale: Multiple reputable fact-checkers examined a widely shared image from Jan. 6, 2021, and determined it had been digitally altered to add flames and make the Capitol appear on fire. Reverse-image checks showed the original photo did not contain the added blaze or lighting effects.

claim: "Military arrests former President George W. Bush."
rationale: There are no credible reports or official statements indicating that U.S. military forces have arrested former President George W. Bush. An arrest of a former president would be an extraordinary, widely reported event and would require legal processes and involvement beyond the military alone.

claim: Says Congress gave Wall Street "trillions of dollars of zero interest loans."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Congress did authorize rescue and support programs (e.g., TARP, CARES) and the Federal Reserve provided trillions in emergency liquidity, but Congress did not directly give Wall Street 'trillions of dollars of zero-interest loans.' Many interventions were loans or asset purchases that charged fees or interest, were collateralized, and some funds were repaid.

claim: "If Trump had just put his father’s money in a mutual fund ... he’d have $8 billion."
rationale: The statement is a speculative counterfactual that depends on the exact amount, timing, and rate of return of the inheritance; public estimates of what Donald Trump received from his father combined with historical stock-market returns do not plausibly compound to $8 billion under realistic assumptions. Analyses by journalists and financial calculations show far smaller outcomes once taxes, fees, and the likely size/timing of transfers are accounted for. The claim therefore overstates the outcome and is not supported by available evidence.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke wants "open borders and wants to take our guns."
rationale: The claim conflates two different assertions. O'Rourke has not advocated 'open borders'—he supports immigration reform with enforcement and pathways to citizenship—while he has publicly supported banning certain assault-style weapons and a mandatory buyback, even saying 'hell yes, we're going to take your AR-15.' Thus the 'open borders' part is false and the 'take our guns' part is a partially accurate but simplified characterization of his policy on specific firearms.

claim: Says Qassem Soleimani "assisted in the clandestine travel to Afghanistan of 10 of the 12 terrorists who carried out the September 11 terrorist attacks in the United States."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Qassem Soleimani personally assisted clandestine travel of 10 of the 12 9/11 hijackers. Major investigations (including the 9/11 Commission and U.S. intelligence reviews) found no indication that Iran or senior Iranian commanders, including Soleimani, orchestrated or enabled the attackers' travel; specific claims tying him to ten hijackers are unsupported by the record.

claim: Sarah Palin was repeating "Abraham Lincoln's words" in discussing the war in Iraq.
rationale: There is no well-documented instance or widely reported transcript showing Sarah Palin verbatim repeating Abraham Lincoln's words in the context of discussing the Iraq war. Palin used contemporary political rhetoric and occasional historical references during the 2008 campaign, but major news transcripts and fact-checkers did not identify her as quoting Lincoln on Iraq.

claim: Since 2009, the Ohio Republican Party has made more contacts with voters — nearly 6.6 million — than any other GOP state organization in the nation.
rationale: There is no independent, verifiable national dataset showing every state GOP's total voter contacts since 2009; while the Ohio Republican Party has at times reported large contact totals (around 6.6 million), that figure is self-reported and cannot be confirmed as greater than every other state GOP. Without standardized definitions and centralized reporting, the claim that Ohio has made more contacts than any other GOP state organization is not verifiable and thus cannot be treated as factual.

claim: "In Florida, for eight years we cut taxes every year, totaling $19 billion."
rationale: I cannot confirm the precise claim as stated. Public summaries and fact-checks indicate Florida has enacted various tax relief measures across multiple years, but the totals and whether cuts occurred in each of eight consecutive years depend on counting methods (one‑time rebates, rate changes, exemptions). No clear, uncontested record in my knowledge base unequivocally supports the specific assertion of eight straight years of cuts summing to $19 billion.

claim: "95 percent of teachers and principals are not implicated in the [Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal] report at all."
rationale: The official investigation and news accounts named specific teachers and administrators implicated in the Atlanta Public Schools cheating scandal, but they do not support the precise claim that 95% of teachers and principals were "not implicated". While most APS staff were never charged, the 95% figure is not substantiated by the report and depends on how the denominator (which staff and which time period) is defined.

claim: "One of the first nurses to receive the vaccine in AL is now dead."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that one of the very first nurses to receive the COVID-19 vaccine in Alabama (AL) subsequently died as a result of or in connection with being an early vaccine recipient. Reports that circulate claiming an early vaccinated nurse in Alabama died have not been corroborated by local health authorities or credible news outlets and appear to be rumor or misinformation.

claim: His biography says he was the top ROTC officer in the nation.
rationale: The statement is unverified as presented because no individual or source is named and I cannot confirm a biography claiming a person was the "top ROTC officer in the nation." Moreover, "top ROTC officer in the nation" is not a standard, well-defined national title—ROTC has various awards (e.g., Distinguished Military Graduate, top cadet awards) but no single universally recognized nationwide "top officer" designation. Without a specific person, time, and source, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: MSNBC’s Mika Brzezinski said, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That’s our job."
rationale: Mika Brzezinski did make that remark on-air during MSNBC's Morning Joe while criticizing Elon Musk's actions around Twitter, saying roughly, "Elon Musk is trying to control how people think. That's our job." The quote was reported by multiple media outlets and appears in program transcripts and video of the segment as a rhetorical critique of Musk's influence and platform changes.

claim: "Now there is a new threat that we’re seeing up close: the risk of exposure to powerful drugs that can kill in even tiny amounts."
rationale: Powerful synthetic opioids (notably fentanyl and even more potent analogs like carfentanil) are pharmacologically lethal at very small doses (milligram-to-microgram range), and their increasing contamination of the illicit drug supply has raised the risk of accidental exposures and overdoses. Public-health authorities have documented rising deaths and warned about the heightened danger, though the actual risk of fatality depends strongly on route and amount of exposure.

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: While many of the poorest counties by some measures are in Appalachia, the very poorest U.S. counties overall include places in the Mississippi Delta and on Native American reservations and are not overwhelmingly white. County-level poverty and low median incomes are found across regions and include counties that are majority Black, Native American, or Hispanic. Thus the blanket claim that the poorest counties are in Appalachia and 'happen to be more than 90 percent white' is inaccurate and misleading.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The statement is too categorical. Research and practical experience show that visible cameras can deter some opportunistic property crimes, but they do not 'certainly' prevent robberies — determined offenders can use masks, plan around cameras, or be undeterred by cameras alone. The effectiveness of CCTV depends on visibility, quality, accompanying security measures, and the perceived likelihood of arrest and prosecution.

claim: "We became a net exporter of natural gas in 2017, and until recently, our exports have exceeded our imports."
rationale: U.S. Energy Information Administration data indicate the United States became a net exporter of natural gas on an annual basis in 2017, and total exports have continued to exceed imports in subsequent years through at least 2022–2023. The substantive claim is accurate, though exact interpretation of 'until recently' depends on the specific current date and short-term monthly fluctuations.

claim: Says Sandra Bullock said to Hillary Clinton, "If you don’t like our president you can leave and never come back again."
rationale: There is no credible reporting, transcript, or video showing Sandra Bullock telling Hillary Clinton the quoted line; the statement appears to originate from social media/meme circulation and is not corroborated by reputable sources. Fact‑checking norms and searches of mainstream coverage find this as a misattribution rather than a documented public remark.

claim: Federal prosecutions for lying on background checks to buy guns are "down 40 percent" under President Barack Obama.
rationale: Fact-checkers and Justice Department data show that federal prosecutions under the false-statement statute for firearm purchases (18 U.S.C. 922(a)(6)) did not fall 40% across the Obama years overall; totals rose relative to some earlier baselines and fluctuated year-to-year. The claim appears to cherry-pick a particular year-to-year comparison without specifying the baseline and contradicts published DOJ prosecution statistics and independent fact-checks.

claim: The effort to recall California Gov. Gavin Newsom is "a coup."
rationale: California's recall process is a constitutional, legal procedure that requires collecting a statutory number of valid petition signatures and then a statewide election; it is not an extralegal seizure of power. A 'coup' by definition involves the illegal or forceful overthrow of a government, which does not describe the petition-and-vote mechanism used in this recall. While critics may use 'coup' rhetorically to express political opposition, that characterization is misleading as a factual claim.

claim: Says Dan Feehan "would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty, putting Minnesota families at risk."
rationale: There is no verified public statement in which Dan Feehan explicitly says he "would vote with Pelosi for open borders and amnesty." The phrasing appears to be a partisan attack that conflates support for immigration reform with the extreme terms "open borders" and "amnesty," which Feehan has not endorsed in those words. Without a direct quote or voting record supporting that claim, it is unsupported.

claim: "No one has died of cancer or heart disease since the COVID-19 thing started."
rationale: This claim is demonstrably false. National and international vital statistics, death certificates, and ongoing hospital reports show that people have continued to die from cancer and heart disease throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, with thousands of such deaths recorded every week/month.

claim: "Many of the countries in question (in Trump’s travel ban) don't even have a U.S. embassy there to help us vet."
rationale: This overstates the situation. While a handful of countries targeted by Trump-era travel bans did not have full, operational U.S. embassies at the time (notably Iran, which has no U.S. embassy, and Syria, Libya and Yemen where missions were closed or evacuated), several other listed countries (for example Iraq) did have U.S. diplomatic missions. Embassy presence varied by country and date, so saying "many" had no U.S. embassy is misleading.

claim: In Iraq, "violence is down to an all-time low" since the start of the war.
rationale: This statement is not accurate as a general claim. Although violence in Iraq has fallen from major peaks (notably 2006–2007 and the 2014–2017 ISIS period) and some years have seen relatively low levels, the country has experienced resurgences and persistent militia/insurgent attacks, so it is incorrect to say violence is at an all-time low for the entire period since the war began.

claim: "Trump on revamping the military: We’re bringing back the draft."
rationale: There is no reliable public record that Donald Trump announced an official policy to "bring back the draft." Reinstating conscription would require Congress to pass legislation and the president to sign it; Trump promoted a larger volunteer force and did not pursue a formal draft proposal. Claims that he said "we're bringing back the draft" appear to be misquotes, taken out of context, or speculative commentary rather than an enacted policy or confirmed pledge.

claim: "There’s no wildlife" in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.
rationale: The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge supports abundant wildlife, including the Porcupine caribou herd calving grounds, polar bear denning areas, muskoxen, wolves, Arctic foxes, numerous migratory birds, and coastal marine mammals and fish. It was established to protect these species and their habitats, so the blanket statement that there is "no wildlife" is incorrect.

claim: John Boozman supports "privatizing Social Security"
rationale: There is not a clear public record that Senator John Boozman has advocated outright "privatizing Social Security." He has expressed support for measures to shore up or reform Social Security and for private retirement savings more generally, but he has not publicly championed full privatization of the program as a stated policy goal.

claim: "95 percent of the income gains in the last few years have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is presented as a broad fact but is imprecise and therefore misleading. Some academic analyses (notably by Piketty and Saez) found that roughly 95% of income gains went to the top 1% during a narrowly defined post‑recession window (e.g., roughly 2009–2012), but that result depends strongly on the exact years chosen and on whether pre‑tax, market, or after‑tax household income is used. Over longer periods or using different income measures multiple data sources (CBO, tax-data analyses) show much smaller shares going to the top 1%.

claim: U.S. sanctions mean "Cuba can’t trade with any country or any company whatsoever."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. U.S. sanctions (the long-standing embargo) restrict transactions by U.S. persons and certain categories of goods and financial flows, but they do not make it impossible for Cuba to trade with any country or any company; many nations and private firms trade with Cuba. While secondary sanctions and banking restrictions can complicate and deter some commercial activity, they do not amount to an absolute global ban.

claim: "California has added twice as many jobs as Florida" over the past year.
rationale: The statement gives no precise 12‑month window or data source, so it cannot be verified as stated. While California's labor market is larger and it often records bigger absolute job gains than Florida, the claim that California added exactly twice as many jobs is a specific numeric assertion that requires BLS/state payroll data for the stated year and is not reliably true without that evidence.

claim: Says Wisconsin payday loans have a 574% average annual interest rate, "exploitative lending that keeps Americans trapped in debt"
rationale: The specific claim that Wisconsin payday loans have a 574% average APR is misleading: payday loan APRs are often extremely high (triple‑digit) and some studies of short‑term loans report figures in the hundreds, but reported averages vary by dataset, year, and calculation method and 574% is not a consistently supported statewide average. The description as "exploitative lending" is an evaluative judgment commonly made by consumer advocates but is not an objective fact about the numeric rate.

claim: "Candidate Slotkin had presented herself as a moderate and as someone who’d be independent-minded, but her time in office was making it increasingly clear that no, she was very partisan, voting 96% of the time with Speaker Pelosi."
rationale: The claim mixes a plausible political narrative (Slotkin marketed herself as a moderate) with a precise numeric voting claim that is not reliably supported without more context. Public vote-with-leader/party metrics vary by source and time period; different trackers report different percentages and a 96% figure has not been consistently documented as a definitive long-term rate. Because the percentage depends on the chosen time window and which votes are counted, the absolute 96% assertion is misleading as stated.

claim: In Arizona, "there are only one and a half (Border Patrol) agents per every 10 square miles."
rationale: The claim is not supported by available context and appears misleading. Arizona's land area is about 114,000 square miles and Border Patrol has roughly tens of thousands of agents nationwide; even allocating several thousand agents to Arizona yields far fewer than 1.5 agents per 10 square miles statewide. Moreover, Border Patrol staffing is concentrated along border corridors, so simple statewide density figures are misleading without a clear timeframe or definition of the area measured.

claim: Banks paid Hillary Clinton "over $1 million and are contributing millions more to elect her."
rationale: The claim conflates different things and overstates or misstates the facts. Hillary Clinton did accept paid speeches and received substantial contributions from the financial sector, and banks/financial-industry PACs and employees gave millions to her campaign and allied groups, but there is no clear, documented instance that 'banks paid Hillary Clinton over $1 million' as a single, direct payment; the statement is ambiguous and misleading.

claim: Says Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "didn't change his position" on a two-state solution.
rationale: Public record shows Netanyahu's stance has shifted over time: he gave a conditional endorsement of a demilitarized Palestinian state in his 2009 Bar-Ilan speech but later repeatedly rejected a sovereign Palestinian state in election campaigns and statements. Because his rhetoric and policy positions have varied by audience and over years, the claim that he "didn't change his position" is inaccurate.

claim: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security warned that the SAVE "database is not a foolproof means of verifying (citizenship on) the voter rolls."
rationale: DHS (through USCIS) has publicly warned that the SAVE system is intended to verify immigration status for benefits and is not a foolproof or sole method to establish U.S. citizenship for voter-registration purposes. Officials and agency guidance have noted SAVE can produce incomplete or inaccurate results and should not be relied upon as the only means to verify citizenship on voter rolls.

claim: Says the late Lady Bird Johnson sicced the CIA on actress and singer Eartha Kitt after Kitt spoke out against the Vietnam War during a White House luncheon in January 1968.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and later declassified documents show that after Eartha Kitt's January 1968 White House remarks criticizing the Vietnam War, the Johnson administration reacted angrily and sought to punish her. Records and historical accounts indicate intelligence and law-enforcement files were opened and information was gathered on Kitt at the administration's behest, effectively blacklisting her career.

claim: "California is 49th out of 50 in the United States in per capita housing units. Only Utah can lay claim to being lowest in per capita production."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated: rankings of housing units per person vary by year and by the exact metric used, and Census data do not consistently place California 49th with only Utah below it. Several states (for example New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Hawaii) commonly rank among the lowest in housing units per capita depending on the dataset and year, so the assertion that only Utah is lower than California is misleading or incorrect.

claim: 52 jobs have been saved or created in Florida's 34th Congressional District.
rationale: The claim is presented without a source, time period, or supporting documentation and I cannot confirm a specific, independently verifiable record that exactly 52 jobs were saved or created in Florida's 34th Congressional District. Such precise employment claims typically come from local press releases or grant announcements and require a cited program or employer to verify. Without that context or an authoritative data source, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: Rob Portman’s "plan to tax, slash and privatize" Social Security "would devastate Ohioans."
rationale: There is no verifiable record that Rob Portman proposed a single, explicit plan to simultaneously 'tax, slash and privatize' Social Security. Public records and press coverage show he supported limited benefit-reform ideas (such as changes to cost-of-living indexing, means-testing, or raising retirement ages) typical of bipartisan deficit discussions, but not wholesale privatization or an across-the-board tax-and-cut package described here. The claim is therefore misleading and overstates his documented positions and their projected impact on Ohioans.

claim: Says House Republicans "tried to change the definition of rape."
rationale: The statement is too broad and misleading as written. While individual Republican lawmakers and some GOP-backed bills have at times proposed narrowing statutory language (for example by adding terms like "forcible" or tightening reporting requirements) these were isolated proposals tied to specific bills and contexts, not a single House Republicans action to universally "change the definition of rape." Without a specific bill, date, or sponsor the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: "The daughter of Sen. Coons (D-DE), along with 7 other underaged girls are featured on Hunter's laptop! - Breitbart News"
rationale: There is no credible, publicly verified evidence that Senator Chris Coons's daughter appears on Hunter Biden’s laptop or that seven underaged girls are featured. Major fact-checkers and mainstream news outlets have found no corroboration for Breitbart’s assertion, and the claim has not been substantiated by law enforcement or independent verification.

claim: Democrats already agreed to "a deal that Republicans wanted, that Eric Cantor said would be a win."
rationale: The statement lacks any specific deal, date, or source for Eric Cantor's alleged quote, so it cannot be verified as presented. Without identifying the particular agreement and a reliable record of Cantor's remark it is not possible to confirm that Democrats had already agreed to a deal Republicans wanted and that Cantor called it a 'win.'

claim: The federal tax code has "loopholes that are giving incentives for companies that are shipping jobs overseas."
rationale: For decades U.S. tax rules (for example deferral of U.S. tax on foreign earnings, favorable treatment of some foreign income, and permissive transfer-pricing rules) have been identified by experts and policymakers as creating financial incentives for corporations to shift profits and operations—and in some cases headquarters—abroad. While the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act introduced measures (e.g., GILTI, BEAT, and a move toward a territorial system) that reduced some of those incentives, many analysts conclude that tax-driven incentives for offshoring were real and not entirely eliminated.

claim: "Fifty percent of the Ottawa police force have all turned in their resignation."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official confirmation that half of the Ottawa Police Service submitted resignations; an event of that magnitude would have been widely documented by major news outlets and the police service. Available public statements and routine media coverage instead show normal personnel changes rather than a 50% mass resignation.

claim: Says Nikita Khrushchev brought an extra shoe to a United Nations session in 1960, which he banged on the desk in protest.
rationale: Contemporary news reports and many historical accounts record that at the October 1960 UN General Assembly Nikita Khrushchev removed a shoe and brandished (and by many witnesses banged) it in protest. However, film and photographic evidence is inconclusive and some eyewitnesses later said he may have waved rather than actually striking the desk, so details are disputed.

claim: Says in U.S. Congress, members "don’t even have to be on the floor for debates or votes."
rationale: As a general rule members of the House and Senate must be physically present (or at their desk in the Senate) for recognized debate and for roll-call votes; quorum and voting rules require presence. A temporary House proxy-voting system was authorized during the COVID pandemic, and members can insert statements into the Congressional Record without being on the floor, but those are exceptions rather than the standard practice.

claim: "Texas now has the second-highest high school graduation rate in the country. And it has the highest graduation rate for African Americans and Hispanics."
rationale: Most recent national graduation-rate rankings (based on the adjusted cohort graduation rate) do not show Texas as the overall No. 2 state; other states such as Iowa, New Jersey, and several New England states typically rank higher. Likewise, Texas does not consistently top the country for Black and Hispanic graduation rates — other states often post higher subgroup rates depending on the year and metric.

claim: "Common welfare programs give income of $43,330 or $20.83 an hour."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as written: no single set of common welfare programs reliably gives recipients $43,330 a year (about $20.83/hr for a 40-hour week). Typical cash assistance programs (e.g., TANF) and in-kind benefits (SNAP, Medicaid) provide much smaller monthly or annual values; combined benefit totals vary widely by program, household composition, and whether noncash benefits are monetized. The claim appears to conflate or misstate benefit measures or average spending per program rather than actual direct income to beneficiaries.

claim: To abide by Environmental Protection Agency rules when mining or drilling you have "to take caution not to disturb bodies of water barely bigger than a puddle."
rationale: Federal EPA/Clean Water Act rules do not categorically prohibit disturbing every tiny or isolated puddle. Jurisdiction under the Clean Water Act is limited to "waters of the United States," which recent court rulings and agency definitions have narrowed to relatively permanent waters or those with a significant connection to navigable waters, so many very small, isolated water features are not federally regulated. However, some small bodies are regulated if they are connected to larger waters or if state laws impose stricter protections.

claim: A congressional laundry closed due to the partial government shutdown.
rationale: There is no well-documented, widely reported instance that a 'congressional laundry' was closed specifically because of a partial government shutdown. Many services used by members of Congress (including in-house or privately contracted amenities) either continued operating or were funded outside the appropriations that caused shutdowns, so this claim lacks corroboration and is likely a confusion with other service disruptions.

claim: Facebook video shows "counting Biden’s votes at 2 a.m."
rationale: The statement as given is unverified and likely misleading because no specific Facebook video, link, location, or metadata is provided to confirm that it shows ballots for Biden being counted at 2 a.m. During recent elections many social posts have miscaptioned or taken videos out of context; verifying such a claim requires the original video, timestamp, and provenance. Without that evidence the claim cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Annual precipitation "has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century."
rationale: Observed records and federal assessments show that precipitation in the Northeast (including Rhode Island) has increased over the last century, but the magnitude reported is typically a few inches to around 6–10 inches rather than a uniform statewide increase of more than 12 inches. A 12-inch (one-foot) rise as a statewide annual increase is larger than the changes documented in NOAA/EPA/National Climate Assessment summaries.

claim: Georgia has led the nation in student fatalities caused by motorists illegally passing stopped school buses.
rationale: The statement is presented as an absolute but no authoritative, time‑bounded data show Georgia consistently leads the nation in student fatalities from motorists illegally passing stopped school buses. Georgia has had several high‑profile incidents, but national traffic‑fatality counts are typically higher in larger states and vary by year; without a specific timeframe or source the broad claim is not supported.

claim: "When I became mayor of Los Angeles, we had a 44 percent (high school) graduation rate. I said that was unacceptable. I challenged that notion. I said the mayor needs to be involved with our schools. We need to partner together. As I left, after a number of reforms, we grew our graduation rate from 44 percent to 72."
rationale: The claim mixes non‑comparable metrics and overstates attribution. LAUSD graduation rates did rise in the late 2000s/early 2010s, but California changed how it calculated graduation (adopting the four‑year adjusted cohort method) and earlier and later figures are not directly comparable; moreover the mayor does not run the school district. Fact‑checks concluded the 44→72 percentage framing is misleading rather than a straightforward factual increase solely due to the mayor's actions.

claim: Says a study indicates up to $8.5 billion in lost GDP and up to 185,000 lost jobs if Texas lawmakers approve a measure limiting transgender bathroom choices.
rationale: I am not aware of a credible, widely-cited study that specifically finds Texas would lose up to $8.5 billion in GDP and up to 185,000 jobs solely from approving a bathroom-limiting measure; those figures do not match the better-known economic estimates for similar laws (for example, North Carolina's HB2 estimates were much smaller). The claim appears to conflate or misattribute numbers without identifying a clear study, timeframe, or methodology.

claim: "I'm the only candidate in the Democratic primary, or actually on either side, who Wall Street financiers and hedge fund managers are actually running ads against."
rationale: The claim of uniqueness is not supported: wealthy Wall Street financiers, financial industry PACs, and hedge-fund donors have funded negative advertising against multiple candidates in both Democratic and Republican contests. Public reporting and campaign‑finance disclosures have documented that financial‑sector interests target several candidates whose policies they oppose, so it is very unlikely that any single candidate is the only one being opposed by such ad spending.

claim: "Texas law enforcement officer fatally shot upon arriving for work by 3 Muslim refugee."
rationale: This specific claim is unsubstantiated: no credible contemporary reporting or official records up to mid‑2024 document a case in which a Texas law‑enforcement officer was fatally shot upon arriving for work by three Muslim refugees. A violent incident of that scale and clear motive would have been widely reported and documented by major news outlets and law‑enforcement statements, but none match this description.

claim: "We are in the sixth year of recovery, and median income is below what it was at the start of the recovery."
rationale: The claim is vague about which country and which recovery period it refers to, and when applied to the recent U.S. recovery after the 2007–2009 recession (which is commonly described as ending in mid-2009), by the sixth year of recovery median household income had generally risen relative to the start of the recovery rather than fallen. Public economic series (Census and BLS) show median income and typical earnings largely recovered through the mid-2010s, so a blanket statement that median income was below the start of the recovery in the sixth year is misleading. Without a specific jurisdiction and defined start date the claim cannot be verified as stated.

claim: "We have cut taxes more than 40 times in four years."
rationale: The claim provides no jurisdiction or definition of what counts as a “tax cut,” and there is no clear evidence that any national government enacted more than 40 distinct tax-cutting laws in a single four-year span. At the U.S. federal level, major tax-cut packages are relatively infrequent and would be well-documented; smaller administrative or technical changes are sometimes counted by politicians to inflate totals. Without specifics, the blanket statement is unsupported and therefore likely false.

claim: The Chamber of Commerce says new carbon regulations will kill "244,000 jobs a year" and cost average families "$1,200 a year."
rationale: I cannot verify that the Chamber of Commerce made that precise, standalone claim; while the U.S. Chamber and allied groups have frequently cited studies projecting large job losses and household cost increases from new carbon rules, the specific figures quoted here ("244,000 jobs a year" and "$1,200 a year" per family) do not match a single, clearly attributable Chamber statement I can confirm. Such numbers are often drawn from modeling studies and are selectively reported or framed by advocacy statements, so attributing this exact phrasing directly to the Chamber is not supported with high confidence.

claim: "Less than 500 people a year killed by all rifles combined" and "4,000 a year killed by illegals."
rationale: The first part is largely true in that rifles account for a small fraction of U.S. homicides and in recent years rifle-involved homicides have generally been under 500 annually. The second part is not supported by credible data: there is no evidence that undocumented immigrants kill 4,000 people per year in the U.S.; official homicide statistics and independent analyses indicate far fewer homicides attributable to undocumented perpetrators and immigration status is often not reliably recorded.

claim: Says in the last 20 years, the French have not "stood by" the United States on foreign policy.
rationale: The statement that the French have not 'stood by' the United States on foreign policy in the last 20 years is inaccurate: France has both cooperated closely with the U.S. (for example in the 2011 Libya intervention, in sanctions and diplomatic efforts after Russia's 2014 actions in Ukraine, and in NATO and counterterrorism partnerships) and disagreed at times (notably over AUKUS and other policy differences). The record shows a mix of alignment and disagreement rather than a total refusal to stand by the U.S.

claim: "Repeated requests for additional security in Benghazi were routinely denied" by Hillary "Clinton’s State Department."
rationale: Official investigations found that diplomatic security in Benghazi was inadequate and that some requests for additional protection were not granted or were not adequately processed, but they did not conclude that Secretary Clinton's State Department routinely and deliberately denied repeated security requests as a consistent policy. Reviews attributed failures to systemic shortages, miscommunication, and process breakdowns rather than a pattern of routine denials directed by Clinton.

claim: "Registered Republican not allowed to vote."
rationale: The claim as stated is inaccurate: being a registered Republican does not bar someone from voting. In the U.S. and most democracies, party registration determines primary participation rules in some places but does not prohibit voting in general elections; only narrow legal disqualifications (e.g., certain felony convictions or court-ordered incapacity) remove the right to vote.

claim: After Hurricane Katrina, "Dallas and San Antonio took in 5,000 to 10,000 refugees each, but (Bill) White brought in 250,000 and put them up in his 'buddies' empty apartment buildings and let the federal government pay their rents for over two years. They did not return to New Orleans, most of them are on welfare."
rationale: This claim mixes exaggeration and unverified assertions. Houston did take in a very large number of Katrina evacuees, but credible counts do not support that Mayor Bill White 'brought in 250,000' into pals' empty apartments as a coordinated scheme, nor that the federal government simply paid rents for over two years for such an arrangement. While FEMA provided temporary shelter and some rental assistance and many evacuees relocated permanently, the sweeping claim that most never returned and are 'on welfare' is unsupported and misleading.

claim: Says "about 100,000 kids in this country leave their home state and go to another state to be educated. Out of that 100,000 young people, 30,000 of them are from New Jersey, by far the largest amount."
rationale: The numbers are inconsistent with known enrollment statistics: far more than 100,000 U.S. students attend school outside their home state (on the order of hundreds of thousands to millions when counting college students each year), so the 100,000 total is a large understatement. It is also implausible that New Jersey alone would supply 30,000 of that 100,000 and be "by far the largest amount," since larger states like California, Texas, and Florida have many more residents and college-age students who go out of state.

claim: Photo shows R. Kelly being released from prison in 2021.
rationale: No image was provided and there is no credible reporting that R.
